en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Jātaka (Second Part)
2. The Second Book of Pairs (Dukanipāta) 1.
The Chapter on the Firm (Daḷhavagga) [151] 1.
The Explanation of the Birth Story of the Advice to the King (Rājovādajātaka)
"He throws the strong against the strong"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the "Advice to the King.

This will be made clear in the Tesakuṇa Jātaka. On a certain day, however, the King of Kosala, having decided a difficult legal case involving one who had gone astray, ate his morning meal and, with hands still wet from washing, mounted his decorated chariot.
Having approached the Teacher, he prostrated at his feet, which were as beautiful as full-blown lotuses, and after paying homage to the Teacher, he sat down to one side.
Then the Teacher said to him: "Well now, Great King, from where have you come so early in the day?
"Venerable Sir, today I was deciding a lawsuit that had reached a dead end and was difficult to resolve."
“Having failed to find an opportunity [to settle it earlier], I have now come to attend upon you with my hands still wet from having finished that case and eaten.
The Teacher said, “Great King, it is indeed wholesome to settle legal disputes according to the Dhamma and in accordance with justice;
this is the path to heaven. Yet it is not surprising that you, receiving instruction from a teacher like me, a Sammasambuddha, should act according to the Dhamma...”
"You should settle lawsuits with impartiality. This alone is marvelous:
that in the past, kings—even after hearing the words of wise men who were not omniscient—settled lawsuits according to the Dhamma and with impartiality;
and having avoided the four ways of going to ruin, having not violated the ten duties of a king, and having ruled the kingdom righteously, they departed filling the city of heaven."
Having spoken thus, being requested by him, he related a past event.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of his chief queen;
having received the necessary care for the pregnancy, he emerged safely from his mother’s womb. On the day of the naming ceremony—
They gave him the name "Prince Brahmadatta. In due course, having reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā at the age of sixteen and attained mastery in all the arts.
Upon his father’s passing, he was established in the kingdom and ruled with righteousness and equity;
he administered justice without being swayed by favoritism or other such biases. While he was thus ruling righteously...

While he was ruling the kingdom, even the ministers decided legal cases solely according to the Dhamma. As legal cases were being decided according to the Dhamma, there were no longer those known as "fraudulent litigants.
Because of their absence, the clamor for the sake of lawsuits ceased in the royal courtyard.
Even though the ministers sat in the place of judgment all day long, they did not see anyone coming for the purpose of a legal decision.
Rising up, they departed, and the place of justice reached a state where it was to be abandoned.
The Bodhisatta thought: "While I am ruling the kingdom according to the Dhamma, there are none who come to the place of justice;
the clamor has ceased, and the place of justice has become something to be cast aside. Now, by me—"
“It is fitting to search for one’s own faults; having heard, ‘This indeed is my fault,’ I shall abandon it and conduct myself only in virtues.
From that time forth, searching to see if there were anyone who spoke of his faults, he saw no one among those in his inner circle who spoke of a fault.
Hearing only talk of his own virtues, he thought: “These [people] speak of my faults even out of fear...”
Thinking, "Let them speak only of my virtues," he searched among the people outside the city; finding no one there who spoke otherwise, he searched within the city.
He searched at the four gates of the city and throughout the four surrounding villages;
still finding no one who spoke ill of him and hearing only reports of his own virtues, he thought, "I shall search the countryside," and having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, he departed.
Having mounted his chariot and taken hold of the charioteer, he departed from the city in an unknown guise and, while surveying the countryside,
traveled as far as the frontier regions. Finding no one who spoke ill of him and hearing only reports of his own virtues,
he turned back toward the city by the great highway from the borderlands.
At that time, the King of Kosala named Ballika, while ruling righteously, was seeking out reports of faults;
yet, finding no one speaking ill within his inner apartments or elsewhere, and hearing only accounts of his own virtues, he traveled to that region while surveying the countryside.
Both of them arrived at a low-lying spot on a cart-track facing one another.

There was no room for the chariot to pass. Then the charioteer of King Ballika said to the charioteer of the King of Bārāṇasī, “Move your chariot aside. He replied, “O charioteer, move your chariot aside;
seated in this chariot is the Great King Brahmadatta, the lord of the kingdom of Bārāṇasī. The other also said to him, “O—”
“Charioteer, the great King Ballika, the lord of the kingdom of Kosala, is seated in this chariot;
turn your chariot aside and give way for our king’s chariot,” he said. The charioteer of the King of Bārāṇasī thought, “This too is surely a king;
what indeed should be done? Then, thinking, “There is a way,” he asked, “Whose chariot is this? [and was told,] “It is the young man’s chariot.”
Having made the decision, "I will have the torch extinguished and give way to the elder," he questioned the charioteer regarding the age of the King of Kosala;
having ascertained that both were of equal age, and having inquired about everything— the extent of their kingdoms,
their armies, their wealth, their fame, their birth, their clan, and their lineage— he [concluded] that "both [belong] to the three-hundred-league [realm]."
Having learned that the king’s sovereign power was equal [to his own] and that they were of the same strength,
wealth, birth, lineage, family, and country, he thought, "I shall grant an opportunity to the virtuous one," and asked,
"O charioteer, what is the moral conduct and behavior of your king? He, proclaiming his own king's very faults as virtues, spoke the first verse:
“The strong man hurls back the strong; Ballika hurls back the weak with the weak;
he conquers the good with goodness, and the wicked with wickedness.
Such is this king: drive away from the road, O charioteer!”

In this context, "he hurls the strong at the strong" means that one who is strong, against someone who must be overcome by a powerful blow or speech, hurls a blow or speech that is equally strong. This shows that he overcomes the other only by being strong himself.
"Ballika" is the name of that king. "With the mild, the mild" means [he treats] a person of mild nature himself...
"Having become mild, he conquers by means of mildness alone. Regarding "he conquers the good by means of the good":
those who are good and true persons, having themselves become good, conquer by means of a good method alone. Furthermore, regarding "he conquers the wicked by means of wickedness":
this shows that those who are wicked, having themselves become wicked, conquer by means of a wicked method alone. "Such is this king."
"This King of Kosala of ours is such in his moral conduct and behavior. "Drive away from the path, charioteer!
he said, causing his own chariot to move off the road, saying, "Go by a wrong way; give our king the path.
Then the charioteer of the King of Bārāṇasī asked him, "Sir, have you been speaking of your own king's virtues?"
Having said this, when [the other] replied, “Yes,” he asked, “If you say these are virtues, then what are non-virtues?
When [the other] replied, “Let these for now be non-virtues, but what kind of virtue does your king possess? he said, “In that case, listen,” and recited the second verse:
“Conquer anger with non-anger; conquer the wicked with goodness.”
"Conquer the miser with generosity, and the speaker of falsehood with truth.
Such is this king; drive out from the path, O charioteer!
In this context, "such as this" means endowed with those qualities stated in such passages as "conquer anger with non-anger."
For this person, being himself free from anger, conquers the angry individual through non-anger;
being himself virtuous, he conquers the unvirtuous by means of virtue alone; being himself a donor, he conquers the miserly and the stubborn stingy through giving;
and being himself a speaker of truth, he conquers the liar through truth. Thus, "by truth, [he conquers] the speaker of falsehood."
"Depart from the path, charioteer! "My lord charioteer, move away from the road.
Grant the way to our king, who is endowed with such virtue, conduct, and qualities; our king is worthy of this path.
When this was said, both King Ballika and the charioteer descended from the chariot, unyoked the horses, and moved the chariot aside.

They showed the way to the King of Bārāṇasī. Having given advice to King Ballika, saying, "Indeed, it is fitting for a king to do this and that," the King of Bārāṇasī went to Bārāṇasī, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and at the end of his life, filled the city of heaven.
King Ballika, too, having taken his advice and governed his own realm, [proceeded with his own affairs].
Without seeing anyone who spoke ill of him, he returned to his own city, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and at the end of his life, filled the heavenly realm alone.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching for the sake of advising the King of Kosala, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying:
"At that time, Moggallāna was the charioteer of King Ballika; King Ballika was Ānanda; and [the charioteer] of the King of Bārāṇasī..."
"Sāriputta was the charioteer, while I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī.
This concludes the first commentary, the Rājovāda Jātaka.
[152] 2. The Commentary on the Siṅgāla Jātaka.
"Unexamined Action": This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Gabled Hall concerning a certain barber’s son from Vesālī.

It is said that his father, being faithful and devoted, performed all the services for the kings, the royal concubines, the princes, and the princesses, such as grooming their beards, dressing their hair, and arranging their ornaments.
Having gone for refuge to the Triple Gem and undertaken the five precepts, he spent his time from time to time listening to the Dhamma of the Teacher.
One day, while going to perform work at the royal palace, he took his son with him.
There, having seen a Licchavi maiden who resembled a celestial nymph (*devaccharā*), adorned and prepared, he was overcome by defilement (*kilesa*).
With his heart bound by passion, he departed from the royal palace with his father and said, "If I obtain this maiden, I shall live;
if I do not obtain her, my death shall be right here. Having cut off all food and taken to a bed, he lay down.
Then his father approached him and said, "Dear son, do not harbor desire and lust for one who is not a fit object; you are of low birth."
“The barber’s son is a Licchavi maiden, a daughter of the Kṣatriya caste, well-born; she is not suitable for you.
We shall bring you another maiden who is equal to you in birth and lineage,” he said. But he did not heed his father’s words.
Then his mother, brother, sister, paternal uncle, maternal aunt, and all his kinsmen and friends [spoke to him].
Having assembled, they tried to revive him, but they were unable to do so. Right there, having withered and completely dried up, he reached the end of his life.
Then his father, having performed the funeral rites and the rites for the deceased, and being somewhat relieved of his grief, thought, "I shall pay homage to the Teacher.
Taking many perfumes, garlands, and ointments, he went to the Great Forest, paid homage to the Teacher, and—
Having paid homage, he sat to one side. When [the Teacher] asked, "Lay follower, why have you not been seen for many days?", he related the matter.
The Teacher said, "Lay follower, it is not only now that your son has met his destruction by giving rise to desire and lust for what is not a proper object;
in the past, too, he did exactly the same. At his request, the Teacher related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the region of the Himalayas in the womb of a lioness.
He had six younger brothers and one sister; they all lived together in a golden cave.
Not far from that cave, on a silver mountain, there was a crystal cave, and in it lived one...
A jackal lived there. Later on, the parents of the lions passed away.
Having placed their sister, the lioness, in the Golden Cave, they departed for the sake of foraging and, having brought back meat, gave it to her.
That jackal, seeing the lioness, became infatuated with her. However, while her parents were still alive—

He did not obtain permission; therefore, when those seven had departed for their own range, he descended into the crystal cave, went to the door of the golden cave, and spoke such a secret discourse connected with worldly gain before the lioness cub:
"O lioness cub, I too am a four-footed creature, and you are a four-footed creature; you become my wife."
“I shall be your husband; we shall live together in harmony and mutual affection. From this day forward, you must cherish me with passion.

Having heard his words, she thought: “This jackal is the lowest and most despised among quadrupeds, like a *caṇḍāla*, whereas we are esteemed as belonging to a noble royal lineage. How can he [be with] me?”
“He speaks words that are ignoble and unbecoming; having heard such talk, what would I do with my life?
I shall not die until I have stopped this wind. Then it occurred to her: “Death for me in this manner is improper;
let my brothers come first, and after speaking to them, I will die. The jackal also [thought] to her—
Failing to receive a reply from her, he thought, "Now she is angry with me," and overcome with dejection, he entered a crystal cave and lay down.

Then a young lion, having slain one of the various animals such as a buffalo or an elephant, ate some of the meat and brought a portion for his sister, saying, "Sister, eat the meat. She replied, "Brother, I do not eat meat; I shall die."
“Why? she asked. He told her what had happened. When he asked, “Where is that jackal now?
she, thinking the jackal lying in the crystal cave was lying in the sky, said, “Brother, do you not see?
There he is, lying in the sky on the Silver Mountain. The lion cub, unaware that he was lying in the crystal cave, thought, “He is lying in the sky.”
Being conscious, thinking, "I shall kill him," he leaped forward with the speed of a lion and struck the crystal cave with his very heart.
With his heart split open, he met his end right there and fell at the foot of the mountain.
Then another came, and she spoke to him in the same way. He too did exactly as before and, meeting his end, fell at the foot of the mountain.
When all six brothers had thus passed away, the Bodhisatta arrived last.
She informed him of that same matter and, when asked, "Where is he now?", she replied, "He is lying in the air at the summit of the Silver Mountain.
The Bodhisatta thought: "Jackals have no foothold in the air; he must be lying in the Crystal Cave."

“...will come to pass. Having descended to the foot of the mountain and seen his six brothers dead, he said, “These men, through their own foolishness and lack of discerning wisdom, did not recognize that this was a crystal cave; they have died from striking their chests with their hands.
Such is the karma of those who act with reckless haste without due consideration. Having said this, he spoke the first verse:
“The deeds of one who has not examined his course of action, who acts with hasty precipitation— those very deeds burn him,
like hot food placed in the mouth. Herein, “one who has not examined his course of action, who acts with hasty precipitation” refers to that person who, desiring to perform a certain deed...

When there is such a deed, if one—without examining or investigating it—hastens and, with sheer speed, rushes headlong into, leaps into, and engages in that action, then those actions of one who has acted without examination and who has rushed in with haste burn him, grieve him, and exhaust him. How so?
Just as if one were to swallow hot molten brass.
Just as one who eats, without reflecting that "this is cold" or "this is hot," swallows a hot morsel fit for consumption;
and once it has entered the mouth, it burns the mouth, the throat, and the stomach, causing pain, grief, and exhaustion—
so too do those very karmas torment such a person.
Having spoken this verse, the lion said, "My brothers, through their lack of skill in means, rushed forward with excessive speed thinking 'we shall kill the jackal,' and thus died themselves;
but I, not acting in such a way, shall split open the heart of the jackal while he is still lying in his crystal cave.
Having observed the path for the jackal's ascent and descent, he turned toward it.
Having roared the lion’s roar three times, the earth and the sky became one in sound.
Even as he lay in his crystal cave, the jackal’s heart burst from the cold and fear, and he met his death right there.
The Teacher, having said, "Thus that jackal met his death upon hearing the lion’s roar," spoke the second verse after attaining full enlightenment:
“The lion, with his lion’s roar, made the daddara drum resound;
hearing the lion’s cry, the jackal dwelling in the daddara drum became terrified and seized by panic, and his heart failed him.”
In this context, "lion" refers to four types of lions: the grass lion, the pale lion, the black lion, and the maned lion with reddish-brown hands and feet.
Among these, it is the maned lion that is intended here.

"He made the mountain resound" means that by means of that terrifying lion’s roar, which resembled the sound of a thunderbolt falling, he caused that Silver Mountain to resound, making it ring out with a single, uniform noise. In the *Daddara* [Sutta].
They were dwelling on a silver mountain interspersed with crystal.
"Terrified, he fell into a state of panic" means that, terrified by the fear of death, he experienced a mental dread. "And his heart burst" means that because of that fear, his heart burst.
Thus, having brought the jackal to the end of its life, the lion concealed his brothers in one place and—
Having explained his intention to his sister and comforted her, he lived in the Kañcanaguha cave for the rest of his life and then passed away according to his karma.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the jackal was the barber’s son, and the lioness cub was the Licchavi maiden."
"The six younger brothers became certain elders, but as for me, I was the elder brother, Siha.
This concludes the second commentary, the Siṅgāla Jātaka.
[153] 3. The Commentary on the Sūkara Jātaka.
"I am four-footed, O Venerable Sir"— this was said by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana,
concerning a certain elder monk. For one day, when the hearing of the Dhamma was taking place at night,
the Teacher stood upon the delightful stair-landing at the door of the Gandhakuṭī, gave the Sugata’s exhortation to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and entered the Gandhakuṭī.
The Dhammasenāpati, having paid homage to the Teacher, went to his own pariveṇa.
Mahāmoggallāna also went to his own pariveṇa, rested for a moment, and then came into the presence of the Elder and asked questions.
As each question was asked, the Dhammasenāpati answered them and made them clear, like raising the full moon in the sky. All four—
The assembly sat listening to the Dhamma. There, one elderly elder thought:
"If I ask a question while agitating Sāriputta in the midst of this assembly, this assembly, knowing that 'this man is very learned,' will show him honor and respect.
Rising from his seat in the midst of the assembly, he approached the elder.
Standing to one side, he said, "Friend Sāriputta, we too wish to ask you a question; please grant us the opportunity.
Give me a judgment—whether by piercing or by striking home, by refutation or by support, by distinction or by specific distinction.
The Elder looked at him and thought, "This old man is established in a life of desire and is empty."
Thinking, "He knows nothing at all," [the other monk], feeling ashamed, did not speak with him; instead, he set down his fan, descended from his seat, and entered his own cell.
The Elder Moggallāna also went to his own cell.
People stood up and said, "Seize this empty old man! He does not wish to hear us listen to the sweet Dhamma."
“Do not be a slave! they pursued him. As he fled, he fell into a broken-down latrine at the edge of the monastery and stood there smeared with excrement.
When people saw him, they were filled with remorse and went into the presence of the Teacher.
Seeing them, the Teacher asked, “Why have you come, lay followers, at such an unseasonable hour? The people then related the matter to him.
The Teacher said, “Lay followers, it is not only now that this old man, being overweening and unaware of his own strength, engaged with those of great strength and became smeared with excrement;

in the past as well, being overweening and unaware of his own strength, he engaged with those of great strength and was smeared with excrement. Having said this, at their request, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having become a lion, made his dwelling in a mountain cave in the Himalayan region.
Not far from there, many wild boars made their home near a certain lake.
Near that same lake, ascetics also made their dwellings in leaf huts. Then, one day—
A lion, having slain one of the various animals such as buffaloes or elephants, ate as much meat as he desired;
then, descending into that lake, he drank water and emerged. At that moment, a certain fat pig was foraging for food near that lake.
Seeing him, the lion thought, "I shall eat this one another day, but once he sees me, he may not return."
Fearing that he would not return, the jackal climbed out from under his belly and began to move away to one side.
The boar looked back and thought, "Seeing me, this creature is unable to approach out of fear and is fleeing in terror;
today it is fitting for me to engage with this lion. Raising its head and challenging him to battle, he spoke the first verse:
“I am four-footed, my friend, and you too, my friend, are four-footed.
Come, my friend, let us turn back; why do you flee in fear?
When the lion heard his words, he said, “My friend, boar, today there is no battle for us with you.”
"Let the battle take place right here on this very spot on the seventh day from now," he said, and then he departed.
The boar, overjoyed at the thought, "I shall fight with the lion," reported this news to his kinsmen.
Upon hearing his words, they were terrified and cried out, "Now you will destroy us all; without knowing your own strength, you [have challenged] the lion..."
“Desiring to engage in battle,” they said, “a lion will come and bring us all to our death;
do not commit such a rash act! He too, terrified and trembling, asked, “What shall I do now?
The boars replied, “Friend, go to the latrine of these ascetics and let your body remain in the putrid excrement for seven days.”
"Wrap it, dry it, and on the seventh day, moisten the body with drops of dew.
Go there earlier than the lion’s arrival; perceiving the movement of the wind, stand in the upper wind.
A pure-born lion, having smelled the scent of your body, will grant you victory and depart," they said. He did accordingly, and on the seventh day, he was there.
He stood there. Having smelled the odor of his body and realized he was smeared with excrement, Sīha said, "My dear boar, you have thought up a clever trick!
Had you not been smeared with excrement, I would have brought about the end of your life right here.
But now, it is impossible for me to bite your body with my mouth or strike it with my foot."
Having said, "I give you victory," he spoke the second verse:
"You are impure, with putrid hair; you smell like a foul-smelling pig.
If you wish to contend, my good man, I give you victory."

In this context, "one with rotten hair" means one whose hair is foul-smelling because it is smeared with filth. "One who dwells in a foul odor" means that he dwells having become possessed of an undesirable, loathsome, and repulsive smell.
Saying, "Victory, my dear friend, I give to you," meaning "I grant you victory; I am defeated;
you may go," the lion turned back right there, took his food, drank water from the lake, and [went] to the mountain cave itself.
The lion departed. The boar, thinking "I have defeated the lion," announced this to his kinsmen.
Terrified and trembling, they thought, "If the lion comes again one day, he will bring us all to our death," and so they fled and went elsewhere.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the boar was the elder, and the lion was none other than myself."
The third: The Explanation of the Boar Birth Story (Sūkarajātakavaṇṇanā).
[154] 4. The Explanation of the Snake Birth Story (Uragajātakavaṇṇanā):
"Here has entered the most excellent of snakes"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the quarrel of the Seṇi clan.
The Teacher related the story. It seems that two high ministers of the King of Kosala, headed by Seṇi, were quarreling with one another whenever they met;
their state of enmity became well known throughout the entire city. Neither the king nor their kinsmen and friends were able to reconcile them.
Then, one day, at the time of dawn, the Teacher surveyed those among his kinsmen who were ready to be trained.
Seeing that both of them possessed the necessary support (*upanissaya*) for the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*), on the following day he entered Sāvatthī for alms alone.

He stood at the door of one of their houses. That man came out, took his bowl, led the Teacher into the house, prepared a seat, and made him sit down. Once the Teacher was seated, [he taught] to him the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*).
Having explained the benefits and knowing his mind was ready, he proclaimed the Truths; at the conclusion of the Truths, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The Teacher, knowing his attainment of stream-entry, had him take that very bowl, rose, and went to the door of the other’s house.
He too came out, paid homage to the Teacher, and saying, "Please enter, venerable sir," ushered him into the house.
He had him sit down. The other, too, took his bowl and entered together with the Teacher.
The Teacher, having praised the eleven benefits of loving-kindness (*mettā*) to him and knowing that his mind was ready, proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*).

At the conclusion of the Truths, he also became established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Thus, both of them, having become stream-enterers, confessed their transgressions to one another.
Having asked for forgiveness, they became reconciled, harmonious, and of one mind. On that very day, they ate together in the presence of the Blessed One.

When the Teacher had finished his meal, he went to the monastery. Taking with them many garlands, perfumes, ointments, and such things as ghee, honey, and molasses, they set out together with the Teacher. The Teacher, accompanied by the community of monks—
Having displayed his conduct and given the Sugata’s exhortation, he entered the fragrant chamber.
In the evening, the bhikkhus in the Dhamma Hall initiated a discussion on the Teacher’s virtues: "Friends, the Teacher is the tamer of the untamed;
for even though the King had been striving for a long time, he was unable to bring those two high ministers into harmony."
“Neither kinsmen nor friends were able [to reconcile them], for they were subdued by the Tathāgata in a single day.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?

When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it was not only now that I made these two people harmonious; in the past as well, they were already reconciled by me. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, a great festival was proclaimed in the city on account of a public celebration.
Many people, as well as devas, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others, gathered together for the sake of seeing the festivities.
In one place, a certain nāga and a supaṇṇa stood side by side, watching the spectacle. The nāga—
Not knowing that he was a supaṇṇa, the man placed his hand upon the supaṇṇa’s shoulder. The supaṇṇa, asking, “Who has placed a hand on my shoulder?
turned around and looked; seeing it was a nāga, he recognized him.

The nāga also looked back, and recognizing the supaṇṇa, terrified by the fear of death, he fled from the city and escaped along the bank of the river. The supaṇṇa, thinking, “I shall seize him,” pursued him.

...was connected [to this]. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become an ascetic and dwelling in a leaf-hut on the bank of that river, would put on his water-cloth (*udakasāṭikā*) and set aside his bark-garment (*vakkala*) for the sake of allaying the fatigue of the day;
he would then descend into the river and bathe. The Nāga, thinking, "I shall obtain my livelihood by depending on this renunciant," assumed his natural form.
Having cast off his body, which was the color of a mass of jewels, he fashioned himself into the form of a bark garment and entered it.
The supaṇṇa, pursuing him, saw that he had entered there; failing to grasp the bark garment because of its great weight, he addressed the Bodhisatta and spoke this matter to him:
"Venerable sir, I am hungry; take your bark garment, and I shall eat this nāga."
He spoke the first verse:
“Here, the most excellent among those from afar has entered, desiring liberation through the splendor of the mountain;
honoring the splendor of Brahmā, though famished, I do not give him food to eat.”
In this context, "the best of serpents has entered here" means that the preeminent king of nagas has entered this bark-garment.
"With the color of a rock" means with the color of a jewel; the sense is that he has entered having become a mass of jewels.
"Desiring deliverance" means desiring release from my presence. "And honoring the color of Brahmā" refers to me, for I am [Brahmā] to you.
"Honoring and respecting the Brahma-like, supreme form [of the Naga]," he said. "Though I am hungry, I do not eat;
though I am famished, I am unable to devour this Naga who has entered between my feathers.
While still standing in the water, the Bodhisatta offered praise to the king of the Supaṇṇas and spoke the second verse:
“Thus, O Brahmagutta, may you live for a long time, and may divine foods appear before you;
you who, honoring the form of a brahmin, do not yield to hunger and eat.
In this context, “O Brahmagutta” means you, being protected by the brahmins and guarded by the brahmins. And may divine foods appear before you.
"May there be food fit for the enjoyment of deities, and may such food appear for you; do not, having committed the taking of life, become an eater of naga-flesh.
Thus the Bodhisatta, while still standing in the water, offered this expression of thanks, and having emerged, he put on his bark garment and [addressed] both of them.
Having taken [the child], he went to the hermitage, spoke in praise of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*), and reconciled the two people.
From then on, they lived together in harmony and mutual affection, dwelling in happiness.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Nāga and the Supaṇṇa were these two high ministers, while the ascetic was none other than myself."
The fourth: The Commentary on the Uragajāta­ka.
[155] 5. The Commentary on the Bhaggajāta­ka.
"Live a hundred years, O broken one!"—this was spoken by the Teacher near the Jeta Grove in a monastery built by King Pasenadi of Kosala.
While dwelling in the Royal Park, he spoke concerning his own coughing fit.

For one day, while the Teacher was seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly in the Royal Park teaching the Dhamma, he coughed. The bhikkhus raised a loud clamor, crying out, "May the Blessed One live!
May the Sugata live! Because of that noise, there was an interruption to the discourse on the Dhamma.
It happened that the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, if one were to say ‘Live!
to someone who has been shot, would he live or die because of that? “Certainly not, Bhante. “Bhikkhus, one should not say ‘Live! to someone who has been shot;
whoever should say so commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Now at that time, people...
When people spat at the bhikkhus, they said, “Live on, venerable sirs! The bhikkhus, being anxious, did not speak to them.
People complained, saying, “How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, not speak when they are told, ‘Live on, venerable sirs!’?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Householders, bhikkhus, are superstitious; I allow [you to speak].”
“Monks, when householders say to you, ‘Live long, venerable sirs,’ you may reply, ‘May you live long.
The monks asked the Blessed One, “Venerable sir, when did this so-called ‘live-and-return-the-greeting’ originate?
The Teacher said, “Monks, the so-called ‘live-and-return-the-greeting’ originated in ancient times,” and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a certain brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi.

His father made his living by trade; when the Bodhisatta reached the age of sixteen, his father had him carry a load of jeweled goods and, traveling through villages, market towns, and other places, they arrived at Benares and stayed at the house of a gatekeeper.
Having had food prepared and eaten himself, and finding no place to stay, he asked, "Where do these guests who have arrived out of hours reside?
Then the people said to him, "There is a hall outside the city, but it is possessed by non-human beings (amanussa).
If you wish, you may stay there. The Bodhisatta said, "Come, dear ones, let us go; do not [fear] the yakkha..."
“I am afraid; I shall tame him and place him at your feet. Having said this, he took his father and went there.
Then his father lay down upon a wooden plank, while he himself sat fanning his father’s feet.
A *yakkha* residing there, who had served Vessavaṇa for twelve years and had obtained that *sālā* as his reward, [thought]: “Among those who have entered this *sālā*...”
"Except for those who say 'It lives' when it is thrown, and those who say 'It lives back' when it is said 'It lives,' you may eat all the rest. He lived by a pillar of the back-bone.
Thinking, "I will cause the Bodhisatta’s father to be thrown," he released fine powder through his own supernatural power; the powder came and—
It entered his nostrils. While still lying on the wooden plank, he spat it out; the Bodhisatta did not say, "He lives.
The yakkha descended from the pillar to devour him. Seeing him descending, the Bodhisatta thought: "This must be the one who made my father spit it out;
this is that very yakkha who devours one who does not say 'he lives' when [the food] has been spat out."
Addressing his father, he spoke this first verse:
“Live for a hundred years, O Blessed One, and another twenty;
let not the piśācas devour me; live you for a hundred autumns.”
In this context, "O broken one" (bhagga) is an address to her father by name. "And another twenty" means: may you live for another twenty years.
"May the piśācas not devour me" means: may the piśācas not eat me. "Live you, O hundred-and-eight" means:
may you, however, live for more than a hundred years. For when "hundred-and-eight" (saradosata) is calculated, it amounts to exactly one hundred years.
That [number] together with the previous twenty is intended here as "twenty-one.
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, the yakkha thought, "Since this young man has been told 'Live!', it is not possible to eat him;
however, I shall eat his father," and he went into the presence of the father. As he was approaching, [the father saw him].
Seeing him, he thought: “This must be that ‘Paṭijīva’ (the ‘Live-on-another’) demon who devours those who do not speak for their own livelihood.
I shall provide a livelihood. Addressing his son, he spoke this second verse:
“May you too live for a hundred years, and another twenty as well!”
"Let the piśācas eat the poison; you live for a hundred autumns!
Therein, "let the piśācas eat the poison" means let the piśācas eat the halāhala poison.
Having heard his words, the yakkha thought, "It is impossible for me to eat both," and he turned back. Then him—
The Bodhisatta asked, “O yakkha, why do you devour the people who have entered this sāla tree?
“Because I obtained it after serving Vessavaṇa for twelve years,” he replied. “But can you eat everyone?
“I eat all except those who speak of their livelihood and their means of subsistence. “Yakkha, formerly too you—”
"Having committed unwholesome deeds, you were reborn as one who is harsh, cruel, and a tormentor of others;
now, having performed such karma once more, you will become one who goes from darkness to darkness. Therefore, from this day forward, refrain from killing living beings and other such acts.
Having thus subdued the yakkha, terrified him with the fear of hell, and established him in the five precepts, he made the yakkha like a mere messenger.
On the following day, people passing by saw the yakkha and, learning that he had been subdued by the Bodhisatta, reported it to the king:
"Your Majesty, a young man has tamed that yakkha and stands by him like a servant.
The king summoned the Bodhisatta and appointed him to the position of commander-in-chief, bestowing upon him great honor equal to his father's.
Thus, having made the yakkha the recipient of his offerings and abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and filled the city of heaven.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "At that time there arose what is called 'living off one's own life' (jīvapaṭijīva)," and he identified the Jātaka:
"The yakkha at that time was Aṅgulimāla; the king was Ānanda; the father was Kassapa; and the son was [the Buddha himself]."
"But it was I myself who was he.
Thus ends the fifth commentary, the Bhaggajātakavaṇṇanā. [156] 6.
Alīnacittajātakavaṇṇanā (The Commentary on the Birth Story of the Undaunted Heart)
"Depending on a depressed mind": this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who had slackened his energy.
The story will appear in the *Saṃvarajātaka* in the *Ekādasanipāta*.
When the Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you have slackened your energy?", he replied, "It is true, Blessed One."

The Teacher said to him: "Bhikkhu, did you not formerly, without relaxing your energy, seize the kingdom of the city of Benares twelve yojanas in extent for a young boy who was like a mere lump of flesh and give it to him?
Why then, having now gone forth into such a teaching as this, do you relax your energy? Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī,
there was a village of carpenters not far from Bārāṇasī where five hundred carpenters lived. They would go upstream by boat into the forest,
chop timber for building materials, and right there prepare various types of house components— single-storied, two-storied, and so forth— beginning with the pillars.
Having marked out all the timber, they led it to the riverbank, loaded it onto boats, and traveled downstream to the city.
There, they built houses of whatever kind each person desired, took their fees in kahāpaṇas, and returned once more to that same place to fetch the materials for the houses.
While they were thus maintaining their livelihood, at one time, a royal camp...
While they were binding the timber and splitting it, an elephant nearby stepped on a khadira wood stake.
The stake pierced his foot, and powerful pains arose; his foot swelled and became infected with pus.
Overcome by the pain, upon hearing the sound of them splitting the timber, he thought, "Relying on these carpenters, my safety will be secured."
Having gone to them on three legs, he lay down not far away. When the carpenter saw that his foot was swollen, he approached him;
seeing the stump in the foot, he cut around the stump with a sharp axe, bound it with a rope, and by pulling it out, extracted the stump.
He then released the pus, washed it with warm water, and [attended to him].
Having smeared it with appropriate medicines, they soon made the wound healthy.
Once the elephant had recovered, he thought: "It is by depending on these carpenters that I have regained my life;
now it is right for me to do them a favor. From then on, he began to carry timber for the carpenters.
Having cut it and turned it over, he gives it [to the elephant]; he provides tools such as axes; having wrapped it with his trunk, he grasps it at the end of a black cord.
At mealtime, carpenters give him five hundred morsels of food, giving one morsel each.
Now, that elephant had a son, a pure white noble elephant calf; because of this, the thought occurred to him:
“I am now old. It is fitting for me to go now, having given my son to these carpenters to serve as their laborer.
Without informing the carpenters, he entered the forest, brought back his son, and said: “This young elephant calf is my son;
you have given me my life. For the sake of your medical fee, I shall give this young elephant calf to you.”
Having said, "I give this one; from now on, he shall perform your work," and having instructed his son,
"From now on, my dear son, you must do whatever work is to be done by me," he gave him to the carpenters and entered the forest himself.
From that time forth, the young elephant became obedient to the carpenters' words and patient with their instructions, performing all his duties.
They, in turn, nourished him with five hundred mouthfuls of food. Having finished his work, he would descend into the river, bathe, and play before returning;
meanwhile, the carpenter’s boys would seize him by his trunk and other limbs, whether in the water or on dry land, and sport together with him.
They played about. However, noble elephants, horses, and men do not void excrement or urine in the water;
therefore, he too, without voiding excrement or urine in the water, did so only outside the riverbank.
Then one day it rained upstream, and consequently, dry elephant dung was carried down by the water as it flowed into the river.
Having tied [the elephant] to a tree in a grove at a bathing place in the city of Bārāṇasī, he stood there.

Then the king’s elephant-keepers brought five hundred elephants, thinking, "We shall bathe the elephant. But having smelled the scent of the noble stallion's dung, not even a single elephant ventured to descend into the river. They all raised their trunks and began to flee.
The elephant-keepers informed the elephant-trainers. Thinking, "There must be an obstacle in the water," they had the water cleared.
Seeing that stallion's dung in that thicket, they realized, "This is the cause here.
Having had a tub brought and filled with water, they crushed it there and had the elephants sprinkle it over their bodies; [thus] their bodies...
They became fragrant. At that time, they descended into the river and bathed.
The elephant trainers, having reported this matter to the king, said, "Your Majesty, it is fitting to search for and bring back that noble elephant.
The king then launched a flotilla of boats onto the river and, with those boats moving upstream—
He reached the carpenters' dwelling place. While playing in the river, the young elephant calf heard the sound of drums, went there, and stood near the carpenters.
The carpenters went out to meet the king and said, "Your Majesty, if you have need of timber, for what reason have you come? Would it not be better to send someone to have it brought?"
“I have not come for the sake of wood, my man; rather, we have come for the sake of this elephant.
“Have it seized and let us go, Your Majesty. The young elephant did not wish to go. “What is the elephant doing, my man?
“It is having the carpenters’ wages brought, Your Majesty. “Very well, my man,” said the king to the elephant.
He had one hundred thousand times one hundred thousand kahāpaṇas placed near the elephant’s trunk, its tusks, and its tail.

Even with such an amount, the elephant would not go; rather, when pairs of garments were given to all the carpenters, and lower and upper cloths to the carpenters’ wives, and when gifts for children were provided for the boys who played together, the elephant turned back toward the carpenters and the women.
Having looked at the two children, she went along with the king.

The king, taking her with him, entered the city; having had the city and the elephant stable decorated, he had the elephant perform a circumambulation of the city, led it into the elephant stable, adorned it with all ornaments, and bestowed upon it the consecration.
Having made him a riding elephant and established him in the position of his own companion, he gave half the kingdom to the elephant and accorded him honors equal to his own.
From the time the elephant arrived, the king’s sovereignty over all Jambudīpa remained firmly in his hands.
As time passed in this manner, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the king’s chief queen.
She took conception. While her pregnancy was reaching maturity, the king passed away.
However, if the elephant were to know that the king had died, his heart would have burst right then and there; therefore, they attended to him without letting him know the king’s death.
But when they heard of the king’s passing, [they thought], "The kingdom is indeed empty."
The neighboring King of Kosala arrived with a great army and besieged the city.
The city-dwellers closed the gates and sent a message to the King of Kosala: "The chief queen of our king is pregnant;
the readers of the science of bodily marks have declared, 'On the seventh day from now, she will give birth to a son. If she gives birth to a son..."
“He will give birth; on the seventh day we shall give battle, not for the sake of the kingdom, so wait for this much time.
The king accepted, saying, “Very well.
On the seventh day, the queen gave birth to a son. However, on the day of the naming ceremony, the hearts of the great multitude were undaunted.
Because he was born grasping [his hands], they gave him the name “Prince Alīnacitta.
From the very day of his birth, however, the citizens fought against the King of Kosala.
Because the battle lacked a leader, even though their great army was fighting, it gradually retreated. The ministers informed the Queen of this matter and said, “We—”
“As our army thus retreats, we fear the state of defeat;
yet our king’s elephant, Maṅgala, who is the king’s companion, does not know of our king’s death, the birth of his son, or that the King of Kosala has arrived to fight.
Let us inform him,” they asked. She consented, saying, “Very well,” and having adorned her son, she—
Having laid him down upon a pillow of fine *dukūla* cloth, he descended from the palace and, surrounded by his assembly of ministers, went to the elephant stable.
There, having laid the Bodhisatta at the foot of an elephant, he said: "Master, your friend has passed away;
we did not inform you out of fear that it would break your heart. This is your friend’s son. King Kosala has arrived and is coming to the city..."
"Surrounding him, he fights together with your son; his army is retreating. Either you yourself must slay your son, or seize his kingdom and give it back to him," he said.
At that moment, the elephant touched the Bodhisatta with its trunk, lifted him up, placed him upon its forehead, and wept.
Having caused the Bodhisatta to descend and placed him in the hands of the queen, [the elephant] emerged from the elephant stable with the thought, "I shall seize the King of Kosala.
Then his ministers, having fastened his armor and adorned him, opened the city gate and went out surrounding him.
Having emerged from the city, the elephant let out a trumpeting cry and [frightened] the great multitude.
Having terrified him and caused him to flee, he broke through the fortified gate, seized the King of Kosala by the topknot, and brought him back.
He made the king prostrate at the feet of the Bodhisatta and, restraining those who had risen to kill him, exhorted him, saying, "From this day forth, be vigilant;
do not entertain the notion that 'the prince is still young,'" and then dismissed him. From that time on—
The sovereignty over the entire Jambudīpa came entirely into the hands of the Bodhisatta;
there was no other rival capable of rising up against him. Having been consecrated at the age of seven, the Bodhisatta became known as King Alīnacitta;
ruling righteously, he filled the city of heaven at the conclusion of his life.
The Teacher, having brought up this past event and having attained full enlightenment, spoke these two verses:
“Relying on an undaunted heart, the great army, exultant,
seized the King of Kosala alive while he was complacent in his camp.”
“Thus endowed with support, a bhikkhu who has aroused energy,
developing wholesome states for the attainment of security from bondage, will reach,
step by step, the destruction of all fetters.”
In that context, "relying on one of undaunted mind" means relying on a prince whose mind was not cowed.
"A great army, exultant" refers to a vast host that had become joyful and delighted, thinking, "We have seen our ancestral sovereignty.

"The Kosalan army, dissatisfied" refers to the king of Kosala who, being dissatisfied with his own kingdom, had come out of greed for another's realm. "He seized him alive" means he captured him while still living.
Without killing that army at all, he had the king captured alive by means of an elephant.

"Thus endowed with a support" means that just as that army was, so too another son of good family who is endowed with a support, having obtained a support such as the Buddha or a disciple of the Buddha who is a virtuous friend.
"Bhikkhu" is a designation for one who is utterly pure. "Aroused in energy" means one whose energy is exerted.
Endowed with energy free from the four faults; "cultivating wholesome states" means developing the wholesome, blameless states known as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
"for the attainment of security from bondage" means cultivating those states for the sake of reaching Nibbāna, which is secure from the four bonds; he would attain it step by step.

"Regarding 'the destruction of all fetters' (*sabbasaṃyojanakkhaya*): as this bhikkhu, endowed with the necessary support of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*), cultivates this wholesome state (*kusala-dhamma*) starting from insight (*vipassanā*), he gradually attains the various knowledges of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and the lower paths and fruits.
Finally, because it has arisen at the point of the destruction of even the ten fetters, it is designated as 'the destruction of all fetters.'"
One attains arahantship. Or, because all fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted by resorting to Nibbāna, that too is simply the exhaustion of all fetters;
thus the meaning is that one gradually reaches the exhaustion of all fetters known as Nibbāna.
Thus the Blessed One, having taken up the pinnacle of the teaching of the Dhamma with the great Nibbāna of the Deathless, further elucidated the Truths.
He brought the Jātaka to its conclusion; at the conclusion of the Truths (Saccapariyosāna), the monk who had slackened his energy established himself in Arahatship.
"At that time, the mother was Mahāmāyā and the father was the Great King Suddhodana.

Having taken over the kingdom, this elephant given away was this very monk who had slackened his energy. The elephant’s father was Sāriputta, the neighboring King of Kosala was Moggallāna, and Prince Alīnacitta was [the Bodhisatta]."
"But it was indeed I who was he.
This concludes the sixth commentary, the *Alīnacittajātaka*.
[157] 7. The *Guṇajātaka* Commentary.
"By which he sends forth his desire"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the Elder Ānanda’s acquisition of a thousand robes.
The account of the Elder preaching the Dhamma in the royal palace of the King of Kosala has already been related below in the Mahāsāra Jātaka.
Thus, while the Elder was preaching the Dhamma in the king’s palace, [the king gave him] robes worth a thousand pieces of gold.
A thousand [pieces of cloth] were brought forth. From that, the king gave five hundred garments to his five hundred queens.
They all set those garments aside and, on the following day, gave them to the Elder Ānanda;
then, having dressed themselves in their old garments, they went to the place where the king was taking his morning meal.
The king asked, “I had a thousand pieces of cloth given to you; why have you come without wearing them?
“Your Majesty, we gave them to the Elder Ānanda. “Did the Elder Ānanda take all of them? “Yes, Your Majesty.
“The Perfectly Enlightened One has permitted only the three robes; the Elder Ānanda [is engaged in] the trade of cloth.”
"I suspect he will do so; he has taken far too many robes," he thought. Feeling resentment toward the elder, the man went to the monastery after finishing his breakfast.
Entering the elder’s cell, he paid homage to the elder and sat down, then asked:
"Venerable sir, do the women in our house learn or hear the Dhamma from you?"
“Yes, great king, they take what is fit to be taken and listen to what is fit to be heard.
“But do they merely listen, or do they also give you their lower garments or upper robes?
“Today, great king, they gave five hundred cloths worth a thousand pieces of money each. “Were those accepted by you, venerable sir? “Yes, great king.”
“But, venerable sir, has not the Teacher himself authorized only the triple robe? “Yes, great king, the Blessed One authorized the triple robe for a single monk by way of its use;
however, its acceptance was not forbidden. Therefore, I accepted those garments in order to give them to other monks whose robes were worn out. “But what about those monks...”

“Having obtained a robe from you, what will you do with your old robes? “We will make them into an outer cloak (saṅghāṭī) and an upper robe (uttarāsaṅga). “What will you do with the old upper robe? “We will make it into an inner robe (antaravāsaka).
“What will you do with the old inner robe? “We will make it into a bedspread (paccattharaṇa).”
“What will they do with the old coverlet? “They will make it into a floor-covering. “What will they do with the old floor-covering?
“They will make it into a foot-wiper. “What will they do with the old foot-wiper?
“Great King, that which is given out of faith cannot be cast away; therefore, the old foot-wiper is cut with an axe...”
“Having pounded it and mixed it with clay, they will apply a coating of clay to the lodgings.
“Venerable sir, what has been given to you cannot even be lost, not even as much as a foot-wiping cloth? “Yes, great king, what has been given to us cannot be lost;
it simply becomes our use.”
The king, being satisfied and filled with joy, had the other five hundred robes kept in his house brought out;
having given them to the Elder and heard the words of thanksgiving, he paid homage to the Elder, circumambulated him, and departed.
The Elder gave the first five hundred robes he had received to those monks whose robes were worn out. But as for the Elder’s own—
There were about five hundred *saddhivihārika* disciples; among them was one young bhikkhu who was of great service to the elder.

He swept the courtyard, provided drinking water and water for washing, gave him tooth-sticks, water for rinsing the mouth, and water for bathing, and he maintained the latrines, the sauna, and the lodgings, as well as performing services such as massaging his hands, feet, and back.
The Elder, having later obtained five hundred robes, gave them all to him alone on the grounds that he had been very helpful to him.
He, in turn, distributed all those robes among his own co-residents.
Thus, all those monks who had received robes cut and dyed them until they were the color of *kaṇikāra* flowers.
Having put on the saffron robes and donned them, they approached the Teacher, paid homage, sat down to one side, and said:
"Venerable sir, there is such a thing as a 'gift of a face-lifting' for a noble disciple who has attained the stream.
"Monks, there is no such thing as a 'gift of a face-lifting' for noble disciples. "Venerable sir, by our preceptor..."
“The Elder Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika gave five hundred robes worth a thousand pieces of money to a single young bhikkhu;
that bhikkhu, having shared what he had received, gave it to us. “Bhikkhus, Ānanda does not give alms by looking at faces;
rather, that bhikkhu was very helpful to him, and therefore, as a token of his own assistance—”

"Out of a sense of gratitude and thankfulness, thinking, 'It is fitting to make a return for one who has been helpful,' he gave it away by way of assistance, by way of virtue, and by way of what was appropriate.
For even the ancient wise men performed returns for those who had helped them.
Having said this, being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta lived as a lion in a mountain cave.
One day, having emerged from his cave, he looked toward the foot of the mountain;
surrounding that mountain foot was a great lake. On one high spot, upon a surface of thick, hardened mud—
Tender green grass grew there. Hares, deer, and other small animals wandered upon the surface of the mud and ate it.
On that very day, one deer was also wandering about eating it.
The lion, thinking, "I shall seize that deer," sprang from the mountain peak and leaped with the speed of a lion; the deer, however, was terrified by the fear of death.
The brave ones fled. Unable to restrain his momentum, the lion fell upon the surface of the mud;
sinking down, he was unable to rise up, and with his four legs sunk in like pillars, he remained there for seven days without food.
Then a certain jackal, intent on its own prey, saw him and fled in fear. The lion called out to it.
“O jackal, do not flee! I am stuck in the mud; give me my life! he said.
The jackal went to him and said, “I could lift you out, but I fear that once you are lifted out, you will eat me. “Do not fear,” he replied. “I will not eat you;
rather, I shall do you a great service by means of a certain stratagem. [He then took] me...
"Pull me out! Having obtained his consent, the jackal cleared away the mud from around all four of the lion's paws, dug four channels for each of the four paws, and directed them toward the water;
the water entered and softened the mud. At that moment, the jackal thrust its head into the lion's belly.
"Make an effort, Master! shouting thus, he struck the lion’s belly with his head.
The lion, exerting his strength, leaped up from the mud and, having bounded forth, stood upon dry land.
After resting for a moment, he descended into the lake, washed away the mud, bathed, and relieved his exhaustion; then, having slain a buffalo, he tore it apart with his fangs.
Having cut off some flesh and placed it before the jackal, saying, "Eat, friend," he ate it after the jackal had eaten.
Again, the jackal bit and seized a piece of meat. When asked, "For what purpose is this, friend?
he replied, "You have a female slave; this shall be her portion. The lion said, "Take it."
Having taken some meat for the sake of the lioness, he said, "Come, friend,
let us go to our friend's dwelling place while standing upon the summit of our mountain. Having gone there, he had her eat the meat,
comforted both the male and female jackals, and said, "From now on, I shall henceforth look after you," and [returned] to his own dwelling place.
Having led them to another cave, he settled them at its entrance. From then on, when they went out for their food, they would leave behind the lioness and the female leopard;
instead, they would go with the male leopard, kill various wild animals, eat the meat right there themselves, and bring some back to give to the other two.
As time passed in this way, the lioness gave birth to two cubs, and the female jackal also gave birth to two cubs.
They all lived together in harmony. Then one day, it occurred to the lioness:
"This lion loves the jackal, the female jackal, and the jackal cubs exceedingly; surely he has a close intimacy with the female jackal, and therefore—"
She showed such affection [for the jackal] that she thought, "What if I were now to squeeze and threaten this one, and drive him away from here?
When the lion had gone out for his prey, she seized the jackal and squeezed and threatened her, saying, "For what reason do you live in this place;
why do you not flee? Her sons, the young jackals, likewise threatened them in the same way. The female jackal [reported] this matter...
Having told the jackal, they said, "We do not even know whether she acted thus at the lion’s command; we have lived here for a long time, and he might even cause us to be expelled.
Let us go back to our own dwelling place. When the jackal heard their words, he approached the lion and said, "Master, we have lived in your presence for a long time—indeed, for too long."

Springtime is indeed unpleasant; when we have departed for our own range, the lioness harasses the female jackal, threatening her, “Why do you dwell in this place? Get out! and the lion cubs likewise threaten the jackal cubs.
Indeed, whoever does not find it pleasing to live near another must be driven away with the command, “Go!”—this is harassment.
Having asked, "What is the purpose of this name?", he spoke the first verse:
"Know that the doe of the powerful ones, who flees at will,
is crying out loudly because she perceives danger arising from her own offspring."
In this context, "he sends him away wherever he wishes" means that because the Dhamma is powerful, it is called "powerful";
just as a lord sends his servant away in whichever direction he desires, so too does he send him out.
This is the nature of those who possess power, the natural law (*paveṇidhamma*) of those who are masters; therefore, if you do not find our dwelling agreeable, [you may go] directly.
"Do not take it out; what is the use of causing harm?"—speaking thus to show this, he said. "O doe" (*migī*) is how he addresses the lioness.
For she is a "doe" (*migī*) because she possesses deer (*miga*) by virtue of being the queen of deer (*migarājā*). "O high-tusked one" (*unnadantī*) is also how he addresses her.
For she is "high-tusked" (*unnadantī*) because she possesses high (*unnata*) tusks (*danta*); "O high-tusked one" (*unnatadantī*) is likewise a reading.
"Understand this": understand that "this is the way of the lords. "Fear has arisen from the refuge":
we have you as our refuge in the sense of being our support, yet fear has arisen from you yourself; therefore, he indicates, "we shall go back to our own dwelling place.
Another interpretation: "O doe, the lioness, roaring and threatening my children and wife, drives them away wherever she pleases."
In whatever manner he desires, he drives them away, causes them to proceed, harasses them, and even makes them flee;
"Know this for certain: what can we do in that matter? This is the law of the powerful, the very nature of those who possess strength;
we shall depart now. Why? Because fear arises from birth.

Having heard his words, the lion said to the lioness, "My dear, do you remember that at such-and-such a time, having gone out for my prey, on the seventh day I returned together with this male jackal and this female jackal?
"Yes, I remember," she replied. "But do you know the reason why I did not return for seven days? "I do not know."
"Yes, Master. "Bhadde, having missed my aim while thinking, 'I will catch a deer,' I fell into a swamp.
Unable to get out, I remained there for seven days without food. It was by depending on this jackal that I regained my life;
he is my friend who gave me my life. For there is no such thing as a weak friend who is incapable of standing firm in the duty of friendship."
“From this day forward, do not treat my companion, his wife,
and their children with such contempt,” he said, and the lion spoke the second verse:
“Even if a friend is weak, as long as he abides by the duties of friendship;”

"He is my kinsman and my relative; he is my friend and my companion. O tusked one, do not despise him as a mere mother; he is a jackal who gave me my life. In this passage, there are two uses of the particle *api*:

one has the sense of "even," and the other has the sense of "indeed. This is the construction [of the verse]: [the first *api*] expresses favor, while [the second] expresses esteem. Therein, this is the application [of the meaning].
"Even if a friend is weak, as long as he abides in the duties of a friend—if he is able to remain so—he is a kinsman and a relative;
he is a friend by virtue of his loving-kindness, and he is my comrade in the sense of being a companion.
'Do not despise the tusked one, O Mother,' Bhaddā—do not despise my companion or comrade, the tusked lion; for this jackal is the giver of my life."
Having heard his words, she asked the female jackal for forgiveness; from then on, she lived in harmony with her and her son.
The lion cubs also played and frolicked together with the jackal cubs, and even after their parents had passed away, they continued to live in harmony, never breaking their bond of friendship.
Indeed, it is said that their mutual affection remained unbroken for seven generations.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
at the conclusion of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some became arahants.
"At that time, the jackal was Ānanda, but the lion was none other than myself."
The seventh is the commentary on the Guṇa-jātaka.
[158] 8. The commentary on the Suhanu-jātaka:
"This is not for one of uneven character"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning two fierce bhikkhus.
At that time, there was also a certain monk at Jetavana who was fierce, harsh, and violent, just like the one in the countryside.
One day, the country monk came to Jetavana on some business; the novices and junior monks knew of his fierce nature.
Out of curiosity, thinking, "We shall witness a quarrel between these two fierce men," they gathered.
They sent that monk to the courtyard of a resident of Jetavana. Although both were fierce, as soon as they saw one another, they became reconciled and lived together in harmony;
they massaged each other’s hands, feet, and backs, and so forth. In the Hall of Truth, the monks started a conversation:
"Friends, fierce monks are fierce and harsh toward others."
“Though they were violent, they have now become harmonious, joyful, and living in mutual affection with one another.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “For this very discussion,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now; formerly these two, as well as others, were fierce, harsh, and violent toward one another.”
Having said, "But they were in harmony, living together in mutual affection," he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister, who accomplished all his aims and instructed him in both material prosperity and the Dhamma.
That king, however, was somewhat inclined toward greed for wealth, and he had a fraudulent horse named Mahāsoṇa.
There were. Then horse-dealers from the Northern Country brought five hundred horses and informed the king that the horses had arrived.
However, previously, the Bodhisatta had had the horses appraised and caused their price to be paid without any reduction.
The king, feeling aggrieved by this, summoned another minister and said, "Dear son, have the horses appraised; while appraising them..."
"And first, you should release Mahāsoṇa so that he enters among those horses;
having had him bite them and cause them to be wounded, you should have the horses appraised at a time when they are weakened and their value has been lost," he said.
He agreed, saying "Very well," and did exactly so.
The horse-dealers, being displeased, reported what had been done by him to the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta asked, "But is there no counterfeit horse in your city? "There is, sir; there is a counterfeit horse named Suhanu who is fierce and cruel," they replied.
"In that case, bring that horse back when you return next time. Having agreed, saying "Very well," they departed.
Returning once more, they brought him back after having him seize that peak.
When the king heard, "The horse-traders have arrived," he opened the lion-window, looked at the horses, and released Mahāsoṇa. Seeing Mahāsoṇa approaching, the horse-traders also released Suhanu.
Having met one another, they licked each other's bodies and greeted one another with joy.
They stood there. The king asked the Bodhisatta: "Do you see these two peak-white horses?
While others are fierce, harsh, and violent, and cause other horses to suffer illness by biting them, these two now stand together, licking each other’s bodies and greeting one another with joy.
What does this mean? The Bodhisatta replied: "Great King, these are not of uneven character; they are of equal character."
Having said, "And these belong to the same element," he spoke these two verses:
"This is not for one of uneven virtue, Soṇa, together with Suhanu;
Suhanu is likewise just such as he, who is the range of Soṇa."
“With one who is impetuous and reckless, constantly devouring his bonds, evil meets with evil; the wicked meets with the wicked.
In this regard, it is not by one of uneven virtue that the jaw-bone meets the jaw-bone; for this jaw-bone of the stallion meets the jaw-bone of the ram.
He forms an affectionate bond with one who is of equal virtue, not with one of uneven virtue; rather, he forms it only with one whose virtue is equal to his own.
Both of these are of equal virtue and of the same temperament because of their own improper conduct and lack of morality. Suhanu was exactly like that;
whoever was within Soṇa’s range of activity was just like Soṇa himself—Suhanu was exactly like that, whoever was within Soṇa’s range of activity.
Whatever is the range of the dog is also the range of the horse. For just as the dog, whose range is horses, roams about biting horses, so too does the horse;

by this he shows their commonality of range. However, in order to show their conduct and range together as one, it is said: “by one who is leaping forward,” and so forth. Therein, “by one who is leaping forward” (pakkhandinā) means...
By "leaping" (*pakkhandana*), he means one who has the habit of leaping upon horses; by "leaping-range" (*pakkhandana-gocara*), he means one whose range of activity is leaping.

By "reckless" (*pagabbha*), he means one who is immoral, possessed of bodily recklessness and so forth. By "always eating his own tether" (*niccaṃ sandāna-khādin*), he means one who has the habit of eating his own binding rope, and whose range of activity is such eating.
"Evil meets with evil" (*sameti pāpaṃ pāpena*) means that the immorality of one [person] coincides with the evil of another among these [types].
"It meets. This means that when one who is non-existent—meaning one who lacks proper conduct and resort—meets with another who is likewise non-existent, their unwholesome deed "meets" [the other's];
like excrement meeting excrement, they blend together, becoming identical and indistinguishable.
Having said this, the Bodhisatta continued: "Great King, a king must not be excessively greedy; toward another..."
"It is not right to destroy what belongs to another," he said, advising the king; then, having had the horses appraised, he caused the actual price to be paid.
Having received the price exactly according to the true value, the horse-traders departed joyful and satisfied.
The king, too, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s counsel, passed away according to his karma.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the two horses were these two wicked bhikkhus; the king was Ānanda; and the wise minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the eighth narration, the Suhanu Jātaka.
9. The Narration of the Mora Jātaka (The Peacock Jātaka)
"This one-eyed man is the sole king," said the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning a certain dissatisfied monk.
When that monk was brought before the Teacher by the other monks, they asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?
He replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir. When they asked, "What did you see? he said, "A body adorned and prepared for display..."
“...having looked at a woman,” he said. Then the Teacher said to him: “Bhikkhu, why would a woman not agitate the mind of one such as you?

For even among the ancient wise men, when they heard the sound of a woman, defilements that had not been active for seven hundred years arose in an instant once an opportunity was found. Even beings who are pure become defiled.”
"Even those possessing supreme fame fall into servitude, let alone those who are impure," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a peacock;
even while in the egg, the shell was the color of a *kaṇikāra* flower bud, and having broken the egg, he emerged golden-hued.
He was beautiful to behold and inspiring, shining with well-colored streaks between his wings;
protecting his own life, he crossed three mountain ranges and made his dwelling on the surface of the Daṇḍaka-Hirañña mountain, the fourth range.
At dawn, sitting upon the mountain peak, he watched the rising sun.
Having observed this, and binding a Brahma-spell for the sake of protection and defense upon his own range of activity, he spoke the verse beginning with "Udetayaṃ":
"This one with eyes, the sole king, rises, the color of Hari,
the illuminator of the earth."
"I pay homage to that one, the color of a lotus, who illuminates the earth;
through him, may we dwell protected this day.
Therein, "rises" means he emerges from the eastern world-system. "The Eyeful One" refers to [the dispelling] of the darkness for all those dwelling within the entire cakkavāḷa.
Having dispelled [the darkness], by means of providing them with the acquisition of sight, he gave them eyes; thus, by means of those eyes, he is "possessed of eyes" (cakkhumā).
He is a "sole king" (ekarājā) in the sense of being the most excellent and distinguished among those who bring light throughout the entire world-system (cakkavāḷa).

He is "of the color of gold" (harissavaṇṇo), meaning his color is like that of gold; the sense is that he is golden-hued. He is "illuminating the earth" (pathavippabhāso), meaning he shines upon the earth. This and this...
"I shall pay homage"—therefore, I pay homage and bow down to such a venerable one as you.
"Protected by you today, may we dwell happily this day": being guarded and protected by you today, may we dwell in comfort throughout this day with the four postures.
Thus, having paid homage to the sun with this verse, the Bodhisatta pays homage in the second verse to the Buddhas who have attained final Nibbāna in the past and to the qualities of the Buddhas.
“Those brahmins who are masters of the Vedas and all phenomena—to them I bow, and may they protect me.
Homage to the Buddhas, homage to Awakening; homage to those liberated, homage to Liberation.
Having made this protection, the peacock wanders in search of food.”
In this context, "those who are brahmins" refers to those who have cast out evil—the purified brahmins. A "Vedagū" is one who has gone to the further shore (*pāra*) of the Vedas;
thus he is a Vedagū. Alternatively, he is a Vedagū because he has gone beyond the Vedas.

Here, however, he is a Vedagū because he has made all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena known and manifest, and has thus gone beyond them. For this very reason it says, "all phenomena. This refers to all phenomena consisting of the aggregates, bases, and elements.
Having made their own knowledge known and manifest by way of both specific and general characteristics, they have gone;

having crushed the heads of the three Māras and caused the ten-thousandfold world-system to resound, they attained perfect enlightenment at the foot of the Bodhi tree and have thus transcended *saṃsāra*—this is the meaning.
"May they accept my homage" means: may they receive this salutation from me.
"And may they protect me"—thus, may those Blessed Ones whom I have thus honored protect, guard, and shield me.

"Homage to the Buddhas, homage to Awakening; homage to the Liberated, homage to Liberation"—may this salutation of mine be for the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, and likewise for the four paths within them.
May there be [success] for the enlightenment (bodhi) defined as knowledge regarding the four fruits; likewise,

may there be [success] for those who are liberated through the liberation of the fruit of arhatship, and for their fivefold liberation— namely, liberation by way of factor (tadaṅga-vimutti), suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti), eradication (samuccheda-vimutti),
subsidence (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti), and escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti)— may there be [success] for that liberation of theirs as well.

"May this homage of mine be for my benefit. However, these two lines—"Having made this protection, the peacock wanders in search"—were spoken by the Teacher after he had attained full enlightenment. Their meaning is as follows:
"O monks, having made this protection, this safeguard, that peacock wanders in his own feeding ground, seeking various kinds of food such as flowers and fruits."
Having thus spent the day, he sat upon the mountain peak in the evening;

gazing at the sun as it set and reflecting upon the qualities of the Buddha, he recited the words beginning with "Apetayam" while once again binding the Brahma-spell for protection and defense of his dwelling place.
“The One-Eyed King, golden-hued, the radiance of the earth—him, the golden-hued radiance of the earth, I revere. Protected by you, may we dwell safely this night.
To those brahmins who have mastered all things, I pay homage; may they protect me.”
"Homage to the Buddhas, homage to Awakening; homage to those who are liberated, homage to Liberation.
Having made this protection (paritta), the peacock established its dwelling.
