In this context, "it departs" (apeti) means it goes away. "Having made this protection, the peacock established its dwelling" means:
Having attained full enlightenment, he spoke this as well. Its meaning is:

"Monks, that peacock, having performed this protective chant (paritta), this safeguard, made his dwelling in his own place of residence; by the power of this protective chant, neither fear nor horripilation occurred for him, whether by night or by day."

Then, a certain hunter living in a village near Bārāṇasī, while wandering in the Himalayan region, saw the Bodhisatta seated on the summit of Mount Daṇḍaka-hirañña; having returned, he reported this to his son.
Then one day, the queen of the King of Bārāṇasī, named Khemā, saw in a dream a golden-colored peacock preaching the Dhamma.
Seeing him descending, when he had awakened, he informed the king: "Your Majesty, I wish to hear the Dhamma from a golden-colored peacock.
The king questioned his ministers. The ministers said, "The brahmins will know.
When the brahmins heard this, they said, "There are indeed such things as golden-colored peacocks," but when asked, "Where are they? they replied, "The hunters will know."
They said: "The king, having assembled the hunters, questioned them. Then that son of a hunter said, 'Yes, Great King, there is a mountain called Daṇḍaka-Hiraññapabbata;
there dwells a golden-colored peacock. 'In that case, bring that peacock back, but do not kill it—bind it alive.
The hunter went and set a snare in its feeding ground. Even at the spot where the peacock had stepped..."
The snare did not move. Unable to capture it, the hunter wandered for seven years and died right there.
Queen Khemā, too, died because she did not obtain what she had desired.
The king, becoming angry, thought, "It is because of that peacock that the queen has died," and [ordered] that in the Himalayan region, on Mount Daṇḍaka-Hirañña...
There is a peacock of golden hue who dwells there; those who eat its flesh become ageless and immortal.
Having had these words inscribed on a golden plate, he had the golden plate placed inside a casket.
When that king passed away, another king ascended the throne, read the golden plate, and [thought], “I shall become ageless and immortal.”
He sent another hunter. He too, having gone there, was unable to capture the Bodhisatta and died right then and there.
In this very manner, six royal successions passed by. Then, the seventh king, having attained the kingdom, dispatched a hunter.
He went and [observed] that even at the spot where the Bodhisatta had stepped, the snare did not move, and [he saw] his own protective charm...

Having understood his intention to go out foraging, he descended to the borderlands, captured a peahen, and trained her so that she would dance at the sound of hand-clapping and cry out at the sound of snapping fingers.
Taking her with him, he went to a place where no protective charms had been made; there, early in the morning, he erected stakes for snares, set the traps, and caused the peahen to cry out.
Hearing the discordant sound of women, the Bodhisatta became afflicted by defilements; unable to recite a protective charm (*paritta*), he went forth and was caught in a snare.
Then, the hunter took him and went to present him to the King of Bārāṇasī.
Upon seeing his physical perfection, the King was delighted in heart and had a seat prepared for him. The Bodhisatta sat upon the prepared seat.
Having sat down, he asked, "Great King, why did you have me seized? [The king replied,] "It is said that those who eat your flesh become free from old age and death;
therefore, desiring to become free from old age and death by eating your flesh, I had you seized.
[The ascetic asked,] "Great King, let those who eat my flesh indeed become free from old age and death, but as for me, I shall die. [The king replied,] "Yes."
“You will die,” he said. “But when I have died, why will they not die after eating only my flesh?
“You are golden-hued; therefore, it is said, those who eat your flesh shall become ageless and immortal.
“Great King, I did not become golden-hued without cause; formerly, I was a wheel-turning monarch in this very city.”
Having been a king, I myself observed the five precepts and caused all the inhabitants of the entire Cakkavāḷa to observe them as well.

Having passed away from there, I was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; after remaining there for the full span of my lifespan, when I fell from that state, I was reborn in the womb of a peacock due to the outflow of another unwholesome deed, yet by the power of my former virtue, I am golden-hued.

“You were born,” he said. “How are we to believe this—that you became a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti), and by guarding your virtue, you were born with a golden complexion as the fruit of that virtue?
Is there anyone who can bear witness for us? “There is, Great King. “Who is his name?
“Great King, during my time as a Wheel-turning Monarch, I traveled through the air seated in a jeweled chariot.”
“Therefore, my chariot was buried within the ground inside the Maṅgala lotus pond;
have it excavated from the Maṅgala lotus pond, for it shall serve as my witness.
The king, having assented with “Very well,” had the water removed from the pond and the chariot brought out for the Bodhisatta.
“Believe me,” said the Bodhisatta. “Great King, apart from the great Nibbāna of the Deathless, all remaining conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhammā) are non-existent once they have arisen;
they are impermanent and subject only to decay and destruction. Having thus taught the Dhamma to the king, he established him in the five precepts.
The king, being filled with faith, honored the Bodhisatta with his kingdom and rendered him great service.
Thus, having restored the kingdom to him and stayed for a few days, he exhorted him, saying, "Be heedful,
O Great King," and then, leaping into the air, he went back to Mount Daṇḍaka Hirañña. The king, too, remaining steadfast in the Bodhisatta’s advice,
performed meritorious deeds such as giving and departed according to his karma.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in Arahatship. “At that time, King Ānanda was [the king], but the golden peacock was none other than myself.
This is the ninth narration of the Mora-jātaka.
[160] 10. The Commentary on the Vinīlaka Jātaka:
"In this very way, surely the king..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta’s construction of a Sugata-ālaya.
For Devadatta, having shown the Sugata-ālaya to the two Chief Disciples who had gone to Gayāsīsa, [proceeded to build one for himself].
When both elders had lain down, they taught the Dhamma and, taking their own dependents with them, went to Veḷuvana.
When the Teacher asked them, “Sāriputta, what did Devadatta do upon seeing you?
they reported, “Venerable sir, having shown him the abode of the Sugata, he met with great destruction. The Teacher said, “Sāriputta, it is not only now that Devadatta has done this.”
"By imitating me, he has met with destruction; even in the past, he would have surely come to the same end. Having said this, being requested by the elders, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while the King of Videha was ruling his kingdom from Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, and after his father passed away...
He was established in the kingdom. At that time, there was a mating between a female crow and a golden swan king on the feeding ground of the swans.
She gave birth to a son; he bore neither the likeness of his mother nor that of his father.
Because his physical elements were of a bluish hue (*vinīlaka-dhātu*), they gave him the name "Vinīlaka. The swan king went frequently and looked upon his son. Now, others...
He had two young swan cubs as sons. Seeing their father frequently going to the human path, they asked him, "Father, why do you go so often to the human path?
"Sons, through my dwelling together with a certain female crow, one son was born to me; his name is Vinīlaka, and I go to see him."
“I am going,” he said. “But where do they live? “In the kingdom of Videha, not far from Mithilā, they live upon a certain palm tree in such-and-such a place.
“Dear father, the path of men is full of suspicion and danger;
you must not go. We shall go and bring them back. Thus spoke two young swans, having understood the signal given by their father.
Having gone there, they made that livid corpse sit upon a single bamboo pole, bit the tip of the pole with their snouts, and carried it along the road toward the city of Mithilā.
At that moment, the King of Videha was circumambulating the city, seated in a magnificent, excellent chariot yoked to four all-white thoroughbreds.
Seeing him, the livid corpse thought: "The King of Videha [is passing by]..."
“What is the reason for this difference? He travels about the city seated in a chariot yoked with four horses, but I go seated in a chariot yoked with swans.
As he traveled through the air, he spoke the first verse:
“Surely it is thus that the King of Videha, the captor of Mithilā, [travels].”
"The thoroughbred horses carry him along, like swans in the blue sky.
In this context, "evameva" means "just so"; "nūna" is a particle used for reflection, though it may also be used for emphasis. "Vedehaṃ" refers to the ruler of the kingdom of Videha.
"Mithilaggahaṃ" means the house of Mithilā; that is, having taken possession of the residence in Mithilā.
"Vasamānaṃ" means "dwelling. "Ājaññā" refers to those who know what is right and what is wrong. "Yathā haṃsā vinīlakaṃ" means:
"Just as these swans carry me, Vinīlaka, so too do they carry him.
Having heard his words, the young swans became angry and thought: "We shall drop him right here and go on our way."

Even after producing [the fire], out of fear of reproach—thinking, "What will our father say when this has been done?"—they led him into his father's presence and reported to the father what he had done. Then the father, becoming angry, said:
"Are you someone superior to my sons, that you treat my sons as if they were horses harnessed to a chariot? You yourself—"
“You do not know moderation. This place is not your domain; go instead to the dwelling place of your own mother.
Having thus rebuked him, he spoke the second verse:
“O dear one, you frequent a foul-smelling ravine; you resort to a ground that is unfit for you.”
“Frequent the outskirts of villages; this is your mother’s home.
Therein, “Vinīlā” is an address to her by name. “You frequent difficult terrain” means that by means of these [cremation grounds], you frequent mountain fastnesses.
“My dear, you frequent what is not your domain”: my dear, the mountain wilderness is indeed not your domain, yet you frequent it—you approach it.
"This village edge, this place for refuse heaps, and this raw charnel ground are your mother’s abode, her home, her dwelling place; go there!
Having thus rebuked him, he commanded his sons, "Go, set him down right at the refuse heap of Mithilā city and return! They did accordingly.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Devadatta was the Vinīlaka;
the two young swans were the two Chief Disciples; the father was Ānanda; and the King of Videha was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Vinīla Jātaka, the tenth.

The Advice to the King, the Jackal, the Boar, the Snake, and the Broken.

2. Santhavavagga [161] 1.
Indasamānagottajātaka Commentary.
"One should not form intimacy with a base person"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain man of a harsh-voiced disposition.
The story of this individual will be revealed in the Gijjha Jātaka of the Navaka Nipāta. However, the Teacher said to that bhikkhu:
"Bhikkhu, even in the past, because of your harshness of speech, you did not follow the words of the wise, and were trampled by the feet of an intoxicated elephant."
Having said, "He was crushed," he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic, becoming the leader of a community of five hundred seers.

Having offered the sacrifice, he established his residence in a region of the Himalayas. At that time, among those ascetics, there was one named Indasamānagotta who was ill-behaved and unresponsive to instruction.
He was rearing a young elephant calf. Having heard of this, the Bodhisatta summoned him and asked, "Is it true, as I have heard, that you are rearing a young elephant calf?
"It is true, Teacher; [I am rearing] one whose mother is dead."
“I am rearing a young elephant,” he said. “Elephants, once they have reached maturity, kill their very keepers; do not rear him,” [the teacher replied].
“I cannot live without him, Teacher,” he said. “In that case, you will become known by his name,” [the teacher said].
Being reared by him, in time the elephant became large-bodied.
Then, at one time, those seers went far into the forest for the sake of roots and fruits and remained there for several days.
A certain elephant, having become rutting in the southeast wind, demolished his leaf-hut,
broke the water-jar, hurled the stone slab, tore up the support-beam, and [sought] that ascetic...
Thinking, “I will kill him and go,” he entered a dense thicket and stood watching the path by which [the elephant] would come.
Indasamānagotta, having taken up his feeding ground, was coming right at the front of the herd;
seeing him, he approached the elephant with the ordinary perception of a human. Then that elephant emerged from the thicket and—

Having seized him by the trunk, he threw him to the ground, trampled his head with his foot, brought him to his death, and having crushed him, let out a loud cry and entered the forest. The remaining ascetics reported this occurrence to the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta, saying, "One should not associate with such base men," spoke these verses:
“One should not form intimacy with a base person, for the noble one understands the goal of what is ignoble;
even after dwelling together for a long time, such a person commits evil, just as the elephant [killed] Indasamānagotta.
But if one should know someone who is equal to oneself in virtue, wisdom, and learning...”
"Therefore, one should make friends with him; for indeed, association with a true person is pleasant.
In this context, "one should not make intimacy with a base person" means that one should not form either an intimacy of craving or an intimacy of friendship with a despicable, angry person.
"The Noble One knows the purpose of the ignoble"—here, "Noble Ones" refers to the four [noble persons].
The noble ones are those who are noble in conduct, noble in outward signs, noble in appearance, and noble in penetration. Among these, it is the one noble in conduct who is intended here.

The meaning is that such a person—understanding what is beneficial and understanding the benefit, skilled in what is beneficial and what is not beneficial, and established in noble conduct—should not associate with one who is ignoble, shameless, and immoral.
Why is this? Because even if [the association] has continued for a long time...
"He commits evil" means that because the ignoble person, even if he has lived with another for a long time, disregards that cohabitation and commits evil—that is, performs base deeds.
How is this like what? "As the elephant [who killed] one of the same clan as Indra":
the meaning is that just as that elephant committed evil by killing one who was of the same clan as Indra. Regarding the passage beginning, "But when he knows: 'He is my equal,'" and so forth...
However, if one should recognize a person as being "equal to me in virtue and other qualities," one should form friendship with that very person, for association with a true person brings happiness.
Thus the Bodhisatta thought: "One must not be someone who fails to offer advice; it is necessary to be well-trained."
Having exhorted the group of ascetics and performed the funeral rites for Indasamānagotta, he cultivated the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) and was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Indasamānagotta was this ill-behaved man, and I myself was the leader of the group.
This is the first commentary on the Indasamānagotta Jātaka.
[162] 2. The Commentary on the *Santhava Jātaka*.
"There is nothing more evil than intimacy"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the offering of fire.
The story is exactly as told below in the *Naṅguṭṭha Jātaka*. The monks were offering fire.
Having seen this, they asked the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, these matted-hair ascetics perform various kinds of wrong austerities;
is there perhaps any progress to be found here? "Monks, there is no such thing as progress here," the Blessed One replied.
"Even the ancient sages, thinking there was progress in making offerings to the fire, maintained their fires for a long time, yet they saw only a lack of progress in that practice."
"Having extinguished the fire with water and struck it with branches and such, even though they turned back again, they did not look [at it]," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family.
When his mother and father took him for the birth-fire ceremony and he had reached the age of sixteen years, they said to him: "What, dear son, regarding the birth-fire..."
“Will you take this fire and tend it in the forest, or will you master the three Vedas, establish a household, and live the life of a householder?
He replied, “I have no need for the life of a householder; having tended the fire in the forest, I shall make the Brahma-world my goal.
Taking the fire, he paid homage to his parents, entered the forest, and [built] a leaf-hut.

Having established his residence, he attended upon the sacrificial fire. One day, having gone to a place where he was invited and received milk-rice with ghee, he thought, "I shall offer this milk-rice to Mahābrahmā.
Bringing that milk-rice back, he kindled the fire and said, "First, venerable sir, I offer this milk-rice mixed with ghee to you, the fire," and he cast the milk-rice into the fire. It was very oily.
As soon as the milk-rice was placed in the fire, the flames blazed up and, with ascending crests of fire, consumed the leaf-hut.
Terrified and trembling, the brahmin fled and stood outside, saying, "One should not form friendships with base men;
now this hut, which I have built with such great difficulty, has been burnt down by this fire," and he spoke the first verse:
“There is nothing worse than intimacy, namely, intimacy with a base person;
though he was gratified with ghee and milk-rice, he burned down the leaf-hut built with such hardship.
In this context, “than intimacy” refers to both the two kinds of intimacy: intimacy through craving and intimacy through friendship.
There is no intimacy more evil, more base—this is the meaning.
"No other intimacy is more evil than that with a base man" means that there is no other intimacy, of either of the two kinds, that is more evil than that with a wicked, base person.
Why? Because, even though he was satisfied with ghee and milk-rice... [he] did not burn. Because, although he was satisfied with ghee and milk-rice... [he] did not burn.
The meaning is: "This fire has consumed the leaf-hut that I built with great difficulty.
Having said this, [the elephant] thought, "I have no need for you, a betrayer of friends," and extinguished that fire with water.
Then, striking it with his trunk, he entered deep into the Himalayas and [sought out] a female deer belonging to a lion, a tiger, and a leopard.
And seeing her licking his face, he thought, "There is nothing better than intimacy with virtuous persons," and spoke this second verse:
"There is nothing better than intimacy, Which is the intimacy that one has with a virtuous person."
"The female deer licks the face of the lion, the tiger, and the leopard out of intimacy.
In this context, "the female deer licks their faces out of intimacy" means that the female deer, by way of intimacy—that is, affection—licks the faces of these three beings.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta entered the interior of the Himalayas, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, I myself was the ascetic.
This concludes the second commentary, the Saṇṭhava Jātaka.
[163] 3. The Commentary on the Susīma Jātaka.
"Black deer with white teeth, you are strong"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the gift of a horse-keeper.
For at times in Sāvatthī, a single family would give alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha;
at other times, they gave to those of other sects; and at other times, many people, having joined together in groups, would give.
Sometimes they give alms by way of a street procession, and sometimes all the inhabitants of the city gather their contributions and give a gift.
But at this time, all the inhabitants of the city gathered their contributions, prepared a gift of all requisites, and divided into two groups;
some said, "We shall give this gift of all requisites to those of other sects."

Some said, "To the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. As this discussion proceeded again and again, the disciples of other sects [spoke] only for the followers of other sects, while the disciples of the Buddha said, "'To the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha'—let us make it many.
Thus, through that extensive discussion, they said, "To the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha."
Even as they were saying, "We shall give," many people gathered, and their discussion alone prevailed.
The disciples of other sects were unable to create an obstacle to the giving that should be given to the Buddhas.
The citizens, having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, offered a great almsgiving for seven days; on the seventh day, they gave all the requisites. The Teacher—
Having offered his appreciation and awakened the great multitude to the fruits of the Path, he went back to the Jetavana Monastery.
When the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had performed their duties, he stood before the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), gave them the Sugata’s exhortation, and entered the Fragrant Chamber.
In the evening, the bhikkhus assembled in the Dhamma Hall and raised this discussion: "Friends,..."
"Even though the disciples of other sects strove to create obstacles for the gifts that should be given to the Buddhas, they were unable to do so;
all those offerings of requisites came back to the very feet of the Buddhas themselves. Oh, how great indeed is the power of the Buddhas!
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?"

Having asked, "Is it indeed by her? and being told that it was, he said: "Monks, these disciples of other sects are not only striving now to create obstacles for what should be given to me; they strove to do so in the past as well.
Yet, that requisite always comes back to my very feet. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Susīma. At that time, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the brahmin wife of his royal chaplain.
When he reached the age of sixteen, his father passed away. During his father’s lifetime, he had served as the king’s elephant-omen-maker.
He also [managed] the equipment and requisites brought for the purpose of performing auspicious rites for the elephants.
He alone received all the hand-ornaments. In this way, at each auspicious ceremony, wealth amounting to ten million arose for him.

Then, at that time, the festival of the elephant-auspiciousness arrived. The other brahmins approached the king and said, "Great King, the festival of the elephant-auspiciousness has arrived; it is fitting to perform the auspicious rite. [It belongs] to the royal chaplain brahmin..."
"But the son is still too young; he knows neither the three Vedas nor the *Hatthisutta*.
We shall perform the elephant festival ourselves," they said. The king agreed, saying, "Very well. The brahmins, however, did not allow the high priest’s son to perform the elephant festival;
instead, thinking, "We shall receive the wealth after performing the elephant festival," they wandered about joyful and delighted.
Then, on the fourth day, having heard the news that the elephant festival was to take place, the Bodhisatta’s mother wept in lamentation, thinking:
"The performance of the elephant festival is our family tradition for seven generations;
our lineage will decline, and our wealth will diminish."
The Bodhisatta asked, "Mother, why do you weep? and having heard the reason, he said, "Mother, shall I not perform the auspicious ceremony?
"Dear son, you know neither the three Vedas nor the elephant-treatises; how will you perform the auspicious ceremony?
"Mother, on what day, then, will the elephant-auspicious ceremony take place? "On the fourth day from now."
“Father! [he said]. “Mother, where does that teacher who, having mastered the three Vedas, knows the *Hatthisutta*, reside?
“Son, such a world-renowned teacher lives two hundred yojanas from here, in Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra.
“Mother, I shall not let our lineage perish; tomorrow I shall go to Takkasilā in a single day.”
"Having gone there, I shall master the three Vedas and the *Hatthisutta* in a single night;
returning on the following day, I will perform the elephant-consecration ceremony on the fourth day. Do not weep," he said, thus comforting his mother.
On the next day, the Bodhisatta ate his morning meal and departed alone. Traveling for a single day, he reached Takkasilā, where he paid homage to his teacher and sat down to one side.
Then the teacher asked him, "Where have you come from, dear boy? "From Bārāṇasī, teacher. "For what purpose?
"To learn the three Vedas and the *Hatthisutta* from you, teacher. "Very well, dear boy, learn them," he said.
The Bodhisatta, saying, "Teacher, my business is urgent," related the whole situation and added, "I [will learn] in a single day..."
"Having come from two hundred yojanas away, grant me your permission this very night;
on the third day from now, there will be the auspicious festival of the elephant, and I shall master everything through a single recitation session.
Having said this, he requested leave from his teacher, and after the teacher had finished eating, he himself ate, washed the teacher's feet, and—
Having placed a thousand-fold bundle of palm leaves before him and paid homage, he sat to one side;
then, having begun his study, he completed the three Vedas and the *Hatthisutta* as the dawn was rising.
He asked, "Is there anything else, Teacher? When [the teacher] replied, "No, dear son, everything is finished," he said, "Teacher, in this book..."
“This much is the extent of the confusion regarding the recitation of the words; from now on, you should teach your pupils in this manner.
Having thus refined his teacher’s craft, he ate his morning meal, paid homage to his teacher, and returned to Bārāṇasī in a single day.
There, after paying homage to his mother, she asked, “My son, have you mastered the craft?”
When this was said, he replied, “Yes, mother,” and thus satisfied his mother.
On the following day, the auspicious elephant festival was prepared. They fashioned about a hundred elephant trappings and golden banners covered with nets of gold and set them out;
they adorned the royal courtyard. The brahmins [prepared] the elephant festival...

“We shall do it, we shall do it! they stood there, adorned and arrayed. King Susīma too, decorated with all his ornaments and having had his equipment and requisites brought along, went to the auspicious place.
The Bodhisatta also, adorned with the honors due to a prince and surrounded by his own retinue, approached the king and asked, “Is it true, indeed?”

“Great King, you have spoken thus: ‘Having destroyed both our lineage and your own lineage, we shall have other brahmins perform the elephant-omen ceremony and give them the elephant’s ornaments and equipment. Having said this, he recited the first verse:
“These black deer of yours, with white tusks, more than a hundred in number, covered with nets of gold;”
"‘I give those to you,’ Susīma, you say, recollecting your ancestors and grandfathers.

Therein, “‘I give those to you,’ Susīma, you say”: it is true that you said, regarding these hundreds of elephants exceeding one hundred in number—belonging to you, adorned with every ornament, and described as ‘black deer with white teeth’—that you would give them to other brahmins.
"Indeed, sir Susīma, it means you speak thus. 'Remembering our ancestors and grandfathers' means remembering exactly what was practiced by our own ancestors and grandfathers in our lineage.
This is what is meant: 'O Great King, as far back as seven generations of your ancestors and our own ancestors have performed the elephant-omen ceremony, you—'"
Even as he was recollecting in this way, having destroyed both his own lineage and ours, [the king thought], "Is it true that you speak thus?
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, King Susīma spoke this second verse:
"These black deer with white teeth, more than a hundred in number, covered with nets of gold—these are mine."
“I say to you, young man, ‘I give those to you,’ remembering the deeds of my ancestors.
In this context, “I give those to you” means: “I truly say, young man, that I give these elephants to other brahmins;
it is not the case that I am giving the elephants to the brahmins [of this lineage]. “Remembering the deeds of my ancestors” means remembering the conduct of their fathers and grandfathers.

"I do indeed remember; I do not fail to remember. Even though I am remembering that your ancestors performed the Elephant Auspiciousness ceremony for our ancestors, I speak thus," he said with this intention.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him: "Great King, it is precisely while remembering both our own lineage and your own that I say this."

“Why, setting me aside, do you have the elephant-omen performed by others? “It is said, dear sir, that you do not know the three Vedas and the elephant-treatises,” they informed me; therefore, I am having it performed by other brahmins.
“In that case, Great King, among all these brahmins, not even a single brahmin [is proficient] in the three Vedas or the elephant-treatises.”
"If there is anyone capable of even discussing a single portion with me, let him stand up!
Apart from me, there is no one else in the entire Jambudīpa who knows the three Vedas along with the *Hatthisutta* and the performance of elephant-omens.
Thus he roared his lion’s roar. Not even a single brahmin was able to rise up as his opponent. The Bodhisatta—
Having established his own family lineage, performed auspicious rites, and taken much wealth with him, he returned to his own home.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some attained Arahatship.
“At that time, Mahāmāyā was my mother, the great king Suddhodana was my father, King Susīma was Ānanda,
the world-renowned teacher was Sāriputta, and I myself was the young brahmin.
This concludes the third commentary, the Susīma Jātaka.
[164] 4. The Commentary on the Vulture Birth Story (*Gijjhajātakavaṇṇanā*).
"Would that a vulture [could fly] a hundred leagues..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who supported his mother.
The background story will be revealed in the *Sāmajātaka*. However, the Teacher said to that monk, "Is it true...?"
Having asked, "Is it true, monk, that you support a householder? and being told, "It is true," he then asked, "Who are they?
When he replied, "They are my mother and father, venerable sir," [the Buddha] gave him his approval, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
and said, "Monks, do not find fault with this monk; even the wise men of old, by virtue of their qualities, [supported] even those who were strangers."
“They have rendered assistance, but for this [child], the task of providing assistance to his parents is indeed a heavy burden,” he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a vulture on Vulture Peak Mountain and supported his mother and father.
Then, at one time, there was a great storm of wind and rain. The vultures [sought shelter] from the storm...
Unable to endure it, they went to Benares out of fear of the cold and sat down near the city wall and the moat, trembling from the chill.
At that time, the merchant of Benares, having gone out from the city to bathe, saw those vultures exhausted;
he gathered them together in a place sheltered from the rain, had a fire lit, and [provided] cow dung...
Having sent [men] and had ox-flesh brought, he gave it to them and established a guard over the site.
When the wind and rain had subsided, the vultures, their bodies now fit for action, went back to the mountain itself. Gathering together right there, they deliberated thus:
"The merchant of Bārāṇasī has done us a service; and indeed, one ought to repay a service that has been rendered."
"It is permissible; therefore, from this time forward, whichever of you receives a cloth or an ornament must drop it onto the open courtyard of the house of the Chief Merchant of Bārāṇasī.
From then on, the vultures, observing the negligence of people as they were drying their clothes and ornaments in the sun, [acted accordingly].
Like an army, they suddenly seized the lump of flesh and dropped it into the courtyard of the merchant’s house in Bārāṇasī.
Having realized that this was the vultures’ means of bringing [the meat], he set them all aside separately.
When they reported to the king, "The vultures are plundering the city," the king said, "Seize even a single vulture first; I shall have them all brought back. Thereupon—
There he set snares and nets. A vulture that supported its mother became caught in a snare; they seized it and led it away, saying, "We shall show this to the king.

As the merchant of Benares was going to attend upon the king, he saw those men leading the vulture away and went along with them, thinking, "Let them not harm this vulture. [He presented] the vulture to the king.
They gave them away. Then the king asked him: "Did you plunder the city and take the clothes and other goods?
"Yes, Great King. "To whom were they given? "To the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī.
"For what reason? "Our lives were saved by him; it is right to repay a favor, therefore—"
“I am. Then the king said to him, “Vultures, it is said, can see carrion from a hundred leagues away;
why then do you not see the snare set for yourself? Having said this, he spoke the first verse:
“That vulture which beholds carrion from a hundred leagues away—”
"Why do you not wake up even after encountering the net and the snare?
In this context, *yaṃ* is a mere particle; *nū* is a particle used in the sense of "indeed.
A vulture, it is said, surveys and sees carcasses situated even a hundred *yojanas* away—this is the meaning. *Āsajjāpi* means "even having encountered," that is, "even having reached."
“Sir,” he replied. “Having encountered both the net and the snare set for your own sake, why do you not wake up?
Having heard his words, the vulture spoke the second verse:
“When ruin comes, when a person’s life is at its end;”
“Then, having encountered both net and snare, he does not even wake up.
In this context, *parābhava* means destruction; *pōsa* means a living being.
Having heard the vulture’s words, the king asked the merchant: “Is it true, Great Merchant, that by the vultures...”
“Clothing and other goods have been brought for you in your house,” he said. “It is true, Your Majesty,” they replied. “Where are they?
“Your Majesty, I have set all of them aside separately; I shall give to each person what belongs to them.
Release this vulture! Having had the vulture released, the Great Merchant caused all the belongings to be given to those to whom they belonged.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:

"At that time, the king was Ānanda; the merchant of Bārāṇasī was Sāriputta; and I myself was the vulture who supported his mother. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The fourth is the Commentary on the Vulture Jātaka.
[165] 5. The Commentary on the Mongoose Jātaka:
"Having allied with an enemy"—this was told by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a quarrel among the Seṇi clan.
The background story is exactly as told in the *Uragajātaka* below. Here too, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have brought these two chief ministers into harmony;
in the past, I also made them harmonious," and having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a certain village.
Having been reborn and reached maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkaśilā. Abandoning the life of a householder, he went forth as an ascetic;

having attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he made his dwelling in a region of the Himalayas, subsisting on forest roots and fruits through the practice of gleaning.
At the edge of his walking path, there was a termite mound where a mongoose lived.
Nearby, in a certain tree hollow, a snake also made its dwelling. Those two, the mongoose and the snake, were constantly quarreling.

The Bodhisatta, having explained to them the danger of quarreling and the benefit of cultivating loving-kindness (*mettā*), advised them, saying, "It is fitting to live in harmony rather than engaging in quarrels," and thus he brought them both into a state of concord.

Then, when the snake had gone outside, the mongoose lay down at the edge of his walking path by the opening of the anthill, thrusting his head out and opening his mouth, and fell asleep while breathing in and out.
Seeing him thus sleeping, the Bodhisatta asked, "What indeed is it that you rely upon such that fear has arisen? and questioned him.
He spoke the first verse:
“Having made an alliance with an enemy, O egg-born one and womb-born one, you lie there baring your fangs;
from where has fear come upon you?”

Therein, "having made an alliance" means having established friendship. "By the egg-born" refers to the nāga born from an egg-shell. "The water-born" is an address to the mongoose; for he is called "water-born" because he was produced within a watery membrane (*jalābu*). "Having opened" means having opened [the egg].
Thus addressed by the Bodhisatta, the mongoose said, "Sir, an enemy must not be disregarded; he should indeed be suspected," and spoke this second verse:
"One should indeed be wary of an enemy, and one should not trust even a friend."
"Abhayā cuts away even the roots of fear that has arisen.
In this context, "Abhayā" means one from whom no fear arises; who is he? A friend.
For when fear arises from even a trusted friend, it cuts away even the very roots—the entire vulnerabilities—of that friend.
The meaning is that through such knowledge, it leads to the destruction of the root [of suffering].
Then the Bodhisatta, having exhorted him, saying, "Do not fear; I shall act in such a way that the snake will not harm you;
from now on, do not harbor any apprehension toward him," and having cultivated the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra),...
He became one whose ultimate goal was the Brahma-world. They, too, departed according to their respective kamma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the snake and the mongoose were these two chief ministers, while the ascetic was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Nakula Jātaka, the fifth.
[166] 6. The Commentary on the Upasāḷaka Jātaka.
Regarding the phrase "named Upasāḷaka," this was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana with reference to a certain brahmin named Upasāḷaka who practiced purification at a cemetery.
It is said that he was wealthy and possessed great riches; however, because he held wrong views, he did not reside in the principal monastery.
Even toward the Buddhas of the past, he did not offer any act of veneration. However, his son was wise and endowed with insight.
When the father had grown old, he said to his son: "My dear son, do not burn me in a cemetery where other outcasts have been cremated;
rather, you should burn me in a part of the cemetery that has never been defiled by food scraps. "Father, as for you..."
“I do not know a place suitable for cremation; it would be well indeed if you yourselves were to take me and go, pointing out the spot where you might cremate me.

The brahmin said, “Very well, dear one,” and taking him, he departed from the city, ascended to the summit of Vulture Peak, and said, “Dear one, this is a place where no other outcaste has ever been cremated; here—”
Having said, "You should cremate me," she began to descend from the mountain with her son.

But on that day, at the time of dawn, the Teacher, surveying those kinsmen who were ready to be enlightened, saw that they possessed the necessary potential (*upanissaya*) for the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
Therefore, like a hunter waiting by the path, he stood at the foot of the mountain.
Having gone there, he sat waiting for them as they were descending from the mountain peak; seeing the Teacher, they approached him.
The Teacher, extending a greeting, asked, "Where are you going, brahmins?
The young man explained the matter to him. The Teacher said, "In that case, come; let us go to the place indicated by your father."
Taking both father and son, he climbed to the summit of the mountain and asked, "Which place?
The young man replied, "Venerable sir, he pointed to the space between these three mountains. The Teacher said, "Young man, it is not only now that your father is a 'purifier by the cemetery';
in the past, too, he was a purifier by the cemetery. And it is not only now that he..."
"He tells you that he would have me cremated in this very place; indeed, in the past as well, he declared that he had been cremated in this very spot.
Having said this, at his request, he related the past:
"In the past, in this very city of Rājagaha, this same Brāhmaṇa Upasāḷaka was his father, and this very person was his son. At that time..."
The Bodhisatta, having been reborn in a brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha, completed his mastery of the arts and went forth as an ascetic.
Having attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he dwelt for a long time in the Himalayan region sporting in the play of *jhāna*.
Then, for the sake of partaking of salt and sour food, he lived in a leaf-hut on Vulture Peak (*Gijjhakūṭa*). At that time, that brahmin, by this very method—
Having spoken thus to his son, when the son replied, "Point out such a place to me yourself," he said, "This very place is it.
As they were descending together with the son, he saw the Bodhisatta and approached him.
The Bodhisatta questioned him in this same manner, and having heard the young man's words, he said, "Come; [this is] the place pointed out by your father..."
“Let us find out whether it is a state of being defiled or a state of being undefiled.

Having climbed to the summit of the mountain with them, when the young brahmin said, “This space between the three mountains is a place that is undefiled,” [the Teacher replied], “Young brahmin, there is no measure for those who have been cremated in this very spot;
even your own father was born right here in this very brahmin family in Rājagaha.”
“Having been reborn and becoming known simply as Upasāḷaka, he was cremated for fourteen thousand births right here within this mountain range.
For it is impossible to find on earth a place where his heads were not cremated, or a place where they were not offered as food, or a place where they were not placed.
Having thus delimited the matter through the knowledge of past lives, he spoke these two verses:
“Fourteen thousand Upasāḷakas by name were burned in this place;
there is nothing in the world that is not subject to death.
In whom truth and Dhamma, non-violence, self-restraint, and self-control reside—”
“The noble ones cultivate this; this in the world is the deathless (amata).
In that context, *anāmata* means a place of death (*mataṭṭhāna*). For, by way of proximity, it is called “the deathless”;
negating that, he says “*anāmata*. There is also the reading *anamata*; for in the world there is no place called a non-cemetery (*anamata*) where death does not occur.

Meaning: "In whom truth and Dhamma exist" means that in whichever person there exists both the knowledge of the truths pertaining to the preliminary stage—which has the Four Truths as its object—and the supramundane Dhamma.
"Non-violence" means non-harming and non-afflicting of others. "Restraint" means restraint by virtue.
"Taming" means the taming of the sense faculties. And since these various qualities exist in whichever person, the Noble Ones attend upon him.
The Noble Ones—the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha—frequent this place; the meaning is that they approach and associate with such a person.
"This is called 'the Deathless' in the world" means that this collection of qualities is called "the Deathless" because it is the means for attaining the state of deathlessness in the world.
Thus, having taught the Dhamma to his father and son and having cultivated the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras), the Bodhisatta became destined for the Brahma-world.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, both father and son were established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, those who were father and son were indeed the father and son of the present day;
as for the ascetic, he was none other than myself."
The Sixth: The Commentary on the Upasāḷaka Jātaka.
[167] 7. The Commentary on the Samiddhi Jātaka:
"O Bhikkhu, you beg without having eaten"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at the Tapodārāma near Rājagaha.
He spoke concerning the Elder Samiddhi. One day, after the Venerable Samiddhi had exerted himself in meditation throughout the entire night, he bathed at the time of sunrise.
Drying his golden-hued body, he put on his inner robe and stood holding his upper robe in his hand, looking like a well-polished golden statue.
Indeed, it was because of the excellence of his physical being that he received the name “Samiddhi.
Then, seeing the beauty of his body, a certain goddess became enamored with him and spoke thus to the Elder:
“Bhikkhu, you are young, a youth, with black hair, endowed with noble youthfulness, handsome, pleasing to behold, and inspiring; for one such as you—”
“What is the point of going forth without having enjoyed sensual pleasures? Enjoy sensual pleasures for now;
later, after you have gone forth, you can practice the duty of a recluse. Then the Elder said to her:
“Daughter of a deva, I do not know the time of my death, thinking, ‘I shall die when I have reached such-and-such an age. This time of mine is hidden; therefore, while I am still young—”
“Having fulfilled the duty of a recluse, I shall bring an end to suffering.
Having failed to receive a hospitable greeting from the Elder, she vanished right there. The Elder approached the Teacher and reported this matter to him.
The Teacher said, “Samiddhi, it is not only now that you have been seduced by a celestial maiden; in the past as well, celestial maidens [seduced you].”
Having said, “They indeed tempted those who had gone forth,” he was requested by him to relate a past event.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in a certain village of Kāsi.
Upon reaching maturity and attaining proficiency in all arts and sciences, he went forth as an ascetic and attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Having attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he took up residence in a region of the Himalayas near a certain mountain lake.

After exerting himself in spiritual striving throughout the entire night, at the time of sunrise, he bathed, put on a single bark garment, and stood holding one end of it in his hand while sprinkling water over his body. Then, his physical beauty reached its peak—
Having observed his physical form, a certain goddess whose heart was bound to him spoke the first verse, attempting to seduce the Bodhisatta:
“O monk, you beg without having eaten; for you do not beg after having eaten.
O monk, eat first and then beg; let not the time pass you by.”

In this context: "You beg as a monk without having eaten"—this means that you, O monk, during your youth, wander for alms without having partaken of sense-pleasures (*vatthukāma*) through the influence of defiled desires (*kilesakāma*).
"For you do not beg after having eaten"—surely one ought to wander for alms after having enjoyed the five strands of sensual pleasure;
yet you have entered upon the practice of begging without having partaken of such pleasures at all. "Having eaten, O monk, you should beg."
“Bhikkhu, first enjoy sensual pleasures during your youth, and later, in old age, become a monk. Let not the time pass you by.
This means: “This is the time for enjoying sensual pleasures—your youth; let it not elapse.
Having heard the words of the deity, the Bodhisatta, revealing his own inner inclination, spoke the second verse:
“I do not know the time; the time is hidden and is not seen.
Therefore, I wander for alms without eating, lest the time should pass me by.
In this context, “voham na jānāmi” (I do not know): *vo* is merely a particle. As for myself, [thinking] “In my first stage of life... [the rest follows].
"One should die in middle age or in old age"—thus I do not know the time of my own death.
For a wise person [should consider]:
"Life, illness, time, the casting off of the body, and the destination."
"These five in the world of the living / Are signless and do not stir.

Regarding "the opportune time is not seen": because even for me, this time—which might be thought, "I must die at such-and-such an age or during such-and-such a season like winter"—is not seen as it passes, remaining well-concealed.

"It is not perceived. Therefore, "I wander for alms without having enjoyed [sensual pleasures]" means that for that reason, I wander for alms without having enjoyed the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*).
"Lest time should overtake me" means: "May the time for performing the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) not pass me by"—this is the meaning.
For this reason, "having gone forth while still young, I shall perform the duty of a recluse. Thus spoke the daughter of a deity to the Bodhisatta.
Having heard this, she vanished right then and there.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the celestial maiden was this very celestial maiden, and I myself was the ascetic at that period.
This is the seventh commentary on the Samiddhi Jātaka.
[168] 8. The Commentary on the Sakuṇagghi-jātaka:
"The hawk, swooping down with force..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the *Sakuṇovāda-sutta* (The Bird’s Exhortation) based on his own personal inclination.
For one day, the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus, saying: "Bhikkhus, go forth for alms."
While reciting this sutta from the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, beginning with the words, “In one’s own paternal domain,” he said: “Let alone you;

even in the past, animals who had abandoned their own paternal domain and were wandering in improper places—even when they came within the reach of their enemies—by means of their own perfection of wisdom and skill in means, [escaped] from the hands of those enemies.”
Having said, "They released me," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a lapwing (*lāpa-sakuṇa*) and made his dwelling on a heap of clods where ploughing was done.
One day, he thought, "I shall seek food within my own domain..."
"Abandoning the range in another's domain, we shall take our food," he said, and went to the edge of the forest.
Then, seeing him taking his food there, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized him.
As he was being carried off by the hawk, he lamented thus: "We are indeed unfortunate; we are of little merit, we who have roamed in a place that is not our proper range."
“If we were to roam today within our own domain, our ancestral territory, this hawk would not have been capable of engaging me in battle.
“But what, Lāpa, is that domain of yours, that ancestral territory?
“It is the place where the ploughing is done and clods of earth are thrown. Then the hawk, no longer overconfident in its own strength, [let him go].
He released him, saying, “Go now, you quail; even having gone there, you shall not escape me.
Having gone there, he climbed onto a large clod of earth and stood there calling out to the hawk, “Come now, you bird-hawk!
The hawk, overconfident in her own strength, folded both wings and swooped down suddenly upon the quail.
But when the quail realized, "This hawk has come very close," he turned around and hid himself within that very clod of earth.
The hawk, unable to sustain her momentum, struck her breast right there.
Thus, with her heart shattered and her eyes bulging out, she met her death.
Having shown this past event, the Teacher said: "Thus, monks, even those who are animals, when wandering in what is not their proper range, fall into the hands of their enemies;
but when they wander in their own range, their ancestral domain, they overcome their rivals. Therefore, you too must not wander in what is not your proper range, in the domain of others.
For monks who wander in what is not their proper range, in the domain of others, Māra will find them."
“Māra will find an opportunity, monks, he will find a foothold. And what, monks, is the non-range, the alien domain of a monk?
It is the five cords of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*). Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye... [and so on] ... This, monks, is the non-range, the alien domain of a monk.
Having said this, and having attained full enlightenment, he spoke the first verse:
“Flying down with force upon a quail standing in its feeding ground, having suddenly reached it, he met his death thereby.
In this passage, *balasā patamāno* means flying down with power and strength, thinking, “I shall seize the quail. *Gocaraṭhāyinti* means [standing] in its feeding ground.
Having departed from his own domain, he went to stand on the edge of a forest for the sake of grazing. "Arrived" means having reached it.
"He met with death because of that" means he attained death by reason of that.

But when he had met with death, the quail emerged and, thinking, "I have indeed seen the back of my enemy," he stood upon the enemy's heart and, uttering an inspired exclamation (*udāna*), spoke the second verse:
“Endowed with this method, delighting in my ancestral domain, I rejoice, free from enemies, clearly perceiving my own welfare.
In this context, “method” means skillful means (*upāya*). “My own welfare” refers to one’s own growth characterized by health.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:

"At that time, the hawk was Devadatta, but the quail was none other than myself. This concludes the eighth narration, the Sakuṇagghijātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, many bhikkhus attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other stages of enlightenment.
[169] 9. The Commentary on the Arahagga Jātaka.
"He who indeed with a mind of loving-kindness..."—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Metta Sutta.
For on one occasion the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been cultivated..."
When [this meditation] is cultivated, practiced frequently, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken, eleven benefits are to be expected.
What are the eleven? One sleeps happily; one wakes up happily; one does not see evil dreams;
one is dear to human beings; one is dear to non-human beings; the deities protect one;...

Neither fire, nor poison, nor weapon can affect him; his mind quickly becomes concentrated, the complexion of his face becomes serene, he dies unconfused, and if he does not penetrate further, he is reborn in the Brahma-world.
Monks, when the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness is cultivated... [and so on] ...when it is well undertaken, these eleven benefits arise.
“...is to be expected. Having thus praised the development of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*) by taking up these eleven benefits, [the Buddha said]:
“Monks, a monk indeed should develop loving-kindness toward all beings, both specifically and generally. One who is a benefactor should be pervaded with kindness;
one who is a non-benefactor should be pervaded with kindness; and one who is neutral should also be pervaded with kindness. In this way, toward all beings...”
Loving-kindness should be developed both specifically and generally; compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity should also be developed.
One must indeed perform the practice within the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). For by doing so, even if one does not attain the Path or the Fruit, one becomes destined for the Brahma-world.
Even the ancient wise ones, having developed loving-kindness for seven years, [remained] for seven aeons of cosmic contraction and expansion (*saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappa*).
"Having said, 'They dwelt indeed in the Brahma-world,' he related a past event.

In a past eon, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family; having reached maturity, he abandoned sensual pleasures, went forth as an ascetic, and becoming a teacher named Araka who had attained the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), he lived in a region of the Himalayas."

He established a residence there, and he came to have a great retinue. While instructing the group of seers, he spoke these verses, proclaiming the benefits of loving-kindness (*mettā*), saying: "One who has gone forth must indeed cultivate loving-kindness;
compassion (*karuṇā*), appreciative joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*) must be cultivated.
For this state of a mind filled with loving-kindness, when it reaches absorption (*appanā*), accomplishes rebirth in the Brahma-world as its ultimate goal. Thus he spoke:
“He who, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, sympathizes with the entire world—
above, below, across, and everywhere, with a measureless mind;
whose immeasurable mind of benevolence is fulfilled and well-developed.”
“Whatever action is performed with a limited measure, that will not remain there.

In this context, “he who indeed with a mind of loving-kindness has compassion for the whole world” refers to anyone—whether among the kṣatriyas and so forth, or among recluses and brahmins—who, with a boundless mind of loving-kindness, feels compassion for the entire world of sentient beings. “Above” means from the earth.
"Upwards" means as far as the Brahma-world of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. "Below" means beneath the earth, in the great Avīci hell.

"Across" means in the human world; in all those world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) that exist, may all beings born in such places be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness. Thus it is with this developed [mind].
"With a mind of loving-kindness" means with a benevolent mind. "Immeasurable" means immeasurable because it has immeasurable beings as its object and is itself immeasurable.
"In every way" means in all modes—upward, downward, and across; this is the meaning in terms of all happy and miserable realms of rebirth.
"An immeasurable mind of welfare" refers to a mind of benevolence toward all beings that has been developed by making it immeasurable. "Complete" means...
"Unimpaired. "Well-developed" means well-increased; this is a name for the mind of absorption (*appanā-citta*).

"That karma which is made limited" refers to that limited sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) karma which, instead of being developed by way of the triad of objects—namely, as "immeasurable" and "having an immeasurable object"—and by way of attaining mastery, remains small. "It will not remain there" refers to that limited [karma].
As for that kamma which is reckoned as "immeasurable and beneficial consciousness"—namely, form-sphere kamma—it does not remain there.
Just as, for example, a small amount of water submerged by a great flood is not left behind within the flood because it is swept away by it, nor does it stay;
rather, the great flood itself remains after having submerged it.
In the same way, that limited kamma remains within that sublime kamma;
having been cut off by that sublime kamma, it finds no opportunity for its result to arise, does not remain, and does not persist.
It is unable to give its own result; rather, the sublime kamma alone overwhelms it, persists, and gives its result.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having explained the benefits of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*) to his disciples, was reborn in the Brahma-world with his meditative absorption (*jhāna*) undiminished; for seven aeons of world-contraction and expansion (*saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappa*), he did not return again to this world.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, the company of seers was the assembly of the Buddha, but the teacher Araṇa was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the ninth Jātaka, the Araṇa Jātaka.
[170] 10. The Commentary on the Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka.
"This one does not rise up before me"—this Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka will appear in the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka.
This concludes the tenth commentary, the Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka.
The second chapter: On Acquaintances.
Its summary verse:
Inda, Samānagotta, Acquaintance, Susīma, and the Vulture.
Nakula and Upasāḷaka, Samiddhi and the hawk, Araka and Kakaṇṭaka. 3.
The Chapter on the Beautiful.
[171] 1. The Commentary on the Kalyāṇadhamma Jātaka.
"One of noble character"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain deaf woman.
For in Sāvatthī there was a householder who was faithful and confident, one who had gone for refuge to the Triple Gem and was endowed with the five precepts.

Thus, one day, having taken many medicinal substances such as clarified butter, as well as flowers, perfumes, garments, and so forth, he went [to Sāvatthī], thinking, "I shall hear the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher at Jetavana.
When he had gone there, his mother-in-law, taking food both hard and soft and desiring to see her daughter, went to that house; she, however, was somewhat deaf by nature.
She, having finished her meal together with her daughter and wishing to dispel the drowsiness caused by eating, asked her daughter:
"Daughter, does your husband live in harmony, without quarreling, and in pleasant companionship? "Mother, what need is there to say?
Even if he were a renunciant, he would be exactly like your son-in-law in his virtue and perfection of conduct."
"Hard to find. The female lay devotee, failing to properly attend to her daughter's words, seized only the phrase "gone forth" and cried out in a loud voice, "Mother, why has your husband gone forth?
Hearing this, all the inhabitants of the house wailed, "It seems our master of the household has gone forth! Hearing their cry, those who were passing by the gate...
“What is his name? they asked. “It is said that the householder of this very house has gone forth,” they replied.
That householder, having heard the Dhamma from the One of Ten Powers, emerged from the monastery and entered the city.
Then, on the very path, a certain man saw him and said, “Friend, it is said you have gone forth; [is there anything] in your house?”
“His wife, children, and attendants are lamenting,” he said. Then this thought occurred to him:
“Indeed, even though I have not yet gone forth, they call me ‘one who has gone forth. Now that this auspicious reputation has arisen for me, it should not be allowed to vanish;
it is fitting that I go forth this very day. Turning back from there, he went into the presence of the Teacher and asked: “What now?”

When it was said, "Upāsaka, you have just now attended upon the Buddha and departed, yet you have returned this very moment," he related that matter and said, "Venerable sir, a 'beautiful sound' has arisen and it is not fitting to let it vanish; therefore, desiring to go forth, I have come.
Having received both the going-forth and the full ordination, and practicing rightly, before long—

He attained Arahatship. It is said that this matter became well known throughout the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus. Then one day, in the Dhamma Hall, the Bhikkhus started a conversation: "Friends, such-and-such a householder, thinking 'the arisen good report must not be allowed to fade away,' went forth into homelessness and has now attained Arahatship. The Teacher, having arrived, asked: "What discussion, monks, was underway? [They replied: "This, Lord. The Teacher said: "Monks, it is not easy for a person who has not previously made merit to attain Arahatship after going forth. [He then related the following story: "Monks, in the past, in the city of Benares, there lived a poor man named Kaṇha. He earned his living by working for hire. One day, while he was working for hire at the house of a certain wealthy man, he heard the sound of the Dhamma being preached. Having heard it, he developed a longing for the life of a recluse. When the wealthy man asked him, 'Friend, where are you going? he replied, 'I am going to become a recluse. The wealthy man said, 'If you go forth, I shall give you whatever you need; do not go forth. But Kaṇha, disregarding his words, went forth into homelessness. After some time, he returned to that same wealthy man's house to work for hire. The wealthy man saw him coming from afar and, recognizing him, said, 'Friend, you have gone forth; why have you come back? Kaṇha replied, 'Sir, I went forth because I desired the Dhamma; however, when I could not obtain the Dhamma, I came back. The wealthy man said, 'Friend, what Dhamma did you hear that you went forth? Tell me, and I will give it to you. Kaṇha replied, 'Sir, I heard the Dhamma of the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. The wealthy man said, 'Friend, if that is so, I too wish to hear that Dhamma. Come with me to the Blessed One. Kaṇha agreed. Then the wealthy man took Kaṇha with him and went to the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the discourse, the wealthy man and Kaṇha both attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Then the wealthy man said to Kaṇha, 'Friend, you have attained the fruit of Stream-entry; now you may go wherever you wish. [The Teacher continued: "Monks, it was because he had previously made merit that Kaṇha was able to attain Arahatship after going forth. [The Teacher then identified the births: "At that time, Kaṇha was the householder who has now attained Arahatship; the wealthy man was Ānanda; and the preacher of the Dhamma was myself. Having said this, the Teacher delivered a teaching on the Dhamma. Then the Bhikkhus asked the Teacher, "Lord, how long ago did this householder go forth? The Teacher replied, "Monks, it was not long ago; it was only seven days ago. The Bhikkhus asked, "Lord, how did he go forth? The Teacher told them the entire story from the beginning. Then the Bhikkhus asked, "Lord, how did the householder hear the Dhamma? The Teacher replied, "Monks, it was not by hearing the Dhamma of the Buddhas that he heard the Dhamma; rather, it was by hearing the Dhamma of a Pacceka Buddha. The Bhikkhus asked, "Lord, how was that? The Teacher told them the following story: "Monks, in the past, in the city of Benares, there lived a king named Brahmadatta. At that time, a Pacceka Buddha named Tagarasikhī dwelt in a forest grove near Benares. One day, the king, having mounted an elephant and surrounded by his retinue, went out of the city to pay homage to the Pacceka Buddha. Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. Then the Pacceka Buddha taught the Dhamma to the king. At the conclusion of the discourse, the king invited the Pacceka Buddha, saying, 'Venerable sir, please accept my almsfood tomorrow. The Pacceka Buddha accepted by remaining silent. Then the king, having honored the Pacceka Buddha with great honor, returned to the city. On the following day, the king had various kinds of excellent food prepared in his own palace and sent word to the Pacceka Buddha: 'Venerable sir, please come and eat at my palace. The Pacceka Buddha, taking his bowl and robe, went to the king's palace and sat down on the seat prepared for him. Then the king, having served the Pacceka Buddha with his own hands with various kinds of excellent food, when the meal was finished, provided water for washing the bowl and hands, and having taken a low seat, sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Pacceka Buddha instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the king with a discourse on the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the discourse, the king attained the fruit of Stream-entry. Then the king said to the Pacceka Buddha, 'Venerable sir, please stay here for the three months of the Rains Retreat; I shall provide you with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines for the sick. The Pacceka Buddha consented by remaining silent. Then the king, having honored the Pacceka Buddha with great honor, returned to the city. During the Rains Retreat, the king provided the Pacceka Buddha with all his needs. When the Rains Retreat was over, the Pacceka Buddha, having stayed for the three months, set out on his travels. The king followed after him for a distance, paid homage to him, and then returned to the city. "Monks, the Pacceka Buddha Tagarasikhī, wandering through the countryside, eventually reached a certain mountain cave. There he stayed for the second Rains Retreat. The king again provided him with all his needs during that retreat. When the retreat was over, the Pacceka Buddha set out on his travels once more. The king followed after him for a distance, paid homage to him, and returned to the city. The Pacceka Buddha Tagarasikhī, wandering through the countryside, eventually reached a certain mountain cave. There he stayed for the third Rains Retreat. The king again provided him with all his needs. When the retreat was over, the Pacceka Buddha set out on his travels. The king followed after him for a distance, paid homage to him, and returned to the city. The Pacceka Buddha Tagarasikhī, wandering through the countryside, eventually reached a certain mountain cave. There he stayed for the fourth Rains Retreat. The king again provided him with all his needs. When the retreat was over, the Pacceka Buddha set out on his travels. The king followed after him for a distance, paid homage to him, and returned to the city. The Pacceka Buddha Tagarasikhī, wandering through the countryside, eventually reached a certain mountain cave. There he stayed for the fifth Rains Retreat. The king again provided him with all his needs. When the retreat was over, the Pacceka Buddha set out on his travels. The king followed after him for a distance, paid homage to him, and returned to the city. The Pacceka Buddha Tagarasikhī, wandering through the countryside, eventually reached a certain mountain cave. There he stayed for the sixth Rains Retreat. The king again provided him with all his needs. When the retreat was over, the Pacceka Buddha set out on his travels. The king followed after him for a distance, paid homage to him, and returned to the city. The Pacceka Buddha Tagarasikhī, wandering through the countryside, eventually reached a certain mountain cave. There he stayed for the seventh Rains Retreat. The king again provided him with all his needs. When the retreat was over, the Pacceka Buddha set out on his travels. The king followed after him for a distance, paid homage to him, and returned to the city. "Monks, the Pacceka Buddha Tagarasikhī, wandering through the countryside, eventually reached a certain mountain cave. There he stayed for the eighth Rains Retreat. The king again provided him with all his needs. When the retreat was over, the Pacceka Buddha set out on his travels. The king followed after him for a distance, paid homage to him, and returned to the city. The Pacceka Buddha Tagarasikhī, wandering through the countryside, eventually reached a certain mountain cave. There he stayed for the ninth Rains Retreat. The king again provided him with all his needs. When the retreat was over, the Pacceka Buddha set out on his travels. The king followed after him for a distance, paid homage to him, and returned to the city. The Pacceka Buddha Tagarasikhī, wandering through the countryside, eventually reached a certain mountain cave. There he stayed for the tenth Rains Retreat. The king again provided him with all his
“Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? he asked.

When they replied, “For this very one,” he said, “Monks, even the wise men of old went forth into homelessness thinking, ‘It is not fitting to bring to ruin a noble reputation that has arisen. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of merchants; having reached maturity—
After his father’s passing, he attained the position of treasurer. One day, having departed from his residence, he went to attend upon the king.
Then his father-in-law, thinking, "I shall see my daughter," went to that house;
she was somewhat deaf by nature, and everything else was exactly as in the present narrative. However, after he had gone to attend upon the king and was returning to his own home—
Seeing him, a certain man said, "It seems you have gone forth as renunciants; therefore, a great lamentation is occurring in your house.
The Bodhisatta thought, "A noble sound that has arisen ought not to be allowed to vanish," and so he turned back from that very spot and went into the presence of the king.
When the king asked, "Great merchant, why did you go just now and then come back again? he replied: "Your Majesty,..."
To clarify this matter— that his household folk were lamenting, saying "He has gone forth," even though he had not yet gone forth,
and that once a noble sound has arisen it should not be allowed to vanish, and thus he would go forth and ask for permission to do so—
he spoke these verses:

“When one attains the worldly reputation of being ‘one of virtuous nature,’ O Lord of Men, then a wise man should not be shamed by it; for the righteous undertake their duties out of a sense of shame.
That very reputation, ‘one of virtuous nature,’ has now been attained here in this world, O Lord of Men.”
"Having observed this, I shall go forth here; for I have no desire for the enjoyments of sense-pleasures here.

In this context, "one of beautiful character" (*kalyāṇadhamma*) means one of excellent character. "He attains the state of a recluse" (*samaññaṃ anupāpuṇāti*): when one who is virtuous and of beautiful character has gone forth, he attains this conventional designation.
Therefore, "he does not fall away from it"—that is, he does not fall away from that state of a recluse.

One might fall away. "Even through shame (*hirī*), the virtuous take up the burden," O Great King—meaning that those called "true persons" (*sappurisā*) undertake this burden of the renunciant life through both internal shame and external dread of blame (*ottappa*).
"I have attained it here today"—that is, "I have attained it by me here today. "They look upon me"—that is, they look upon me as one who has acquired that designation by virtue of my qualities.

"Looking upon," meaning observing. "Indeed, there is no desire" means "indeed, I have no desire. "In this world of sensual enjoyment" refers to the enjoyment of the objects of defiled desire (*kilesakāma*) and worldly desire (*vatthukāma*) in this world.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta obtained the king’s permission to go forth; he went to the region of the Himalayas, entered the ascetic life of a seer (*isipabbajjā*), and having realized the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he became one destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, Ānanda was the king, and I myself was the merchant-prince of Bārāṇasī.
The first explanation of the Kalyāṇadhamma Jātaka.
[172] 2. The Explanation of the Daddara Jātaka.
"Who is it that makes such a great noise?"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Kokālika.

At that time, many learned bhikkhus were reciting the *sara-bhāṇa* (the rhythmic chanting) in the midst of the Saṅgha on the Manosilā Terrace, roaring like young lions and as if causing the celestial Ganges to descend. While they were thus reciting the *sara-bhāṇa*, Kokālika...

Without realizing his own worthlessness, thinking, "I too shall recite the *sara-bhāṇa*," he entered among the monks and wandered about here and there, speaking without mentioning the name of the Saṅgha of monks:
"They do not give us the *sara-bhāṇa*. If they were to give it to us as well, we too would recite it. His talk—
He became well-known within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. The bhikkhus, thinking, "Let us first test him," spoke thus with that intention:
"Friend Kokālika, recite the *Sārabbhāṇa* today for the Saṅgha.
Without knowing his own strength, he accepted, saying "Very well," and thinking, "I shall recite the *Sārabbhāṇa* today," he drank rice-gruel suitable for himself.
He ate the hard food and took his meal with suitable soup.
When the sun had set and the time for hearing the Dhamma had been announced, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus assembled.
He put on the saffron robe the color of the *kaṇṭakuraṇḍaka* flower and donned the outer cloak the color of the *kaṇikāra* flower; having entered into the midst of the Saṅgha, he...
