There, having paid homage and ascended the excellent Dhamma throne prepared in the pavilion adorned with various jewels, he took up a variegated fan and sat down, thinking, "I shall deliver the recitation. At that very moment, sweat broke out from his body and he was overcome by trepidation.
Having uttered the first word of the opening verse, he could see nothing beyond it. Trembling, he rose from his seat.
Having descended [from his seat], he departed from the midst of the Saṅgha feeling ashamed and went to his own cell.
Another learned bhikkhu delivered a formal recitation (*sarabhāṇa*). From that time on, the bhikkhus recognized his emptiness.
Then one day, in the Hall of Dhamma, the bhikkhus initiated this discussion: "Friends, first was the emptiness of Kokālika..."
“Difficult to know [in the past], but now he has become famous by shouting for himself.

The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has become famous by shouting;
in the past as well, he became famous by shouting. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the region of the Himalayas in the womb of a lioness and became the king of many lions.
Surrounded by a great retinue of lions, he made his dwelling in a silver cave.
Not far from there, a single jackal also lived in a cave. Now, one day after it had rained,
When all the lions had departed, they gathered at the entrance of the lion-king’s cave and, letting out lion-roars, engaged in lion-sports.

While they were thus roaring and sporting, that jackal also roared. Hearing his sound, the lions thought, “This jackal is roaring along with us,” and being ashamed, they became silent. When they had become silent—
The Bodhisatta’s son, the lion cub, asked his father, saying the first verse:
“Father, these lions, having roared and been playing their lion-sports, have become silent out of shame upon hearing this sound; who indeed is this that makes himself known by his own voice?”
“Who is it that makes the mountain Daddara resound with a great noise?
Why do the lions not roar back at him? Who indeed is this lord of beasts?

Therein, “makes the mountain Daddara resound” means he makes the silver mountain Daddara emit a single sound. “Lord of beasts” is an address to his father. This is the meaning here: “O lord of beasts, chief of animals, O king of lions, I ask you: ‘Who indeed is this?’”
Having heard his words, his father spoke this second verse:
“O dear one, among the species of deer, the jackal is the lowest;
out of loathing for his birth, the lions remain silent.”

In this context, *samaccare* means “they remain silent”; *santi* is merely a prefix, and the sense is “they go beyond” (or “they cease”). What is meant is that they sit down in silence. However, in the manuscripts, it is written as *samacchare*.
The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika makes himself known by his own shouting;
he did so even in the past,” and having delivered this Dhamma teaching, he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the jackal was...”
“Kokālika was he; Rāhula was the lion cub; and as for the lion king, that was I myself.
This concludes the second commentary, the Daddara Jātaka.
3. The Commentary on the Makkaṭa Jātaka.
“This is a fatherly young brahmin”—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain hypocritical monk.
The story will appear in the *Uddālakajātaka* in the *Pakiṇṇakanipāta*. At that time, however, the Teacher said, “Monks, this monk has not been a hypocrite only now;
formerly, too, having been a monkey, he practiced deceit for the sake of fire,” and he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in a certain village of Kāsi.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered his craft at Takkasilā and established a household.
Then, after his brahmin wife had given birth to a son, she passed away while the boy was still running and playing about.
Having performed the funeral rites for her, the Bodhisatta thought, "What use have I now for the household life? I shall take my son and go forth.

Abandoning his circle of kinsmen and friends with tearful faces, he took his son, entered the Himalayas, and having gone forth as an ascetic, he made his dwelling there, subsisting on forest roots and fruits. One day, during the rainy season, while it was raining...
While it was raining, he kindled a fire with dry *sāra* wood and, warming himself, lay down upon a wooden plank.
His son, a young ascetic, sat beside him, massaging his father’s feet.
Then, a certain forest monkey, oppressed by the cold, saw that fire in his leaf-hut and thought, "If I were here..."
"If I enter, they will drive me out, beating me and shouting, 'A monkey! A monkey! and I shall not be allowed to warm myself by the fire.
Now I have a plan: I will enter after assuming the guise of an ascetic and practicing deception.
Having thought this, he put on the bark garments of a deceased ascetic, took a basket and a hook-staff, and stood at the door of the leaf-hut.

He stood huddled against a single palmyra tree. Seeing him, the young ascetic, not knowing he was a monkey, thought, "This must be an old ascetic who has come to warm himself by the fire because he is afflicted by the cold.
Having told his father, the ascetic, he thought, "I will bring him into the leaf-hut and let him warm himself," and [approached] his father.
Addressing him, he spoke this first verse:
"Dear one, this young man is leaning against the base of a palm tree;
there is even a small hut here, so come, let us give him a hut."
In this context, "young man" (*māṇavaka*) is a designation for a sentient being (*satta*). By that term, he illustrates: "Dear one, this is one young man, a sentient being; the other is an ascetic.
"Standing by the base of a palm tree" means standing leaning against the trunk of a palm tree.
"Is there this little hut?"—he says this referring to our hut as renunciants, meaning the leaf-hut (*paṇṇasālā*). "Handa" is used in the sense of an exhortation.
[This is] a particle. "We shall give him a small hut" means we shall give him a small dwelling for the purpose of living in seclusion.
Having heard his son's words, the Bodhisatta rose, stood at the door of the leaf-hut, and looking about, recognized his monkey-nature and said:
"Dear one, such a face as this does not belong to humans; this is a monkey. He must not be summoned here."
Having spoken thus, he recited the second verse:
“Do not call me back, dear one; it would defile our little home.
Such a face as this does not belong to a well-behaved brahmin.”
"In this place, he might defile our hut"—for if he had entered here, he might have defiled this leaf-hut built with such difficulty by burning it with fire or by voiding excrement and so forth.
"He is not like this," [the Bodhisatta thought], and saying, "The mouth of a well-behaved Brahmin is not like this; this is a monkey," the Bodhisatta took a torch and said, "What..."
"Stay right here! he shouted, and having thus driven him away, the monkey cast off his bark garments, climbed a tree, and entered the forest thicket.
The Bodhisatta, having cultivated the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the deceitful monk was this very monkey; the young ascetic was Rāhula; and the ascetic, however, was I myself."
The third is the Commentary on the Monkey Jātaka [174].
4. The Commentary on the Untrustworthy Monkey Jātaka:
"We have given you water in great abundance"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta.

One day, while the monks were sitting in the Hall of Truth discussing Devadatta’s ingratitude and treachery toward his friends, the Teacher approached and said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is ungrateful and treacherous to his friends;
formerly, too, he was of such a nature. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in a certain village of Kāsi.
Upon reaching maturity, he established a household. Now, at that time, along the great highway leading through the kingdom of Kāsi, there was a deep well that was inaccessible to animals;
those seeking merit who had set out upon the road [encountered it].
People used a long rope and a bucket to draw up water, filling a trough and giving it as drinking water to the animals.
Around that place was a vast forest where many monkeys lived.
Then, for two or three days, human traffic on that path was cut off, and the animals could not obtain drinking water.
A certain monkey, afflicted by thirst, was wandering near a well in search of water.

The Bodhisatta, having set out on that road for some business, while traveling there, drew up water, drank, washed his hands and feet, and stood there; he then saw that monkey. Recognizing its state of thirst, [he thought:]
Having drawn up water and poured it into a trough, he gave it to him;
and having given it, thinking, "I shall rest," he lay down at the foot of a tree. The monkey, having drunk the water, sat down nearby and terrified the Bodhisatta by making faces.
Seeing that behavior of his, the Bodhisatta said, "O wicked monkey, I..."
"I gave much water to you when you were thirsty and exhausted; now you make monkey-faces at me.
Alas! A favor done for a wicked person is indeed fruitless. Having said this, he spoke the first verse:
"We gave you abundant water when you were scorched by the heat and parched with thirst;”
"So now, having drunk, you make the sound 'kiri'; it is better not to associate with wicked people.
In this context, "So now, having drunk, you make the sound 'kiri'" means:

having now drunk the water given by me, you make the sound "kiri kiri" while making a monkey-like face. "It is better not to associate with wicked people" means [to avoid] together with wicked people.
“Association is not better; non-association alone is better.

Having heard this, that monkey, who had betrayed his friend, said: “You have formed the perception that ‘this much is enough,’ but now I shall drop excrement upon your head and depart! Having said this, he spoke the second verse:
“Have you ever heard of, or seen, a monkey who is truly virtuous?”
"Now I shall descend upon you; this is our custom. Herein, the summary of the meaning is as follows:

"O Brahmin, where have you heard or seen it said that there is such a thing as a 'monkey' who knows his duties, is endowed with good conduct, and is virtuous? Now I shall descend upon you—I shall void my excrement upon you."
"I shall depart placing him on my head; for this is the custom, this the inherent nature of our species, the monkeys—that excrement must be placed upon the head of one who has been helpful.
Hearing this, the Bodhisatta rose and began to go. At that very moment, the monkey leapt up and [climbed] onto a branch.
Having sat down, as if descending from a hanging branch, he dropped excrement upon his head and, screaming, entered the forest thicket.
The Bodhisatta, having bathed, departed.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta does not recognize the merit I have performed for him; even in the past, he did not know it."
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and brought forth this Jātaka, he identified the births: "At that time, the monkey was Devadatta, and the brahmin was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the fourth Jātaka, the Story of the Untrustworthy Monkey.
[175] 5. Commentary on the Ādiccupaṭṭhāna Jātaka.
"Among all beings," it is said—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain hypocritical bhikkhu. The story is just as told above.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Having reached maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takṣaśilā; then, having gone forth as an ascetic, he developed the supernormal powers and meditative attainments.
Having become a teacher of a large following with a great retinue, he made his dwelling in the Himalayas.
After living there for a long time, he descended from the mountains to visit a village in the borderlands in order to partake of salt and sour gruel.

He took up residence in a leaf-hut nearby. Now, while the company of seers had gone out for alms, a certain mischievous monkey came to the hermitage and began to overturn the leaf-huts, pour out the water from the water-jars, break the water-pots, and defecate in the fire-hall.
After the ascetics had spent the rainy season, they thought, "Now the Himalayas are abundant with flowers and fruits..."
“It is delightful; we shall go right there,” they said, and asked the inhabitants of the border village.
The people replied, “Venerable sirs, tomorrow we shall come to the hermitage bringing almsfood; you may depart only after having consumed it.
Having said this, on the following day they took a great quantity of solid and soft food and went there. Seeing that, [they were amazed].
The monkey thought: "By practicing deception and winning over people, I shall have them bring me food and drink as well.
Acting like one who follows the conduct of ascetics and appearing as if he were virtuous, he stood not far from the ascetics, paying homage to the sun.
When people saw him, they said: "Those who dwell in the presence of the virtuous become virtuous themselves."
Having said, "They exist," he spoke the first verse:
"Indeed, among all beings there are those established in virtue;
behold the jackal Sākhamiga, who stands in attendance upon the sun."
In this context, "there are those endowed with virtue and concentration" means they are found possessing virtue;

the further meaning is that those who are virtuous and concentrated—possessing one-pointed minds—are found there. "Jamma" means base or contemptible. "He attends upon the sun" means he stands worshipping the sun.

Seeing those people speaking thus of his virtues, the Bodhisatta said, "Without knowing the character and conduct of this greedy monkey, you have placed your faith in him without cause," and spoke the second verse:
"You do not know his character; you praise him without understanding.
The sacred fire has been extinguished, and two water-pots are broken."

In this context, *anaññāya* means "without knowing. *Ūhanan* means he was pushed away by that deceitful monkey. *Kamaṇḍalu* refers to a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*). By saying, "And two water-pots were broken by him," he spoke thus of the monkey's faults.
When the people realized the monkey’s deceitful nature, they took up clods of earth and sticks, beat him, and drove him away;

then they gave almsfood to the company of seers. The seers, too, went back to the Himālayas and, without falling away from their meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), became destined for the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the deceitful monk was this monkey; the company of seers was the Buddha’s retinue; and I myself was the leader of the group.
This concludes the fifth commentary, the Ādiccupaṭṭhāna Jātaka.
[176] 6. The Commentary on the Kaḷāyamuṭṭhi Jātaka.
"This man is indeed a fool, whose domain is but the branches of a tree"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the King of Kosala.
For on one occasion during the rainy season, the border regions of the King of Kosala rose in revolt.
The soldiers stationed there, having fought two or three battles and being unable to overcome their enemies, sent a message to the king.
The king, having set out even during the unseasonable rains and encamped his army near the Jeta Grove, thought:
“I have departed at an improper time; the ravines, paths, and other routes are flooded with water, and the road is difficult to traverse. I shall approach the Teacher;
he will ask me, ‘Where are you going, Great King? and then I shall report this matter to him. He did not...
"Furthermore, my Teacher favors me for the sake of the life to come, and he also favors me for the sake of the present life.
If, because of my going there, there will be no progress for me, he will say, 'It is not the right time, Great King.
But if there will be progress, he will remain silent. Having entered Jeta’s Grove and paid homage to the Teacher, he said:
He sat down to one side. The Teacher asked, "Well now, Great King, from where have you come so early in the day?
"Venerable Sir, I set out to pacify the border region; I have come here thinking, 'I shall pay my respects to you before departing.
The Teacher said, "Great King, in the past as well, when kings were about to set out with their armies, they would consult with wise men..."
"Having heard what, did they not go out at an improper time? Having said this, when requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his all-purpose minister, who instructed him in matters of welfare and righteousness.
Then, when the border regions rose in revolt, the frontier soldiers sent a letter to the king.
At the time of the rains, the king went out and established his camp in the park; the Bodhisatta stood near the king.
At that moment, they brought in parched grains for the horses, having soaked them in water, and placed them in a trough.
A certain monkey among the monkeys in the park descended from a tree, took some of those grains from there, filled his mouth with them, and also grasped more with his hands.
Having flown up and perched upon a tree, he began to eat them. While he was eating, a single pea fell from his hand to the ground.
Abandoning all the peas he held in his mouth and hands, he descended from the tree;
looking for that very pea but not seeing it, he climbed back up the tree once more, having lost a thousand coins for half a pea.
Grieving as if he were truly in sorrow, the monkey sat with a dejected face upon a tree branch.
Seeing the monkey’s behavior, the king addressed the Bodhisatta and asked, “Look! What is this that the monkey has done?
The Bodhisatta replied, “Great King, it is only fools of poor intellect who, without looking at the great and observing only the small, act in such a manner.”
He spoke the first verse:
“A fool indeed is this one, whose range is the branches of a tree; wisdom, O Lord of Men, is not found in him.
Having scattered an entire handful of peas, he searches for the single pea that has fallen.”

In this context, "one whose range is the branches of trees" refers to a monkey. For he takes his range among the branches of trees; those very branches constitute his range, serving as the ground upon which he moves.
Therefore, he is called "one whose range is the branches of trees. "O Lord of Men" is a form of address to the king;
for the king is the "Lord of Men" (janinda) because, by virtue of his supreme sovereignty, he is the lord (inda) of people. "A handful of peas" means a handful of chickpeas (*caṇaka*).
They even say, “A handful of black-king rice. *Avakiriya* means having scattered. *Kevalaṃ* means all of it.
*Gavesati* means he searches for only that single grain which has fallen on the ground.
Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta again approached him, addressed the king, and spoke this second verse:
“In the same way, O King, we and others who are overcome by excessive greed—may we conquer much with little, like a monkey with a single pea.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: O Great King, in just this way, both we and all other people who are overwhelmed by greed—
"Only a little would we have gained. For now, traveling on the road during the rainy season when it is not the time for travel, we are losing many benefits for the sake of a small one.
Just as this monkey, while searching for a single pea, has lost all his peas because of that one pea, so too have we, by traveling at an improper time..."

"Traveling through places such as ravines and footpaths, while seeking even a small amount of profit, we shall be deprived of our many elephant mounts, horse mounts, and so forth, as well as our entire army.
Therefore, it is not fitting to go at an improper time. Thus he gave this advice to the king.
Having heard his words, the king turned back from there and entered Bārāṇasī itself. The thieves also [heard that] "the king, it seems, is the Subduer of Thieves..."

Hearing that [the king] had departed from the city with the thought, "I shall do so," they fled from the borderlands. Even in the present day, when robbers heard that "the King of Kosala has indeed set out," they fled.
Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, the king rose from his seat, paid homage, circumambulated him to the right, and entered Sāvatthī itself.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the wise minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the sixth narrative, the Commentary on the Kaḷāyamutthi Jātaka.
7. The Commentary on the Tiṇḍuka Jātaka.
"By means of a quiver with a bow in hand"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the perfection of wisdom.
For the Teacher, having heard his own wisdom praised as in the Mahābodhi-jātaka and the Umaṅga-jātaka, said:
"Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata is wise; in the past, too, he was wise and skilled in means," and he related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a monkey and, accompanied by a retinue of eighty thousand monkeys, made his dwelling in a region of the Himalayas.
Near him there was a certain frontier village that was sometimes inhabited and sometimes deserted. In the center of that village stood a tree, complete with branches and foliage, bearing sweet fruit.
There was a single *tinduka* tree; when the monkeys were in their period of rest, they would come and eat its fruits.

Then, during another fruiting season, that village became a residence once again, being firmly walled and provided with gates, and that tree stood there with its branches bent down by the weight of the fruit.
The troop of monkeys thought: "Previously, we used to eat *tinduka* fruits in such-and-such a village; it has now borne fruit."
"Is this tree still there now, or is it not? Is that village still inhabited, or is it not?
Having thought thus, he sent one monkey, saying, "Go and find out about this matter.
He went and, having learned that the tree had indeed borne fruit and that the village was densely populated, he returned and reported it to the monkeys.
When the monkeys heard that it had borne fruit, they became eager, thinking, "We shall eat the sweet *tinduka* fruits," and reported the matter to the lord of the monkeys.
The lord of the monkeys asked, "Is the village an inhabited place or an uninhabited one? "It is inhabited, O Lord.
"In that case, you must not go; for humans are full of guile. "O Lord, at the time when humans are in seclusion..."
Thinking, "We shall eat at the time of midnight," many of them went and informed the lord of monkeys;
then, descending from the Himalayas, they waited for the time when the people of that village would be in seclusion,
and lying upon a great rock surface, they climbed a tree and ate the fruits during the middle watch when the people had fallen asleep.
Then a certain man, having gone out from his house on some business concerning his body, saw monkeys in the middle of the village and informed the people.

Many people, having equipped themselves with bows and quivers and holding various weapons in their hands, took up clods, sticks, and other implements, and stood surrounding the tree, thinking, "At daybreak we shall capture the monkeys. There were eighty thousand monkeys.
Seeing humans terrified by the fear of death, they went into his presence and, saying,
"We have no other refuge but the Lord of Monkeys," they spoke this first verse:
"With bows in hand and quivers, bearing excellent nets;..."
“We are surrounded on all sides; how will there be liberation?
In this context, “with bundles of bows in hand” means with bows in their hands; the meaning is: standing there having taken up both bows and quivers of arrows.
“Carrying excellent *nettiṃsa* weapons” means that *nettiṃsa* refers to swords; thus, it means those who carry superior swords.
"Meaning. "Surrounded" means we are encircled. "How? means by what means indeed will our liberation come about?
Having heard their words, the Lord of Monkeys said: "Do not fear; humans are indeed busy with many affairs. Even now the middle watch of the night continues;
perhaps, while you are thus surrounded, there may arise for them an obstacle to this task [of killing us]."
Having comforted the monkey with the words, "Perhaps another task might arise," he spoke this second verse:
"Even for those with many duties, some purpose may arise;
There is still something uncut on this tree—eat of the *tinduka* fruit!"
In this context, *taṃ* is a mere particle; the meaning here is simply: "Perhaps some other matter might arise for people who have many duties.

"There is a place where much has been stripped from the tree" means that there is a large portion of this tree from which much has been stripped by way of pulling and dragging off its fruits. "The *tinduka* fruit is indeed fit to be eaten" means that the *tinduka* fruit is certainly edible.
"Eat as much as you need; we shall know the time for our own combat," thus the Great Being reassured the troop of monkeys.
For had they not received such reassurance, all of them would have met their end with broken hearts. Having thus reassured the host of monkeys, the Great Being said, "All of you..."
“Bring the monkey,” he said. While they were searching for him, they did not see his nephew, the monkey named Senaka, and reported, “Senaka has not arrived.
“If Senaka has not arrived, do not be afraid; he will now ensure your safety.
As for Senaka, he had been sleeping at the time the troop of monkeys departed and only woke up afterwards.
Having seen no one, he followed along the footprints as he came; then, seeing people and realizing that fear had arisen for the troop of monkeys, he lit a fire in a house at the edge of the village.
Approaching an old woman who was spinning thread, he took a torch like a village boy going to the fields, and standing upwind, [he set fire to] the village.
He set it on fire. The people abandoned the monkey and went to extinguish the fire.
As the monkeys fled, each one took a fruit for Senaka’s sake and escaped.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Senaka the nephew was Mahānāma the Sakyan; the troop of monkeys was the Buddha’s retinue; and the king of the monkeys was none other than I myself.”
The Seventh: The Exposition of the Tinduka Jātaka.
[178] 8. The Exposition of the Kacchapa Jātaka.
"He was my father; he was my mother"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain man who had been cured of a snake-bite disease.
He spoke concerning this. It is said that once, in a certain family in Sāvatthī, a plague broke out.
The parents said to their son: "Dear son, do not stay in this house; break through the wall, flee, and go wherever you can to save your life.
Later, when you have returned, there will be a great treasure in such-and-such a place; take it."
“Having recovered the treasure and established a household, you shall live in happiness. His son accepted their words, broke through the wall, and fled.

When his illness had subsided, he returned, recovered the great treasure, established a household, and lived the life of a householder. One day, [he provided] ghee, oil, and so forth, as well as clothing and coverings...
Having had [the goods] taken aboard and gone to Jetavana, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat down.
After the Teacher had exchanged greetings with him, he asked, "We heard that a snake-poison epidemic broke out in your house; how did you escape it?
He related the circumstances to him. The Teacher said, "Upāsaka, in the past as well, when danger arose, in your own dwelling place—"
"Those who went elsewhere having made their home [there] met their end, but those who went elsewhere without making their home regained their lives.
Having said this, when requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a potter’s family in a village of Kāsī."
Having been reborn there, he performed the work of a potter and supported his wife and children.
At that time, however, near the Great River in Bārāṇasī, there was a large lake connected to it. During the period of abundant rain, it shared the same water as the river;
when the water diminished, it became separate. But the fish and turtles [thought], "In this year there has been good rainfall..."

“Next year there will be a drought,” they knew. Then, the fish and turtles born in that lake, having realized, “Next year there will be a drought,” departed from that lake for the river while the water was still continuous.
However, one turtle thought, “This is my birthplace and the place where I grew up.”
"This is the place where my parents lived; I cannot abandon it," he said, and did not go to the river.
Then, during the heat of the summer, the water there dried up. That tortoise dug into the earth at the spot where the Bodhisatta had taken the clay and entered it.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I shall take some clay," went there and began digging the ground with a large hoe.
Having split the back of the tortoise and lifted it out like a lump of clay with a hoe, he threw it onto dry land.
Overcome by pain, the tortoise lamented, saying, "Unable to abandon my attachment to my dwelling place, I have thus met with destruction," and spoke these verses:
“I thought, ‘I have been born, I have come into being,’ and so I sank into the mud.
That mud overwhelmed me, just as it would a weakling.
This I say to you, Bhaggava: listen to my words.”
“Whether in the village or in the forest, wherever one attains happiness—
knowing that to be the true kinship and the true wealth of a man—
one should live where it exists and go there; one should not be ruined by a fixed home.”
In this context, "This was my birthplace, this was my place of growth" means:
"Because of this reason—'I relied upon, I lay down in, I made my dwelling in this mire'—it is for this cause [he said it].
"He overcame" (ajjhabhavi) means he surpassed, he brought to destruction. "Bhaggava" refers to the potter.
He addresses him. This is a designation by name and clan for potters, namely, "Bhaggava. "Happiness" refers to physical and mental bliss.

"That which has been produced and cultivated" means both the place where it was born and the place where it was developed. There is also a reading as "jānittam bhāvitam" with a long vowel, which has the same meaning.
"Of one who understands" means of one who knows what is beneficial and what is harmful, and what is the cause and what is not the cause.
"May you not be destroyed by a home" means: having made a home in a dwelling and not going elsewhere, one would be destroyed by that very home;
may you not be brought to such suffering of death.
While speaking thus with the Bodhisatta, he passed away. The Bodhisatta took him [with him] and [addressed] all the inhabitants of the village...
Having gathered those people together, he exhorted them, saying: "Behold this tortoise!
When the other fish and turtles were going down the great river, this one was unable to sever its attachment to its own dwelling place;
thus, instead of going with them, it entered my clay-digging site and lay down there. Then I [took] its clay..."
Seizing him with a large hoe, I split his back and cast him onto dry land like a lump of clay.
Remembering the deed he himself had committed, he lamented with two verses and passed away.
Thus, having formed an attachment to his own dwelling place, he met his death; therefore, from this day forward, you too must not become like this tortoise.
"Do not grasp at them through the power of craving or through the desire for enjoyment, thinking: 'Form is mine, sound is mine, smell is mine, taste is mine, touch is mine;
my son is mine, my daughter is mine, my slaves, maidservants, and attendants are mine, my gold and bullion are mine.
For this single being wanders alone through the three realms of existence. Thus, with the grace of a Buddha, [he spoke] to the great multitude.
He gave this exhortation, and that exhortation spread throughout the entire Jambudīpa and remained for about sixty thousand years.
The great multitude, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s exhortation and performing meritorious deeds such as giving, filled the city of heaven at the end of their lives;
the Bodhisatta likewise performed meritorious deeds and filled the city of heaven.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that clansman was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. “At that time, Ānanda was the tortoise, and I myself was the potter.
This concludes the eighth narrative, the Kacchapa Jātaka.
[179] 9. The Commentary on the *Satadhamma-jātaka*.
This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning twenty-one kinds of improper search (*anesana*).
For at one time, many bhikkhus were engaged in medical practice, acting as messengers, acting as envoys, and serving as foot-couriers.
"By means of alms-food and further alms-food": they maintained their livelihood through such twenty-one kinds of improper search (*anesanā*). This will be made clear in the *Sāketa Jātaka*.
The Teacher, knowing that they were maintaining their livelihood in such a manner, said: "At present, many bhikkhus maintain their livelihood by improper search;
yet, having maintained their livelihood in this way, [they fall] from the state of a *yakkha* or the state of a *peta*..."
“They will not be liberated; they will be reborn as draft-oxen and take rebirth in hell.
It is fitting to deliver a single Dhamma teaching—born of my own inspiration and directed toward my own purpose—for their benefit and for their happiness.
Having thus assembled the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he said: “Bhikkhus, one must not seek alms by means of the twenty-one kinds of improper search.”
[Alms-food] should be obtained by proper means. For alms-food obtained by improper means is like a red-hot iron ball, comparable to deadly *halāhala* poison.
Indeed, such improper means are censured and rejected by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples.
For one who eats alms-food obtained by improper means, there is neither laughter nor joy. Such is the nature of alms-food obtained [in this way].
"In my teaching, [this practice] is like the leftover food of a caṇḍāla; its consumption is like the consumption of the food left over by a caṇḍāla by the young brahmin Satadhamma.
Having said this, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a caṇḍāla..."
Having reached maturity, he set out on a journey for some business, taking provisions of rice and a vessel of food.
At that time, in Bārāṇasī, there was a young brahmin named Satadhamma, born into a prominent family of northern brahmins;
he too set out on a journey for some business, but without taking any rice or a vessel of food.
The two of them met upon the great highway. The young brahmin asked the Bodhisatta, "What is your caste?
He replied, "I am a Caṇḍāla," and then asked the young brahmin, "What is your caste? "I am an Udicca-brāhmaṇa," he said.
"Very well, let us go," they both said, and the two of them proceeded along the road. At the time for the morning meal, the Bodhisatta [arrived] at a place convenient for water.
Having sat down, washed his hands, and opened the food packet, he said, "Young man, eat this meal.
"There is no need, you outcaste; I have no use for your food," [the other replied].
The Bodhisatta said, "Very well," and without making the food in the packet defiled, he placed enough for his own sustenance into another leaf, tied up the food packet, and set it aside.
Having set aside [the food], eaten, drunk water, and washed his hands and feet, he took the rice and the remaining alms-food and set out on the road,
saying, "Let us go, young men. Having traveled all day,
they both bathed in the evening at a pleasant spot by the water and came back out.
The Bodhisatta sat down in a comfortable spot, opened his food-bag, and began to eat without having asked the young brahmin for permission.
The young brahmin, exhausted from traveling all day on the road and famished, stood watching, thinking, "If he gives me some food, I will eat.
The other continued eating without saying anything. The young brahmin thought:
“This outcaste eats everything of mine without even saying ‘no’; it would be permissible to take that [food] even by squeezing it out, throw away the leftover food on top, and eat what remains.
Having done so, he ate the leftover food. As soon as he had finished eating, [he thought]:
“I have done what is unworthy of my own birth, lineage, and family status; [to act thus for] an outcaste...”
The thought, "He has eaten my leftover food," gave rise to intense remorse;

at that very moment, his food, along with blood, vomited from his mouth. Thinking, "Alas, for the sake of such a trifling matter, I have committed an unworthy deed," he uttered the first verse while lamenting under the weight of the grief that had arisen:
“That was little and it was leavings; he gave it to me with great difficulty.
I, being of brahmin birth, ate even that which was vomited.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: what was eaten by me was both little and leavings, and that [food] was given by that outcaste...
"He did not give me [the food] of his own free will; rather, being pressured, he gave it with great difficulty and hardship.
I am of a pure Brahmin birth, yet because of that very act, what I ate has come up along with blood.

Having lamented thus, the young man thought, "What is the use of my life now, having performed such an unworthy deed? He entered the forest and, without showing himself to anyone, met his death as a helpless man.
Having shown this past event, the Teacher said: "Bhikkhus,
just as no laughter or joy arose in the young brahmin Satadhamma after he had eaten that leper’s leavings because of having consumed food unfit for himself, even so,
whoever has gone forth in this Teaching and maintains his life through improper search, consuming requisites obtained in such a manner, [incurs blame]."
"Because his life is censured and condemned by the Buddha, neither laughter nor joy arises in him," he said,
and having attained full enlightenment, he spoke the second verse:
"One who lives by unrighteousness, having thus set aside the Dhamma;..."
“Even though he possesses the Dhamma, he does not rejoice even at what has been gained.
In this context, “Dhamma” refers to the Dhamma of virtue consisting in purity of livelihood. “Having cast aside” means having removed or discarded.
“By un-Dhamma” means by wrong livelihood, which consists of the twenty-one kinds of improper search. “Satadhamma” is his name; it is also [spelled] “Santadhamma.”

The reading is *na nandati*. Just as the young brahmin Satadhamma did not rejoice in the gain he received, thinking, "I have obtained the leavings of a caṇḍāla," so too, a son of good family who has gone forth in this very teaching does not rejoice or find satisfaction while consuming gains obtained through improper search;
rather, he falls into dejection, thinking, "I live a livelihood censured by the Buddha."
Therefore, for one who maintains his livelihood through improper search, it is better to enter the forest and die an orphan’s death, just like the young Brahmin Satadhamma.
Having thus delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths—
Many bhikkhus attained the fruits of stream-entry and the other stages. "At that time, the young brahmin was Ānanda, and I myself was the son of the Caṇḍāla.
This concludes the ninth commentary, the Satadhamma Jātaka.
10. The Commentary on the Duddada Jātaka.
"To those who give what is difficult to give"— this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a gift given to a community.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, two friends who were sons of householders pooled their resources,
prepared a gift of all requisites, invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and for seven days offered a great almsgiving.

On the seventh day, they presented all the requisites. Among them, the leader of the group, having paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side, said, “Venerable Sir, in this act of giving there are both many donors and some who have given little;

for the sake of all of them, I dedicate this gift so that it may be of great fruit. The Teacher said, “Indeed, lay followers, by you [this has been dedicated] to the community headed by the Buddha...”
"Having given a gift to the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus, those who dedicate it in this way perform a great deed;
even the ancient wise ones, having given gifts, dedicated them in just this manner. Having said this, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi."
Having reached maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā; then, abandoning the household life, he went forth as an ascetic and became the leader of a community.
After dwelling for a long time in the Himalayan region, he traveled through the countryside to seek salt and sour flavors.
Upon reaching Bārāṇasī, he stayed in the royal park and, on the following day, went with his retinue to the gate-village for alms.
He went for alms. People gave him alms. On the following day, he wandered in Bārāṇasī;
the people, feeling great affection, gave him alms, and having gathered their offerings through a communal bond, they prepared a gift and presented a great offering to the group of seers.
At the conclusion of the offering, the leader of the group spoke in this very manner and dedicated the gift according to that same method.
The Bodhisatta said, "Friends, when there is confidence in the heart, there is no such thing as a small gift," and while offering words of appreciation,
he spoke these verses:
"For those giving what is hard to give, performing deeds that are difficult to do..."
The wicked do not imitate the good; the way of the virtuous is difficult to follow.
Therefore, the destiny of the virtuous and the wicked is different after this life:
the wicked go to hell, while the virtuous are destined for heaven.
In this context, "difficult to give" means that giving cannot be performed by the foolish who are under the sway of greed and hatred;
therefore, it is called "difficult to give. For those who give it: "they perform a difficult deed" means that this very act of giving cannot be performed by everyone, and thus it is difficult.
For those who perform it: "the non-existent" refers to the foolish and ignorant. "They do not imitate" means they do not follow that [example].
They do not imitate the action. "The Dhamma of the virtuous" refers to the inherent nature of the wise. This was said with reference to giving.
"Difficult to follow" means difficult to understand by way of its connection to the fruit; it is hard to realize that for such a kind of giving, such is the ripening of the fruit.
Furthermore, "difficult to follow" means difficult to attain; [for] having given a gift, the fruit of the gift [is not understood] by those who are unwise.

The meaning is also that it is impossible to obtain [such] a name. "Various are the destinations from here" means that for those passing away from here and going to the world beyond, the taking of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is diverse.
"The wicked go to hell" means that the unwise, being immoral, go to hell without having given gifts or guarded their virtue.
"The virtuous have heaven as their destination" means that the wise, however, having given gifts...
"By guarding their virtue, performing the Uposatha rites, and fulfilling the three types of good conduct, they are destined for heaven and experience the great attainment of heavenly bliss.

Having thus offered his expression of appreciation, the Bodhisatta remained right there for the four months of the rainy season. When the rains had passed, he went to the Himālayas, attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), and, without falling away from those absorptions, was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the company of seers was the assembly of the Buddha, and the leader of the group was none other than myself.
This concludes the tenth story, the Commentary on the Duddada Jātaka.
The third chapter, the Kalyāṇa Vagga, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Kalyāṇadhamma, Daddara, Makkaṭī, Dubbhimakkaṭa;
Ādiccupaṭṭhāna, Kaḷāyamuṭṭhi, and Tinduka.
The Tortoise, the One with a Hundred Qualities, and the Ten who were Hard to Give To—these are ten.
4. The Chapter on the Peerless (Asadisa-vagga). [181] 1. The Commentary on the Peerless Jātaka (Asadisa-jātaka-vaṇṇanā).
“The archer is peerless”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation.
One day, indeed, the bhikkhus, having sat down in the Hall of Truth, were sitting there praising the Blessed One’s perfection of the Great Renunciation.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked: “Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you sitting here now?”
Having asked, "Is it indeed she? and being told that it was, he said, "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has gone forth on the Great Renunciation;
in the past as well, he went forth, having abandoned the white parasol. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen.
He took rebirth, and on the day of the naming ceremony for that child born in safety, they gave him the name "Asadisa Kumāra.
Later, while he was running about and playing, another meritorious being took rebirth in the womb of the queen;
when that child was born in safety, on the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name "Brahmadatta Kumāra."

They gave him a name. Among them, when the Bodhisatta reached the age of sixteen, he went to Takkasilā and, having mastered the three Vedas and eighteen crafts under a world-renowned teacher, became peerless in the art of archery and returned to Bārāṇasī.
As the king was passing away, he said, "Having given the kingdom to the peerless prince, [I shall give it] to Brahmadatta..."

Having said, "Grant me the vice-regency," he passed away. When he had died, although his own kingdom was being offered to him, the Bodhisatta refused it, saying, "I have no need for the kingdom," and they consecrated Brahmadatta upon the throne.
The Bodhisatta desired nothing at all, thinking, "I have no need for the kingdom," while his younger brother was ruling the realm as usual.
He dwelt [there] as if he were wearing it. The courtiers at the king’s feet, saying, “This incomparable prince aspires to the kingdom,” slandered the Bodhisatta in the presence of the king.
Taking their words to heart, his mind became estranged, and he dispatched men, saying, “Seize my brother!”
Then one attendant of the Bodhisatta reported that matter to him.
The Bodhisatta, having become angry with his younger brother, departed from the city and went to another kingdom.
He had it announced to the king, "A certain archer has arrived and is standing at the palace gate. The king asked, "How much wealth do you desire? [He replied,] "In one year..."
"A hundred thousand," he said. "Very well, let him come," [the King replied]. Then, when he had arrived and was standing nearby, [the King] asked him:
"Are you a master archer? "Yes, Your Majesty," he replied. "Very well, attend upon me. From that time forth, he attended upon the King.
Seeing that a salary was being given to him, the veteran archers thought, "He receives too much."
They complained. Then one day, having gone to the park, the king had a screen-wall of grass cloth erected near the auspicious stone slab;

reclining on a great couch at the foot of a mango tree, he looked upward and, seeing a cluster of mangoes at the top of the tree, thought, "It is not possible to climb up and take this," and having summoned his archers, [said]: "This..."
“Will you be able to cut down and bring down a cluster of mangoes with an arrow? he asked. “Your Majesty, that is not difficult for us;
however, Your Majesty has previously seen our work many times, whereas this archer who has just arrived receives more [patronage] than we do.
Therefore, have him bring it down.”
The king summoned the Bodhisatta and asked, "My dear son, will you be able to shoot this?
"Yes, Great King, if I am granted a single opportunity, I shall be able," he replied. "What kind of opportunity? "An opportunity within the space of your own bed.
The king had the bed removed and cleared the space. The Bodhisatta had no bow in his hand; rather, it was inside his lower garment.
Having strung his bow, he wandered about; therefore, he said, "It is necessary to obtain a screen. The king, saying "Very well," had a screen brought and enclosed the area.
The Bodhisatta, having entered the screen, removed the white cloth he was wearing on top, put on a single red cloth as an undergarment, girded his loins, and bound another red cloth around his belly.
Having drawn a sword fitted with a jointed hilt from its scabbard and fastened it at his left side,
having put on a golden tunic and secured a quiver upon his back, having taken up a great bow made of jointed *meṇḍaka* wood and strung it with a coral-colored bowstring,
and having placed a turban upon his head, he twirled a sharp razor-edged arrow with his fingernails.
Having split the hempen cloth in two and cleaved the earth, he emerged like a decorated young Nāga, went to the place where the arrow was fixed, and having nocked his shaft, he said to the king:
"Great King, shall I strike down this cluster of mangoes with an upward-flying arrow, or with one that descends downward? "My son, many [have been struck] by me with an upward-flying arrow."
“I have seen those who shoot with upward-flying arrows before, but I have never seen anyone shooting with a downward-falling arrow;

therefore, shoot with a downward-falling arrow. “Great King, this arrow will ascend far, traveling as far as the realm of the Four Great Kings before falling back down of its own accord. You must endure it until it falls.”
The king accepted, saying, "Very well.
Then he spoke to him again: "Great King, as for this arrow, when being shot upward, it will ascend as far as the middle of the mango cluster's stalk;
and when descending, without deviating even a hair's breadth from this or that direction, it will descend perfectly straight."
“See, Great King! Having fallen, it will descend after taking hold of a cluster of mangoes,” he said, and with great force he shot an arrow.
That arrow ascended, cutting through the stem of the mango cluster right down to its middle.
The Bodhisatta, knowing that the arrow would now reach as far as the realm of the Four Great Kings, [acted] from the first arrow he had shot...
Generating even greater speed, he shot another arrow; it went and struck the feathered end (*puṅkha*) of the first arrow, then returned and ascended to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven itself.
There the deities seized it, and the sound of the returning arrow being severed by the wind was like the roar of a thunderbolt. When the great multitude asked, "What is this sound? the Bodhisatta—

Having said, "It is the sound of the arrow turning back," and perceiving that the arrow was about to fall upon his own body, he reassured the terrified great multitude, saying, "Do not be afraid! He then declared, "I shall not allow the arrow to fall upon the ground.
As the arrow descended, he kept it from moving even a hair's breadth to this side or that, keeping it perfectly straight.
Having fallen, he cut the mango cluster. The Bodhisatta, not allowing the mango cluster and the stalk to fall to the ground, caught them in mid-air;
with one hand he grasped the mango cluster and with the other hand he grasped the stalk.
Seeing that marvel, the great multitude exclaimed, "We have never before seen anything like this! and [they praised] the Great Man.
He praised him, shouted, clapped his hands, snapped his fingers, and waved his garments a thousand times.
When the royal assembly was filled with joy and exultation, the wealth given to the Bodhisatta amounted to many millions.
The king, as if raining down a shower of riches, bestowed upon him vast wealth and great glory.

While the Bodhisatta was thus living there, honored and revered by that king, seven kings arrived and surrounded the city of Bārāṇasī, thinking, "It is said there is no prince equal to him in Bārāṇasī.
They sent a letter to the king, demanding, "Give us either the kingdom or battle.
Terrified by the fear of death, the king asked, "Where does my brother live? and [inquired further].
Hearing that he was attending upon a neighboring king, [the prince] sent messengers with the message: "My brother will not come; I shall have no life if he does not.
Go, in my name, bow at his feet, ask for his forgiveness, and bring him back.
They went and reported this matter to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta [then approached] that king.
Having taken leave and returned to Bārāṇasī, he reassured the king, saying, "Do not fear.

Then, carving letters into his arrow-shaft, he stood upon the watchtower while the seven kings were eating and declared: "I am the Peerless Prince who has arrived; by discharging another single arrow, I shall take away the lives of you all. Those who have need of their lives, let them flee!"
He dropped the arrow right into the hollow of a golden bowl. Seeing those letters, all of them, terrified by the fear of death, fled away.
Thus, the Great Being, without causing even a drop of blood to be drunk by the small flies, caused the seven kings to flee;
then, taking leave of his younger brother, he abandoned sensual pleasures and went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Having produced the supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), at the end of his life he went to the Brahma-world.

After having attained full enlightenment, the Teacher said these verses: “The archer Asadisa, the prince of great strength; having routed the seven kings, he went forth into the ascetic life of a seer.”
He was one who could strike from afar, a sharpshooter, and a destroyer of vast hosts.
Having waged war against all his enemies, yet not harming anyone,
he ensured his brother’s safety and entered upon the path of self-restraint.
In this context, "unrivaled" means he is unrivaled not only by name, but also in strength, energy, and wisdom.

"Possessing great power" means he is mighty both in physical strength and in the power of wisdom. "Long-distance shooter" means he is capable of launching an arrow as far as the realm of the Four Great Kings and the realm of the Thirty-three Gods.
"A shot that never misses" means his aim is unfailing. Alternatively:

A "moment" (*akkhaṇa*) is said to be a flash of lightning; as long as a single flash of lightning occurs, one takes up seven or eight arrows during that brief illumination and shoots them—thus he is called a "marksman who hits the moment" (*akkhaṇavedhī*).

"The crusher of great bodies" (*mahākāyappadālana*) means he crushes large bodies. These are: a body of leather, a body of wood, a body of metal, a body of iron, a body of sand, a body of water, and a body of wooden planks.
The seven great bodies are as follows: there, one [elephant] can pierce through a buffalo hide that crushes leather;
yet another can pierce even a hundred buffalo hides. Another can pierce through a fig-wood plank eight finger-breadths thick, or an acacia-wood plank four finger-breadths thick;
yet another can pierce even a hundred planks bound together as one.
It penetrates [even] a copper-iron plate two finger-breadths thick, or an iron plate one finger-broadth thick.
Having inserted an arrow-shaft behind a cart of sand, a cart of jujube fruits, or a cart of straw, one drives it through from the front;
naturally, an arrow-shaft that enters four *usabhas* deep in water enters eight *usabhas* on dry land—in this way, for these...
Because he shattered the seven great hosts, he is called Mahākāyappadālana (the Shatterer of the Great Hosts).
"All enemies" means all adversaries. "Having made war" means having fought a battle; the sense is that he put them to flight. "And he did not harm anyone" means he did not harm even a single person.
Without harming them at all, however, he waged war against them merely by sending forth his arrows. "He entered into self-restraint" means:
Having entered the homeless life with restraint in virtue, he approached the going-forth.
Thus the Teacher, having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka: "At that time the younger brother was Ānanda, while the Prince Asadisa was none other than myself.
This is the first narrative, the Commentary on the Asadisa Jātaka.
[182] 2. The Commentary on the Saṅgāmāvacara-jātaka.
"The hero who dwells in the midst of battle"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the Elder Nanda.
For when the Teacher went to Kapilavatthu on his first journey, he [converted] Prince Nanda, his younger brother.
Having ordained him and departed from Kapilavatthu, they traveled by stages until they reached Sāvatthī.
While the Blessed One was staying there, the Venerable Nanda took the Buddha’s bowl and followed him as they were leaving the house.
At that time, having heard that "the youth Nanda is going with the Teacher," some people looked out through the window with their hair still half-combed.
“Noble son, you should come soon,” reflecting on these words spoken by Janapadakalyāṇī, he became distressed, discontented, and turned pale; his veins stood out upon his body.
The Teacher, perceiving this state of affairs, thought, “What if I were to establish Nanda in Arahatship? and [went] to the dwelling cell where he resided.
Having gone and sat down on the prepared seat, he asked, "Nanda, do you find delight in this teaching?
"Venerable sir, having my heart bound to Janapadakalyāṇī, I do not find delight. "Nanda, have you ever gone on a journey to the Himalayas before?
"I have not, venerable sir. "In that case, let us go. "Venerable sir, I possess no supernormal power."
“Where shall I go? The Teacher said, “Nanda, I will take you by the power of my supernormal might,” and taking the elder by the hand, he leapt into the air.

Along the way, in a field of burnt wood, he saw a being sitting on a charred stump—one whose ears, nose, and toes were severed, whose hair was singed, whose skin was stripped away, leaving only the hide, and who was smeared with blood.
He showed him a single leaping monkey and said, “Nanda, do you see this monkey? “Yes, Bhante,” he replied.
“Behold it clearly for yourself.
Then, taking hold of it, [he led him] to the sixty-league Manosilātala plateau, the seven great lakes beginning with Lake Anotatta, and so forth.
Having shown him the five great rivers and the Himalayan mountain range adorned with golden mountains, silver mountains, and jewel mountains,
and filled with many hundreds of delightful sights, he asked, "Nanda, have you ever seen the Tāvatiṃsa heaven before?
When Nanda replied, "No, venerable sir, I have not seen it before," [the Buddha said], "Come, Nanda, I will show you the Tāvatiṃsa heaven."
Having led him there, he sat upon the Paṇḍukambala stone seat. Sakka, the king of the gods, arrived from two celestial realms together with a host of deities;

having paid homage, he sat down to one side. His three-and-a-half million attendants and five hundred deva-maidens with peacock-feet also arrived, and having paid homage, they sat down to one side. The Teacher addressed the Venerable...
Those five hundred nymphs, under the influence of defilement, made Nanda look at them again and again. "Do you see these nymphs with the feet of a hen, Nanda?
"Yes, venerable sir. "Are they beautiful, or is Janapadakalyāṇī more so?
"Venerable sir, compared to Janapadakalyāṇī, these are just like a mangy old monkey."
“Compared with Janapadakalyāṇī? “Now what will you do, Nandā?

“By doing what deed, venerable sir, do these nymphs obtain such a state? “By practicing the duty of a recluse. “If, venerable sir, the Blessed One will stand as my guarantor for the acquisition of these nymphs, I shall practice the duty of a recluse. “Do so.”
“Nanda, I am your guarantor. Thus, having taken the Tathāgata as his guarantor in the midst of the assembly of gods, the Elder said, “Venerable Sir, do not make such a long delay;
come, let us go; I shall perform the duties of a recluse.
Taking him with him, the Teacher returned to Jetavana itself. The Elder began to perform the duties of a recluse.

The Teacher addressed the Dhamma-Senāpati, saying, "Sāriputta, my younger brother Nanda took me as his guarantor for the sake of celestial nymphs in the midst of the assembly of gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. He explained this to him.
By this same method, he spoke to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, the Elder Anuruddha, and the Elder Ānanda, the Keeper of the Dhamma-Treasury.
He related this to the eighty great disciples and to most of the remaining bhikkhus. Then the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, approached the Elder Nanda and said:

"Is it true, friend Nanda, that in the midst of the assembly of gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, you took the Ten-Powered One as your guarantor, saying, 'I shall practice the ascetic life while obtaining celestial nymphs'?"
Having said this, he put the Elder to shame and deprived him of his splendor, saying: "If that is so, then your dwelling in the holy life is dependent upon women and dependent upon defilements;

for you who perform the duties of a recluse for the sake of women, what difference is there between you and a hired laborer performing work for wages? By this means, he did the same to all eighty great disciples.
The remaining bhikkhus put that venerable Nanda to shame. Thinking, "Alas, I have done what is improper," he,
through a sense of shame and moral dread, exerted firm energy, developed insight, and having attained arahantship,
approached the Teacher and said, "Venerable sir, I [honour] the Blessed One’s promise..."
“I release you,” he said. The Teacher also said, “Nanda, when you have attained Arahatship, at that very moment I shall be released from my promise.
Having understood this matter, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
“Friends, how patient of admonition is this Elder Nanda! For with only a single exhortation, having established a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, he has practiced the duty of a recluse.”
“Having done so, he attained arahantship. The Teacher returned and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Nanda was indeed capable of receiving instruction.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of elephant trainers.
Having reached maturity, he attained perfection in the art of elephant training and entered the service of a rival king of Benares.
He thoroughly trained and educated that king’s state elephant. Then the king, thinking, "I shall seize the kingdom of Benares," set out.

Taking the Bodhisatta, he mounted the auspicious elephant and, having gone to Bārāṇasī with a great army, surrounded the city and sent a letter to the king, saying: "Either give up the kingdom or give battle.
Brahmadatto, thinking "I shall give battle," stationed his forces at the city walls, gate-towers, and gateways, and gave battle. The rival king [mounted] the auspicious elephant...
Having covered himself in armor and having donned his own armor as well, he mounted the back of an excellent elephant, took up a sharp goad, and dispatched the elephant toward the city, thinking:
"I shall break through the city, bring my enemies to the end of their lives, and place the kingdom in my hands.
It [trampled] the hot mud and various kinds of mechanical stones.
Seeing them discharging their weapons, he was terrified by the fear of death and, unable to approach, retreated.
Then the elephant trainer approached him and said, "Dear son, you are a hero who ranges in battle;
it is not fitting for you to retreat in such a situation. Having spoken thus, while instructing the elephant, he recited these verses:
“You are renowned as a hero who frequents the battlefield and is full of strength;
why then, O elephant, do you retreat upon encountering the gateway?
Crush the crossbar quickly and pull up the pillars!”
"And having trampled the gate-towers, enter quickly, O elephant!"—therein, "thus renowned" means:
dear one, because you move about having trampled the battle where the clash of weapons occurs, you are known as a "warrior of the battlefield" (*saṅgāmāvacara*);
because of your firm heart, you are a "hero" (*sūra*); and because of your possession of strength, you are "powerful" (*balavā*)—thus you are renowned and famous.
"Manifest. "Having reached the gateway" means having arrived at the gateway known as the city gate. "You retreat" means: "Why indeed do you withdraw?
For what reason do you turn back? "Crush them down" means: "Grind them down; cast them below. "And pull out the pillars" means:
[having fixed] the pillars at the city gate by inserting sixteen cubits [of each] into the ground and making them immovable.
"The sand-pillars have been driven in; pull them up quickly and tear them out! he commanded.
"And having crushed the archways" means having crushed the wooden frames at the city gate. "Enter quickly" means enter the city swiftly. "O elephant"—this is how he addresses the nāga.
Upon hearing this, the nāga turned back at the Bodhisatta’s single command, coiled his trunk around the sand-pillars, and...
Having plucked them out like mushrooms, crushed the gate-bar, lowered the crossbar, broken down the city gate, and entered the city, he seized the kingdom and gave it [to him].
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Nanda was the elephant; Ānanda was the king; and I myself was the elephant trainer."
The second commentary on the *Saṅgāmāvacara-jātaka*.
[183] 3. The commentary on the *Vālodaka-jātaka*:
"The water with hair is scanty and base. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning five hundred scavengers.

He spoke concerning this. It is said that in Sāvatthī, five hundred lay followers (upāsakas), having entrusted the burdens of household life to their wives and children, traveled together while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching.

Among them, some were stream-enterers (sotāpanna), some once-returners (sakadāgāmin), and some non-returners (anāgāmin); there was not even a single worldling (puthujjana). Even when they were inviting the Teacher [to their homes],...
They invited [the monks] only after having brought those lay followers inside.
Now, five hundred minor attendants (*cūḷupaṭṭhāka*), who were scavengers (*vighāsāda*) providing tooth-sticks, mouth-washing water, robes, perfumes, and garlands for them, lived there.
Having eaten their morning meal and slept, they would rise and go to the Aciravatī River; shouting on the riverbank, they engaged in wrestling matches. Those five hundred lay followers...
They were quiet and noiseless, devoted to seclusion. When the Teacher heard the loud clamor of those scavengers, he asked the Elder, "Ānanda, what is this sound?

When the Elder replied, "It is the sound of scavengers, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Ānanda, it is not only now that these scavengers roar after eating their scraps; in the past, too, they used to roar."
"These lay followers have not only sat together now; they have sat together in the past as well," the Elder said, and being requested, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers.
Upon reaching maturity, he became the king’s advisor in matters of statecraft and righteousness. Then, on one occasion, that king heard that "the border regions were in revolt."
Having saddled five hundred horses and set out with a fourfold army, he pacified the border regions and returned to Bārāṇasī itself.
He then gave the order: "The horses are exhausted; give them fresh juice as their drink.
Having drunk the fragrant drink, the horses went to the stable and stood each in his own place. But as for the remainder of what had been given to them—
It became turbid and full of sediment. People asked the king, "What shall we do with this?
The king had it kneaded with water, strained through coarse cloth, and gave it away, saying, "Give this to those who sent fodder for the Sindhava horses.
Having drunk the turbid water, the donkeys became intoxicated and brayed loudly in the royal courtyard.
They wandered about. The king, having opened a large window and looking out over the royal courtyard, addressed the Bodhisatta standing nearby:
"Look, these donkeys, having drunk turbid water, wander about bellowing and leaping about in their intoxication;
but the thoroughbreds born of the Sindhu breed, having drunk the scented drink, sit quietly and still."
"Being asked, 'Why is it that they do not become intoxicated? What is the reason? he spoke the first verse:
'Having drunk the water from a horse's tail—thin, tasteless, and inferior—intoxication arises in donkeys;
yet having drunk this excellent juice, no intoxication arises in thoroughbred Sindhu horses.'"
In this context, *vālodaka* means water strained through the fibers of a coarse cloth; there is also a reading, *vāludaka*.

"Inferior" (*nihīna*) means inferior by way of its inferior flavor. "It does not arise" means that the intoxication of Sindhava horses does not arise; [the king] asked, "What indeed is the reason for this?
Then, explaining the reason to him, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
“Having drunk only a little, that man of low birth becomes intoxicated when questioned by you, O Lord of Men;
but one born into a noble family, firm in virtue, does not become intoxicated even after drinking the finest liquor.
In this context, “O Lord of Men” means O supreme king; “that man of low birth” refers to one who, by virtue of his low birth—
When touched [by wine], he becomes intoxicated and grows negligent. "One whose nature is to bear the burden" means one who possesses the conduct of bearing the yoke, like a noble thoroughbred horse.
"Even after drinking the finest liquor" means even after drinking the very first grape juice taken, he does not become intoxicated.

Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, the king had the donkeys removed from the royal courtyard; remaining established in his advice, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the five hundred donkeys were these scavengers;
the five hundred Sindhava horses were these lay followers; King Ānanda was [the king]; and the wise minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the third narrative, the Vālodaka-jātaka.
[184] 4. The Giridatta-jātaka Commentary. "Corrupted by Giridatta":
This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning a certain monk who associated with adversaries.
The story of the incident has already been told below in the Mahiḷāmukha-jātaka. However, the Teacher said: "Monks, not..."
"This monk is now serving those who are opposed; previously, too, he was one who served those opposed," he said, and then related a story of the past.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, King Sāma reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers, and upon reaching maturity, he became the king’s advisor in matters of welfare and righteousness. The king, however, had a state elephant named Paṇḍava. To him—

There was a horse-keeper named Giridatta who was lame. Seeing the horse go ahead while holding the nose-rope, and perceiving that "this man is training me," the horse followed his lead and became lame.
They reported the horse's lameness to the king, and the king sent physicians. Having gone there, they [examined] the horse...
Not seeing any disease in his body, they told the king, "We do not see any disease in him. The king sent the Bodhisatta, saying, "Go, friend;
find out the reason for this. Having gone there, he learned that the man had become lame through association with a lame horse-binder;
he reported the matter to the king, saying, "Indeed, by the fault of association it has come to this..."
Showing that this occurs, he spoke the first verse:
“The horse Paṇḍava of Sāma, corrupted by Giridatta,
having abandoned its former nature, conforms to him alone.”

Therein, "the horse of Sāma" refers to the auspicious horse of King Sāma. "Having abandoned his ancient nature" means having relinquished his own former nature, which was characterized by pride. "He conforms" means he learns after [the example].
Then the king asked him, "Now, young man, what should be done? The Bodhisatta said, "If one obtains a skilled horse-trainer, he will become as he was before," and spoke the second verse:
"And if there is a person born of noble lineage, adorned with the form of a crest..."
“Having taken him by the mouth, one should turn him around in the circle;
having quickly struck him, he will conform to his very will.
In this context, *tanuja* means “his younger brother. For one born in accordance with [the elder] is a younger brother (*anuja*); thus, “his younger brother” is *tanuja*. This is what is meant.
It would be so—provided, O Great King, that the man born to that noble and well-behaved horse is himself noble and well-behaved.

"With his hair and beard trimmed in a crest-like fashion" means that, having taken hold of that horse by the face with his beautiful crest-like [hair], he should move it around in the horse-enclosure; very quickly indeed would he abandon that state of lameness.
"Thinking, 'This Siṅgāla, endowed with good conduct, is training me,' he will quickly conform to him and follow his instruction;
the meaning is that he will remain in his natural state. The king acted accordingly, and the horse was established in its natural state.
The king, thinking, "He even knows the disposition of animals," was delighted in heart.
He bestowed great glory upon the Bodhisatta.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Giridatta was Devadatta; the horse Vipakkhasevaka was a certain monk; the king was Ānanda; and the wise minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Giridatta Jātaka, the fourth.
[185] 5. The Commentary on the *Anabhirati-jātaka*.
"Just as when water is turbid, it is not clear"—the Teacher spoke this while residing at Jetavana, concerning a certain young brahmin.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a young brahmin who had mastered the three Vedas and [instructed] many young kṣatriyas.

And he taught the mantras to the young Brahmin. Later on, after establishing a household, he became preoccupied with the acquisition of clothing, ornaments, male and female slaves, fields, lands, cattle, buffaloes, children, wives, and so forth;

falling under the sway of lust, hatred, and delusion, his mind became turbid. He was unable to recite the mantras in their proper sequence, and the mantras no longer came to him from this or that source.
One day, having taken many perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he—
Having gone to Jetavana, he paid homage to the Teacher, bowed down, and sat to one side.
The Teacher exchanged greetings with him and asked, "Young man, do you recite the mantras? Are your mantras well-mastered?
"Venerable sir, my mantras were well-mastered in the past; however, from the time I took up the life of a householder, my mind..."
"It has become turbid; therefore, my spells are not proficient. Then the Teacher said to him, "Young man, it is not only now;
formerly too, when your mind was unturbid, your spells were proficient, but when it was turbid by passion and the like, your spells did not manifest.
Having said this, at his request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a prominent brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the sacred texts at Takkasilā and became a world-renowned teacher.
Residing in Bārāṇasī, he taught the sacred texts to many princes and brahmin youths. Among those in his presence was a certain brahmin student.
He became proficient in the three Vedas; without doubt even regarding a single word, he served as a tutor and taught the mantras.
Later, after taking up the life of a householder, his mind became turbid with the cares of domestic life, and he was unable to recite the mantras.
Then, when the student came into his presence, the teacher asked him, "Young man, are the mantras still familiar to you?"
When he replied, "Since the time I took up the life of a householder, my mind has become turbid;
I am unable to recite the mantras," [the teacher] said, "Dear son, when the mind is turbid, even well-mastered mantras do not manifest;
but when the mind is unturbid, there is nothing that cannot be spoken. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“Just as when water is turbid and not clear, one does not see the shells and snails,
nor the pebbles, sand, and schools of fish— so too, when the mind is turbid,
one does not see one’s own welfare or the welfare of others.”
“Just as in clear, serene water one sees shells and snails,
gravel, sand, and schools of fish, so too, in an untroubled mind,
one sees one’s own welfare and the welfare of others.”
In this context, *āvile* means stirred up by mud. *Appasanne* means not clear because of that very turbidity.
*Sippikasambukañca* means both a snail and a shell. *Macchagumbaṃ* means a school of fish. *Evaṃ āvilamhi* means "in a mind thus turbid with lust and so forth.
*Attadatthaṃ paratthaṃ* means he sees neither his own welfare nor the welfare of others; such is the meaning.
"He sees thus": in this very way, with a mind undisturbed, that man sees his own welfare and the welfare of others.
Having brought forward this past event and proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*), the Teacher identified the Jātaka;

at the conclusion of the Truths, the young brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). "At that time, the young student was none other than this very young student, and the teacher..."
"But it was indeed I who was he.
