The fifth commentary, the *Anabhirati-jātaka-vaṇṇanā*. [186] 6.
The *Dadhivāhana-jātaka-vaṇṇanā* (Commentary on the Birth Story of Dadhivāhana).
"Endowed with beauty, fragrance, and flavor"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning a monk who associated with those of opposing character.
The background story has already been told above. However, the Teacher said: "Monks, association with the unwholesome is indeed evil and harmful.
In that regard, what need is there to speak of the harm caused by evil association for those who have become human beings?"

"It must be said that previously, even the insentient mango tree, having come into contact with the neem tree—which is neither savory nor sweet—became insipid and bitter, its sweet juice resembling divine nectar. Having said this, he related a story from the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there were four brahmin brothers in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Having gone forth into the ascetic life of a seer, they built leaf huts in succession in the Himalayan region and made their dwelling there.
Their eldest brother passed away and attained the status of Sakka.
Having learned of this situation, he would go to attend upon them every seven or eight days; on one such occasion, after paying homage to the eldest ascetic, he said:
Sitting to one side, he asked, "Venerable sir, what do you require? The ascetic Paṇḍuroga replied, "I require fire.
Having heard this, he gave him an axe and a hatchet. An "axe and hatchet" (vāsipharasuka) is so called because it serves as both an axe and a hatchet by way of being inserted into a handle.
The ascetic thought, "Who will take this for me and fetch wood?"
He said. Then Sakka spoke to him thus: “Venerable sir, whenever you have need of wood, you should strike this axe with your hand and say, ‘Bring me wood and make a fire.
Having brought the wood and made a fire, it will give it to you.
Having given him the axe and the hatchet, he approached him a second time and asked, “Venerable sir, what do you need?”
He asked. An elephant track led to his leaf-hut; being harassed by elephants, he said, "Suffering arises for me because of these elephants; drive them away.
Sakka presented him with a drum and said, "Venerable sir, when this surface is struck, your enemies will flee;
when this surface is struck, they will become possessed of a mind of loving-kindness."
"Having sacrificed, they will surround you with a fourfold army," he said; then, having given that drum, he went to his younger brother and asked, "Venerable sir, what do you need?
He too was of a constitution afflicted by jaundice, and therefore he replied, "I need curd.
Sakka gave him a jar of curd and said, "If you so desire, you may pour this out."
"Having become a great river and set in motion a mighty flood, he will even be capable of seizing your kingdom and returning it to you," he said, and then departed.
From that time forth, the axe and hatchet provided fire for the elder brother;
when the other struck the surface of a drum, elephants would flee; and the youngest brother consumed curd.
At that time, a certain boar, while wandering in the ruins of an old village, saw a magnificent mass of jewels.
Seizing that mass of jewels in his mouth, he flew up into the air by its power and went to an island in the middle of the ocean.
Thinking, "It is fitting for me to dwell here now," he descended and [settled] in a comfortable spot.
He made his dwelling beneath a single udumbara tree. One day, having placed a cluster of jewels before him at the foot of that tree, he fell asleep.

Then, a man from the kingdom of Kāsi, who had been driven out of his home by his parents with the thought, "This man is of no use to us," went to a port town and became a laborer for the boatmen, [working on] a ship.
Having boarded [the ship], when it was wrecked in the middle of the ocean, he lay upon a plank;
having reached that island and searching for various fruits, he saw that boar sleeping.
Going slowly, he took a cluster of jewels, and by their power, he leaped into the air, sat down upon an udumbara tree, and reflected: "This boar [is the owner] of this..."
"By the power of that cluster of jewels, he has become a sky-walker and seems to be living here;
it would be right for me to kill this pig first, eat its flesh, and then go.
He broke off a stick and struck it upon the pig's head. The pig woke up, and not seeing the jewel, it ran about here and there, trembling.
A man sitting in a tree laughed. A boar, looking about and seeing him, struck that tree with its head and died right there.
The man descended, made a fire, cooked the boar’s meat, and ate it. Then, leaping into the air and traveling over the Himalayas, he saw a hermitage;
he descended into the hermitage of his eldest brother, the ascetic, and stayed for two or three days.
Having stayed there, he performed his duties and services for the ascetic and witnessed the power of the axe and adze.

Thinking, "It is right for me to take this," he demonstrated the power of the crystal cluster to the ascetic and said, "Venerable sir, please take this jewel and give me the axe and adze. Desiring to travel through the air, the ascetic took it.

He gave him a hatchet and an axe. Having taken them, he went a short distance, struck with the hatchet and axe, and said, "Hatchet and axe, cut off the head of the ascetic and bring me the cluster of jewels.
He went, cut off the head of the ascetic, and brought back the cluster of jewels.
[The king] placed the hatchet and axe in a hidden spot and [approached] the middle ascetic.
Having gone into his presence and stayed for a few days, he saw the power of the drum;
having given a mass of jewels and taken the drum, he had his head cut off in the same manner as before. Then, approaching his younger brother, he saw the power of the pot of curd;
having given a mass of jewels and taken the pot of curd, he had his head cut off in the same manner as before.
Having had the heap of jewels cut away and taking his axe, hatchet, drum, and pot of curd, he leapt into the air and,
standing not far from Bārāṇasī, sent a letter in the hand of a man to the King of Bārāṇasī, saying: "Give me either battle or the kingdom."
Upon hearing the royal decree, the king set out, thinking, “I shall seize the thief. He struck a single drum-skin, and his fourfold army surrounded him.
Perceiving the king’s advance, he released a jar of curd, and a great river began to flow.
The multitude of people sank into the curd and were unable to escape. [He] struck with an axe and a hatchet, saying, “Of the king...”
“Bring me the head,” he said. The executioner went, brought the king’s head, and placed it at his feet.

Not a single person was able to lift a weapon. Surrounded by a great force, he entered the city, had himself consecrated, and having become the king named Dadhivāhana, he ruled the kingdom with righteousness and equity.
One day, while he was playing with a fishing net in the Mahānadī River, a mango fruit that had been enjoyed by a deity from the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa Lake came and became caught in the net.
When they were hauling up the net, they saw it and gave it to the king.
It was as large as a water-jar, perfectly round, and golden in color. The king asked, "What kind of fruit is this?"
Having questioned a forest-dweller and heard that it was "mango fruit," he ate it and had its seed planted in his own garden, where he had it watered with milk.
The tree grew and bore fruit in the third year.
The mango received great honor; they watered it with milk, offered scented unguents for the five fingers, and presented garlands of flowers.
They surrounded it and lit lamps with scented oil; its enclosure was made of a curtain of fine cloth.

The fruits became sweet and golden-colored. When King Dadhivāhana sent mango fruits to other kings, fearing that they might sprout while standing upright, he pierced the spot where the sprouts would emerge with a frog-thorn.
He sent [them]. Having eaten the mangoes, they found that the seeds they planted did not grow.
Asking, "What indeed is the reason for this? they discovered the cause.
Then one king, having summoned the park-keeper, said: "Destroy the flavor of King Dadhivāhana’s mango fruits and turn them bitter."
Having asked, "Will you be able to do it? and being told, "Yes, Your Majesty," [the king] said, "In that case, go," gave him a thousand [pieces of gold], and sent him off.
He went to Bārāṇasī, had it announced to the king, "A park-keeper has arrived," and was summoned by him.
Having entered and paid homage to the king, he was asked, "Are you the park-keeper? and he replied, "Yes, Your Majesty."
He praised his own power. The king said, "Go and remain in the presence of our park-keeper.
From then on, those two people tended the park together.
The newly arrived park-keeper made the park delightful by causing out-of-season flowers to bloom beautifully and by having out-of-season fruits gathered. The king, becoming confident in him—
Having evicted the former garden-keeper, he gave the garden back to him.
Once that man realized the garden had come into his own hands, he surrounded the mango tree with nimba trees and *phaggava* creepers. Gradually the nimba trees grew;
their roots entwined with roots, and their branches with branches, until they were completely interlaced and covered. Because of this—
Through contact with something unpleasant and bitter, that mango, which had previously borne sweet fruit, became bitter, its taste resembling that of neem leaves.
When the park-keeper realized the bitterness of the mango fruits, he fled.
Dadhivāhana went to the park and, while eating a mango fruit, [discovered] that the mango juice that had entered his mouth was like the pulp of a neem fruit.
Unable to swallow it, he spat it out after making a sour face. At that time, the Bodhisatta was his minister who instructed him in matters of welfare and Dhamma.
The king addressed the Bodhisatta, saying: "O wise one, there has been no decline in the traditional care given to this tree;
yet, even so, its fruit has become bitter. What could be the reason for this? he asked.
He spoke the first verse:
“Formerly this mango tree was endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor;
while receiving such honor as that, why has the mango now become bitter of fruit?”
Then, explaining the reason for this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
“O Dadhivāhana, your mango tree is surrounded by *pucimanda* trees;
root is joined with root, and branch is attended by branch.”
“Through dwelling with the disagreeable, that mango tree has such bitter fruit.
In this context, “surrounded by *pucimanda* trees” means surrounded by *nimba* trees. “Branches entwine branch” means the branches of the *pucimanda* entwine the branches of the mango tree.
“Through dwelling with the disagreeable” means through dwelling with the non-sweet *pucimanda* trees.
"By living together with it. "Therefore," he said, "for that reason this mango has become bitter-fruited, unpleasant-fruited, and pungent-fruited.

Having heard his words, the king had all the *pucimanda* trees and *phaggava* creepers cut down, had their roots uprooted, had the non-sweet soil removed from all around, and had sweet soil added; then [he watered them] with milk-water, sugar-water, and scented water.
He had his mother cared for. Through that sweet association, he became sweet once again. The king entrusted the garden to the original gardener;
having lived out his lifespan, he passed away according to his karma.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the wise minister."
The Sixth: The Commentary on the Dadhivāhana Jātaka.
[187] 7. The Commentary on the Catumaṭṭha Jātaka.
"Ascending to the high branch... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain elderly bhikkhu.

He spoke concerning this. It is said that one day, while two of the Chief Disciples were sitting together engaged in a discussion of asking and answering questions, an elderly bhikkhu approached them, sat down as a third, and said:
"Venerable sirs, we too shall ask you questions; you also should ask us about your own doubts. The Elders—
Having felt disgust for it, they rose and departed. When the assembly that had sat down to hear the Dhamma from the elders dispersed, they went into the presence of the Teacher.
When he asked, "Why have you come at an improper time?", they reported the reason to him.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta and Moggallāna, having felt disgust for this, depart without speaking."
"Even in the past they departed," he said, and related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in a forest glade.
Then two young swans, having emerged from Mount Cittakūṭa, sat down upon that tree.
Even when returning from their foraging grounds, they would rest right there before proceeding to Cittakūṭa.
As time passed, a bond of friendship developed between them and the Bodhisatta.
Whether going out or coming back, they would greet one another with joy, exchange discourses on the Dhamma, and then depart. Then, one day, while they were at the tops of the trees—
While they were seated and conversing with the Bodhisatta, a certain jackal stood beneath that tree and,
whispering with those young swans, recited the first verse:
“Having climbed to the high branches, you deliberate in private;”
"Descend lower and deliberate; even the king of beasts will hear.
Therein, "having climbed to a high branch" means having climbed to a branch higher than this tree, which is already naturally high.
"Deliberate" means discuss or speak. "Descend lower" means having descended and stood in a lower place.
"Speak here. Thinking that even the king of beasts would hear him, he spoke while identifying himself as the king of beasts.
The young swans, filled with loathing, rose up and went back to Cittakūṭa itself.
When they had departed, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse to the jackal:
“Since the one of beautiful hue consults with the one of beautiful hue, and the god with the god—what concern is that to you, O four-legged one? Enter a hole, jackal!
In this context, *suvaṇṇo* means “of beautiful hue. *Suvaṇṇena* means “with the second young swan. *Devo devena* means...
He speaks by treating those very two as gods. Regarding the phrase *catumaṭṭhassa*:

the literal meaning of the word is "of one who is smooth (*maṭṭha*)—that is, pure—in four respects: body, birth, voice, and virtue. However, he says this while censuring that very impurity through words of praise;
the underlying intention here is: "What is there for you in being base in these four ways? [You are] like a jackal!"—"Enter the hole! he said.
Having displayed this terrifying object and driving him away, the Bodhisatta spoke thus.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the jackal was Mahallaka; the two young swans were Sāriputta and Moggallāna; and the tree deity was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Catumaṭṭha Jātaka, the seventh.
[188] 8. The Commentary on the Sihaṅguli-Sīhanakha Jātaka.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this concerning Kokālika.
It is said that one day, while others who were well-versed in the Dhamma were preaching the Dhamma, Kokālika himself also desired to preach; thus [the story] is told in its entirety.

This should be expanded upon according to the method explained below. Having heard that account of his conduct, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has become notorious for his own voice;
in the past, too, he was notorious. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a lion in the Himalayan region.
Living together with a single female jackal, he obtained a son.
In terms of these characteristics—his fingers, claws, mane, color, and shape—he resembled his father, while in his voice he resembled his mother.
Then one day, when the rain had ceased and the lions were roaring and playing their lion-sports, he too desired to roar among them.
Having uttered a lion-like roar, he let out a cry. Hearing his sound, the lions became silent.
Hearing that sound, another son of the Bodhisatta born of the same clan asked, "Father, this lion is equal to us in appearance and other qualities, yet his voice is different;
who indeed is he? and spoke the first verse:
“With lion-like fingers and lion-like claws, with feet planted like those of a lion—he is a lion who roars differently, alone within the lion-herd.

In this context, “with feet planted like those of a lion” means he stands firmly on lion-like feet. “He roars differently, alone” means that he alone, roaring with a jackal’s cry unlike that of the remaining lions, roars in a different manner.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta said, "Dear one, this is your brother; in appearance he is like me, and in voice he is like his mother.
Then, addressing the son of the female jackal, he admonished him, saying, "Dear one, from now on, while living here, live quietly;
if you roar again, they will discover your true nature as a jackal," and spoke the second verse:
“Do not roar, O prince, dwell silently in the forest;
they would recognize you by your voice, for it is not like your father’s.
There, ‘prince’ refers to the son of the lion, the king of beasts. Having heard this admonition, he did not venture to roar again.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Kokālika was the jackal; Rāhula was the son of the same clan; and as for the lion-king, he was none other than myself.
This concludes the eighth narrative, the Siha-Kotthu Jātaka.
[189] 9. The Siha-Camma Jātaka (The Lion’s Hide Jātaka) Narrative:

"This is not the lion’s roar"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing in Jeta’s Grove concerning Kokālika himself. At that time, Kokālika desired to recite the *sara-bhañña* (the rhythmic chanting of the Dhamma). Having heard of this occurrence, the Teacher related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of farmers;
having reached maturity, he made his living through the work of plowing. At that time, a certain merchant was conducting business using a load of donkeys.
He wandered about. In every place he went, he would unload a load from the back of a donkey, cover the donkey with a lion’s skin, and let it loose in the rice and barley fields.
Seeing him, the field-watchers were unable to approach because they perceived it as a "lion.
Then one day, that merchant took up residence at the gate of a certain village.
While preparing his morning meal, he put a lion’s skin over a donkey and released it into a barley field.
The field-watchers, perceiving it to be a "lion," were unable to approach; they went home and reported the matter.
The inhabitants of the entire village took up their weapons, blew conchs, beat drums, and went near the field, shouting loudly.
Terrified by the fear of death, the donkey brayed with the cry of a donkey. Then, recognizing his donkey nature, the Bodhisatta spoke the first verse:
“This is not the roar of a lion, nor of a tiger, nor of a leopard.”
“Covered with a lion’s skin, the base donkey brays.
Therein, “base” (*jammo*) means contemptible. Even the villagers, having recognized his state as a donkey, broke his bones, beat him, and departed taking the lion’s skin.
Then the merchant, having returned and seen that the donkey had met with such disaster, spoke the second verse:
“Even for a long time this donkey might eat the green barley;
yet, though covered with a lion’s skin, he only brought disgrace by braying.
In this passage, *taṃ* is a mere particle; this donkey, without making known his own donkey-nature, [donned] a lion’s skin.
The meaning is that even after a long time had passed, he might eat green barley.
"He defiled himself while braying" means that he defiled himself by braying his own donkey-bray; there was no fault here on the part of the lion’s skin.
Even as he was speaking thus, the donkey, lying right there, died, and the merchant also left, abandoning it.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the merchant was Devadatta; the donkey was Kokālika; and the wise farmer was none other than myself.
This concludes the ninth narrative, the Siṅgālacamma-jātaka. 10.
The Narrative of the Benefits of Virtue (Sīlānisaṃsa-jātaka)
"Behold through faith and virtue"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain faithful lay follower.
It is said that one day this faithful, confident noble disciple, while going to Jetavana, arrived at the bank of the Aciravatī River in the evening.
Having had the boatmen moor the boat on the shore, he went to the landing place where they had gone for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
Without seeing the boat, he took up joy directed toward the Buddha and descended into the river; his feet did not sink into the water.
As he walked as if upon the surface of the earth, when he reached the middle of the stream, he saw the waves.
Then the joy directed toward the Buddha grew weak, and his feet began to sink. He again made firm the joy directed toward the Buddha.
Having traveled by way of the water’s edge and entered Jetavana, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side.
The Teacher exchanged greetings with him and asked, “Lay follower, I hope you have come along the road without much fatigue?
He replied, “Venerable sir, having taken up rapture directed toward the Buddha, I established myself upon the surface of the water.”

When he said, "Having obtained the earth, I have come here as if trampling it," the Teacher replied, "Lay follower, you are not the only one who has gained a firm footing by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha;
in the past, too, lay followers whose ship was wrecked in the middle of the ocean gained a firm footing by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha.
Having said this, at his request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, a noble disciple who was a stream-enterer boarded a boat together with a barber-householder.

The barber’s wife said, "Noble sir, the pleasure and pain of this man is your responsibility," and she placed the barber into the hands of that lay follower. Then, on the seventh day, that boat was in the middle of the ocean.
Separated from one another, those two men, lying on the same plank, reached a single lamp.
There, that barber, having killed and cooked birds, ate them himself and gave some to the lay follower as well. The lay follower said, "Enough for me," and did not eat.
He thought: "In this place, we have no other refuge except for the Three Refuges."
Thus he recollected the virtues of the Three Jewels. As he was thus recollecting them, the Naga king who had been reborn on that island fashioned his own body into a great ship;
the deity of the ocean became the helmsman; the ship was filled with the seven kinds of jewels;
the three masts were made of sapphire (*indanīlamaṇi*); the ornament was made of gold; and [the other parts] were made of silver.
The oars were made of gold, and the rudders were made of ivory.
Standing upon the ship, the ocean deity cried out, "Is there anyone bound for Jambudīpa? The lay follower said, "We shall go.
[The deity replied,] "In that case, come; board the ship. He boarded the ship and called for his barber; then the ocean deity—

“It belongs to you alone, not to him,” he said. “For what reason? “The reason is that this man has no virtue of moral conduct (*sīlaguṇa*) or proper behavior; that is why. For I brought the boat for you, not for him.
“Very well, through the gift I have given myself, the virtue I have guarded, and the meditation I have cultivated, I give my merit to him. The barber replied, “I rejoice, master.”
The deity thought, "I shall take them now," and having placed both men upon it, she brought them out from the ocean and traveled by river to Bārāṇasī.

By her own supernatural power, she established wealth in the homes of both of them and said, "One should indeed associate only with the wise. For if this barber had associated with this lay follower..."
"If he had not come into contact with me, he would have perished right in the middle of the ocean. Speaking thus, describing the virtue of associating with the wise, she spoke these verses:
"Behold this fruit of faith, virtue, and generosity:
The Naga, by means of his ship’s beauty, carries the faithful lay follower across."
“One should associate only with the virtuous; one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
for by dwelling together with the good, even a barber attains safety.
In this context, “look” is an address meaning “look,” without specifying anyone in particular. “With faith” refers to both mundane and supramundane faith.
"Through faith. The same method applies to virtue as well. "Of generosity" means both the relinquishing of material things to be given and the relinquishing of the defilements.
"Behold this fruit" means behold this result; the sense is that it is a quality (*guṇa*) or a benefit (*ānisansa*). Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus:
"Behold the fruit of generosity, like the color of this elephant on the boat"—that is, by means of the boat.
By way of configuration. "Faith" means faith established in the Three Jewels.

"Only with the good" means only with the wise. "One should associate" means one should dwell together; the sense is that one should live in proximity. "One should make" means one should perform. "Familiarity" means intimacy with friends.
However, intimacy born of craving should not be formed with anyone. "The barber" refers to a barber-householder; there is also a reading, "the bath-attendant."
Thus the ocean deity, standing in the air, taught the Dhamma and gave exhortation, then took the Naga king and returned to her own celestial mansion.
The Teacher, having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka.

At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of a Once-returner (sakadāgāmiphala). "At that time, the lay follower who had attained stream-entry (sotāpanna) passed away into Parinibbāna; as for the Naga king..."
"Sāriputta was he, but I myself was the ocean deity.
This concludes the tenth commentary, the Sīlānisaṃsa Jātaka.
The fourth chapter, the Asadisa Vagga, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Asadisa and Saṅgāma, Vālodaka and Giridatta;
Nabhirati and Dadhivāha, Catumaṭṭha and Sīhakoṭṭha.
The Lion’s Hide: The Benefits of Virtue.
5. The Ruhaka Chapter [191]. 1.
The Commentary on the Ruhaka Jātaka.
"Even though the *ruhaka* plant is cut," the Teacher said this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction by his former wife.
The story will be revealed in the *Indriya-jātaka* of the *Aṭṭhaka-nipāta*. However, the Teacher addressed that bhikkhu:
"This woman has brought you harm; even in the past, she caused you shame in the midst of an assembly including the king."
Having said, "He caused the appearance of departing from his home," when requested by him, he related a past event.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen.
Upon reaching maturity, after the death of his father, he was established in the kingdom and ruled it according to the Dhamma. To him—
There was a chaplain named Ruhaka, whose wife was a brahmin woman named Purāṇī.
The king, having adorned the horse with the brahmin’s own trappings, gave it to him. He would mount that horse and go to attend upon the king.
Then, seeing him sitting on the back of the adorned horse as he went to and fro, here and there—
The people standing there praised only the horse, saying, "Oh, what beauty this horse has! Oh, how splendid the horse looks!
Having returned home and ascended the palace, he addressed his wife: "My dear, our horse is exceedingly beautiful;
people standing on both sides are praising only our horse. But that brahmin woman said only a little:
Chinnikā was a procuress; she said this to him: "Noble sir, you do not know the means for a horse to look beautiful.
This horse looks beautiful by virtue of his own decorated horse-trappings.
If you too wish to look beautiful like a horse, you should put on horse-trappings, descend into the middle of the street, and stamp your feet like a horse."
“Go and see the king; the king will praise you, and the people will also praise you.

Having heard her words, that madman, not knowing that she was speaking to him for such a reason, perceived it to be so and acted accordingly. Whomever he saw, they would mock him, saying, “He looks well...”
They said, "He is the teacher. But the king, saying to him, "What is it, teacher? Is your bile disturbed? Have you become insane?

and so forth, put him to shame. At that time, the brahmin, feeling ashamed that he had acted improperly, became angry with his wife and thought, "I have been put to shame here in the midst of this assembly including the king; I shall beat her and cast her out from the house. He went home.
He arrived. The unchaste brahmin woman, having become angry with him and learning of his arrival, departed even earlier through the small gate;
she went to the royal residence and remained there for four or five days.
When the king learned of this matter, he summoned the chaplain and said, "Teacher, it is only natural that a woman has faults; as for this brahmin woman—"
"It is right to forgive," he said, and for the sake of asking for forgiveness, he first spoke this verse:
"Even though it is broken, O Rūhaka, the bowstring can be joined again;
let it be joined with the old one, do not fall under the power of anger."

In this regard, the summary of the meaning is as follows: "O Ruhaka, surely even a bow that has been broken is joined and restored once more; in the same way, you too should be reconciled with your former wife; do not fall under the power of anger.
Having heard this, Ruhaka spoke the second verse:
"When arrows are available, when materials for repair exist..."
"I shall make another string; there is no need for this old one.

Its meaning is: "O Great King, while bow-makers, fletchers, and those who make strings are available, I shall make another string; enough with this old string that has been broken—there is no purpose for me in it."
Having spoken thus, he had her removed and brought another brahmin woman.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka:
at the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, O Brahmin, the former wife was she."
“The monk Ruhaka was one who was weary of the world, while I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī.
This is the first commentary on the Ruhaka Jātaka.
[192] 2. The Commentary on the Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka.
"A woman may be beautiful"—this is the *Sirikāḷakaṇṇi-jātaka*, which will appear in the *Mahā-umaṅga-jātaka*.
The second commentary, the *Sirikāḷakaṇṇi-jātaka-vaṇṇanā*, is finished.
[193] 3. The Commentary on the *Cūḷa-paduma-jātaka* (The Lesser Lotus Birth Story).
“This very one is she; I too am he, not another”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk who was despondent.

The background story will be revealed in the Ummādantī Jātaka. When the Teacher asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are despondent? he replied, “It is true, Blessed One. [The Teacher continued: “But by whom were you...?”
When he said, "I am distressed," he replied, "Venerable sir, having seen a woman adorned and prepared for a tryst, I became subject to defilements and grew distressed.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Bhikkhu, a woman is indeed ungrateful, treacherous to her friends, and full of guile;
even the ancient sages, after making their own blood flow from the right knee, [offered] gifts as long as they lived..."
Having said, "They could not win over the heart of the woman," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen;
on the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name "Padumakumāra. Some time later, six...
They became his younger brothers. When those seven men had gradually reached maturity, they took up the life of householders and lived about like the king's companions.
Then one day, as the king stood watching the royal courtyard, he saw them approaching to wait upon him with a great retinue;
suspecting that "these might kill me and seize the kingdom," he conceived a fear.
Having summoned them, he said: "Sirs, you are not permitted to live in this city;
go elsewhere, and after my passing, come back and take the kingdom that belongs to our lineage.
Accepting their father’s words, they wept and wailed, went to their respective homes, took their wives, and [departed] to wherever it might be.
Or, having gone [elsewhere], we shall live. Having departed from the city and traveled along the road, they reached a wilderness where they found no food or drink.

Unable to endure their hunger, they thought, “If we remain alive, we will obtain women,” and so they killed the youngest brother’s wife, divided her flesh into thirteen portions, and ate it. The Bodhisatta and his own wife...
And among the portions they had obtained, setting aside one, they ate even two. Thus, having killed six women over six days, they ate their flesh.
But the Bodhisatta, day after day, set aside one for each and set apart six portions. On the seventh day—
When they said, “We shall kill the Bodhisatta’s wife,” the Bodhisatta gave those six portions to them and said, “Eat these six portions for today; we shall see tomorrow.
After they had eaten the meat, he took his wife and fled while they were asleep. Having gone a short distance, she said, “I cannot go further, my lord.”
He said: Then the Bodhisatta, taking her upon his shoulder, departed from the wilderness at the time of sunrise.
When the sun had risen, she said, "I am thirsty, my lord. The Bodhisatta replied, "There is no water, dear lady.
When she spoke thus again and again, he struck his right knee with his sword and said, "Dear lady, there is no drinking water; however, this [blood] of mine..."
“Sit down while drinking the blood from your right knee,” he said. She did accordingly. Gradually they reached the Great Gaṅgā;
having drunk, bathed, and eaten various fruits, they rested in a comfortable spot.
Then, establishing a hermitage at a bend in the Gaṅgā, they made their dwelling there.
Then one day, on the upper reaches of the Ganges, they had a criminal who had offended against the king have his hands, feet, ears, and nose cut off;
having laid him down in a wooden tub, they set him adrift upon the great Ganges. He reached that spot crying out with a great cry of distress.
The Bodhisatta, hearing his piteous sound of lamentation, [thought], "He has fallen into suffering..."
Thinking, "While I am here, let not this creature perish," he went to the bank of the Ganges, rescued him, and brought him back to his hermitage.
There, he performed medical treatment for the wound by washing it with yellow robes (*kāṣāya*) and applying medicinal ointments.

However, his wife, saying, "He has married such an immoral, crippled man and is now living with him, tending to him," wandered about loathing that cripple and spitting upon him. Thus the Bodhisatta [acted].
When his wounds had fully healed, he established him right there in the hermitage and, together with his wife, gathered fruits from the forest to support both him and his wife.
While they were living in this manner, that woman became infatuated with the cripple;
having committed immoral acts with him and desiring to kill the Bodhisatta by some means, she spoke as follows:
“Master, while we were departing from the wilderness, I sat upon your shoulder and, seeing a mountain, made this appeal to the deity born on that mountain:
‘If I shall obtain life safely together with my husband, I will perform an offering for you.
Now she is frightening me; let us perform an offering for her.”
The Bodhisatta, not knowing that trick, accepted it saying, “Very well,” prepared the offering, had her take the vessel of offerings, and ascended to the summit of the mountain.
Then she said to him, “Lord, you alone are the supreme deity even among deities;
first, therefore, worship the forest flowers, circumambulate them, and pay homage to them, and only afterwards—”

“I shall perform an offering to the deity. Having placed the Bodhisatta facing toward the precipice, she worshipped him with forest flowers, circumambulated him, and, as if wishing to pay homage, stood behind him.

Striking him on the back, she caused him to fall over the precipice. Thinking, “I have seen the back of my enemy,” she descended from the mountain with a joyful heart and went into the presence of Kuṇṭha.
The Bodhisatta, falling from the mountain following the path of the precipice, caught on a thornless, leaf-covered bough at the top of an udumbara tree;
however, he was unable to descend to the base of the mountain.
Having eaten the udumbara fruits, he sat down among the branches. Then, a large-bodied king of monkeys climbed up from the foot of the lower mountain.
He was eating the udumbara fruits there. Having seen the Bodhisatta on that day, he fled;

on the following day, he returned, ate some fruits from one side, and departed. As he came again and again in this manner, he gained confidence with the Bodhisatta and asked, "For what reason have you come to this place? To which [the Bodhisatta replied], "By this..."
When this was said, he replied, "In that case, do not fear," and having laid the Bodhisatta upon his back,
carried him down from the forest, set him upon the great highway, and dismissed him with the words, "Go by this path," he himself entered the forest once more.
The Bodhisatta went to a certain village and, while staying right there, [sent word] to his father...
Having heard of the king’s death, he went to Bārāṇasī and, being established in the kingdom inherited from his family, became known as King Paduma.
Without violating the ten duties of a king, he ruled righteously;

having constructed six alms-halls—at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the door of his own residence—he bestowed gifts daily, distributing six hundred thousand pieces of money each day.
That woman, having seated the cripple on her shoulder and emerged from the forest, wandered for alms along the public road;
collecting rice gruel and food, she nourished that cripple. When people asked her, "Who is this to you?", she replied, "He is my maternal uncle's daughter;
he is my father's sister's son. They gave me to him."
“Thus, even though my husband had reached the point of being condemned to death, I supported him by carrying him about on my shoulders and wandering for alms.
From that time on, people, thinking, “This woman is devoted to her husband,” gave her much more rice porridge and food.
However, other people said this: “Do not wander about like that; King Paduma rules the kingdom in Bārāṇasī over the whole of Jambudīpa.”
"Agitate him and give alms; when he sees that, he will be pleased, and being pleased, he will give you much wealth.
Leave your husband right here and go! Thus they gave her a sturdy bamboo basket.
That woman of immoral conduct, having seated that cripple in the bamboo basket and lifted up the basket, went to Benares and [stood] at the halls of almsgiving.

She wandered about eating. The Bodhisatta, having gone to the alms-distribution site mounted on the back of a decorated noble elephant, would give alms with his own hands to eight or ten people and then return home.
That woman of improper conduct, having seated that cripple upon a basket and lifted up the basket, stood in the path of his departure.
The king, seeing her, asked, "What is this? "O King, it is a woman devoted to her husband," they replied.
Then, having summoned her and recognized her, he had the cripple removed from the basket and asked, "Who is this to you?
She said, "O King, he is my paternal uncle's son, my husband, given to me by my family. People, unaware of that inner circumstance, exclaimed, "Oh, what a devoted wife! and so forth.
They praised that misconduct. Again the king asked, "Is this your husband, the dull-witted heir of the family?
Not recognizing the king, she spoke boldly, saying, "Yes, Your Majesty. Then the king said to her, "Is he the son of the King of Bārāṇasī?
Are you not the wife of Prince Paduma and the daughter of such-and-such a king? You are named So-and-so, my own kinswoman."
"Having drunk from this well, she whose heart was bound to it threw me down the precipice.
Now, having seized Death by the forehead, you have come to this place thinking, 'He is dead,' yet am I not indeed alive?
Having said this, he addressed his ministers: "O ministers, did I not answer when questioned by you thus: 'My younger brother...'"

Six women killed me and ate my flesh; however, I restored my own wife to health, led her to the banks of the Ganges, and while living in a hermitage, I rescued and cared for a cripple who was destined for execution.
That woman, her heart bound to him, threw me down at the foot of a mountain. Yet, through my own mind of loving-kindness (*mettacitta*), I preserved my life.

“They have obtained [their reward]. She by whom I was cast down from the mountain is none other than this unvirtuous woman; and he who reached the point of execution, the cripple, is none other than this very man.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“This is she indeed, and I am he, no other; this is that very one with the severed hand, no other.”
"He who said, 'She is my wife since childhood,' there is no truth among women in that he avoided other women.
Having struck this wretch with a pestle— this corpse who consorted with another's wife—
cut off the ears and nose of her, his evil wife, while she is still alive."
In that regard, as for what she said, "He is my *komārapati*," meaning she said, "This is my husband, given by my family, my *komārapati*";
it is he himself and no other. There is also the reading, "What they call *komārapati*. For this very reading is written in the manuscripts;
its meaning is also the same, though a transposition of words (*vacanavipallāsa*) should be understood here. For that which was spoken by the king is precisely this.
“Has come here. Regarding “Vajjhitthiyo”: women are called *vajjhitthiyo* because they must be slain (*vajjha*)—that is, they are to be killed.
“There is no truth in women”: among them, there is not even a single inherent nature (*sabhāva*). “And this wretch,” and so forth, is said for the purpose of inflicting punishment upon both of them.
In that context, “wretch” (*jamman*) means base or contemptible. “Having struck with a pestle” means having struck and beaten with a pestle until the bones [are crushed].
"Having broken it, having reduced it to powder and fragments. "Ludda" means cruel. "Chava" means lifeless, like a corpse, due to the absence of virtues.
Regarding the word "ca" in the phrase "imissā ca": here, "ca" is merely a particle;
the meaning is, "Even while she is still alive—this wicked, unchaste, and immoral woman—cut off her ears and nose."
The Bodhisatta, unable to endure his anger, did not act exactly as he had commanded them after issuing the punishment.
Instead, suppressing his wrath, he had her bound more tightly so that she could not lift the basket from her head;
then, having a blunt weapon thrust into it, he had her driven out from his own realm.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
at the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the six brothers were certain elders;
the wife was Ciñcā Māṇavikā; the cripple was Devadatta; the bull-king Godha was Ānanda; and as for the lotus-king, he was none other than myself.”
The third: The Commentary on the Cūḷapaduma Jātaka.
[194] 4. The Commentary on the Maṇicora Jātaka:
"There are no gods; they have surely gone away"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning one who was plotting for his own destruction.
He spoke concerning Devadatta. At that time, however, having heard that "Devadatta is plotting for my death," the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Devadatta plotted for my death, yet even though he plotted, he was unable to kill me.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a household of a householder in a village not far from Benares.
When he had reached maturity, they brought him a daughter of a noble family from Benares;
she was golden-hued, beautiful, lovely to behold, like a celestial nymph, like a flowering creeper, and like a graceful, intoxicated kinnarī.
And Sujātā by name was devoted to her husband, endowed with virtue and good conduct, and perfected in her duties.
She always performed her service toward him, as well as her service toward her mother-in-law and father-in-law; she was dear and pleasing to the Bodhisatta.
Thus, both of them, living in harmony and with one mind, dwelt together in concord.
Then one day, Sujātā said to the Bodhisatta, "We wish to see our parents.
He replied, "Very well, my dear; prepare enough provisions for the journey.
Having had various kinds of snacks prepared and placed them in a carriage, he stood before the carriage driving it, while the other stood behind. They arrived near the city.
Having arrived, they unyoked the carriage, bathed, and ate. Then the Bodhisatta yoked the carriage and sat in the front;
Sujātā changed her clothes, adorned herself, and sat behind him.
As the carriage entered the city, the King of Bārāṇasī, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, came to that place while performing a circumambulation of the city.
Sujātā descended and proceeded on foot behind the carriage. When the king saw her, his eyes were drawn by the perfection of her beauty;
his heart becoming bound to her, he commanded a minister:
"Go, find out whether she has a husband or is without one. Having gone and ascertained that she had a husband, he returned.
“Your Majesty, the man sitting in the carriage is indeed her husband,” he said.
The king, unable to dispel his infatuation and becoming afflicted by passion, thought, “I will kill him by some means or other and take the woman.
Having thus reflected, he addressed a man: “Go, sir, with this crest-jewel...”
"Act as if you were walking along the street, place this in this man's carriage, and then come back," he said, giving him the crest-jewel and sending him away.
"Very well," he replied, took it, went there, placed it in the carriage, and returned to report, "It has been deposited for me, Your Majesty.
The king said, "My crest-jewel is lost! and the people raised a great clamor. The king—
“Close all the gates, cut off all movement, and search for the thief,” he said; the king’s men did accordingly, and the city was thrown into a great commotion.
The other man, taking some people with him, went to the Bodhisatta and said, “Sir, stop the carriage;
the king’s crest-jewel has been lost, and we must clear the carriage. He [stopped] the carriage.
While searching, he found the jewel he himself had placed there; seizing the Bodhisatta, he beat him with his hands and feet, crying out, “Jewel-thief!
He bound the man’s hands behind his back, led him away, and presented him to the king, saying, “This is the jewel-thief.
The king then commanded, “Behead him!”
Then the king’s men, lashing him with whips four by four, drove him out of the city through the southern gate.
Sujātā too, abandoning her carriage and raising her arms, followed behind him wailing, "My lord, it is because of me that you have met with this suffering!
The king’s men, intending to cut off his head, said:
They laid the Bodhisatta down on his back. Seeing him, Sujātā reflected upon her own virtue and said,
"I suppose there are no deities in this world capable of restraining wicked and violent men who would harm those possessed of virtue," and having spoken thus,
she uttered the first verse:
“There are no gods who purify; surely there are no guardians of the world here.
For those who act with violence and are unrestrained, surely there are no restrainers.
In this context, “there are no gods” means that in this world there are none who look after the virtuous nor any who restrain the wicked.
"Surely there are gods. Regarding such matters as these, "surely they wander," meaning they go into exile.
"In this world, O World-Protectors"—even those recluses and brahmins who are regarded as world-protectors in this world, who assist the virtuous, surely do not exist.
"Of those acting with violence, the unrestrained"—that is, those who act with violence without reflection.
Of those who perform cruel deeds and are immoral. "Those who prohibit" means those who forbid them, saying, "Do not do such a deed;
it is not permitted to do this"—the meaning is that they say, "There is no [such thing].
Thus, while she, endowed with virtue, was lamenting, the seat of Sakka, the king of the gods, became hot.
Sakka manifested himself and, reflecting, "Who indeed wishes to displace me from the position of Sakka? he understood this reason.
Thinking, "The King of Bārāṇasī is performing an exceedingly cruel deed; he oppresses Sujāta, who is endowed with virtue.
It is now fitting for me to go," he descended from the world of the gods and, by his own supernatural power, [confronted] that wicked king seated upon the back of an elephant.
Having caused him to descend from the back of the elephant, he had him laid flat on his back upon the stone slab for execution;
then, lifting up the Bodhisatta, he adorned him with all ornaments, had him don the royal attire, and seated him upon the elephant’s back.
The king’s men, raising their axes and severing the head, cut off the king’s head, and at the very moment it was severed, the king—

They recognized his state as that of a prince. Sakka, the king of the gods, approached the Bodhisatta with his visible body, performed the royal consecration for the Bodhisatta, and appointed Sujātā as his chief queen.
When the ministers, brahmins, householders, and others saw Sakka, the king of the gods, they said, "The unrighteous king has been slain; now, by us—"
They were filled with joy, thinking, "A righteous king, a son of Sakka, has been obtained.
Standing in the sky, Sakka said, "This is your king, a son of Sakka; from now on he will rule according to the Dhamma.
For if a king is unrighteous, the rain falls out of season and does not fall at the proper time, and there is fear of drought and fear of disease."
"Regarding 'the fear of weapons,' these three fears have indeed come upon him. Speaking thus as he exhorted him, he spoke the second verse:
"The rain falls for him out of season, and it does not rain for him in season;
he falls from his place in heaven—has he not been slain by that much?"
In that context, "out of season" means it rains during the reign of an unrighteous king, at an improper time, when the crops have ripened, or during the time of harvesting and threshing.
"In season" means it does not rain at the proper and appropriate times, such as during the sowing season, when the young crops are growing, or during the period of conception.
"And he falls from his heavenly state" means he falls from the celestial worlds, which are designated as "heaven."

For an unrighteous king indeed falls from the world of the gods by way of non-attainment; or rather, the meaning is that even while exercising sovereignty in heaven, an unrighteous king falls from there.
"Is he not slain by that much?"—is it not the case that this unrighteous king is slain by just this much?
Alternatively, the particle *nu* here expresses a single-pointed certainty: he is not slain by this much alone with absolute certainty.
The meaning here is that he will be slain for a long time in the eight great hells and the sixteen secondary hells.
Having thus given this exhortation to the great multitude, Sakka returned to his own celestial abode. The Bodhisatta, too, having ruled the kingdom with righteousness, filled the city of heaven.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka: "At that time..."
"The unrighteous king was Devadatta; Sakka was Anuruddha; Sujātā, the mother of Rāhula, was [Sujātā];
and the King Sakkadattiya was none other than myself.
This concludes the fourth commentary, the Maṇicora Jātaka.
[195] 5. The Commentary on the Pabbatūpatthara Jātaka.
“On the delightful mountain-spread,” this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the King of Kosala.
It is said that a certain minister of the King of Kosala became lustful toward a woman in the inner palace. The king, upon investigating the matter, recognized him as he truly was.

Having learned this, thinking, "I shall inform the Teacher," he went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked, "Venerable Sir, a certain minister in our inner palace has become lustful; what should be done with him?
Then the Teacher, having asked, "Great King, that minister and that woman are both dear to you, are they not? he replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir, they are exceedingly dear to me."
When he said, "She supports the entire royal household, and she too is dear to me," [the Elder] replied,
"Great King, 'It is impossible to offend one's benefactors, servants, or beloved wives'— having heard this teaching from the wise in the past,
kings remained impartial. Having said this, when requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of ministers.

Upon reaching maturity, he became the counselor who instructed the king in matters of welfare and righteousness. At that time, one of the king’s ministers became lustful toward a woman in the inner palace.
When the king learned of this as it truly was, he thought: “This minister is very helpful to me, and this woman is dear to me; yet both of these must be destroyed.”
“It is not possible; having asked the wise minister a question, if it can be answered, I shall answer it, but if it cannot, I shall not.

Having thus summoned the Bodhisatta, given him a seat, and said, “Wise man, I shall ask you a question,” and the other having replied, “Ask, Great King, I shall answer,” he asked the question and spoke the first verse:
“In a delightful expanse spread at the foot of a mountain, a lovely lotus pond was formed;
a jackal drank from it, knowing it was protected by a lion.
Therein, “in a delightful expanse spread at the foot of a mountain” means in a courtyard-like area situated at the base of the Himalayan mountains.
The meaning is as follows: "A pleasant lotus pond has arisen" means that a pleasant, cool, and sweet-watered lotus pond has been produced;
furthermore, even a river covered with lotuses is indeed called a "lotus pond. Regarding the word *apāpāyi*: *apa-* is a prefix, and the meaning is "one who does not go away" (*apāyī*).
"Knowing it was protected by a lion" means that the lotus pond was enjoyed by a lion and thus protected by him; he too—
The jackal, knowing full well that "this [water] is protected by the lion," drank it. What do you think?
Would a foolish jackal drink from such a lotus pond without fearing the lion? This is the intended meaning here.
The Bodhisatta, realizing, "Surely there must be a corrupt official in this man's inner court," spoke the second verse:
“If they drink from the great river, O Great King, even though it is full of creatures, it does not thereby cease to be a river; forgive them if they are dear to you.
In this context, “full of creatures” (*sāpadāni*) means not only jackals, but all other predatory animals such as dogs, wild boars, cats, deer, and so forth.
If they drink from that river, which has received the name "Pokkhaṇī" because it is covered with lotuses (*pokkhara*), it does not thereby cease to be a river.
For in a river, both bipeds and quadrupeds, as well as snakes and fish—all who are thirsty—drink the water;
yet for that reason, it does not become what is called a "non-river," nor does it become a "river of leftovers. Why? Because it is common to all.

Just as a river is not defiled by being drunk from by anyone whatsoever, so too a woman who, out of the influence of the defilements (*kilesa*), transgresses her husband and enters into a union with another, does not thereby cease to be a woman. Why? Because she remains common to all. Nor is she a "defiled woman" (*ucchiṭṭhitthī*). Why?
Because of her proximity to water and her state of purity. "Forgive me, if you love me."
"But if that woman is dear to you, and that minister has been very helpful, then forgive both of them and remain in a state of equanimity.
Thus the Great Being gave this counsel to the king. The king, abiding by his advice, said, "Do not commit such an evil deed again," and forgave both of them.
From then on, they desisted. The king as well [practiced] giving and the other perfections.
Having performed meritorious deeds, at the end of his life he filled the city of heaven.
The King of Kosala, having heard this teaching on the Dhamma, forgave both of them and remained impartial toward them.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time the king was Ānanda, but the wise minister was none other than myself."
The fifth: The Commentary on the Pabbatūpatthara Jātaka.
[196] 6. The Commentary on the Valāhaka Jātaka.
"Those who will not follow this advice..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who was dissatisfied with the religious life.
He related it. For that bhikkhu, when asked by the Teacher, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are disenchanted?", said, "It is true.
When asked, "For what reason?", he replied, "Because I saw a woman adorned with ornaments, and through the influence of defilement.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Bhikkhu, these women indeed [possess] their own forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles..."
By means of feminine gestures and charms, they entice men, bring them under their control, and once they know those men have come under their sway,
they are called “yakkhinīs” in the sense that they cause the ruin of virtue and the ruin of wealth.
For in the past as well, yakkhinīs approached a company of men with feminine gestures, enticed the merchants, and [brought them under their power].
"Having made them their vessels, they saw other men again;
having brought all of them to the end of their lives, they filled their mouths with blood streaming from both sides of their jaws and devoured them. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, there was a city of yakkhas called Sirīsavatthu, where yakkhinīs resided.
When the merchants whose ships had been wrecked arrived, she— adorned and dressed in finery,
surrounded by a retinue of female slaves and carrying her children on her hips— approached them. To give them the impression that they had reached a human habitation,
she had people tending cattle and guarding fields, as well as herds of cows and dogs, stationed here and there.
They show themselves and, going to the merchants, say, "Drink this rice-gruel, eat this meal, and consume this hard food.
The merchants, being unaware, partake of what is given by them.
Then, after they have eaten, drunk, and rested, [the women] offer a greeting, saying, "Where do you dwell? From where..."
They asked, "Where have you come from? Where will you go? For what purpose have you come here?
When they replied, "We have come here because our ship was wrecked," [the others said], "Excellent, noble ladies!
Three years have passed since our own masters boarded their ship and departed; they must be dead. You too are surely merchants; we [will take care of] you..."
Having said, "We shall become attendants to your feet," they enticed those merchants with feminine gestures, charms, expressions, and seductive graces;
then, leading them to the city of the *yakkhas*, if there were men previously captured, they bound them with divine chains and cast them into the prison-house.
However, not finding any men from the wrecked ships in their own dwelling place, they [acted as follows].
"Beautiful on one side, like an island of serpents on the other"—thus they wander along the shore of the ocean; this is their natural disposition.
Then one day, five hundred merchants whose ship had been wrecked landed near their city.
They went to them, seduced them, and led them to the city of the *yakkhas*, where they bound the men previously captured with divine chains.
Having bound the chief merchant and cast him into the prison-house,
the senior yakkhinī and the remaining five hundred yakkhinīs made those five hundred merchants their husbands. Then,
when the merchants had fallen asleep during the night, that senior yakkhinī rose, went to the prison-house, and killed the men there, taking their flesh.
Having eaten, she returned; the others did exactly the same.
When the eldest female *yakkha* returned after eating human flesh, her body was cold. As the elder merchant examined her, he realized she was a *yakkhinī*.
Thinking, "These five hundred must be *yakkhinīs*; we ought to flee," he [prepared to depart] early the next morning.
Having gone to wash his face, he informed the remaining merchants: "These are female *yakkhas*, not human women;
when other ships arrive, they will claim those as their owners and devour us as well. Come, let us flee from here!
Of those five hundred, two hundred and fifty said, "We cannot abandon them; you go."
"We shall not flee," they said. The senior merchant, taking two hundred and fifty of his followers who were obedient to his word, fled in fear of them.

At that time, however, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a cloud-demon; he was entirely white, with a black head and hair like muñja grass, possessing supernormal powers and the ability to travel through the air.
He leaped from the Himalayas into the sky and went to the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
There, having eaten wild-growing rice in the Tambapaṇṇi lake-pool, he would depart.
And as he was going, thinking, "There are those who wish to go to the countryside," he spoke three times in a human voice imbued with compassion.
Hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, they approached him, raised their joined palms, and said, "Master, we [wish to go to the countryside]..."
"Let us go," they said. "In that case, mount upon my back," he replied. Some indeed mounted;
among them, some grasped his tail, while others stood right there with their hands joined in reverent salutation.
By his own supernatural power, the Bodhisatta [carried] all those two hundred and fifty merchants, even including those who merely stood with hands joined in salutation.
Having led them to the countryside and established them in their respective places, he returned to his own dwelling place.
Those yakkhinīs, moreover, whenever others arrived, would kill and eat the two hundred and fifty men who had been left behind there.
The Teacher addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, just as those merchants who fell under the power of the yakkhinīs met their end..."
Just as merchants who have reached [their destination] and obey the command of King Valāhaka establish themselves in their respective places,
even so, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who do not follow the instruction of the Buddhas undergo great suffering in the four states of misery (apāya),
in the fivefold bonds, in places of forced labor, and so forth. However, those three who follow the instruction...
"Having attained these stations— the perfections of noble birth in the six heavens of sensual pleasure and the twenty Brahma-worlds—
and having realized the great Nibbāna, the Deathless, they experience great happiness," he said, and having become fully enlightened, he spoke these verses:
"Those men who do not follow the advice taught by the Buddha..."
“They will meet with disaster, like merchants [attacked] by ogresses.
But those men who follow the advice taught by the Buddha will reach safety on the further shore, like merchants [guided] by a favorable wind.”
In this context, "those who will not do so" means those who will not practice. "They will go to ruin" means they will meet with great destruction.
"Like merchants by ogresses" means like merchants enticed by ogresses. "They will reach the further shore in safety" means they will attain *nibbāna* without obstacle.
"Like merchants by a cloud" means like those [merchants] to whom a cloud says, "Come! and so forth.
They are like the merchants who, having been told [to go], carried out his instructions.

For just as they, having gone to the further shore of the ocean, returned to their respective homes, so too those who follow the advice of the Buddhas go to Nibbāna, the further shore of saṃsāra; thus he grasped the pinnacle of the teaching of the Dhamma through the great Nibbāna of the Deathless.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:

at the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and many others likewise attained the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship.
"At that time, the two hundred and fifty merchants who carried out King Valāhakassara’s command were the Buddha’s retinue."
They were those very ones; as for King Valāhakassarā, he was none other than myself.
This concludes the sixth narrative, the Commentary on the Valāhakassara Jātaka.
[197] 7. The Commentary on the Mittāmitta Jātaka.
"He does not smile upon seeing him"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain bhikkhu.

A certain bhikkhu, thinking, "My preceptor will not be angry with me for what I take," took a piece of cloth entrusted to him out of trust by his preceptor and made it into a sandal-bag; afterwards, [he approached] the preceptor...
He took leave of him. Then the preceptor said to him, "For what reason did you take it?
When he replied, "I took it out of confidence in you, thinking that you would not be angry if I had taken it," the preceptor said, "What kind of confidence do you have toward me?
Becoming enraged, he rose up and struck him. That act of his became known among the monks. Then one day, while the monks were in the Dhamma hall...

How did they report it? “Friends, it seems that a certain young man, having taken a piece of cloth out of trust in his preceptor, made a sandal-bag for him. Then the preceptor, saying, ‘What kind of trust do you have toward me?
became angry, rose up, and struck him. The Teacher approached and asked, “Bhikkhus, what is this that you are discussing?”
Having asked, "Are you sitting here now for this discussion? and being told, "Indeed we are," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that this monk has been distrustful toward his own student;
even in the past he was distrustful. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi.

Having reached maturity, he went forth into the ascetic life, developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and having become the leader of a community, he made his dwelling in the Himalayan region.
In that group of seers, one ascetic, disregarding the Bodhisatta’s words, took charge of a dead mother elephant’s calf. When it had grown up, he killed it.

He entered the forest. After performing the funeral rites for his body, the company of seers surrounded the Bodhisatta and asked: "Venerable sir, by what cause or for what reason can friendship or enmity be known?
The Bodhisatta, explaining, "By this and that cause," spoke these verses:
“Seeing him, one does not smile; nor does one greet him back;
one does not even offer a glance, and behaves with hostility.
These are the signs established in an enemy.”
"By seeing and hearing, the wise person should recognize these as enemies.
In this context, "he does not smile upon seeing him" means that one who is an enemy to another does not smile upon seeing that person;
he does not laugh, nor does he display a joyful countenance. "Nor does he greet him back" refers to that [enemy].
Even upon hearing those words, he does not greet that person; he does not rejoice, saying, "Well said, well spoken. And as for "he does not give his eyes":
he does not look by meeting eye with eye face-to-face, but turns his eyes away elsewhere.
And as for "he behaves contrarily": he finds neither the person's bodily action nor their verbal action pleasing, maintaining a contrary attitude.
He adopts a hostile attitude. "Causes" means reasons. By which [causes] one knows an enemy:
by seeing or hearing those reasons, a wise person would know, "This person is my enemy. Conversely, from the opposite of these, friendship is to be known.
Thus, having explained the causes for the states of friend and enemy, the Bodhisatta developed the divine abodes (brahmavihāras) and went to the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the elephant-keeper ascetic was the co-resident disciple, the elephant was the preceptor, the company of seers was the Buddha’s retinue, and I myself was the leader of the group.
The seventh commentary on the *Mittāmitta-jātaka*.
8. The *Rādha-jātaka* Commentary.
"‘I have returned from my journey, dear one’—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain dissatisfied monk.
It is said that when the Teacher asked him, ‘Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?
he replied, ‘It is true, Venerable Sir. When asked, ‘For what reason? he said, ‘Because I saw a well-adorned woman and was overcome by defilement.’"
Then the Teacher said to him, “Monk, women cannot be guarded. Even in the past, those who stationed doorkeepers and tried to guard them were unable to do so.
What use have you for a woman? Even if one is obtained, she cannot be guarded. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a quail; his name was Rādha.
His name was [Mahā] Kaccāna, and his younger brother was named Poṭṭhapāda.
While both were still young, a hunter captured them and gave them to a certain brahmin in Bārāṇasī; the brahmin placed them in the position of sons and cared for them.
However, the brahmin’s wife was unguarded, immoral, and unchaste. Once, while the brahmin was going out on business—
Having addressed his two young sons, he said, "Sons, I am going away for the purpose of conducting business;
whether it be at the proper time or at an improper time, you should keep watch over your mother’s conduct and find out whether or not another man has come to her.
Having thus entrusted the brahmin woman to the care of his two young sons, he departed. From the moment of his departure, she...
From that time on, he behaved improperly; there was no limit to his coming and going, even by night and by day.

Seeing this, Poṭṭhapāda asked Rādha: "The brahmin went away after handing this brahmin woman over to us, yet she commits evil deeds; do you say so? Rādha said, "Do not say so. He [Poṭṭhapāda] [spoke] to him...
Not accepting her words, he said, "Mother, for what reason do you commit such an evil deed?
Desiring to kill him, she called out to him as if with affection, saying, "Dear son, you are indeed my son; from now on I shall not do it. Come, dear son, come for a moment.
Having seized him when he had approached, she said, "You are lecturing me; you do not know your own measure," and she wrung his neck.
Having turned her over and killed her, he threw her into the spaces between the cooking hearths. When the brahmin returned, rested, and asked the Bodhisatta, "What is it, dear Rādha?
Is your mother behaving improperly, or not? he spoke the first verse:
"Dear father, I have returned from my journey; I have just now arrived."
“I hope, dear father, that your mother does not serve another man?

The meaning of this is: “Dear Rādha, I have returned from my journey, and I have only just now arrived, not long ago. Not knowing what has been happening, I ask you: ‘I hope, dear father, that your mother does not serve another man?
Rādha, making it known that “Father, those called wise do not speak of what is real or unreal if it is not conducive to liberation,” spoke the second verse.
“But this is not well-spoken, this speech endowed with truth;
Poṭṭhapāda would rather lie down, roasted upon glowing embers.
In that context, *giraṃ* means speech. For just as it is called *girā* now, so too was it called *giraṃ* at that time; it refers to that young parrot.
He spoke thus without taking [the word] *liṅga* into account. However, this is the meaning here:

"My dear, for one called a wise man, even a statement that is truthful, in accordance with reality, meaningful, and consistent with the nature of things, is not well-spoken if it does not lead to liberation.
And one who speaks a truth that does not lead to liberation would lie like Poṭṭhapāda, being roasted in embers—just as Poṭṭhapāda was scorched in the hot ashes."
“...he lies down, thinking, ‘May I lie down thus. There is also a reading, “upakūḷhito,” which has the same meaning.
Having thus taught the Dhamma to the brahmin, the Bodhisatta thought, “It is not possible for me to dwell in this place either,” and after taking leave of the brahmin, he entered the forest itself.
The Teacher, having brought forward this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths—
The dejected bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, Poṭṭhapāda was Ānanda, while I myself was Rādha.
This is the eighth commentary on the Rādhajātika.
[199] 9. The Commentary on the Householder Jātaka.
"Both of these are not pleasing to me"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was despondent.
And in speaking, he said: "Womenfolk are indeed unprotected; having committed an evil deed, by whatever means..."
"Indeed, she deceives her husband," he said, and then related a story of the past.
Long ago, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a household of gahapatis in the kingdom of Kāsi;
having reached maturity, he entered the life of a householder. His wife was immoral and engaged in unchaste conduct with a village headman.
He moves about. The Bodhisatta, knowing this, moves about while taking it into account.
At that time, however, after the seeds had been removed during the rainy season, a drought occurred and the time for the crops to take root arrived.

All the inhabitants of the village gathered together, saying, "In two months from now, we shall harvest the crops and give you rice," and they [offered] an old bull from the hands of the village headman.
Having taken it, they ate the meat.
Then one day, the village distributor, looking for an opportunity, entered the house at a time when the Bodhisatta had gone out.
Just as they were lying down comfortably, the Bodhisatta entered through the village gate and proceeded toward the house.
That woman, facing toward the village gate, saw him and thought, "Who might this be? Standing on the threshold and looking out, she recognized him as he was and informed the village headman.
The village headman was terrified and trembled. Then she said to him, "Do not fear; there is a way.
We have eaten ox-flesh from your hand; act as if you were settling the price for that meat."
“I will climb onto the granary, stand at its door, and say, ‘There is no rice.
You, standing in the middle of the house, must repeatedly urge him, saying, ‘The children in our house are hungry; give me the price for meat.
Having said this, he climbed the granary and sat down at its door. The other, standing in the middle of the house, said, “Give me the price for meat.”
She spoke. Sitting at the gate of the granary, she said, "There is no rice in the granary; when the harvest is gathered, I will give it to you, so go.
The Bodhisatta entered the house, and seeing their conduct, he realized, "This must be a stratagem devised by this wicked woman.
He then addressed the village headman: "O village headman, while we were eating the meat of your old ox..."
"We were eating with the thought, 'In two months from now we shall give rice'; why have you had it brought right now, without even half a month having passed?
You have not come for this reason; you must have come for some other purpose.
Your conduct does not please me; she too is ill-behaved and of evil character, for she knows the absence of rice in the granary."
Then, having climbed onto the granary, she said, "There is no rice," while you said, "Give it.
The conduct of both of you does not please me. To clarify this matter, she spoke these verses:
"Neither of the two is acceptable to me; neither of the two is pleasing to me."
This woman, having descended into the granary, speaks thus:
"O village headman, I say this to you while my life remains but a little:
having made a compact for two months, [give me] the flesh of an old, emaciated ox."
"To blame me for what has not yet been attained—that too does not please me.
Regarding this, "I say that to you, O village headman": "O chief of the village, for that reason I speak to you.
"In what kind of meager life? means: our life is indeed meager, hard, coarse, difficult, and scanty.
It is meager and scanty while such a life as this is being lived. Having made an agreement for two months, you are emaciating an old ox for us who are taking its meat;
you, by giving an old, lean, and weak ox to those taking its meat, have thus made an agreement and a limit for two months, saying, "The price must be paid within two months."
"Having done so. "You reproached me before the time had come" means that you reproached me while that time had not yet arrived, but in the interim.
"And even that does not please me" refers to this woman of evil character and immoral conduct who, though knowing there was no rice in the granary, acted as if she did not know;
having entered the granary and stood at the door, she said, "I will give none. And... [the rest of the passage].
"You admonish me at the wrong time, and that too"—saying "neither this nor that is acceptable or pleasing to me," he spoke thus;
even as he spoke, he seized the village headman by the topknot, dragged him down, and threw him into the middle of the house.
Then, reviling him with words such as, "Being a village headman, you offend against the goods protected and guarded by another," he beat him and rendered him weak.
Having seized her by the neck and dragged her out of the house, he grabbed that wicked woman by the hair, pulled her down into the storehouse, and beat her, threatening her:
"If you ever do such a thing again, you will know [the consequences]!
