From that time on, the village headman did not even dare to look at that house, and that evil woman was no longer able to transgress against him even in her thoughts.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:

“At that time, Devadatta was the village headman, and I myself was the householder who administered the punishment. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The ninth is the Commentary on the Householder Jātaka.
[200] 10. The Commentary on the Sādhusīla Jātaka:
This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain brahmin.
It is said that he had four daughters. Four men desired them: one was handsome and possessed of a perfect body;
one was of mature age but elderly; one was of noble birth; and one was virtuous. The Brahmin reflected:
"When settling and establishing my daughters in marriage, to whom indeed should they be given? To the one endowed with beauty, or rather to the one who has reached maturity?"
“Of those endowed with noble birth and virtuous conduct, choose one. Even as he reflected, not knowing the answer, he thought, “The Perfectly Enlightened One will know this matter;
having asked him, I shall give [the girl] to one who is suitable among these.
Taking perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and sitting to one side, he related the matter from the beginning.
“Venerable Sir, among these four people, to whom is it appropriate to give? he asked.
The Teacher said, “In the past, too, the wise discussed this question; however, because you have entered into the cycle of existence, you were unable to discern it.
Having been thus requested, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered his craft at Takkasilā; returning to Benares, he became a world-renowned teacher.
Now, a certain brahmin had four daughters, and likewise, four men sought them in marriage.

The brahmin, not knowing to whom it should be given, thought, "I will ask my teacher and give it to one who is worthy," and going into his presence, he asked about the matter, reciting the first verse:
"The body is a gift, the aged are a gift, noble birth and virtuous conduct [are gifts];"
“Brahmin, we ask you this: which of them do you prefer?
Herein, by the words “possessed of bodily wealth,” and so forth, he reveals the existing virtues of those four. This is the intended meaning:
four men desire my daughters; among them, one possesses “bodily wealth,” that is, excellence of body.
The state of being handsome exists. For one, there is the state of being aged, growth, and old age.

For another, there is nobility of birth, noble lineage, and excellence of birth; "sujacca" is also a reading. For another, there is goodness of character, the state of beautiful virtue, and excellence of virtue.
"We ask only the brahmin"—this was said by those who did not know which of these [qualities] should be given to whom by name.
“We ask you, venerable Brahmin, this very question: ‘Whom of them do we choose?’”—that is, he asks, “Of those four persons, whom do we choose?
Whom do we desire? To whom shall we give those maidens?

Having heard that, the Teacher spoke the second verse, elucidating this meaning: “Even though excellence of form and so forth may be present, one who has failed in virtue is contemptible; therefore, that is not the standard for us. It is our possession of virtue that is pleasing.”
“There is excellence in the body; let us pay homage to the one who has grown old.
There is excellence in the well-born; our preference is for virtue.
In this regard, “there is excellence in the body” means that even in a body endowed with physical form, there is indeed a specific excellence or growth.
“I do not say ‘there is none. I pay homage to the state of being aged;
indeed, I perform a salutation toward the condition of old age, for it is the state of being aged that receives veneration and honor.
‘There is purpose in one who is well-born’—even in the case of a man of noble birth there is growth, and excellence of birth is certainly to be desired. ‘Virtue is pleasing to us’—to us...”
"However, virtue alone is what is pleasing. For one who possesses virtue and is perfected in conduct is worthy of honor and praise even when devoid of body and material wealth.
Having heard his words, the brahmin gave him his daughters.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka: at the conclusion of the Truths...
The brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry. [The Buddha said: "At that time, this very brahmin was that brahmin, and I myself was the world-renowned teacher.
This concludes the commentary on the Sādhusīla Jātaka, the tenth.
The fifth chapter, the Ruhaka-vagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
Ruhaka, Sirikāḷaka, Paduma, and Maṇicoraka.
The cloud spread over the mountain, friends and enemies, Rādha, and the householder of virtuous conduct. 6.
The Chapter on Nataṃdaḷha.
[201] 1. The Commentary on the Bandhanāgāra Jātaka.
"The wise do not call that a strong bond," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a prison.
It is said that at that time, many thieves—cut-purses, highwaymen, and robbers—had been brought before the King of Kosala.
They showed themselves. The king had them bound with wooden stocks, rope bonds, and iron chains.
About thirty monks from the countryside, desiring to see the Teacher, arrived; having seen him and paid homage, they went to the prison the following day while wandering for alms.
Seeing those thieves there, they returned from their almsround and approached the Tathāgata in the evening.

“Venerable sir, today while we were wandering for alms, we saw many thieves in the prison who, bound with iron shackles and other fetters, were experiencing great suffering; they were unable to break those bonds and escape.
Is there perhaps another bond more firm than those? they asked. The Teacher said:

“Monks, what indeed are these called ‘bonds’? That bond of defilement known as craving (taṇhā) toward wealth, grain, children, wives, and so forth—is firmer than these bonds by a hundredfold, even a thousandfold.
Yet, having severed this very great and difficult-to-sever bond, the ancient sages went to the Himalayas.”
"Having entered [the city], they went forth," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a certain poor household.
When he reached maturity, his father passed away; he supported his mother by working for wages. Then, to him—
His mother, against his own will, took a daughter of a noble family into their home and later passed away.
Subsequently, a fetus was conceived in the womb of his wife. Not knowing that a fetus had been established there, he said, "My dear, you must earn a living by working for wages;
I shall go forth into the religious life. She replied, "A fetus has been conceived in me; once I have given birth..."
"Upon seeing the boy, you shall go forth," she said. He consented, saying, "Very well.
When she had given birth, he asked her for leave, saying, "Bhadde, you have given birth safely; now I shall go forth.
Then she said to him, "Wait until the time when your son can be weaned from the breast," and she conceived again.
He thought: "It is not possible to depart after having accepted this [proposal];
I shall flee and go forth into homelessness without telling her. Without telling her, he rose during the night and fled.
Then the city guards seized him. He had himself released by them, saying: "Sirs, I am one who supports his mother; please release me."
Having lived in one place, he departed through the main gate, entered the Himalayas, and went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Having realized the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he dwelt there sporting in the play of *jhāna*.
While living there, he thought: "Even such a bond of wife and children, so difficult to sever, and this bond of the defilements (*kilesa*), have been cut by me!"
Uttering this inspired utterance, he spoke these verses:
“The wise say that bond is not strong which is made of iron, wood, or rattan;
rather, it is the longing for jewels and earrings, and the attachment to children and wives, that is the true bond.”
“The wise call this a strong bond, dragging one down, slack yet difficult to release;
having cut even this, the wise go forth, indifferent, having abandoned sensual pleasure.

In this context, “the wise” (*dhīrā*) means those possessing steadfastness (*dhitimantā*); they are called “wise” because they have condemned evil. Alternatively, “wisdom” (*dhī*) is said to be *paññā* (discernment); by that—
"Endowed with wisdom" means they are wise (*dhīra*). Buddhas, paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Buddha, and bodhisattvas—these are what is meant by "the wise.
Regarding the terms *āyasa* and so forth: that which is made of iron and is called an iron chain is *āyasa*; that which consists of wooden bonds is *dāruja*;
and that which is made by taking grasses such as *pabbaja* or other materials like hemp (*vākā*) and making them into a rope...
The wise do not call that "firm" or "stable" which can be cut by means of iron or other tools;
such is the bond of the rope. "Sārattarattā" means being attached and impassioned, that is to say, dyed with intense passion.
"Maṇikuṇḍalesu" refers to gems and earrings, or to earrings set with gems.

"This is strong": the wise have said that this bond consisting of defilements is firm and stable for those who are intensely attached to jewels and earrings—their passion (*sārāga*) and their longing (*taṇhā*) for their children and wives.
"Carrying away" (*ohārina*): it is called "carrying away" because it drags one down and carries one off into the four states of misery;
it "carries away" in the sense that it takes one downward. "Loose" (*sithila*): [in the sense of being loose] at the place of bondage...
It is "loose" because it does not cut the skin, hide, and flesh; it does not draw out the blood;
it does not even make known the state of being bound; and it allows one to perform work on land routes, water routes, and so forth.
It is "difficult to release" because a bond of defilement that has arisen even once through craving and greed is hard to loosen from its place of attachment, like a turtle [from its hole].
"Difficult to release. Having cut even this— having severed with the sword of wisdom this very firm bond of defilements,
like a noble elephant breaking iron chains, or like lion cubs breaking through a cage— the wise,
loathing sense-pleasures (both objective and subjective) as if they were a dung heap, become indifferent and [renounce] sensual happiness.

"Having abandoned [the world], they go forth; having gone forth, they enter the Himālaya mountains, and having taken up the ascetic life of a seer (isipabbajjā), they spend their time in the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna).
Having uttered this inspired utterance (udāna), the Bodhisatta, without falling away from his meditative absorption, became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, some became Stream-enterers, some Once-returners, some Non-returners, and some became Arahants.
"At that time, the mother was Mahāmāyā, the father was King Suddhodana, the wife was Rāhulamātā, and the son was Rāhula. Thus he spoke of his family.
"But it was I myself who, having abandoned [the world], gone forth, and become a renunciant.
Thus ends the first commentary on the *Bandhanāgāra-jātaka*.
2. The Commentary on the *Keḷisīla-jātaka*
"Hamsas, cranes, and peacocks"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya.

It is said that this venerable one was well-known and renowned in the Buddha’s dispensation; he possessed a sweet voice and was a sweet preacher of the Dhamma, having attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and being a great one whose taints were destroyed.
Yet, among the eighty great elders, he was small in stature, a dwarf (lakuṇḍaka).

He was like a novice, as if made small for the sake of play. One day, when the people had gone to the gateway of Jetavana after having paid homage to the Tathāgata, about thirty monks from the countryside entered Jetavana thinking, "We shall pay homage to the One of Ten Powers.
Seeing the Elder at the monastery gateway, they perceived him as a novice and [grabbed] the Elder by the corner of his robe.
Seizing him by the hands, seizing him by the head, touching him on the nose, and taking him by the ears, they shook him and made a fuss with their hands;
then, having put away their bowls and robes and approached the Teacher, they paid homage, sat down, and when the Teacher had exchanged pleasant greetings with them, they asked:
"Venerable sir, it is said that the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya..."
“Bhikkhus, you have one disciple among you who is a sweet speaker of the Dhamma; where is he now?

“But, bhikkhus, do you wish to see him? “Yes, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, that one whom you saw at the gateway and came here having felt hesitation in your hands while grasping the hem of his robe and so forth—that is he. “Venerable sir, such as this...”
“For what reason has this disciple, who had made earnest aspirations and was endowed with a resolute vow, become one of little power?
The Teacher replied, “It was on account of an evil deed committed by himself,” and when they requested him to do so, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, the king of the gods. At that time...
It was impossible for Brahmadatta to show an old elephant, horse, or ox that had reached the end of its life;
being of a playful nature, whenever he saw such a thing, he would have it pursued. Seeing even an old cart, he would have it broken.
Seeing an old woman, he would have her summoned, have her struck in the belly, have her thrown down, and having made her rise again, he would frighten her.
Seeing old men, he made them perform such sports as rolling on the ground like acrobats;
even when he did not see them himself, having merely heard that "there is an old man in such-and-such a house," he would have him summoned and play with him.
People, feeling ashamed, sent their own parents away to other kingdoms, and thus the duty of attending to mothers and the duty of attending to fathers were cut off.
Even the king’s servants were of a playful nature. As they died one after another, they filled the four lower realms, and the assembly of the gods diminished.
Seeing no new sons of the gods, Sakka reflected, "What could be the cause of this?
Having understood the reason, he thought, "I shall subdue them," and assuming the form of an old man, he placed two jars of buttermilk upon a worn-out cart.
Having yoked two old oxen, on a festival day, he mounted a decorated elephant while Brahmadatta was circumambulating the decorated city;
dressed in a coarse hempen garment and driving that carriage, he went toward the king.
Seeing the dilapidated carriage, the king said, "Remove this carriage! The people asked, "Where—?"
"Your Majesty, we do not see them," they said. By his own supernatural power, Sakka caused them to be seen by the king himself.
Then, as the cart had drawn near, he drove it over the upper part of it; causing the king to turn back, he broke the second cart.
From the king's head, curd began to flow out here and there, and he was distressed by it.

He was ashamed and felt loathing. Then, knowing his state of distress, Sakka caused his vehicle to vanish, manifested his own form as Sakka, and standing in the air with the thunderbolt in hand, said: "O wicked, unrighteous king!
Will you not become an old man? Will old age not strike your body? Having been playful by nature, you have committed an act of harassment against the elderly."
"You are doing this; by performing such work while living alone, you cause the dead to fill the states of misery, and humans do not get the chance to care for their mothers and fathers.
If you do not desist from this work, I shall split your head with a thunderbolt. Do not commit this deed from now on! Having thus rebuked him, [he spoke] of the virtues of mother and father.
Having spoken thus, he proclaimed the benefits of the practice of honoring the elders, gave his exhortation, and returned to his own place.
From that time forth, the king did not even conceive the thought of performing such an act.
Having brought up this past event, the Teacher, now having attained full enlightenment, spoke these verses:
“Swans, cranes, and peacocks, elephants, antelopes, and deer—all fear the lion;
there is no equality in their physical bodies.
In the same way, among human beings, even if one is young, if they possess wisdom...”
"For in that case, he is great; the fool is not even equal in body.
In this context, "deer called *pasada*" means deer known as *pasada*; the meaning is also "the *pasada* deer and the remaining deer.
There is also the reading "*pasadamigā*," which has the same meaning as "*pasadā migā*. "There is no equality in the body" refers to the measurement of the physical frame.

There is no such thing. If it were so, large-bodied elephants and deer would kill lions, and the lion would kill only small-bodied creatures like swans; only small beings would fear the lion, not the large ones.
But because this is not the case, all of them fear the lion. Regarding "body," even a fool may have a large body.
"He is not called 'Great' (Mahā) by name; therefore, although Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya was small in body, let him not be thought small in wisdom"—this is the meaning.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, among those bhikkhus, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some attained arahantship.
“At that time, King Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya was he; because of his playful disposition, he became a source of amusement for others, while Sakka was none other than myself.
This is the second commentary, the Keḷisīla Jātaka.
[203] 3. The Commentary on the Khaṇḍa Jātaka.
"May I have loving-kindness toward the Virūpakkhas"—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain bhikkhu.
It is said that as he was splitting wood at the door of a sauna, a rotten tree emerged from between the logs.
A certain snake bit him on a toe; he died right there. His death became known throughout the entire monastery.

In the Hall of Truth, the monks began a discussion: "Friends, it is said that such-and-such a monk, while splitting wood at the entrance to the sauna, was bitten by a snake and died right there. The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what is it that you are discussing?"
Having asked, "Are you sitting here now for this discussion? and being told, "Indeed we are," he said:
"Bhikkhus, if that bhikkhu had cultivated loving-kindness toward the four royal families of snakes, no snake would have bitten him.
Even the ancient ascetics, before the Buddha had arisen, cultivated loving-kindness toward the four royal families of snakes and [avoided harm from] those royal families of snakes."
"Having said, 'They were liberated from fear arising in dependence [on that],' he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Upon reaching maturity, he abandoned sensual pleasures, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and having developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),"
Having established a hermitage at a bend of the Ganges in a region of the Himālayas, he dwelt there surrounded by a company of seers, sporting in the play of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
At that time, various species of long-tailed serpents on the banks of the Ganges were creating obstacles for the seers, and for the most part, the seers met their end.
The ascetics reported this matter to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta...
Having assembled all the ascetics, he said, "If you cultivate loving-kindness toward the four royal families of snakes,
the snakes will not bite you; therefore, from this day forward, cultivate loving-kindness toward the four royal families of snakes," and he spoke this verse:
“I have loving-kindness for the Virūpakkhas, loving-kindness for the Erāpathas;
I have loving-kindness for the Chabyāputtas, and loving-kindness for the Kaṇhāgotamakas.
In this context, “I have loving-kindness for the Virūpakkhas” means that I have loving-kindness toward the families of the Virūpakkha nāga kings. The same applies to the Erāpathas and the others.

The same method applies here. For these too—namely, the royal family of the Erāpatha nāgas, the royal family of the Chabyāputta nāgas, and the royal family of the Kaṇhāgotamaka nāgas—are indeed royal families of nāgas.

Having thus shown the four royal families of nāgas, he said, "If you are able to cultivate loving-kindness toward them, the Dīghajāti nāgas will not bite you nor will they harm you," and then he spoke the second verse:
"May my loving-kindness be toward those without feet; may my loving-kindness be toward those with two feet."
“May my loving-kindness be toward those with four feet; may my loving-kindness be toward those with many feet.
Therein, by the first phrase, having made it specific, the cultivation of loving-kindness toward all footless beings—both those of long-standing birth and fish—is shown;
by the second phrase, [loving-kindness toward] humans and those born as birds is shown; by the third phrase...
Regarding all four-footed creatures such as elephants and horses, [the phrase] "by the fourth foot" refers to those such as scorpions, centipedes, *uccāliṅga* insects, spiders, and so forth.
Having thus shown the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*) by way of its own form, he now spoke this verse to show it by way of supplication:
“May the footless not harm me; may the two-footed not harm me.”
"May no four-footed creature harm me; may no many-footed creature harm me.

In this context, "May no one harm me" means: "May not even a single one among these, such as those without feet and so forth, harm me or cause me distress"—thus, the meaning is that one should cultivate loving-kindness while making such a request.
Now, demonstrating the cultivation of loving-kindness by way of the unspecified (anodissaka), he spoke this verse:
“May all beings, all living creatures, all that have come to be, and everyone without exception—may they all behold what is auspicious; may no evil come upon anyone.
In this context, *satta* (beings) refers to those who are attached, clinging, stuck, and fastened to the five aggregates within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by means of craving and views.
They are "breathing beings" (*pāṇā*) by way of living through the process of the occurrence of inhalation and exhalation;

they are "beings" (*bhūtā*) by way of having come to be, being brought into existence, and being produced. Thus, one should understand that there is only a difference in terminology. However, without distinction, all these terms indeed encompass all sentient beings.
"Kevalā" means "entire. This is indeed a synonym for the word "all" (*sabba*). "May they see what is auspicious"—all these [beings].
"May beings see only what is auspicious, excellent, and beautiful; may no evil come to anyone. This means:

"May not even a single being among these encounter evil—that is, anything base or painful; may it not come, may it not reach them. May all be free from enmity, free from affliction, happy, and without suffering."
Having thus said, "One should cultivate loving-kindness toward all beings in an unspecified manner," he further spoke—
"The Buddha is immeasurable, the Dhamma is immeasurable,
the Saṅgha is immeasurable"— in order to cause them to recollect the virtues of the Three Jewels.
In this context, the Buddha-ratana is immeasurable because of the absence of defilements that create limits and because of the immeasurability of its qualities.
"Dhamma" refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma; since it is impossible to measure even that, it is immeasurable.
Because he is endowed with that immeasurable Dhamma, the Saṅgha is also immeasurable.
Thus the Bodhisatta, having said, "Recall the virtues of these Three Jewels," and having shown the immeasurable qualities of the Three Jewels, spoke as follows to show beings who possess measure:
"The reptiles that have measure—snakes, scorpions, centipedes;
spiders, crabs, and mice."

In this context, "reptiles" (*sarīsapā*) is a name for snakes and long-bodied species. For they move by crawling (*sarantā*), or they glide with their heads (*sirena sapanti*), thus they are called "reptiles.
The phrase beginning with "snakes" (*ahī*) is an illustration of them according to their specific forms. Therein, "spider" (*uṇṇanābhī*) refers to the house-lizard;
for from its navel (*nābhi*) threads resembling wool (*uṇṇā*) emerge, and therefore it is called a "wool-naveled one. "Scorpion" (*sarabū*) refers to the house-glowworm (*gharagoḷikā*).
Thus the Bodhisatta, having shown that "because these creatures possess internal qualities such as passion which act as their measure, therefore those reptiles and others are limited in size," said:
"By the power of the three immeasurable Jewels, may these beings of limited size perform protective rites day and night; thus, you should recollect the virtues of the Three Jewels."
Having said this, he spoke the following verse to show what must be done thereafter:
“Protection has been made for me, a safeguard has been made for me; let the spirits depart!
I pay homage to the Blessed One; I pay homage to the seven Perfectly Enlightened Ones.”
In this context, "Protection has been made for me" means that protection and security have been established by me through recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem.
"The safeguard has been made for me" means that a protective spell (*paritta*) has also been performed by me for myself.
"May the spirits depart" means that those spirits who harbor ill intentions toward me should retreat and go away. "I, having thus performed the safeguard, pay homage to the Blessed One."
"I pay homage to every Buddha, Blessed One, who has passed away and attained *parinibbāna* in the past.
By saying 'Homage to the seven Perfectly Enlightened Ones,' I specifically pay homage to the seven Perfectly Enlightened Ones who have attained *parinibbāna* in succession in the past.
Thus, "Even while paying homage, you should recollect the seven Buddhas"—this is what the Bodhisatta said to the company of seers.
Having bound this protective charm (paritta), he gave it.

However, it should be understood that this specific paritta is spoken here because, from the beginning, loving-kindness (mettā) toward the four royal families of snakes is illustrated by two verses; or alternatively, because two modes of developing loving-kindness—namely, the directed and the undirected—are illustrated.
Or else, another reason should be sought. From that point onward...
The troop of deer, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s instruction, cultivated loving-kindness and recollected the qualities of the Buddha.
While they were thus recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, all the long-eared deer departed. The Bodhisatta, too, having cultivated the divine abodes, was destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the company of seers was the assembly of the Buddha, and the leader of the group was none other than myself.
This concludes the third commentary, the Khaṇḍa-jātaka.
4. The Commentary on the Vīraka-jātaka.
“Api vīraka passesī” (Did Vīraka see it?). This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the abode of the Sugata.
For when the elders had returned having taken Devadatta’s retinue with them, the Teacher asked, “Sāriputta, what did Devadatta do upon seeing you?
When they replied, “He showed us the abode of the Sugata, Bhante,” he said, “Sāriputta, this is not so.”
"Just now Devadatta, by imitating me, has met his destruction; in the past, too, he met his destruction," the Elder said, and being requested, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the womb of a water-crow in the Himalayan region."
Having been reborn, he lived near a certain lake, and his name was Vīraka. At that time, there was a famine in the kingdom of Kāsi;
people were unable to give food to the crows or to perform offerings to the *yakṣas* and *nāgas*.
Due to the drought, the crows for the most part entered the forest. There, a resident of Bārāṇasī named Saviṭṭhaka—
A certain crow, taking a female crow with him, went to Vīraka’s dwelling place and made his home nearby that lake in a secluded spot.
One day, while foraging at that lake, he saw Vīraka descend into the water, eat fish, and come back out to dry his body.
[Seeing this, he thought: "It is possible, by depending on this water-crow..."
Thinking, “Having caught many fish, I will attend upon him,” she approached him. When he asked, “What is it, lady?
she replied, “I wish to attend upon you, Master. He consented, saying, “Very well,” and from then on she attended upon him.
From that time forward, Vīraka too, having eaten only enough for his own sustenance, would pull up the fish.
He gave [the fish] to Saviṭṭhaka. He too, having eaten just enough for his own sustenance, gave the remainder to the female crow.
Later, conceit arose in him: "This water-crow is black, and I am black;
there is no difference between him and me in terms of eyes, beak, or feet. From now on, my work shall be with the fish caught by this one."
“There is no need; I myself will catch them. He approached Vīraka and said, “Friend, from now on I myself shall descend into the lake and catch the fish.

Although he was restrained by him with the words, “Friend, you were not born into a family that descends into the water to catch fish; do not perish,” he disregarded those words and descended into the lake.
Having entered the water, as he was emerging, he was unable to get out because he had cut through the algae;
he became stuck amidst the algae, and only the tip of his beak remained visible. Breathless, he met his death right there within the water.
Then his wife, not seeing him return and wishing to learn what had happened, went to Vīraka and said, "Husband,"
“Saviṭṭhaka is not to be seen; where indeed could he be? asking thus, she spoke the first verse:
“Do you see, Vīraka, that sweet-voiced bird, Resembling a peacock’s neck, my husband Saviṭṭhaka?”
In that regard, Vīraka, you see? "Yes, Master Vīraka, I do see.
"Mañjubhāṇaka" means one who speaks sweetly. For she, out of lust, thinks, "My husband has a sweet voice," and therefore she says this.
"Resembling a peacock's neck" means having a color similar to a peacock's neck.
Having heard this, Vīraka said, "Yes, I know where your husband has gone," and spoke the second verse:
"The bird that moves on water and land, Who constantly feeds on raw fish—
Saviṭṭhaka, imitating him, Is dead, entangled in the seaweed."
In this context, "capable of moving both on water and on land" means one who is able to travel upon both water and dry ground.
"A bird" he says referring to himself. "Imitating him" means acting in imitation of him.
"Dead, enveloped in seaweed" means that having entered the water and being unable to cut through the seaweed to emerge, he remains submerged within the water itself, completely covered by seaweed.
“Look, it is dead; its beak is visible. Having heard this, the female crow lamented and went back to Bārāṇasī itself.
The Teacher, having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Savitṭhaka was Devadatta, but Vīraka was none other than myself.
This is the fourth narrative of the Vīraka Jātaka.
[205] 5. The Commentary on the Gaṅgeyya Jātaka.
"The fish of the Ganges shines"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning two young bhikkhus.
It is said that these two sons of good family from Sāvatthī, having gone forth in the Dispensation and applied themselves to the meditation on the foul (asubhabhāvanā),...
Being fond of physical beauty, they wandered about praising their own forms. One day, having fallen into a dispute over their appearance, saying, "You do not look beautiful;
I look beautiful," and seeing an elderly elder monk sitting not far away, they thought, "He will know whether we are beautiful or not. Approaching him, they said, "Venerable sir,..."
“Who among us is the most handsome? they asked. He replied, “Friends, I am indeed more handsome than you.
The young monks rebuked him, saying, “This old man, instead of answering what we asked, tells us what we did not ask,” and then they departed.
Their conduct became well known throughout the Saṅgha of monks. Then, one day in the Dhamma Hall—
How did they initiate it? They said, "Friend, it is said that such-and-such an elder has put those young monks who are devoted to form to shame.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "For this very discussion," he said, "Monks, these two young men have not only now been devoted to praising form."
“Formerly, these too wandered about fondling only forms,” he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity on the bank of the Ganges.
At that time, at the confluence of the Ganges and the Yamunā, there were two fish—one from the Ganges and one from the Yamunā—who said, “I am more beautiful.”
Disputing over their beauty, saying, "You do not shine," they saw a turtle lying on the bank of the Ganges nearby and thought, "He will know whether we are beautiful or not.
Approaching him, they asked, "Friend turtle, which shines more: she of the Ganges or she of the Yamunā? The turtle—
“Both the fish of the Gaṅgā shines, and the fish of the Yamunā shines; yet, between you two, I alone shine even more brightly.
Proclaiming this meaning, he spoke the first verse:
“The fish of the Gaṅgā shines, and likewise the fish of the Yamunā;”
“This man has four limbs, his proportions are like a banyan tree, and with his neck slightly bent, he outshines them all.
Therein, “four-limbed” means having four limbs. “Man” (purisa) is said referring to himself. “Proportions like a banyan tree” (nigrodhaparimaṇḍala) means—
"Born well, like a banyan tree, he is perfectly rounded. "With a neck slightly elongated" means his neck is as long as that of a chariot-steed.
"He outshines everyone"—thus, being endowed with such physical proportions, the tortoise outshines everyone;
he says, "I alone, surpassing all of you, am resplendent."
The fish, having become his interlocutors, said, “O friend! Wicked tortoise, without answering what we asked you, you have spoken something else entirely,” and they spoke this second verse:
“What was asked, that you did not declare; instead, being questioned, you declared something else.
This man who praises his own purpose does not please us.”
In this context, "one who praises himself" refers to a person whose habit is to praise themselves, one who exalts themselves.
"This does not please us" means, "This wicked tortoise is not pleasing or acceptable to us"; having thus splashed water over the tortoise, they went back to their own places.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the two fish were the two young bhikkhus;
the tortoise was the elder; and I myself was the tree deity who arose on the bank of the Ganges and witnessed these events."
The fifth: The Commentary on the Gaṅgeyya Jātaka.
[206] 6. The Commentary on the Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka:
"Come now, let them set a snare made of a ring. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana grove concerning Devadatta.
At that time, having heard that Devadatta was plotting for his murder, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has plotted for my murder;
he has plotted against me even in the past," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having become a kurunga deer, lived in the forest.
He made his dwelling in a thicket not far from a certain lake.
Not far from that same lake, upon the branch of a tree, lived a *satapatta* bird, while a tortoise made its home in the lake. Thus, those three friends lived together in mutual affection.
Then, as a deer-hunter was wandering in the forest, he [saw] the Bodhisatta at the drinking-place on the shore of the water.
Seeing the tracks, he set a circular snare like an iron chain and departed.
The Bodhisatta, having come to drink water, was caught in the snare during the very first watch of the night and let out a cry of distress.
Hearing that sound, a peacock from the top of a tree and a tortoise from the water approached and deliberated, "What indeed should be done?"
Then Satapatta, addressing the tortoise, spoke the first verse, explaining this matter: "Friend, you have teeth; you cut this snare.
I will go and act in such a way that he does not return.
Thus, through the effort exerted by us both, our companion shall regain his life."
“Come now, tortoise, cut through this snare made of rope with your teeth!
I shall act in such a way that the hunter will not catch you.
Then the tortoise began to gnaw the leather thong, and Satapatta went to the hunter’s village.
He sat down in a tree nearby. At the very break of dawn, the hunter took his spear and set out.
The bird, perceiving his departure, cried out and flapped its wings; as the man was exiting through the front door, it struck him in the face.
The hunter thought, "I have been struck by an ill-omened bird," and turning back, he lay down for a short while.
Taking up his spear again, he rose up. The bird, knowing that "this man first went out by the eastern gate;
now he will go out by the western gate," went and sat down at the western house.
The hunter thought, "When I went out by the eastern gate, I saw an ill-omened bird; now I shall go out by the western gate. And so he went out by the western gate.
The bird flew out, but after returning and perching again, it struck him on the face. The hunter thought, “Once more I have been struck by this ill-omened bird;
it will not let me go out now. He turned back and slept until sunrise.
At the moment of dawn, he took up his spear and went out. The bird flew away with great speed and informed the Bodhisatta, “The hunter is coming!”
At that moment, the tortoise had already chewed through all the leather thongs except for one;
his tusks were on the verge of breaking off and blood was streaming from his mouth.
Seeing the hunter’s son approaching with a spear like a bolt of lightning, the Bodhisatta cut that remaining thong and entered the forest.
The bird perched on the top of a tree, while the tortoise, being weak, remained lying right there.
The hunter, having caught the tortoise and placed it in a bag, tied it to a wooden stake. The Bodhisatta turned back and, looking down, realized that the tortoise had been captured;
thinking, "I shall give the gift of life to my companion," he acted as if he were weak.
He showed himself to the hunter. Thinking, "This one will be weak; I shall kill him," the hunter took up his spear and pursued him.
The Bodhisatta, walking neither too far nor too near, led him into the forest.
Knowing that he had gone a great distance, he feigned a loss of track and, taking another path, went with the speed of the wind until, with his horn, he [struck] the hunter's bag.
Having tossed him up, dropped him to the ground, and split him open, he extracted the tortoise. The hundred-winged bird also descended from the tree.
The Bodhisatta, giving advice to both of them, said: "It was through you that I obtained my life;
you have done for me what a friend ought to do for a friend. Now, if the hunter comes and captures you, therefore, my friend—"
“Satapatta, take your two young ones and go elsewhere; you too, dear tortoise, enter the water,” he said. They did accordingly.
Having attained full enlightenment, the Teacher spoke the second verse:
“The tortoise entered the water, the antelope entered the forest;
the hundred-winged bird [fled] from the tree-top, leading its young far away.
In this context, “he led away” (*apānayi*) means he brought them; the sense is that he took them and departed.

The hunter also came to that place; finding no one there, he took the severed skin-bag and returned home overcome with grief. Those three companions, having lived their lives without betraying one another’s trust, passed away according to their respective karma.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the hunter was Devadatta; Sāriputta was the hundred-footed bird; Moggallāna was the tortoise; and I myself was the kuruṅga deer. This is the sixth narrative, the Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka.
[207] 7. The Commentary on the Assaka-jātaka.
This story, beginning with the words "By King Assaka," was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the seduction of a former wife.
For that bhikkhu, when asked by the Teacher, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are dissatisfied? replied:
When he said, “Truth,” and was asked, “By whom were you made despondent? he replied, “By my former wife.
Then the Teacher said to him, “It is not only now that this bhikkhu has had affection for that woman;
in the past as well, you fell into great suffering on her account,” and he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kāsi, in the city of Pāṭalipura, a king named Assaka reigned.
His chief queen, named Upari, was dear to him, beloved, beautiful, fair to behold, gracious, surpassing human beauty, yet not having attained divine beauty.
She passed away; because of her death, the king was overcome with grief, suffering, and dejected. He, for her—
Having laid the body down in a trough, having had oil and mud poured over it, and having placed it upon a lower bed, he lay down fasting, weeping and lamenting.

His parents, the remaining kinsmen, friends, ministers, brahmins, householders, and others were unable to console him, saying, "Do not grieve, Great King; conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and so forth. To him—

Seven days passed while he was thus lamenting. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become an ascetic who had attained the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, was dwelling in a region of the Himalayas.
Increasing his light and surveying Jambudīpa with his divine eye, he saw the king lamenting in such a manner and thought, "I must become his refuge."
By means of his supernormal power, he leapt into the air, descended into the king’s park, and sat upon the auspicious stone slab like a golden statue.
Then, a young brahmin student residing in Pāṭaliputta went to the park; seeing the Bodhisatta, he paid homage and sat down.
After the Bodhisatta had exchanged greetings with him, he asked, "Young man, is the king righteous?"
“Yes, venerable sir, King Dhammika is righteous, but his wife has passed away. Having had her body placed in a trough, he lies there lamenting;
today is the seventh day. Why do you not release the king from such suffering?
Is it fitting for the king to experience such grief while virtuous men like yourselves are present?”
“I do not know the king, young man, but if he were to come and ask me,
I would point out the place where he was reborn and have him speak with the king right there. “In that case, venerable sir,
please remain seated here until I bring the king,” the young man said, having received the Bodhisatta’s consent.
Having taken [the message] and gone into the presence of the king, he reported the matter and said, "It is fitting to go into the presence of that one who possesses the divine eye.
The king, his mind delighted at the thought, "I shall indeed be able to see what is above," mounted his chariot and went there.
Having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, he sat down to one side and asked: "Is it true, as it is said, that you know the place where the queen has been reborn?
"Yes, Great King," [the Bodhisatta replied]. "Where has she been reborn?
"Great King, having become intoxicated with physical beauty and through negligence, she failed to perform wholesome deeds; she has been reborn right here in this park in the womb of a dung-worm."
“I do not believe it,” he said. “In that case, I shall show it to you and make you speak,” replied the Bodhisatta. “Do so, please,” he requested.
By his own supernatural power, the Bodhisatta caused them both to come before the king while rolling balls of cow dung, saying, “Let them both come.
They came exactly as instructed. Showing it to him, the Bodhisatta said, “This, Great King, is for you...”
“Uparidevī, having abandoned that [status], follows closely behind a dung-beetle; do you see her?
he asked. “Venerable sir, we do not believe that she will be reborn in the womb of a dung-beetle,” they replied.
“I shall explain it to him, Great King,” said the Buddha. “Please explain it, venerable sir.”
The Bodhisatta, explaining it by means of his own supernatural power, said, "Uparī.
She replied in the human tongue, "What is it, venerable sir? "In a past birth, what was your name? "Venerable sir, I was the chief queen of King Assaka, named Uparī.
"But now, is King Assaka dear to you, or is he the dung-beetle?"
“Venerable sir, he was my husband in a previous birth; at that time, I wandered in this very park with him, experiencing forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects.
But now, since the time I have entered this cycle of existence, what has become of him?
For I have now killed the king of horses and, with his throat-blood, [have fed] my husband, the dung-beetle.”
Having said, "I shall anoint your feet," she spoke these verses in the human tongue in the midst of the assembly:
"This region has been traversed by me together with King Assaka,
according to my desire and will, along with my beloved husband."
“By internal pleasure and pain, the past is covered over;
therefore, even a mere insect is dearer to me than the kingdom of Assaka.

In this regard, [the verse] “This region was traversed by King Assaka, and this delightful park-land was formerly [traversed] by me” means that this beautiful park-land was previously [visited] by me.
He wandered together with the king of horses. Regarding the phrase *anukāmaya kāmena*: *anu* is merely a particle;
the meaning is, "by him who desires me, together with me who desire him. Regarding *piyena*: it means "by what is dear" in that particular state of existence.
"By new pleasure and pain, the old is covered over," venerable sir; for by new pleasure the old pleasure is covered, and by new pain [the old pain is covered].
"The ancient suffering is covered over and concealed; this is the nature of the world," he thus demonstrates.

Therefore, "even a worm is dearer to me than the king of the Assakas": because the new covers over the old, therefore even a mere worm is a hundredfold and a thousandfold dearer to me than the king of the Assakas.
Having heard this, the king of horses was filled with remorse; standing right there, he had the carcass removed, bathed his head, and paid homage to the Bodhisatta.
He then entered the city, appointed another as chief queen, and ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma.
The Bodhisatta, too, having exhorted the king and freed him from grief, departed for the Himālayas.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
at the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the former second wife was Uppalavaṇṇā;
the horse-king was the despondent monk; the young brahmin was Sāriputta; and the ascetic was none other than myself.”
The seventh is the Commentary on the Assaka-jātaka.
[208] 8. The Commentary on the Susumāra-jātaka:
"Enough with these mothers!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Devadatta’s plotting for his own destruction.
He spoke with reference to this. For at that time, having heard that Devadatta was plotting for his life, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has plotted for my life;
he plotted even in the past, yet he was unable to cause even the slightest alarm. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a monkey womb in the Himalayan region.
Possessing the strength of an elephant, endowed with great power, and having a massive body, he attained a state of supreme beauty and made his dwelling in a forest glade at the bend of the Ganges.
At that time, a certain crocodile lived in the Ganges. Then his wife [approached] the Bodhisatta...
Having seen his body, she conceived a longing for the heart-flesh of that king of monkeys and said to the crocodile:
"My lord, I wish to eat the heart-flesh of this monkey king. "My dear lady, we are water-dwellers while he is a land-dweller;
how shall we be able to catch him? "By whatever means possible, catch him; if I do not obtain it," she continued, [she would die].
“I shall die. “In that case, do not grieve; there is a remedy.
I will have you eat his heart-flesh,” she said, and having thus reassured the crocodile, she went to the Bodhisatta while he was sitting on the bank of the Ganges after drinking water from the river.
Approaching him, she spoke thus: “O Lord of Monkeys, why are you eating bitter fruits in this place?”
“You are wandering right where you have settled; there is no end to the sweet fruits such as the *ambalabuja* on the far side of the Gaṅgā.
Is it not fitting for you to go there and eat various fruits? “O King of Crocodiles, the Gaṅgā has vast waters and is wide;
how shall I go there? “If you wish, I will place you upon my back and [carry you across].”
“I will carry you. Having placed his trust in him, he accepted, saying, “Very well. When the crocodile said, “In that case, come and climb onto my back,” he climbed up.
After leading him a short distance, the crocodile caused him to sink into the water.

The Bodhisatta asked, “Friend, you have made me sink into the water; what is this about? [The crocodile replied: “It is not out of respect for the excellence of the Dhamma that I am doing this to you.”
“I shall take it and go; however, my wife has developed a craving for the flesh of your heart, and I wish to have you eat your own heart.
“My dear, you have done well by speaking thus. For if there were a heart within our bellies, it would have been ground to dust as we moved about on the tips of branches. “But where [is it] for you?”
"Leave it," [the hunter said]. The Bodhisatta, pointing to a nearby udumbara tree covered with clusters of ripe fruit, said, "See these hearts of ours hanging from this udumbara tree.
"If you will show me your heart, I shall not kill you. "In that case, lead me there; I will show it to you hanging from the tree."
So, taking him, he went there. The Bodhisatta, leaping onto his back and sitting upon an udumbara tree, said:
"Friend, foolish crocodile, you were under the impression that 'the hearts of these beings are at the top of the tree';
you are a fool. I deceived you; let your fruit remain yours alone, for your body is indeed large."
"But there is no wisdom," he said, and in order to clarify this point, he spoke these verses:
"Enough for me with these mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits;
though they are on the far shore of the ocean, a fig tree is better for me."
“Great indeed is your body, yet your wisdom is not commensurate with it.
You have been deceived like a crocodile; now go as you please.
In this context, “Enough for me with these things” means: “I have had enough of those things which you have pointed out regarding the island. It is better for me—”
"Udumbara" means: "This very udumbara tree is my choice. "Bondī" means the body. "Tadūpikā" means:
but your wisdom is not *tadūpikā*, that is, it is not suitable for that body. "Gaccha dāni yathāsukhaṃ" means: go now as you please;
there is no means for you to seize the flesh of my heart—this is the meaning. Thus the crocodile was defeated by the thousand.
Like one who is pained and dejected, as if brooding, he went back to his own dwelling place.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, the female crocodile was Ciñcā Māṇavikā, and the king of the monkeys was none other than myself.
This concludes the eighth narrative, the Susumāra-jātaka.
[209] 9. The Commentary on the Kukkuṭa Jātaka.

"I have seen trees in the forest"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a young bhikkhu who was a co-resident disciple of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma.
It is said that he was engaged in the protection of his own body.
He became skillful. Out of fear that "there might be no comfort for my body," he did not consume food that was too cold or too hot;
out of fear that "my body might be exhausted by cold and heat," he did not go outside; and he did not eat rice and other foods that were excessively soaked or parched.
This skill of his in protecting the body became well known in the midst of the Saṅgha. The monks, in the Dhamma-hall...
How did they initiate the conversation? "Friends, it is said that a certain young bhikkhu is skilled in the art of bodily protection.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Bhikkhus, with what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "With this very one," he said, "Bhikkhus, this youth is not only skilled in the art of bodily protection now; formerly, too..."
Having said, "How did she come to be so?", he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in a forest glade.
Then, a certain bird-trapper, taking a wild jungle fowl along with a hair-rope and a stick, [set out].
While binding the domestic fowl in the forest, the hunter began to bind an ancient wild cock that had fled and entered the woods.
Due to his skill with hair-loops, the bird would not allow itself to be caught;
rising up again and again, it hid itself away. The hunter, concealing himself among the branches and foliage, repeatedly set out his staff and snares.
Desiring to put her to shame, the cock uttered human speech and spoke this first verse:
“I have seen in the forest trees such as the *assakaṇṇa* and the *vibhītaka*;
they are not able to do what you, O tree, are able to do.”
The meaning of this is: "O hunter, many *assakaṇṇa* and *vibhīṭaka* trees have been seen by me growing in this forest;
yet those trees are not able, as you are able, to move from here to there or to wander about."
Having spoken thus, the cock fled and went elsewhere. When he had fled and gone, the hunter recited the second verse:
"This is an ancient cock; having broken through the cage, he has come out.
Skilled in the trap-stones, he departs while still crowing."
In that context, "skilled with hair-traps" means being skilled regarding traps made of hair; he does not allow himself to be bound, but rather retreats and speaks, and having spoken, he flees.
Having said this, the hunter went back to his very home, taking whatever he had found after wandering through the forest.
The Teacher, having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the hunter was Devadatta."
“I was the young bhikkhu Kukkuṭa, skilled in guarding the body;
and as for the tree deity who witnessed that event, she was none other than myself.
The ninth explanation, the Commentary on the Kukkuṭa Jātaka.
[210] 10. The Explanation of the Kandagalaka Jātaka.
“O, what tree is this?”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana grove, concerning the abode of the Sugata.
For at that time, having heard that Devadatta had made an abode for the Sugata, the Teacher said: “Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has done so.”
“Having acted against me, he has met his destruction; indeed, he would have met it even before,” he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the region of the Himālaya in the womb of a woodpecker, and his name was Khadiravaniya.
He took his food solely in a *khadira* forest, and one [of his companions]...
He had a companion named Kandagalaka, who used to graze in the Simbali-pālibhaddaka forest. One day, he went to the presence of Khadiravaniya.
Thinking, "My companion has arrived," Khadiravaniya took hold of Kandagalaka, entered the acacia forest, struck an acacia trunk with his beak, and [extracted] the insects from the tree.
Having brought it out, he gave it to him. Kandagalaka ate it, cutting it up again and again as if it were sweet cakes.
As he was eating, pride arose within him: "This one too has been reborn in the womb of a woodpecker;
what use have I for this food given to me? I shall seek my own fodder in the acacia forest. He [went] to the acacia forest.
He said, "Friend, do not experience suffering; I myself will seek my food in the Khadira forest.
Then he replied to him, "Come now, friend, you were born into a family that seeks its food in worthless places such as the forests of *simbali*, *pāli*, and *bhaddaka*;
but the *khadira* trees are full of pith and are hard—do not let this displease you. Kandagalaka asked, "What then shall I..."
Disregarding his words, [the bird] rushed forward and struck a *khadira* tree with its beak.
At that very moment, its beak was shattered, its eyes became bulging as if about to pop out, and its head split open.
Unable to remain balanced on the trunk, it fell to the ground and spoke this first verse:
“O friend, what indeed is this tree, with its withered leaves and thorns, where my head has been split asunder by a single blow?
Therein, “O friend, what indeed is this tree? means: O you who dwell in the acacia forest, what indeed is this tree? “What indeed... [is the remainder].
"So" is also a reading. "Sinnapatta" means a thin leaf. "Where, with a single blow" means upon which tree [he struck] with just one blow.
"His head was split open" means the head was broken; and not only the head, but the beak was also broken.
Because he had reached such a state of pain, being unable to recognize the acacia tree, thinking, "What kind of tree is this?", he was overcome by agony.
Having offered the sacrifice, he lamented with this verse.
Hearing those words, Khadiravaniya spoke this second verse:
“Truly, he has wandered through the forests piercing them, among trees of wood and branches that are pithless.”
"Then he found a khadira tree that had reached its core, whereupon the Garuḷa struck his head.
In this context, *acāri vatāyaṃ* means "indeed, he moved about. *Vitudaṃ vanāni* means "piercing and striking through forests," specifically forests of sapless *simbalī* and *pālibhaddaka* trees.
*Kaṭṭhaṅgarukkhesu* refers to trees in the forest sections consisting of mere wood. *Asārakesu* means "in those lacking pith."
"Among those that escape" refers to the *pālibhaddaka*, *simbalī*, and other such trees. "Then he reached the khadira tree that had produced heartwood":
from the time it was a mere sapling, he eventually reached the khadira tree that had developed a core of solid wood. "Where the garuḷa split his supreme limb":
"where" means in which khadira tree he split or tore [the branch]. "Garuḷa" is a bird; for this is a term used with respect and reverence toward all birds.

Having spoken thus to him, Khadiravaniya said, "O Kandagalaka, that place where you shattered your head is where this tree called the Khadira grows; it is a tree of solid heartwood. He met his death right there.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Kandagalaka was Devadatta, and Khadiravaniya was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Kandagalaka Jātaka, the tenth.
The sixth chapter is the Nataṃdaḷha-vagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
Bandhanāgāra, Keḷisīla, Khaṇḍa, Vīraka, and Gaṅgeyya.
Kuruṅgamāssaka, Susumāra, Kukkuṭa, and Kandagalaka—these are the ten. 7.
The Chapter on the Bīraṇa-Stump.
[211] 1. The Commentary on the Somadatta Jātaka.
"He made himself ready"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyin.
For he was unable to speak even a single word in harmony with two or three people; he was full of timidity.
Thinking, "I will speak of something else," he spoke of something entirely different. The monks sat in the Dhamma hall discussing that incident of his.
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Lāḷudāyī is full of passion; formerly, too, he was so."
"Indeed, he was full of passion," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a certain brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Having reached maturity and mastered his craft at Takkasilā, he returned home to his parents.
Realizing his state of poverty, [the son] thought, "I shall establish him from a lowly family into a merchant's family.
Having taken leave of his parents, he went to Bārāṇasī and attended upon the king. He became dear and pleasing to the king.
Then, while his father—who was making a living by farming with only two oxen—lost one ox, he approached the Bodhisatta.
“Father, one ox has died; the farming work cannot proceed. Go and ask the king for one ox,” he said.
“Father, I have seen the king not long ago; it is not appropriate to ask for an ox right now. You all should ask.
“Father, you do not know how full of timidity I am; for in the presence of two or three people, I—”
"How can I manage this? If I go to the king to ask for the ox, he will give it to me and then return.
"Dear son, let it be as it may; I cannot ask the king, but nevertheless, I shall have you trained.
"In that case, please do have me trained."
The Bodhisatta, taking his father, went to the Bīraṇatthambhaka cemetery;

there, having tied bundles of grass in various places and assigned names to them—“This is the king,” “This is the viceroy,” “This is the commander-in-chief”—he showed them to his father in succession and said, “Father, go into the presence of the king and recite this verse: ‘Victory to you, Great King!’”
Having said this, he had him learn the verse:
"I have two oxen, O Great King, with which we plow the field;
one of them is dead, O Lord, give me the second, O Kshatriya."
The Brahmin, having mastered this verse within a single year, said to the Bodhisatta: "Dear Somadatta, the verse has become familiar to me;
now I am able to recite it before anyone. Take me into the presence of the King.
He replied, "Very well, dear father," and having had him take such a gift, he led his father to the King.
He led him into his presence. The brahmin, saying, "Victory to you, Great King," presented the gift.
The king asked, "Somadatta, what is this brahmin to you? "He is my father, Great King. "For what purpose has he come?
At that moment, the brahmin, speaking a verse for the sake of requesting oxen, said:
“Great King, I have two oxen with which we plow the field;
one of them is dead, O Lord, so take the second, O Kṣatriya,” he said.
The king, having been disappointed by the brahmin and perceiving the state of what was said, smiled and said, “Somadatta, for you...”
“There must be many oxen in your house,” he said. “They will have been given by you, Great King,” [the Brahmin replied].
The King, being pleased with the Bodhisatta, gave the Brahmin sixteen oxen, ornaments, and a village as his royal grant (*brahmadeyya*);
then, with great honor, he sent the Brahmin away. The Brahmin [mounted] a chariot yoked with all-white thoroughbred horses.
Having mounted [the chariot], he went to the village with a great retinue.
As the Bodhisatta was traveling seated in the chariot together with his father, he said, "Father, for an entire year I had you prepare the team;
yet at the time of the final decision, you gave the oxen to the king," and spoke the first verse:
“He constantly practiced his craft with diligence for a year on a stalk of *bīraṇa* grass;
having entered the assembly, he gave his explanation: ‘Discipline does not protect one of little wisdom.
In this regard, “He constantly practiced his craft with diligence for a year on a stalk of *bīraṇa* grass,” [the Buddha said]: “My dear son, you...”
Being constantly heedful, he prepared a meditation seat in the charnel ground made of a bundle of *bīraṇa* grass. "He manifested his perception, having entered the assembly":
moreover, having entered the assembly, he manifested that perception; he brought it to transformation—that is the meaning—and he reversed it.
"Restraint does not protect one of little wisdom": restraint, namely the practice of yoga, does not protect a person who is lacking in discernment (*appañña*).
"It does not save, it does not protect one's feet.
Then, having heard his words, the brahmin spoke this second verse:
"O dear Somadatta, a beggar encounters two things:"
“Whether there is loss or gain of wealth, such is the nature of begging.
In this context, “such is the nature of begging” means that begging has such an inherent character.
The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Lāḷudāyī is full of passion; formerly, too, he was full of passion.”
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and brought forth this Jātaka, he identified the births: "At that time, King Ānanda was Lāḷudāyī, the father of Somadatta;
but Somadatta was none other than myself.
This is the first commentary on the Somadatta Jātaka.
[212] 2. The Commentary on the Ucchiṭṭhabhatta Jātaka.
"Another higher description": this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction by his former wife.
For that bhikkhu, when asked by the Teacher, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are dissatisfied? replied:
Having said, “It was Truth,” when asked, “Who caused you such distress? he replied, “My former wife.
Then the Teacher said to him, “Monk, this woman has brought you harm; even in the past, she fed the leftovers of her own paramour. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, having wandered for alms at a certain place, [continued...]
Having been reborn into a poor family of actors who made their living by such means, he grew up to be destitute and ill-favored;

thus, he sustained his life by wandering for alms. At that time, in a certain village in the kingdom of Kāsi, there was a Brahmin whose wife was unchaste and of evil character, committing adultery. Then one day, while the Brahmin was away on some business...
When he had gone outside, her lover, having watched for that moment, entered the house. Having committed adultery with him, she said, "Wait a moment;

you shall go after you have eaten. She prepared a meal, adding hot food along with soup and condiments, and giving it to him with the words, "You eat," she herself waited, looking out for the arrival of the brahmin.
He stood at the door. The Bodhisatta stood there, waiting for alms-food at the place where the Brahmin’s paramour was eating.
At that moment, the Brahmin was returning toward the house. Seeing him approaching, the Brahmin woman hurried inside, saying, "Get up!
The Brahmin is coming! She then lowered her paramour into a store-room and, having entered herself, [waited for the Brahmin].

When he was seated, [the man] brought forward a wooden board, provided him with water for washing his hands, and added hot food on top of the cold food remaining from what the other had eaten, then gave it to the brahmin.
When the brahmin dipped his hand into the food, seeing that the upper portion was hot while the lower portion was cold, he thought: "This man has given me the leftover, discarded food of another."
"It must be so. Then, questioning the brahmin woman, he spoke this first verse:
"One caste is higher, and another caste is lower;
O brahmin woman, I ask you: what is below, and what is above?"
In this context, "color" (*vaṇṇa*) means appearance. For he asks about the hot nature of the upper part and the cold nature of the lower part, saying thus:
"What is below, and what is above? Indeed, by the very fact of being boiled rice, the upper part ought to be cool and the lower part hot;
yet this is not so. Therefore, I ask you: "For what reason is the rice above..."
"The upper part is hot, the lower part is cool.
Although the brahmin spoke again and again, the brahmin woman remained silent out of fear that the deed she had committed would be exposed.
At that moment, it occurred to the actor’s son: "By this wicked man who has been seated in the granary, my mistress..."
"This must be so; however, this brahmin woman says nothing out of fear that the deed she has committed might become known.
Well then, I shall reveal her deed and tell the brahmin that he was made to sit at the gate by her paramour.
From the moment he left the brahmin’s house, he [watched] the other’s entry into the house.

Having related the entire incident—including his transgression, eating the first portion of the meal, standing at the door of the brahmin woman and watching the road, and the fact that the other had been brought down into the storehouse—he spoke the second verse:
“I am a dancer, O venerable sir; I have come here as a beggar.”
"For he has descended from the rafters; this is he whom you seek.
In that regard, "I am a dancer, venerable sir" means, "Master, I am by nature a dancer.
"I have come here as a beggar" means that I have come to this place seeking alms as a beggar. "For he has descended from the rafters"—this refers to the rafters of the house.
"But this paramour of hers, while eating this meal, has entered the storehouse out of fear of you.
This is he whom you seek. "This is he whom you were seeking, wondering, 'Whose leavings could this possibly be?
Having seized him by the crest-lock and dragged him out from the storehouse, she acted in such a way that he would not commit such an evil deed again.

"Be mindful," he said, and then departed. The brahmin, having instructed both of them with threats and beatings so that they would never again commit such an evil deed, departed according to his own business.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths—
The monk Ukkhaṇṭhita was established in the fruit of stream-entry. [The Buddha said: "At that time, the brahmin woman was my former wife;
the brahmin who was the monk Ukkhaṇṭhita was [my son]; but as for the actor's son, it was I myself.
This is the second commentary on the Ucchiṭṭhabhatta Jātaka.
[213] 3. The Commentary on the Bharu Jātaka.

"Having placed the sages in between"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the King of Kosala. For the Blessed One and the community of monks received great gain and honor. As it is said:
"At that time, the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, and was a recipient of..."
“[The Blessed One] is honored with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is also honored... [with] medicinal requisites for the sick.
But the wanderers of other sects are not honored... [with] medicinal requisites.
Thus, having lost their gains and honor, they held secret assemblies day and night and consulted together: “Of the ascetic...”
"From the time Gotama appeared, we have become deprived of gain and honor; the ascetic Gotama has attained the pinnacle of gain and the summit of fame.
By what cause, then, has he come to possess such success? Thereupon, some said this:
"The ascetic Gotama dwells at the most excellent place, the highest spot on earth in all of Jambudīpa. For that reason, gain and honor arise for him."
The others said, "There is this reason: we too shall have a monastery for the non-Buddhist sects built on the grounds of the Jeta Grove; in this way, we shall become recipients of gain.

They all reached the conclusion, "So be it," and thought, "Even if we were to build the monastery without informing the king, the monks would prevent us; yet, having received a bribe, there is such a thing as a 'corruptible' person."
"There is no [other way]; therefore, let us give a bribe to the king and take the site for the monastery.

Having thus deliberated, they requested attendants, gave one hundred thousand pieces of money to the king, and said: "Great King, we shall establish a monastery for the non-Buddhist sects on the grounds of Jetavana.
If the monks inform you that they will not allow it to be built, our reply to them is—"
"It should not be given," they said. Out of greed for the bribe, the king accepted, saying, "Very well.
Having won over the king, the sectarians summoned a carpenter and began the work; there was a great clamor.
The Teacher asked, "Ānanda, what is this loud noise, this great clamor? "It is the followers of other sects, venerable sir."
“They are building a monastery for the non-Buddhist sects (tīrthika-ārāma) on the back of the Jeta Grove; that is where this noise comes from.
“Ānanda, this place is not suitable for a monastery for the non-Buddhist sects. Non-Buddhists are fond of loud noises; it is not possible to live with them,” he said.
Having spoken thus, he convened the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and said, “Go, bhikkhus, inform the king regarding the construction of the monastery for the non-Buddhist sects.”
“...you must prevent them,” he said. The community of monks went and stood at the gate of the king’s residence.
Although the king heard that the Saṅgha had arrived, because he had accepted a bribe, thinking, “They must have come on account of the heretics’ monastery,” he had it announced:
“The king is not at home. The monks went and reported this to the Teacher. The Teacher said, “On account of the bribe...”
“...act in this way,” he sent forth his two chief disciples. When the king heard that they too had arrived, he made them speak in the same manner.
They also came and informed the Teacher. The Teacher said, “Sāriputta, from now on the king will no longer be permitted to sit inside his house;
he will go outside. Then, on the following day at the time of morning, the Teacher dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and [set out] with the five hundred monks.
Accompanied by hundreds of bhikkhus, he went to the gate of the king’s palace. Having heard this, the king descended from his palace, took a bowl, and escorted the Teacher inside.

After providing rice gruel and solid food to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side. The Teacher, beginning a gradual discourse on the Dhamma for the king, said: “Great King,…”
"Former kings, having accepted bribes and incited mutual quarrels among those possessed of virtue, became non-rulers of their own kingdoms and met with great destruction," he said;
and being requested by him, he related a story of the past.

In the past, in the kingdom of Bharu, a king named Bharu reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was one who had attained the five super-knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*aṣṭasamāpatti*).

Having lived for a long time in the Himalayan region as an ascetic who was the leader of a community, he descended from the Himalayas surrounded by five hundred ascetics in order to partake of salt and sour gruel.
Arriving in due course at the city of Bharu, he went there for alms;
having departed from the city, he sat at the foot of a banyan tree—abounding in branches and foliage—at the northern gate, and performed his meal duties.

He took up residence right there at the foot of that tree. While that community of seers was dwelling there in this manner, after the lapse of half a month, another leader of a group, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, arrived.
Having wandered for alms in the city and departed from it, he sat down at the foot of a similar banyan tree at the southern gate; having finished his meal, he remained there.
He took up residence at the foot of a tree. Thus, those two groups of seers dwelt there as long as they pleased and then returned to the Himālaya.
When they had departed, the banyan tree at the southern gate was dry.
Later, when they were returning, the inhabitants of the banyan tree at the southern gate arrived first; perceiving that their own banyan tree was dry, [they went] for alms.
Having wandered for alms and departed from the city, they went to the foot of a banyan tree at the northern gate; having performed their meal-duty, they took up residence there.
The other seers, however, arrived later, wandered for alms in the city, went to their own respective trees, performed their meal-duty, and took up residence. They said, "That tree is not yours."
"This tree is ours," they said, and leaning against the tree, they quarreled with one another; the quarrel was great.
Some said, "This was our first dwelling place; you shall not have it.
Others said, "We arrived here earlier this time; you shall not have it. Thus they said, "We are the owners..."
Quarreling over the matter of "who is the owner?", they went to the royal palace for the sake of settling the dispute at the foot of a tree.
The king declared the first group of birds that had nested there to be the owners. The others, thinking, "Now we must ensure that we are not defeated by these," looked with their divine eye;
seeing a chariot-fender that was the possession of a wheel-turning monarch, they brought it back and [presented it] to the king.
Having given a bribe, they said, "Great King, please make us your masters as well.
The king, having accepted the bribe, said, "Let both groups dwell together," and thus he made them both his masters.
The other seers, having removed the wheels from that chariot-fender and given a bribe, said, "Great King, please make us alone your masters."

They said, "The king did so. The company of seers, filled with remorse, thought, "It was improper for us—having gone forth after abandoning both material desires and the desires of the defilements—to quarrel over the root of a tree and offer bribes.
Having fled in haste, they went back to the Himālayas. All the deities dwelling throughout the kingdom of Bharu gathered together.

Having made the offering, he thought, "It was improper for the King to engage in a quarrel with one who is virtuous," and becoming enraged at King Bharu, he caused the ocean to surge up three hundred leagues and submerged the kingdom of Bharu.
Thus, because of one King Bharu, all the inhabitants of the entire kingdom met their destruction.
Having brought forth this past event, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke these verses:
“Having placed the seers between us, I have heard,
