O King Bharu, that the king perished along with his kingdom and fell from his power.
Therefore, the wise do not praise acting out of desire.”
“One with a mind free from hatred should speak words endowed with truth.
In this context, “having made an opening” means having created a rift by way of following one’s own desire (*chandāgati*). “King Bharu” refers to the king in the kingdom of Bharu.
“Thus have I heard” means that previously this was heard by me. “Therefore, indeed, following one’s own desire” means because of following one’s own desire.
Having gone there, Bharu the king was destroyed along with his kingdom; therefore, the wise do not praise the following of one's own desires.
"With a mind free from malice" means having a mind that has not been defiled by the *kilesas*.

"One should speak words endowed with truth" means one should speak only those words that are based on what is natural, based on the meaning, and based on reason. For those who, in that situation, were taking bribes from King Bharu...
Protesting, "This is improper," they spoke words endowed with truth; even today, at the place where they stood on Nāḷikeradīpa, a thousand lamps are still visible.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Great King, one should not be a slave to one's own desires."
"It is not permissible for two groups of renunciants to engage in quarreling," he said, and then he identified the Jātaka:

"At that time, I was the elder king. When the King had finished his meal with the Tathāgata and departed, he dispatched men and had the monastery of the sectarians demolished; the sectarians were left without a base.
The third *Bharujātaka* commentary.
[214] 4. The *Puṇṇanadījātaka* commentary.
"The river Puṇṇā"—this the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke concerning the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*). For once, when...
One day in the Dhamma Hall, the bhikkhus initiated a discussion concerning the wisdom of the Tathāgata, saying:

“Friends, the Perfectly Enlightened One possesses great wisdom, vast wisdom, radiant wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, profound wisdom, penetrative wisdom, and he is endowed with skillful means in wisdom.
The Teacher approached and asked: “Bhikkhus, what is it that you are discussing?”
Having asked, "Are you sitting here now for this discussion? and being told, "Indeed we are," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, the Tathāgata was wise and skilled in means," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of a royal chaplain.

Having reached maturity and mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, he obtained the position of court chaplain upon his father’s passing and became the counselor in matters of welfare and righteousness to the King of Bārāṇasī.

Later, the king, having taken up the words of those who sought to cause dissension, became angry with the Bodhisatta and banished him from Bārāṇasī, saying, "Do not dwell in my presence. Thus the Bodhisatta departed.
Taking his wife and children, he made his home in a certain village in Kāsī. Later on, the king, remembering the teacher’s virtue, thought:
"It is not fitting for me to send anyone to summon the teacher;
rather, I shall compose a verse, write it upon a leaf, have some crow-flesh cooked, wrap both the leaf and the meat in a white cloth, and [send them]."
“I will have it sent by means of a royal seal. If he is wise, he will read the letter, recognize that it is crow’s flesh, and return;
if not, he will not return. Thus, he wrote this verse on the letter:
“‘The river is full,’ they say, where one drinks; ‘the barley has grown,’ they say in secret.”
"He whom they call one who has gone far away—come, O brahmins, eat from his generosity.
In this context, "to that full river which they call drinkable by crows" refers to rivers that are called "drinkable by crows" because they are full;
for a river that is not full is not called "drinkable by crows. Even when standing on the riverbank, [if] the neck...
When it has grown so that a crow can drink from it by stretching out its neck, then they call it "crow-drinkable" (*kākapeyya*).

Regarding the phrase "that which is called *guhya* when the barley has grown," the term *yava* is merely a heading for the teaching; however, what is intended here is all the grain that has grown, risen, and become fully matured.
For when it is able to conceal a crow that has entered within, it is then called *guhya*, meaning "hidden."

What is hidden? A crow. Thus, that which is the secret of a crow is called "crow-secret" (*kākaguyha*); speaking thus, they call it "secret" (*guyha*) because of the crow, which serves as the cause for the word "secret.
Therefore it is said: "and by which they call it secret. And "by which they call one who has gone afar":
seeing a beloved person who has gone afar, who is living away, having come and sat down...

"If such-and-such a person comes"—either upon hearing him crying "caw, caw" or simply hearing him crying out—those who, saying "Just as the crow cries, such-and-such a person will arrive," summon him;
this means they speak, converse, deliberate, and utter [these words].
"He has been brought by you" means he has been brought to you. "Come, eat, O Brahmin! means: take it, Brahmin, and eat.
"Naṃ" means "this," and "khāda" means "eat this crow's flesh"—this is the meaning.
Thus the king wrote this verse on a leaf and sent it to the Bodhisatta. Having read the leaf and realized, "The king wishes to see me," he spoke the second verse:
"Since the king remembers me Even to the point of sending for a crow..."
“Swans, cranes, and peacocks—these are indeed worse than a wanton woman.
In this context, “since the king remembers me, he will even have the crow killed” means that when the king obtains the flesh of a crow, he remembers me so that even that may be killed.
“Swans, cranes, and peacocks” refers to when these swans and others are presented to him.

The meaning is: "When he will obtain some swan-flesh and so forth, why then will he not remember me? In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, the reading is "of swans, cranes, and peacocks. That is better; the meaning is: "Having obtained the flesh of these—swans and so on—why will he not remember me? He will certainly remember me. [The phrase] "But one who is ungrateful is worse" means: *Asatīyeva pāpiyā* (but one who is ungrateful is worse). This is a compound (*samāsa*) consisting of three words: *a-satī* (ungrateful), *eva* (indeed), and *pāpiyā* (worse). It means that one who is ungrateful is indeed worse than even those previously mentioned. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *bahubbīhi* compound: "one who is worse than even an ungrateful person. This is because such a person is extremely wicked. Or it may be analyzed as a *kammadhāraya*: "one who is both ungrateful and worse," meaning one who is both ungrateful and more evil than others. Thus, the sense is that one who is ungrateful is worse than even a person who has committed a grave offense. For example, if someone were to kill his mother, father, or an arahant, or shed the blood of a Buddha, he would still be considered a transgressor; yet one who is ungrateful is even worse than such a person. Therefore, it is said: "But one who is ungrateful is worse. In this context, the term "ungrateful" (*asatī*) refers specifically to one who does not acknowledge the kindness received from another. Because of this, it is said: "One who is ungrateful is worse. Furthermore, the word *pāpiyā* is derived from the superlative suffix *-tama*; thus, it means "the most wicked among all wicked people. It is like saying, "Among all the wicked people in the world, this one is the worst. Therefore, it is said: "But one who is ungrateful is worse. This concludes the commentary on the verse beginning with "But one who is ungrateful is worse. Now follows the commentary on the verse beginning with "He who gives to one who is ungrateful... (Dhp 178). Here, "he who gives" (*dadāti yo*) refers to one who bestows gifts upon an ungrateful person. "To one who is ungrateful" (*asatimhi*) means to one who does not acknowledge the favor received. "He gives to him" (*tam dadāti*) means he offers that gift to him. "For what purpose? (*kimatthāya*)—it is for the sake of merit (*puññatthāya*). "Merit" (*puñña*) refers to wholesome karma (*kusala-kamma*). "For the sake of" (*atthāya*) means for the purpose of. "He gives to him for the sake of merit" means he offers a gift to that ungrateful person for the purpose of acquiring merit. "What does he receive? (*so kim labhati*)—what does he obtain? "He receives suffering" (*so dukkham nigacchati*) means he encounters suffering. "Suffering" (*dukkha*) refers to the result of unwholesome karma (*akusala-vipāka*). "He receives" (*nigacchati*) means he undergoes or experiences it. "He receives suffering" means he encounters the fruit of unwholesome karma. Why is this? Because he gave a gift to one who is ungrateful. Just as a person who sows seeds in salty soil reaps nothing but salt, so too, one who gives to an ungrateful person receives only suffering. Therefore, it is said: "He who gives to one who is ungrateful... he receives suffering. This concludes the commentary on the verse beginning with "He who gives to one who is ungrateful... Now follows the commentary on the verse beginning with "But he who gives to one who is grateful... (Dhp 179). Here, "he who gives" (*dadāti yo*) refers to one who bestows gifts upon a grateful person. "To one who is grateful" (*satimhi*) means to one who acknowledges the favor received. "He gives to him" (*tam dadāti*) means he offers that gift to him. "For what purpose? (*kimatthāya*)—it is for the sake of merit (*puññatthāya*). "Merit" (*puñña*) refers to wholesome karma (*kusala-kamma*). "For the sake of" (*atthāya*) means for the purpose of. "He gives to him for the sake of merit" means he offers a gift to that grateful person for the purpose of acquiring merit. "What does he receive? (*so kim labhati*)—what does he obtain? "He receives happiness" (*so sukham nigacchati*) means he encounters happiness. "Happiness" (*sukha*) refers to the result of wholesome karma (*kusala-vipāka*). "He receives" (*nigacchati*) means he undergoes or experiences it. "He receives happiness" means he encounters the fruit of wholesome karma. Why is this? Because he gave a gift to one who is grateful. Just as a person who sows seeds in fertile soil reaps an abundant harvest, so too, one who gives to a grateful person receives only happiness. Therefore, it is said: "But he who gives to one who is grateful... he receives happiness. This concludes the commentary on the verse beginning with "But he who gives to one who is grateful... Now follows the commentary on the verse beginning with "Therefore, knowing the ungrateful person... (Dhp 180). Here, "therefore" (*tasmā*) means for that reason. "Knowing the ungrateful person" (*asataṃ viditvā*) means having understood the nature of the ungrateful person. "And the grateful person" (*satañca*) means and the grateful person. "Knowing" (*viditvā*) means having understood. "Both of them" (*ubho*) means both the ungrateful and the grateful persons. "Having known both of them" (*ubho viditvā*) means having understood both the ungrateful and the grateful persons. "The wise man" (*paṇḍito*) means one who possesses wisdom. "Should give to the grateful person" (*dajjā satimhi*) means he should offer a gift to the grateful person. "Not to the ungrateful person" (*no asatimhi*) means he should not offer a gift to the ungrateful person. "Why? (*kiṃkāraṇā*)—for what reason? Because the ungrateful person is a vessel for suffering (*dukkhassa āvāso*), while the grateful person is a vessel for happiness (*sukhassa āvāso*). Therefore, it is said: "Therefore, knowing the ungrateful person... not to the ungrateful person. This concludes the commentary on the verse beginning with "Therefore, knowing the ungrateful person... Now follows the commentary on the verse beginning with "Just as rain falling on a high mountain... (Dhp 181). Here, "just as" (*seyyathāpi*) means just as. "Rain falling" (*udakaṃ vassamānaṃ*) means water falling. "On a high mountain" (*upari pabbate*) means on a high mountain. "High mountain" (*upari pabbate*) means on a lofty mountain. "Falling" (*vassamānaṃ*) means pouring down. "Water" (*udakaṃ*) means rainwater. "Just as rain falling on a high mountain" means just as rainwater falling on a high mountain. "Does not reach the lower valleys" (*na heṭṭhimāni pūreti*) means it does not fill the lower valleys. "Lower valleys" (*heṭṭhimāni padesāni*) means the lower regions. "Does not reach" (*na pūreti*) means it does not fill. "Just as rain falling on a high mountain does not reach the lower valleys" means just as rainwater falling on a high mountain does not fill the lower valleys. "So too, the gift given to an ungrateful person" (*evameva dānaṃ datvā asatimhi*) means just so, having given a gift to an ungrateful person. "Does not reach the giver" (*na taṃ dātāram-eti*) means it does not reach that donor. "Does not reach" (*na eti*) means it does not go to or reach. "The gift given to an ungrateful person does not reach the giver" means the gift offered to an ungrateful person does not reach the donor. Why is this? Because the ungrateful person is a vessel for suffering. Therefore, it is said: "So too, the gift given to an ungrateful person... does not reach the giver. This concludes the commentary on the verse beginning with "Just as rain falling on a high mountain
"Whatever refuge one obtains, even if it is called 'beautiful,' it is actually the worst in the world;
for being forgetful is itself base and wretched, yet that is not the case for our king. Thinking, 'The king remembers me; he awaits my arrival;
therefore I shall go,' he had his carriage prepared, went, and saw the king. The king was pleased and established him in the very position of domestic priest."
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the king, and I myself was the chaplain.
This concludes the commentary on the Puṇṇanadī Jātaka, the fourth.
5. The Commentary on the Kacchapa Jātaka.
“Alas, one has slain oneself!”—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning Kokālika. The background story will be revealed in the Mahātakkāri Jātaka.
At that time, however, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has been slain by his own speech;
in the past as well, he was slain by his own speech,” and he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers;

having reached maturity, he became the counselor who instructed him in matters of profit and righteousness. That king, however, was a man of many words, and while he was speaking, there was no opportunity for the speech of others.
Desiring to restrain the king’s excessive talkativeness, the Bodhisatta devised a certain stratagem.
He wandered about reflecting. At that time, a tortoise lived in a certain lake in the Himalayan region;
two young swans, while wandering for food, became friends with him.
Having become close friends, one day they said to the tortoise: "Friend tortoise, in our Himalayas, on the slopes of Mount Cittakūṭa..."
“The dwelling place in the Golden Cave is a delightful spot; will you go with us?
“What must I do to go? “We shall take you along, provided you can guard your mouth and say nothing to anyone. “I will guard it, Master; take me and go.”
Saying "Very well," they had the tortoise bite onto one stick, and having themselves bitten onto both ends of it,
they sprang into the air. As they were being carried away by the swans in this manner, the village children saw them and said, "Two swans are carrying a tortoise on a stick."

The tortoise, wishing to say, "If my friends are taking me away, what are you wicked servants doing here?", released his stick from the spot where he had been holding it as they reached the upper part of the royal palace in the city of Bārāṇasī due to the swiftness of the geese's speed;
he fell onto the courtyard of the sky and was split in two. [The people said: "The tortoise has fallen from the sky..."
“[The tortoise] has split in two!”—thus there was a great clamor. The king, taking the Bodhisatta and surrounded by his retinue of ministers, went to that place;
seeing the tortoise, he asked the Bodhisatta: “O wise one, what did he do to fall into this? The Bodhisatta replied:
“For a long time I have been wandering, seeking a means to advise the king, as I desired to do so. [He continued: “By this...”
The tortoise must have formed a friendship with the geese; they must have bitten him with their beaks, saying, "We will carry you to the Himalayas," and then flown up into the sky.
Then, having heard something from someone, because he failed to guard his mouth and desired to say something, he let go of the beaks; thus he fell from the sky.
Thinking, "He must have met with the destruction of his life," he said, "Yes, Great King, those called 'excessively talkative'—
those whose speech is boundless— indeed encounter such suffering as this," and spoke these verses:
"Alas, the tortoise has slain himself by uttering a voice!"
“When the wood was firmly grasped, he was killed with a single word.
Having seen this too, O best of men in valor, let not your speech release unwholesome words in excess;
you see the tortoise who met with disaster because of his excessive talking.”
In this context, *avadhī vatā* means "alas, he has killed. *Byāharanti* means "while speaking.
*Suggahītasmiṃ kaṭṭhasmiṃ* means when the stick had been firmly grasped with the mouth, having bitten it well.

*Vācāya sakiyāvadhī* means that due to excessive talkativeness, while uttering speech at an improper time, he released his grip on the place where he was biting and, by that very speech of his own, he struck and killed himself.
"Thus he has met his end, and not otherwise. "Having seen this too" means having seen this reason as well.

"O best of men in vigor" means O supreme king of excellent vigor, foremost among men by virtue of your energy. "A wise person should utter wholesome speech, but not excessively" means that a wise man should release—that is, utter—only what is wholesome, connected with truth and so forth;
and even that should be beneficial, appropriate for the occasion, and not excessive.
One should not speak words that exceed the proper time or are limitless. "Do you see?"—does he not indeed see it directly? "By much speaking"—by means of excessive talk.
"The tortoise has met with disaster"—this means the tortoise has reached the end of its life.
The king, realizing, "He is speaking with reference to me," said, "O wise ones, he was speaking about us. Thus spoke the Bodhisatta.
"Great King, whether it be you or anyone else, whoever speaks beyond measure meets with such a calamity," he said, making this clear.
From that time forward, the king refrained from speaking and became one who speaks sparingly.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the tortoise was Kokālika; the two young swans were the two Great Elders; the king was Ānanda; and the wise minister was none other than myself."
The fifth: The Commentary on the Kacchapa Jātaka.
[216] 6. The Commentary on the Maccha Jātaka.
"This fire of lust does not burn"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction of his former wife.
He related the story. For the Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?
When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," and was asked, "By whom have you been made dissatisfied? he said, "By my former wife.
Then the Teacher said to him, "This woman has brought you harm; even in the past, because of her, you were impaled on a stake."
“Having been pierced and cooked over glowing coals, he reached the state of being eaten; yet, by relying on a wise man, he obtained his life. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his domestic priest.
Now one day, some fishermen hauled up a fish caught in their net, placed it upon hot sand, and said, “We shall cook it over glowing coals and eat it.”
Thinking, “We shall eat him,” they carved the spit. As the fish lamented, addressing the female fish, he spoke these verses:
“This fire does not burn me, nor does this spit, though well-carved;
it is because the female fish thinks of me that another has gone to his pleasure.”
“Thus the fire of passion burns me, it scorches my mind;
O Noble Ones, release me from the snare! One is never slain by sensual desires.
In this context, “this fire does not burn me” means that this fire does not scorch me, does not produce heat, and does not cause grief.
The meaning is as follows: "Not the stake"—even this stake, being well-hewn, does not burn me, nor does it produce grief in me.

But that which she thinks of me—namely, what that female fish thinks thus of me, "He has gone to another female fish for the pleasure of the five strands of sensual desire"—that alone burns me, that alone causes me grief.
"It consumes me"—it is this fire of passion that consumes me.
It burns. It consumes the mind; indeed, it is the mind associated with passion that consumes me, afflicts me, and torments me.
"O fishers," he addresses them; for they are called "the netters" because they possess nets.
"Release me, O masters," he entreats; "nowhere is one slain by sensual pleasures."
"A being established in sensual desire, led away by sensual desire, is not killed anywhere. For those like you are not fit to kill him," he lamented.
Alternatively, "kāme" is used in the locative case with the sense of a cause; thus he lamented:
"One who follows a fish for the sake of sensual desire is not killed anywhere by people like you. At that moment, the Bodhisatta [reached] the riverbank.
Having gone there and heard the sound of that fish’s lamentation, he approached the fishermen and released the fish.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (*saccāni*), the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the dejected monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). "At that time, the female fish was his former wife; the male fish..."
"The dejected monk was none other than myself, while the chaplain was I indeed.
This concludes the sixth *Jātaka*, the Story of the Fish.
[217] 7. The Story of the Seggu Bird (*Seggu-jātaka*).
“The whole world,” this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain lay follower who was a dealer in leaves.
The story is already detailed in the Ekakanipāta. Here too, the Teacher asked him, “Lay follower, why have you come so late?
The lay follower replied, “Venerable sir, my daughter always has a smiling face; having wished to test her—”
"I gave her to a young man of a certain family; because of the duties involved therein, I had no opportunity to come and see you," he said.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Lay follower, this Sīlavatī was not virtuous only now; she was virtuous in the past as well.
And you did not only now test her; you tested her in the past as well. Having said this, at his request, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity.
At that time, this very same lay disciple, a merchant, thinking, "I shall test my daughter," took her into the forest and, as if out of lust, seized her by the hand.
Then, as she was lamenting, he addressed her with the first verse:
“The whole world was delighted, for they were ignorant of the ways of village life;
O maiden, what kind of dhamma is this of yours, that you, having been taken into the forest, are weeping?
In this context, “the whole world was delighted” means, “Mother, the entire world of beings [was delighted] by her indulgence in sensual pleasure.”
He became delighted. "Seggū" means one who is unskilled in the ways of the village; that was her name. Therefore, it is said:
"But you, mother Seggū, being unskilled in the ways of the village, are unskillful in this way of the village, this way of the outcastes.
"What kind of maidenly nature (*komāri*) do you have today, mother? means, "Mother, what indeed is this natural character (*sabhāva*) of yours today as a young girl?"

"Since you, when taken by me in this forest, wept 'O heavens!'—you were taken by me in this forest on account of intimacy, yet you wept and did not accept it; what is this nature of yours? Are you indeed just a young maiden? he asked.
Hearing that, the young maiden said, "Yes, father, I am indeed a young maiden; I do not know what is called the act of sexual intercourse," and lamenting, she spoke the second verse.
“He who would be a refuge for one touched by suffering—that father of mine does wrong in the forest!
To whom shall I cry out in the midst of the woods? He who was my protector now acts with violence!
This has already been explained below. Thus, having tested his daughter at that time, the merchant took her home, gave her to a young man of good family, and departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
at the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower Paṇṇika was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the daughter was indeed the daughter, and the father was indeed the father;
but as for the tree deity who witnessed the event firsthand, she was none other than myself.”
The seventh is the commentary on the Seggu Jātaka.
[218] 8. The commentary on the Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka:
"Deceit belongs to the deceitful"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a fraudulent merchant.

He related the story. For two merchants living in Sāvatthī, a fraudulent merchant and a wise merchant, having become friends, filled five hundred carts with merchandise and, traveling from the eastern region to the western region, conducted trade and, having gained much profit, returned to Sāvatthī. The wise merchant said to the fraudulent merchant: "Friend,..."
“Let us divide the merchandise. The fraudulent merchant thought, “This man has long been exhausted by a wretched bed and poor food;
he will eat various kinds of choice meals at his own home and die from indigestion.
Then all this merchandise will belong to me alone. Having thought this, he said, “The constellation is unfavorable; the day is unfavorable.”
"I will find out myself; I will find out on the following day," he said, thus wasting time.

Then the wise merchant, having pressed him and made him share the profit, took the perfumes and garlands, went into the presence of the Teacher, and after worshipping and paying homage to the Teacher, sat down to one side.
The Teacher asked, "When did you arrive? and he replied, "It has been only half a month since I arrived, Bhante."
Having said this, when he was asked, "Now why have you come to attend upon the Buddha after making such a fuss? he related the circumstances.
The Teacher said, "Lay follower, it is not only now that this man has been a fraudulent trader; he was so even in the past.
At his request, the Teacher related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers;
having reached maturity, he became the king’s judge. At that time, there were two merchants who were friends, one living in the countryside and the other in the city.
The country dweller deposited five hundred ploughshares with the city dweller. Having sold those ploughshares, [the city dweller...]
Having taken the plow-shares, he placed rat droppings in the spot where they had been set down and left them there.
Later, a village dweller came and said, "Give me my plow-shares. The fraudulent merchant said, "Your plow-shares have been eaten by rats," and showed him the rat droppings.
The other replied, "Let them be eaten; what can one do when things are eaten by rats? and [went] for the sake of bathing.

Taking his son with him, as he was going along, he said to a friend’s house, "Do not let him go anywhere," and having seated him inside the inner chamber, he himself bathed and went to the house of the fraudulent merchant. The merchant asked, "Where is my son?
[The friend replied,] "Good sir, having placed your son on the bank, while I was submerged in the water, a hawk—"
"Having come and seized your son with his talons, he flew into the sky;
though I struck my hands together and cried out, struggling as I did, I was unable to free him. "You speak falsely! There are no hawks capable of seizing a child and flying away.
"My dear sir, let it be; even if it were improper, what could I do? It was by a hawk alone..."
“Your son has been taken away! Having threatened him, he said, “Hey, you wicked thief, murderer of men! Now I shall take you before the court and have you dragged there.
Saying, “You are doing exactly what pleases me,” he went with him to the place of judgment.
The fraudulent merchant said to the Bodhisatta: “Master, this man took my son and went to bathe; when asked, ‘Where is my son?
he replied, ‘He was carried off by a hawk. Judge my lawsuit. The Bodhisatta asked the other, “Tell the truth.
He replied: “Yes, Master, I took him with me; as for his being struck down by a hawk—”
“It is true, Master. “But what, in this world, do hawks do when they seize children? “Master, I too ask you this:
‘Are hawks unable to fly through the air after seizing children, while mice are able to chew iron ploughshares?
“What is this supposed to mean? “Master, five hundred iron ploughshares were placed by me in this man’s house.”
Saying, "Your plow has been eaten by mice," he showed him excrement, saying, "This is the dung of the mice that ate your plow.
"Master, if mice eat the plow, hawks will carry off the children;
but if they do not eat it, even the army will not carry them off. Yet this man says, 'Your plow has been eaten by mice.'"
“Find out whether they have been eaten or not eaten, and then decide my case. The Bodhisatta,
knowing that this had been thought by one who intended to win by practicing deception against a deceiver,
said, “Very well thought of by you,” and spoke these verses:
“O Indra, the deceit of the deceiver is well-considered; the fraud of the fraudulent is well-executed.
If mice were to eat the ploughshare, why would hawks not carry off the prince?
For indeed, there are frauds for the fraudulent, and there is also deception for the deceiver.”
"Give the ploughshare to one who has lost his son through ploughing; let not the loss of your son through ploughing be yours.
In this context, "of the crafty" means of one who is crafty by way of craftiness (*kerāṭika*), thinking, "It is permissible to consume another's property after employing some stratagem.
"This craftiness is well-considered" refers to you who were considering this counter-stratagem (*paṭisāṭheyya*).
"Well thought out. Regarding "the snare set against the rogue": you have well set a snare against that rogue person;
the meaning is that you have made it as if it were actually laid down by creating a likeness.
"If mice were to gnaw the plowshare" means if mice were to gnaw the plowshare. "Why would falcons not carry off the boy? [is asked] regarding the mice.
While the hawks are devouring the entrails, for what reason would they not carry off the prince?

For there are indeed "frauds upon frauds" (kūṭakūṭā) in this world; you think, "I am a man whose entrails were made to be eaten by mice, I am a fraud," but for such a fraud as you, there are many other frauds in this world—frauds upon frauds, that is, those who are the counter-frauds of the frauds.
This is the name; it is said that there are "counter-deceits" (*paṭikūṭa*) for a deceitful person (*kūṭa*).
Furthermore, there is indeed another deceitful person, a deceiver, who acts as a counter-deceiver (*nikati*) against a deceitful person, a deceiver—someone who is himself dishonest.
"Give [it] to me," they say, "for the sake of the lost son, for the sake of the plowing. "O man whose son is lost, for this..."
“Give the plowshare to him whose plowshare is lost. Do not let your son be lost for the sake of a plowshare.
For if you do not give him the plowshare, he will take your son; let him not take him from you—give him the plowshare.
“I will give it, sir, if you give me my son. “I will give it, sir, if you give me the plowshare. Thus, one who has lost a son [seeks] a son.
The one whose plough was lost recovered his plough, and both went their separate ways according to their karma.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the fraudulent merchant was the fraudulent merchant of today; the wise merchant was the wise merchant of today; and the judge-minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the eighth narrative, the Commentary on the Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka.
[219] 9. The Commentary on the Garahitajātika.
"Gold is mine, gold is mine"—the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a certain monk who was weary and dissatisfied with the religious life.
For this monk had no specific object of attachment; rather, it was a state of dissatisfaction that dwelt within him.
They then brought him, while he was still in the springtime of his youth, into the presence of the Teacher. When the Teacher asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?
he replied, "It is true. When asked, "For what reason? he said, "On account of the defilements.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Monk, these so-called 'defilements' have been censured even by animals in the past; you, in such a state..."
"Having gone forth in the Dispensation, why are you dissatisfied through the influence of defilements that are censured even by animals? Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Himālaya region in the womb of a monkey.
A certain forest-dweller captured him, brought him back, and gave him to the king. Having lived for a long time in the royal palace, [he...]
He was perfect in his duties; he understood for the most part the activities prevailing in the world of humans.
The king, having gained confidence in his conduct, summoned a forest ranger and commanded him, “Release this monkey at the very place where it was captured.
He did accordingly. The troop of monkeys, knowing that the Bodhisatta had arrived, [gathered] to see him.
Having gathered on a large stone slab and exchanged friendly greetings with the Bodhisatta, he asked, "Friend, where have you been living for all this time?
"In Bārāṇasī, at the royal palace," he replied. "Then how were you released?
"The king made me his pet monkey; becoming pleased with my conduct, he set me free."
Then those monkeys said to him, "You must know the activities currently taking place in the human world;
please tell us first, for we wish to hear. [The Bodhisatta replied,] "Do not ask me about the activities of humans. "Tell us, for we wish to hear," they urged.
The Bodhisatta then said, "As for humans—whether they be kshatriyas or brahmins—they say, 'It is mine, it is mine!'"
“They speak thus, yet having become [so], they do not know impermanence in the sense of non-existence.
Now listen to the reasoning of those blind fools,” and having said this, he spoke these verses:
“‘Silver is mine, gold is mine’—this is their talk by night and by day;”
Of foolish people who do not see the noble Dhamma:
"In the house of each pair of householders, one among them is hairless;
he has a hanging belly, is covered in veins, and moreover has his ears pierced."
"Like a moth [drawn] by abundant wealth, he strikes at that person.
In this context, the phrases "silver is mine" and "gold is mine" are merely the headings for the teaching;
however, by these two lines, he shows all ten kinds of treasures, as well as all primary and secondary grain, fields and lands, and all bipeds and quadrupeds.
"This is mine, this is mine," he said. This is the talk of people by night and by day, at all times.
But they do not know anything else, such as "the five aggregates are impermanent" or "having come to be, they do not remain";
thus they wander about lamenting. "Of the dull-witted" means of those with little wisdom. The noble Dhamma...
"Those who do not see" refers to those who do not see the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas, or the Noble, faultless, ninefold supramundane Dhamma;
it is only of them that this statement is made. For others, however, there is no talk of "the impermanent" or "suffering.
"Householders" means those who are masters in their homes. "One among them" refers to the woman among those two householders.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). In this context, "one who has braided hair" (*veṇikato*) means one who has fashioned a braid, that is to say, a mass of hair arranged in various ways.
Furthermore, "one who has marked ears" (*aṅkitakaṇṇako*) refers to one whose ears have been pierced—that is, one with perforated ears—stating this with reference to having long, hanging ears.

Moreover, "bought for much wealth" (*kīto dhanena bahunā*) refers to him being without a beard, having long limbs, having braided hair, having marked ears, and [being the offspring] of his mother and father.
Having been purchased for much wealth, adorned and beautified, and placed upon a vehicle, he was brought home with a great retinue.

From the moment of his arrival, that householder began to strike the people in the house—whether they were slaves, laborers, or others—with verbal daggers, saying, "Hey, you wicked slave! You wicked slave-woman! Why do you not do this? and so forth.
He prods them about and, acting like their master, interrogates the great multitude. Thus, first of all, he censured the human world, saying, "It is utterly unfitting in the world of men.
Hearing this, all the monkeys cried out, "Do not speak! Do not speak! We have heard what ought not to be heard! And with both hands—
They firmly closed their ears with their hands. Thinking, "In this place we have heard what is improper," they censured that spot as well and departed for another location.
That back-rock became known as the "Censured Back-Rock.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, [the listeners were established in the fruits of the path].
That bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the troop of monkeys was the Buddha’s retinue, and the lord of the monkeys was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Garahitajātakaya, the ninth.
[220] 10. The Commentary on the Dhammadhajajātakaya.
“You live happily,” this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta’s attempt to kill him.
At that time, the Teacher said: “Monks, it is not only now; formerly as well, Devadatta sought my death.”
"Though he strove to kill him, he was unable to cause even the slightest bit of fear," he said, and then related a story of the past:
"In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Yasapāṇi reigned, and he had a general named Kāḷaka.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was his own court priest, named Dhammadhaja, while there was also a barber who attended to the king's head."
He was named Chattapāṇi. The king administered the kingdom with righteousness, but his general, while conducting legal proceedings, took bribes and acted as a backbiter;
having accepted bribes, he made those who were not owners appear to be owners.
Then one day, a man defeated in a legal case emerged from the court, wailing and raising his arms, and went to wait upon the king.

Seeing the Bodhisatta as he was passing by, [Kāḷaka] fell at his feet and said, “My lord, while you, such as you are, are instructing the king in both worldly profit and the Dhamma, Kāḷaka the general has accepted a bribe and is making those who do not own property appear as owners.
Thus he told the Bodhisatta of his own defeat. The Bodhisatta, having aroused compassion, said, “Come here, friend!”
“I shall settle your lawsuit,” he said, and taking him with him, he went to the place of judgment. A great crowd gathered;
the Bodhisatta, having adjudicated that lawsuit, restored the rightful owner to his own property.
The great crowd gave a shout of approval, and that sound was loud. Hearing it, the king asked, “What is this noise?”
He asked, “Your Majesty, the case poorly adjudicated by the scholar Dhammadhaja has been well adjudicated by you; there is a sound of applause for that.
The king was delighted and, having summoned the Bodhisatta, asked, “Teacher, it is said that the case was adjudicated by you?
When he replied, “Yes, Great King, I have adjudicated the case which Kālaka adjudicated poorly,” the king said, “From this day forward—”
“You yourselves must decide the case; it will be pleasing to my ears and a benefit to the world,” he said.
Then, having entreated him, saying, “Sit in judgment out of compassion for living beings,” even though he was unwilling, he caused him to accept.
From that time forth, the Bodhisatta sat in judgment; he restored property to its rightful owners.

From that time on, Kāḷaka, receiving no bribes and falling away from his gains, harbored resentment toward the Bodhisatta and slandered him to the king, saying, "Great King, the wise Dhammadhaja covets your kingdom.
The king, not believing him, rejected it, saying, "Do not speak thus! But when Kāḷaka spoke again, [the king said], "If you do not believe me..."
"When he arrives, look through the window; then you will see that the entire city has been placed in his hands," he said.
When this was said, the king saw the general’s retinue and, perceiving it to be "his very retinue," broke ranks and asked, "General, what shall we do?
"Your Majesty, it is right to kill him. "He has committed a grave offense..."
“How shall we kill him if we do not see him? “There is a certain stratagem. “What kind of stratagem?
“By charging him with an impossible task; when he is unable to perform it, we shall kill him for that offense. “But what is an impossible task?
“Your Majesty, a garden planted in fertile soil and tended with care [will, in three or four years]—”
“He will give you the fruit. You should summon him and say, ‘Tomorrow we shall go for recreation in the park; build me a park.
He will not be able to build it, and then we shall have him executed for that offense.
The king addressed the Bodhisatta: “O wise one, I have long enjoyed myself in my old park; now, in this new park—”
“We wish to play; we shall play tomorrow. Build us a pleasure garden; if you are unable to build it, you shall have no life.

The Bodhisatta, knowing that King Antara would be ruined by Kāḷaka because he had not obtained the bribe, said, “I shall see if I am able, Great King,” and having gone home, eaten a fine meal, he reflected.
As he lay down upon his bed, he caused the palace of Sakka to appear hot.
Sakka, reflecting and perceiving the Bodhisatta’s thought, came with great speed, entered the inner chamber, stood in the air, and asked, "What are you thinking, O wise one?
"Who are you? "I am Sakka. "The king told me, 'Build a pleasure grove'; that is what I am thinking."
“O wise one, do not worry; I shall construct for you a pleasure grove like the Nandana Grove or the Cittalatā Grove.
In which place shall I build it? “Build it in such-and-such a place. Having had it constructed, Sakka returned to the city of the gods.
On the following day, the Bodhisatta, seeing the pleasure grove before his eyes, went and informed the king: “It is finished.”
“Go, Great King, and enjoy yourself in the pleasure garden.

The king went and saw the park, which was enclosed by a wall eighteen cubits high with the color of red arsenic, provided with gate-towers, and adorned with various trees laden with an abundance of flowers and fruits.
Seeing it, he asked Kālaka, “The wise man has carried out our word; what shall we do now?”
“Great King, if you are able to have a pleasure grove constructed in a single night, why would you not be able to seize the kingdom?
“What shall we do now? “Let us have him perform another task that requires great effort. “What kind of work is it?
“Have him construct a lotus pond made of the seven precious gems. The king said, “Very well,” and addressed the Bodhisatta: “Teacher, …”
"First, your garden has been laid out; now, construct for it a lotus pond made of the seven precious gems worthy of it.
If you are unable to construct it, you shall have no life," he said. The Bodhisatta replied, "Very well, Great King;
if I am able, I shall construct it. Then Sakka constructed for him a lotus pond that had reached the pinnacle of beauty and possessed eternal bathing places.
It had a thousand curves, was covered with five-colored lotuses, and resembled the Nandana lotus pond.
On the following day, the Bodhisatta, having personally inspected it as well, informed the king: "The lotus pond has been constructed, Your Majesty.
When the king saw it as well, he asked Kāḷaka, "What shall we do now? [Kāḷaka replied: "A house suitable for the pleasure garden..."
“Have it built, O King,” he said. The King addressed the Bodhisatta, saying, “Now, Teacher, build a house made entirely of ivory that is suitable for this park and lotus pond;
if you do not build it, you shall have no life. Then Sakka built the house for him as well. On the following day, the Bodhisatta—
Having witnessed it firsthand, he reported it to the king. When the king saw that as well, he asked Kāḷaka, "What shall we do now?
He replied, "Great King, command him to fashion a gem suitable for this house; we shall move about by the light of that gem.
The king addressed the Bodhisatta, saying, "Wise one, fashion a gem suitable for this ivory house; we shall travel by the light of the gem."
"If you cannot create it, you shall have no life," he said. Then Sakka created a jewel for him as well.
On the following day, the Bodhisatta verified this for himself and reported it to the king. When the king saw that too, he asked Kāḷaka, "What shall we do now?
"Great King, there is the Dhammadhaja Brahmin, who grants whatever is desired."
“I imagine there are deities; now, command that which even the deities are unable to create.
For even the deities cannot create a human being endowed with the four factors; therefore, say to him:
‘Create for me a park-keeper endowed with the four factors. The King addressed the Bodhisatta: “Teacher, by you our park—”
“A lotus pond has been built, and a palace made of ivory; a jewel-treasure has also been fashioned for the purpose of providing light.
Now, build for me a park-keeper, a garden guardian endowed with the fourfold qualities; if you do not build him, you shall have no life.
The Bodhisatta said, “Very well, I shall know when I find one,” and having gone home, he took a fine meal.
Having eaten and lain down, he woke at the time of dawn and, sitting upon his couch, reflected:
"Sakka, the king of the gods, has created everything that it is possible for him to create; however, he was unable to create a park-keeper endowed with the four qualities.
This being so, death in the forest without a protector is indeed better than death at the hands of others."
Thus, without telling anyone, he descended from the palace, departed from the city by way of the main gate, entered the forest,
and sat at the foot of a certain tree reflecting upon the Dhamma of the hundred verses.
Sakka, having understood this situation, approached the Bodhisatta in the guise of a forest-dweller and said, "Brāhmaṇa,..."

"You are one who has lived in luxury, appearing as though you have never before experienced suffering; having entered this forest, what are you doing sitting here?"—asking this matter, he spoke the first verse:
"You appear to live in comfort, having come from the kingdom to the wilderness."
“Thus you meditate alone at the foot of a tree, like a pauper.
In this context, “you live as if in happiness” means you are like one who lives in comfort, nurtured by ease and shielded by pleasure.
“From the realm” means from a place crowded with people. “Come to the forest” means you have entered a wilderness devoid of water. “At the foot of a tree” means...
"Near the tree. "You meditate like a pauper," he asked; "you sit alone like a pauper, meditating and brooding—what is it that you are thinking about?
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
“I am one who lives happily, having come from the kingdom to the forest;
alone at the foot of a tree, I meditate like a pauper,
recollecting the Dhamma of the Arahants.”
"In this regard, friends, they recollect the Dhamma of the virtuous; this is indeed the truth.
I have come from the kingdom to the forest in the form of one seeking happiness, yet here, sitting alone at the foot of this tree, I meditate like a pauper.
As for what you asked, 'What is it that you are thinking?', I shall explain it to you as the 'Dhamma of the virtuous. For I—"
"Recalling the Dhamma of the virtuous, seated here. "The Dhamma of the virtuous" refers to the Dhamma of the virtuous, noble, wise persons—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha.
For this eightfold worldly condition consists of gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. But the virtuous, being struck by these, do not waver.
“They clash against one another; this is the Dhamma of the noble ones, characterized here by imperturbability, which I am sitting here recollecting,” he explained.

Then Sakka asked him, “That being so, brahmin, why are you sitting in this place? “The king has had a park-keeper endowed with four qualities brought to him, yet I am unable to find anyone such as that.
Therefore I thought, ‘What is the use of my dying at the hands of another?’”
“Having entered the forest and thinking, ‘I shall die an orphan’s death,’ he has come here and sat down.
“Brahmin, I am Sakka, the king of the gods; it was I who had the gardens and such things laid out for you.
It is not possible for me to create a park-keeper endowed with the four qualities; rather, your king’s head-groom named Chattapāṇi is the one who possesses those four qualities.”
“Tell the gardener who is endowed with the four qualities that, when there is need, he should be appointed as the barber.
Having thus given this advice to the Bodhisatta and comforted him, saying, “Do not fear,” Sakka returned to his own celestial city.
The Bodhisatta went home, and after eating his morning meal, he went to the palace gate; there he saw the umbrella-bearer as well.
Taking him by the hand, he asked, "Friend Chattapāṇi, it is said that you possess the four factors.
When Chattapāṇi replied, "Who told you that I possess the four factors? he said, "Sakka, the king of the gods.
When asked, "For what reason did he tell you?", he explained everything, saying, "For this very reason. Chattapāṇi then said, "Yes, I..."

“He is endowed with the four qualities,” he said. Then the Bodhisatta took him by the hand and went into the presence of the king, saying, “Great King, this Chattapāṇi is endowed with the four qualities;
if there is need for a park-keeper endowed with those four qualities, you should appoint this man as park-keeper. Then the king said to him, “It seems that you—”
“You are endowed with four factors,” he asked. “Yes, Great King,” he replied. “With which four factors are you endowed?
“I am free from envy, O Lord; I do not drink intoxicants; I am free from lust, O Lord; and I am resolved upon non-anger.”
“Great King, I have no envy; I have never drunk intoxicants; neither affection nor anger has ever arisen toward others. I am endowed with these four qualities.
Then the king said to him, “O Chatta-pāṇi, you say that you are free from envy? “Yes, Your Majesty, I am free from envy.
“What object did you see that made you become free from envy? “Listen, Your Majesty,” he replied, and [related] the reason for his freedom from envy.
Speaking thus, he recited this verse:
“O King, it was for the sake of a woman that I had the chaplain bound;
he informed me of the matter, and therefore I am free from resentment.”
The meaning of this is as follows: "O King, in the past, having been a king just like you in this very city of Bārāṇasī, I had a family priest imprisoned for the sake of a woman.
For: 'Those who are not bound there are bound where fools shine forth;
even those who are bound are released where the wise shine forth.'"

For in this Jātaka, according to the method set forth therein, at one time this King Chattapāṇi, having conspired with sixty-four courtiers, became estranged from the Bodhisatta because he did not fulfill his own desire;
he had him bound by a queen who wished to destroy him. When the Bodhisatta was brought there after being bound, [the queen spoke to him] exactly as it was.

Having cleared himself of the charge, he released all those who had been bound by the king at the foot of the tree, and exhorted them, saying, "Great King, forgive the offense of these men and of the queen.
All of this should be understood in detail according to the method already stated below.
With reference to that, he said:
“O King, it was for the sake of a woman that I had the chaplain imprisoned;
he informed me of the matter, and therefore I am free from malice.
At that time, however, I thought: “Having abandoned sixteen thousand women, I have come here alone because of defilement.”

Even while supporting them, I was unable to satisfy them; thus, getting angry with women who are so difficult to satisfy is like getting angry at a garment for becoming soiled, saying, "Why do you get soiled?
or like getting angry at food after it has been eaten for turning into excrement, saying, "Why do you turn into this nature? From here—
“From this day forth, until I attain Arahantship, let no envy arise in me on account of defilements,” he resolved.
From that time on, he became free from envy. It was with reference to this that he said, “Therefore I am free from envy.
Then the king asked him, “Friend Chattapāṇi, what object did you see that caused you to become a non-drinker of intoxicants? Explaining the reason for it, he spoke this verse:
“I was intoxicated, O Great King, when I ate the flesh of my own sons;
touched by grief for them, I abstained from drinking liquor.
“In the past, O Great King, having been such a king of Bārāṇasī, I was unable to live without liquor.”
I was unable even to eat food without meat. On the Uposatha days in the city, the slaughterhouse was closed;
however, the cook had taken meat on the thirteenth day of the fortnight and set it aside, and because it was poorly stored, dogs ate it.
On the Uposatha day, the cook being unable to obtain meat, cooked various exquisite dishes for the king and [ascended] the palace.
Being unable to lift it up and present it, he approached the queen and said, "Queen, today I have found no meat;
I am unable to present food that is meatless. What shall I do?
"Dear one, my son is dear and pleasing to the king. When the king sees my son, he kisses and embraces him so much that he forgets even his own presence."
She did not know that she should say, "Having adorned my son, I shall have him sit upon the king's lap; when the king plays with his son, you must bring the food.
Having said this, she adorned her own son with ornaments and had him sit upon the king's lap. When the king played with his son, the cook [brought] the food...
He presented it. The king, intoxicated by liquor, not seeing the meat in the bowl, asked, "Where is the meat?

When told, "Today, Your Majesty, is the Uposatha day; no meat was obtained for slaughter," he remarked, "Meat is indeed difficult for me to obtain," and having twisted the neck of his beloved son who was sitting on his lap, he brought him to the end of his life.
Having thrown [the child] before the cook, he said, "Prepare it with speed and bring it here!
The cook did exactly so, and the king ate his meal with the flesh of his own son.
Out of fear of the king, not a single person was able to weep, cry, or even speak.
Having eaten, the king went to sleep on his couch; waking at dawn, his intoxication gone, he said, "Bring my son.
At that moment, the queen fell at his feet weeping. When he asked, "What is it, lady?
she replied, "Your Majesty, yesterday you killed your son and ate a meal of his flesh. The king, out of grief for his son—
Weeping and wailing, he perceived the fault in drinking liquor, thinking, "This suffering of mine has arisen on account of drinking liquor. He resolved:
"From this day forth, until I attain Arahantship, I shall not drink such a ruinous thing as liquor.
Having taken some dust and wiped his mouth, he made this firm resolve. From that time on, [he abstained from] intoxicants.
“I did not drink [the wine]. It was with reference to this matter that he spoke this verse: “I am intoxicated, O Great King.
Then the king asked him, “But what object, my dear Chattapāṇi, have you seen that has caused you to lose your affection? Explaining the reason for it, he spoke this verse:
“O King, I am Kitavāsa by name; my son is a Paccekabuddha.”
“Having broken his bowl, he has passed away; he was without affection because of that.
“Great King, formerly I myself was a king named Kitavāsa in Bārāṇasī. A son was born to me. When the readers of omens saw him, they said:
‘Great King, this prince will die without obtaining water. ‘This is a wicked prince,’ they said of him.”
This was his name. When he reached the age of discretion, he served as viceroy. The king went about with the prince either in front of him or behind him.

Fearing that the prince might die from thirst, the king had lotus ponds constructed here and there—at the four gates, within the city, and in various other places—and having erected pavilions at the crossroads and other locations, he stationed water-jars there.
Thus, one day, while traveling to the park early in the morning, having prepared himself in full regalia, he saw a Paccekabuddha on the way.
When the great multitude saw the Paccekabuddha, they paid him homage, praised him, and raised their joined palms in salutation to him.
The prince thought: "People traveling with someone like me pay homage to this shaven-headed man, praise him, and raise their joined palms to him."
“...is receiving it. Enraged, he dismounted from the back of the elephant, approached the Paccekabuddha, and said, “Have you received your meal, ascetic?
When the other replied, “Yes, young man,” he took the bowl from his hand, dashed it to the ground, and together with the food, crushed it to powder with a kick of his foot. The Paccekabuddha—

"Alas, this being is lost! he said, and looked up at his face. The prince replied, "I am the son of King Kitavāsara, O ascetic, known by the name Duṭṭhakumāra; what can you do by looking at me with wide-open eyes while you are angry?
Having been deprived of his meal, the paccekabuddha rose up into the air and went to the Nandana-mūla cave in the northern Himalayas.
He departed. At that very moment, the prince’s evil karma ripened as well. Crying out, “I am burning! I am burning!
with a fever of the body arising within him, he fell right there. Wherever he fell, all the water was cut off;
the irrigation channels dried up, and having met his end right there, he was reborn in the Avīci hell. The king [learned] of this occurrence...
Having heard this, overcome with grief for his son, he thought: "This sorrow of mine has arisen from an object of affection;
if I had no affection, this sorrow would not have arisen. From this day forward, may no such thing as 'affection' arise in me toward any object whatsoever, whether conscious or unconscious.
Having thus resolved, from that time forth, there was no more affection.
There was no other name [for him]. With reference to that, he spoke the verse: “I am known as Kitavāsa.
Therein, “my son has fallen from the state of a Paccekabuddha” means that my son, having broken the attainment of Paccekabodhi, has passed away.
“Because of a lack of affection for him” means because of the cause of the affection that had arisen toward him at that time.
The meaning is: "I have become free from affection.
Then the king asked him, "But friend, what object did you see that caused you to become free from anger? Explaining the reason for this, he spoke this verse:
"Having become an Araka, I cultivated a mind of loving-kindness for seven years."
"For seven eons in the Brahma-world, therefore I am free from anger.

Its meaning is this: "Great King, having been an ascetic named Araka, I developed a mind of loving-kindness for seven years and dwelt in the Brahma-world for seven eons of world-dissolution and evolution; therefore, because of my long-term cultivation of loving-kindness..."
"Because he has practiced and cultivated [this habit], he has become free from anger.
When the umbrella-bearer had thus spoken regarding his own four qualities, the king gave a sign to the assembly by his gesture.
At that very moment, the ministers, brahmins, householders, and others rose up and cried out, "O you bribe-eating, wicked thief!
“Having failed to obtain a bribe, you have become intent on slaying the wise man after having slandered him.

Thus saying, they seized the general Kāḷaka by his hands and feet, brought him down from the royal palace, and having smashed his head with stone mallets as they were being taken up one after another, they brought about his death.
Then, dragging him by the feet, they cast him away in a place of refuse. From that time forth, the king [ruled] according to the Dhamma...
While exercising his sovereignty, he passed away according to his karma.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Kāḷakasena the general was Devadatta; the umbrella-bearer Chatta was Sāriputta; Sakka was Anuruddha; and as for Dhammadhaja, it was I myself.
This is the tenth commentary on the Dhammadhaja Jātaka.
The seventh chapter is the Bīraṇathambhava-vagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows: Somadatta, Ucchiṭṭha, Kuru, Puṇṇa, and Nadī.
The Tortoise, the Fish, the Heap, and the Fraudulent Trader—these ten are the "Dharma-Banner" [chapter]. 8.
The Chapter on the Saṃghāṭī Robe.
[221] 1. The Commentary on the Kāsāva Jātaka.
“One who is not free from impurity wears the saffron robe”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Devadatta.
However, the story originated in Rājagaha. On one occasion, the General of the Dhamma, together with five hundred bhikkhus...
He was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove. Devadatta, too, was dwelling on Gayāsīsa surrounded by his own assembly of the unvirtuous.
At that time, the residents of Rājagaha gathered their offerings and prepared a gift.
Then, a merchant who had come for business purposes offered this garment, saying, "Make me a recipient as well," and [gave] a very costly [robe].
He gave him a fragrant yellow robe. The citizens of the city held a great almsgiving, and everything collected by Chandaka was completed using only kahāpaṇa coins.
That robe remained as a surplus. The great multitude gathered together and deliberated:
"This fragrant yellow robe is a surplus. To whom shall we give it? To the Elder Sāriputta, or rather to Devadatta?"
Regarding this, some said, "To the Elder Sāriputta. Others said, "The Elder Sāriputta will stay for a few days and then depart as he pleases;
however, the Elder Devadatta dwells constantly depending on our very city.
In matters of both auspicious and inauspicious events, he alone is our refuge; let us give it to Devadatta."
Even when they were making it in large quantities, those who said, "We shall give it to Devadatta," were more numerous;
so they gave it to Devadatta. Devadatta had its fringes cut off, had it sewn with a border, had it dyed, and having made it the color of a gold band, he put it on.
At that time, about thirty monks departed from Rājagaha.

Having gone to Sāvatthī, paid homage to the Teacher, and exchanged greetings, they reported that occurrence to him, saying, "Venerable Sir, thus has he donned the banner of an Arahant, which is unbecoming to himself.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta dons the banner of an Arahant which is unsuitable to himself; in the past, too, he used to don it. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a herd of elephants in the Himalayan region.
Upon reaching maturity, he became the leader of a troop consisting of eighty thousand elephants and lived in a forest glade.
Now, a certain poor man living in Benares went to the ivory-workers' street and [saw] the ivory-workers making ivory bracelets and other such items.
Seeing them doing so, he asked, "Will you take the elephant tusks once you have obtained them?

They replied, "Yes, we will take them. Taking up a weapon, dressed in saffron robes and assuming the guise of a Paccekabuddha, he put on a head-covering, stood in the elephant path, killed the elephant with his weapon, took the tusks, and [went] to Bārāṇasī.
He made his living by selling them. Later on, he began to slaughter the very last of the Bodhisatta’s herd elephants.
As the number of elephants decreased day by day, they informed the Bodhisatta, "For what reason are the elephants diminishing?"
While the Bodhisatta was observing, he thought, "A man dressed in the guise of a Paccekabuddha stands at the edge of the elephant road;
I wonder if he will kill me? I shall watch him closely. One day, placing the elephant in front, he himself followed behind.
Seeing the Bodhisatta, the man took up his weapon and sprang forward. The Bodhisatta—
Turning back and standing there, thinking, "I will kill him by trampling him on the ground," he extended his trunk;
but seeing the saffron robes wrapped around him, he thought, "It is right for me to show respect for this banner of the Arahants.
Withdrawing his trunk, he said, "O man, is this banner of the Arahants not unbecoming to you? Why do you wrap yourself in it? And he spoke these verses:
“He who, being impure, shall wear the saffron robe,
devoid of self-control and truthfulness— he does not deserve the saffron robe.
But he who has vomited out impurity and is well-established in moral virtues— ”
“Endowed with self-control and truth, he indeed is worthy of the saffron robe.

In this context, “one who is not free from stain” (*anikkaṣāva*): “stain” (*kaṣāva*) is said to be lust, hatred, delusion, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, guile, obstinacy, aggression, pride, arrogance, intoxication, and negligence—all unwholesome states. All [these]...
All misconduct, all karma leading to existence, and the one thousand five hundred defilements—this is called "stain" (*kasāva*).
That person for whom this has not been abandoned, who has not relinquished it from their continuum, and has not emerged from it, is called "one who is not free from stain" (*anikkasāva*).

"Kāsāva" refers to that which is dyed with an astringent taste, serving as the banner of the Arahants. "Whoever shall wear the robe" means whoever, having become such [a person], shall wear such [a garment].
"He will wear clothes" means he both dresses in them and wraps himself in them.

"Devoid of self-control and truth" means devoid of and shunned by that which is called self-control—namely, the restraint of the sense faculties—and that which is called truth—namely, ultimate reality (paramattha-sacca).

Alternatively, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the ablative; the meaning is "devoid of [and departed from] this self-control and truth. And here, "truth" refers both to verbal truth and to the Four Truths.

It is indeed permissible. "He does not deserve the saffron robe" means that because this person has not cast out the stain (*kasāva*), he does not deserve the saffron robe which is the banner of the Arahant; it is unsuitable for him.
"But he who has vomited out the stain" refers to that person who, by having vomited out the aforementioned stain, is one whose stain has been vomited out (*vantakasāva*).
He is well-composed in the precepts (*sīlesu susamāhito*): he is properly established in both the precepts of the Path and the precepts of the Fruit, as if brought and placed there;
this is a designation for one who is endowed with those precepts. "Endowed" (*upeto*) means possessed of.
"By self-control and truth" (*damasaccena*) means by the aforementioned kind of self-control and truth. "He indeed is worthy of the saffron robe" (*sa ve kāsāvamarahati*) refers to such a person.
“This person is worthy of this saffron robe, the banner of the Arahants.
Having thus explained the reason to that man, the Bodhisatta threatened him, saying, “From now on, do not come here; if you do come, you shall lose your life,” and made him flee.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the elephant-killer was Devadatta, and the leader of the herd was none other than I myself.”
The first commentary on the Kāsāva Jātaka.
[222] 2. The commentary on the Cūḷanandiya Jātaka:
"This is that word of the Teacher" was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta.
One day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth: “Friends, Devadatta is indeed harsh, cruel, and violent;
he plotted against the Perfectly Enlightened One, hurled a rock at him, and incited Nāḷāgiri against him;
he possesses not even a trace of patience, loving-kindness, or compassion toward the Tathāgata. The Teacher approached and asked, “What is it that you are discussing? [He continued: “...kāya...”
"Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? he asked. When they replied, "For this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Devadatta was indeed harsh, cruel, and pitiless. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta [lived] in the Himalayan region as Mahānandika.
There was a monkey named Nāma, and his younger brother was named Cūḷanandiya.
Both of them, accompanied by a retinue of eighty thousand monkeys, lived in a region of the Himalayas caring for their blind mother.
Having placed their mother in a thicket of trees, they would enter the forest and send sweet fruits back to her. These were the monkeys who brought the provisions.
They did not give her any; oppressed by hunger, she became emaciated, reduced to mere skin and bone.
Then the Bodhisatta said to her, "Mother, we send you sweet fruits and various kinds of fruit; why are you wasting away? "Dear son, I do not receive them," she replied.
The Bodhisatta thought, "While I am looking after the herd, my mother will perish."
“Leaving the herd, I shall look after my mother alone. He summoned Cūḷanandiya and said, “Dear brother, you take charge of the herd;
I shall look after our mother. He too replied, “Brother, I have no need for the task of looking after the herd;
I too shall look after our mother alone. Thus, both of them were of one mind.
Having sacrificed their herd and left it behind, they took their mother and descended from the Himalayas;
settling at a banyan tree in the borderlands, they looked after her.
Now, a certain brahmin youth residing in Bārāṇasī was in the presence of a world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā.
Having mastered all the crafts, he asked his teacher for leave, saying, "I shall go.
Through the power of his knowledge of bodily signs (*aṅgavijjā*), the teacher perceived his harshness, cruelty, and recklessness, and said: "Dear son, you are harsh, cruel, and reckless;
for those such as you, things do not always succeed in the same way. You will meet with great ruin and great suffering."
"Do not be harsh; do not perform an action that will cause you regret later," he advised, and then sent him away.

He paid homage to his teacher and went to Bārāṇasī. Having entered the life of a householder, and being unable to maintain himself through other crafts, he thought, "I shall live by means of the tip of a bow;
I will make my living by practicing the hunter's trade."
Having departed from Bārāṇasī and living in a frontier village, he entered the forest equipped with a quiver and bow,
and made his living by killing various wild animals and selling their meat. One day, returning from the forest empty-handed,
he saw a banyan tree standing at the edge of a clearing and thought, "Perhaps there might be something here."
He set out toward the banyan tree.
At that moment, both brothers, having fed their mother with fruits and placed her in front, were sitting within the fork of a branch;
seeing him approaching, they thought, "What will he do to our mother? and hid themselves among the branches.
That violent man, having come to the foot of the tree and seeing their mother—blind and weakened by old age—thought:
"What is the use of my going with empty hands? I shall shoot this female monkey and take her away.
He took up his bow for the purpose of shooting her. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta said: "Dear Cūḷanandiya, this..."

Having said, "A man wishes to pierce my mother; I shall grant her the gift of life, and you should look after my mother after my passing," he emerged from among the branches and said, "O man, do not pierce my mother!
She is blind and weakened by old age; I give her the gift of life. Do not kill her, but kill me instead."
Having obtained his promise, he sat down in a place near the stream.
That merciless man, having pierced and felled the Bodhisatta, readied his bow once more to pierce his mother as well. Seeing this, Cūḷanandiya thought, "This man wishes to pierce my mother;
it would be better for my mother to live for even a single day, having truly gained her life."
Thinking, "There is someone here; I shall give her the gift of life," he emerged from between the branches and said, "O man, do not pierce my mother!
I will give her the gift of life. You, however, must pierce me, take us two brothers, and give the gift of life to our mother.
Having obtained his promise, he sat down in a place near the river. He [the hunter] also—
Having pierced and struck them down, thinking, "This female monkey will become the mother of the children in the house," he likewise pierced and struck down their mother;
then, taking all three upon a carrying-pole, he set out toward the house.
Then, while that wicked man was at the house, a thunderbolt fell, and his wife and two children were destroyed along with the house itself.
He burned it until only the pillar of the backbone remained. Then, a certain man saw it right at the village gate and reported what had happened to him.
Overwhelmed by grief for his wife and children, he abandoned his meat-hook and bow right there, cast off his clothes, and went home naked, wailing with his arms outstretched.
He entered. Then that pillar broke, fell upon his head, and shattered it; the earth opened up, and flames from the Avīci hell rose up.

As he was being swallowed by the earth, he remembered the teacher’s instruction and, lamenting, "It was indeed seeing this very circumstance that the Brahmin Pārāsariya gave me this advice," he spoke these two verses:
“This is the word of the Teacher, which Pārāsariya spoke:
‘Do not commit evil, lest you suffer for what you have done later.
Whatever a person does, that they will see within themselves.’”
“The doer of good reaps good, and the doer of evil reaps evil;
as one sows the seed, so one reaps the fruit.
This is its meaning: that which the Brahmin Pārāsariya spoke—“Do not commit evil, for what has been done will later [be experienced]...”

"You alone shall experience [the results]"—this is the teacher’s statement. Whatever kamma a person performs through the doors of body, speech, and mind, when receiving its result, he sees those very actions within himself.
One who performs wholesome kamma experiences a wholesome fruit; and one who performs evil kamma experiences only evil—a low, wretched, and undesirable fruit.
"For even in the world, whatever kind of seed one sows, such is the fruit one reaps; one reaps, takes, and experiences a fruit that corresponds exactly to the seed and is appropriate to the seed.
Thus, while lamenting, he entered the earth and was reborn in the Avīci Great Hell.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is harsh, cruel, and merciless; even in the past, he was just the same."
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and brought forth this Jātaka, he identified the births: "At that time, the hunter was Devadatta;
the world-renowned teacher was Sāriputta; Cūḷanandiya was Ānanda; the mother was Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī;
and Mahānandiya was none other than myself."
The second [story], the Explanation of the Cūḷanandiya Jātaka.
[223] 3. The Explanation of the Puṭabhatta Jātaka:
"One who bows down should associate with one who associates"—this [verse] the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke concerning a certain householder.
He spoke with reference to this. It is said that a certain householder living in the city of Sāvatthī engaged in business with a householder from a certain country.
Taking his own wife with him, he went to the presence of that debtor.
The debtor, saying "I am unable to pay," gave him nothing; the other, becoming angry, departed without even eating his meal.
Then, seeing her on the way with her stomach rumbling from hunger, some men traveling along the road gave her a bowl of food, saying, "Eat this, even if you must give it to your wife.
Taking it, he—having no desire to give it to her—urged her forward, saying, "My dear, this is a place where bandits lurk;
you go on ahead," and having eaten all the food himself, he left her with an empty bowl.
Having shown it, he said, "Bhadde, they gave me an empty bowl instead of food.

Knowing from that single sign alone that she had eaten, she became filled with dejection. As the two of them were walking along the Jetavana back road, they entered the Jetavana thinking, "We shall drink some water."
The Teacher, anticipating their arrival, took his seat in the shadow of the Perfumed Chamber like a hunter stationed on the path;
seeing the Teacher, they approached, paid homage, and sat down.
After exchanging greetings with them, the Teacher asked, "Laywomen, does this husband of yours desire your welfare and is he affectionate toward you? "Venerable Sir," they replied.
"I am full of affection for him, but he has no affection for me. Let alone other days;
even today, having obtained a meal on the road, he ate it himself without giving any to me.
"Laywoman, you have always been desirous of his welfare and full of affection for him, yet he remains without affection. However, when, by relying upon the wise, your..."
“When he recognizes his virtues, then he entrusts all sovereignty to him,” having said this, and being requested by her, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers;
upon reaching maturity, he became the advisor on matters of state and dharma to the king. Then the king, thinking, “This man might even rebel against me,” [entrusted the kingdom] to his own son.
Fearing [the consequences], he fled. Taking his own wife, he departed from the city and took up residence in a certain village of Kāsi.
