Later, having heard that his father had passed away, thinking, "I shall take the kingdom inherited by my family," he was returning to Benares when, on the way, he received a bowl of food with the instruction, "Give some to your wife and eat."
Without giving her any, he ate it himself. She became dejected, thinking, "How cruel this man is!

After he had taken the kingdom of Bārāṇasī and established her in the position of chief queen, he thought, "This much alone is enough for her," and so he gave her no further honor or respect, nor did he even ask her, "How are you getting by?"
The Bodhisatta thought: "This queen has been very helpful to the king and is full of affection for him, yet the king does not consider her as such;
I shall cause her to receive honor and respect. Approaching her, he performed the customary salutation and stood to one side.
When she asked, "What is it, dear?", he replied, "How may we serve you, O Queen, so that we may ensure your well-being?"
"What, indeed, is wrong with giving even a scrap of cloth or a morsel of food to our elderly parents?
he asked. "Dear son, I do not receive anything for myself; what then shall I give to you?
Did I not give when there was something to be received? But now the King gives me nothing. Let alone other gifts; even when he came to seize the kingdom—"
“Having received a food parcel on the way, she would eat it herself without giving even a portion of the food to me.
“But, mother, will you be able to speak thus in the presence of the king? “I shall be able, dear father.
“In that case, this very day, while I am standing in the presence of the king, when I ask you, speak thus: ‘This very day your virtue [was tested].’”
Having said, "I shall cause her to know," the Bodhisatta went on ahead and stood before the king.
She too went and stood near the king.
Then the Bodhisatta said to her, "Mother, you are exceedingly harsh; what indeed [is this] regarding a scrap of cloth from your parents?"
“Or even to give you so much as a morsel of food is not permitted,” he said. “Dear father, I myself receive nothing at all from the King;
what shall I give to you? “Did you not obtain the position of chief queen?
“Dear father, when there is no honor whatsoever, what will the position of chief queen avail? Now, what does the King have for you?”
“...he will give it; having received a bowl of food on the way, he will eat it himself without giving any of it away.
The Bodhisatta asked, “Is that so, Great King? The King consented.
The Bodhisatta, understanding his consent, said, “In that case, Mother, what is the use of your staying here from the time the King became displeased? For in this world...”
“Association with the unpleasant is suffering; if you remain here, association with what is unpleasant to the king will surely become your suffering.
These beings indeed associate with those they associate with; knowing their nature of associating, one should go elsewhere, for the world’s habitation is vast.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“One should associate with one who associates, and do what is to be done for one who does what is to be done.
One should not do what is beneficial for one who desires no benefit, nor should one associate with one who does not associate.
One should abandon one who abandons, and not harbor resentment; one should not associate with one whose mind has departed.”
"Knowing that the tree has exhausted its fruit, the great world would surely look for another.
In this context, "one who bows to one who bows, should associate with one who associates": one should return the bow to whoever bows to oneself;
and one should associate with whoever associates with oneself. "One who does what is to be done for oneself, should do what is to be done": one should perform the duty that has arisen for oneself.
One should indeed repay the service rendered by that person who acts for one’s benefit.
One should abandon the one who abandons [one], but one should not harbor the "woodiness" (vanatha)—that is, craving—toward them.
"With a departed mind" means with a mind that has strayed or is perverted. "One should not associate" means one should not come together with such a person.

He said: "Just as a bird, when the fruit of a tree has previously ripened but is now exhausted, realizes 'this one's fruit is gone,' abandons it, and looks for and seeks another—so too should you look for another.
For this world is vast; perhaps you will find another man who still possesses affection."
Having heard this, the King of Bārāṇasī granted the queen full sovereignty. From that time forth, they lived together in harmony and mutual affection.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the royal couple was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. "The royal couple of that time were these very two, husband and wife."
“...they were [the others], but the wise minister was none other than myself.
The third narrative, the Commentary on the Puṭabhatta Jātaka.
[224] 4. The Commentary on the Kumbhīla Jātaka.
"Whosoever possesses these four qualities..."— this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana grove concerning Devadatta:
"O Lord of Monkeys, he who possesses these four qualities as you do—
truth, righteousness, fortitude, and generosity— he transcends even what has been seen."
“But for whom these most excellent qualities do not exist—
truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity— he does not transcend what is seen. In this context,
“most excellent qualities” refers to those four most excellent qualities which, for someone, exist in the sense of a heap and in the sense of a mass.
"Virtues do not exist; he is unable to overcome his enemy. All else here is exactly as explained below in the *Kumbhila Jātaka*, together with the summary.
This concludes the commentary on the fourth *Kumbhila Jātaka*.
[225] 5. The Exposition of the Khantivaṇṇa Jātaka.
"I have a man, O King," with these words the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke concerning the King of Kosala.

It is said that one of his ministers, who had been very helpful to him, became enamored of a woman in the inner palace. The King, recognizing that he was a benefactor, endured it out of consideration for him.
He reported this to the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Great King, even ancient kings endured in this very same way," and being requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a certain minister became lustful toward his harem; [the same happened] to the minister as well.
A servant became enamored with his wife. Unable to endure her transgression, he took her with him and went into the presence of the king.
Asking, "Your Majesty, I have an attendant who performs all my duties; he has become enamored with my wife.
What should be done with him? he spoke the first verse:
“O King, I have a man who is occupied with all my affairs;
if that man should commit even a single offense, what do you think of that?
In this context, “if that man should commit even a single offense” means that there is one offense committed by that man. Regarding that, you—
"What do you think?"—by this he indicates: "Regarding that man's offense, what do you think should be done?
According to how your mind inclines, propose a punishment for him accordingly.
Having heard that, the king spoke the second verse:
“We too have such a man; one such as this is found here among us.
One endowed with all limbs is rare; patience is what we prefer.
The meaning of this is: “We kings also have such a man in our homes who is of great service—a man who is difficult to find.”
"He is indeed found here; even now he is present right here. Although we ourselves are kings, we have consented out of consideration for his great helpfulness;
but for you, even though you are in the forest, this burden of consent has arisen.
For a man endowed with all limbs and possessed of every portion of virtue is truly rare; for that reason, [we have acted] toward us..."
"In such circumstances, only patience through endurance is appropriate.

The minister, realizing that the King had spoken with reference to himself, was unable from that time forward to commit any offense within the inner palace. And the servant, knowing that the King had informed him of the matter, was likewise unable from that time forward to perform that deed.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī."
"It was so. That minister, having learned from the Teacher that the King had spoken thus, was unable to perform that deed from that time forward.
This concludes the fifth commentary, the Khantivaṇṇa Jātaka.
[226] 6. The Commentary on the Kosiya Jātaka.

"It is good to depart at the proper time. The Teacher spoke this while residing at Jetavana concerning the King of Kosala. The King of Kosala had departed at an improper time for the purpose of suppressing a border disturbance.

The background story is exactly as related above. However, the Teacher, having brought up a past event, said: "Great King, in the past, the King of Bārāṇasī departed at an improper time and established his camp in a park.
At that time, a certain owl bird entered a bamboo thicket and hid there."
The crow-army arrived and, thinking, "We shall seize him while he has just departed," surrounded him.
Without waiting for the setting of the sun, he set out at an improper time and began to flee. Then the crows surrounded him and, pecking at him with their beaks, threw him down.
The king addressed the Bodhisatta: "What is this, wise one? Why are these crows [attacking] Kosiya?"
“Are they causing harm? he asked. The Bodhisatta, explaining this matter by saying, “Great King, those who leave their own dwelling place at an improper time certainly encounter such suffering;
therefore, it is not right to leave one’s own dwelling place at an improper time,” spoke these two verses:
“Departure at the right time is good; departure at the wrong time is not good.
For by departing at the wrong time, even a great multitude achieves no purpose at all, like a flock of vultures against a quail.”
“The wise man, knowing the proper method and discerning the vulnerabilities of others, having brought all enemies under his control, shall be happy like Kosiya.
In this regard, O Great King, it is said that departing at the right time is excellent; for “departing” means either going forth or exerting oneself.
Or it is good [to go] at the time when one is properly engaged. But it is not good to depart at the wrong time;
for "departing at the wrong time" means that going out from one's own dwelling place to another place—whether as a departure or an exertion—is not good.
Regarding the four phrases beginning with "At the wrong time," the meaning should be understood by correlating the third with the first and the fourth with the second.
For indeed, if a certain man leaves his dwelling place at an improper time or exerts himself at an improper time, he does not illuminate any purpose;
he is unable to produce even the slightest increase for himself.
On the contrary, whether he is alone or surrounded by many people—even if those many are his enemies—[they all perceive] him as one who is departing or exerting himself at an improper time.
Having surrounded him, it brings about his great destruction. Herein is this simile: like a flock of hawks [attacking] a quail.

Just as this flock of hawks, when the quail emerges at an improper time and attempts to escape, peck at him with their beaks and bring about his great destruction, so too, starting from any animal, if one [emerges] at an improper time from one's own dwelling place—
"One should not go out, nor should one exert oneself.
In the second verse, "the wise man" (*dhīra*) means the learned one. "The method" (*vidhi*) refers to the tradition established by ancient sages.
"Arrangement" (*vidhāna*) means either a division or a distribution. "One who follows the openings" (*vivarānugū*) means one who knows while following the openings. "All friends" (*sabbāmitte*)...
"All enemies. "Having brought under one's own control" means having made them subject to oneself. "Like a weaver" means like another wise weaver, distinct from this foolish weaver.
This is what is meant: that wise person who, according to the tradition established by ancient sages—namely, "at this time one should go forth and exert oneself;
at this time one should not go forth nor exert oneself"—[acts accordingly].

One who knows the method— that is, the arrangement known as the division of parts, or the planning and execution of that method— knows how to carry it out. Such a person, knowing the vulnerability of others who are his adversaries,
acts just as the wise Kosiyas did, having gone forth and exerted themselves at their own appointed time during the night, here and there.
"Just as one who cuts off the heads of crows while they are still lying there might bring all those enemies under his control and become happy, so too, a wise man,
by departing at the right time and exerting himself, brings his adversaries under his control and becomes happy and free from suffering.
Having heard the words of the Bodhisatta, the king desisted.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Ānanda was the king, and the wise minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the sixth commentary, the Kosiyajātakavaṇṇanā.
7. Gūthapāṇajātakavaṇṇanā (The Story of the Dung-Worm)
“Hero meeting hero”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain bhikkhu.

It is said that at that time, about two and a half *yojanas* from Jeta’s Grove, there was a market town where many *salākabhatta* (ticket-meals) and *pakkhiyabhatta* (fortnightly meals) were provided. There lived a certain Koṇḍañña who was a questioner. He...
When young novices arrived for the sake of *salākabhatta* (tickets for food) and *pakkhiyabhatta* (fortnightly meals), he would ask them, "Who eats?
Who drinks? Who consumes? and, when they were unable to answer, he put them to shame.
Out of fear of him, they did not go to that village for the sake of the *salākabhatta* and *pakkhiyabhatta*. Then one day, a certain...
The bhikkhu went to the hall where the voting sticks were kept and asked, "Venerable sir, is there alms-food by ticket or fortnightly meal-offering in such-and-such a village?
When he was told, "There is, friend; however, a certain Koṇḍañña asks questions there, and if anyone is unable to answer him, he reviles and insults them;
out of fear of him, no one is able to go," he said, "Venerable sir..."

"Therefore, serve me meals there; having tamed him and rendered him harmless, from that time forth I will ensure that he flees upon seeing you," he said. The bhikkhus, accepting with "Very well," served him meals there.
So, having gone there, he put on his robe at the village gate. Seeing him, Koṇḍañña Caṇḍameṇḍaka approached with speed like a fierce bull and said, "Tell me a question, ascetic!
[The Buddha replied,] "Lay follower, go about the village, bring some rice-gruel, and first let me come to the assembly hall.
When he had brought the gruel and arrived at the assembly hall, [the other] was still acting in the same way.
He said: That monk also said to him, "First give me rice-gruel to drink; first let me sweep the sitting hall;

first bring me my ticket-meal. Having brought the ticket-meal, he had him take that very bowl and said, "Come, I will explain the question to you," and leading him outside the village, he gathered up his robe and placed it on his shoulder.
Having taken the bowl from his hand, he stood there. There too, the man said to him, "Ascetic, answer my question.
Then, saying "I shall answer your question," he struck him with such force that it was as if crushing his bones all at once;
he stuffed excrement into his mouth and said, "From this day forward, whatever monk comes to this village..."
“I shall know when it is time to ask the question,” he said, and having thus intimidated him, he departed.
From that time forth, whenever he saw monks, he would flee. Later on, that monk’s conduct became well known among the Saṅgha of monks.
Then one day, in the Hall of Truth, the monks started a discussion: “Friends, it is said that such-and-such a monk [fled] from Koṇḍañña...”
“Having thrown excrement into his mouth, he departed. The Teacher, having arrived, asked, “Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, that monk does not defile him with filth only now;
in the past, too, he defiled him. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, when inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha were traveling from one kingdom to the other, they stayed one day by a certain lake on the border between the two kingdoms.
Having drunk liquor and eaten fish and meat, they harnessed their vehicles at dawn and departed.
After they had gone, a certain dung-eating insect came along, drawn by the scent of excrement.
Seeing the liquor discarded where they had drunk, he drank it out of thirst; becoming intoxicated, he climbed upon a heap of dung.
As he climbed, the fresh dung sank down slightly. He cried out, "The earth cannot support me!
At that very moment, a noble elephant in rut arrived at that place, and smelling the odor of the dung, he felt loathing.
He retreated. Seeing him, the other—perceiving, "This one is fleeing out of fear of me"—thought, "It is fitting to engage in battle with this one," and calling out to him, he spoke the first verse:
"A hero, having encountered a hero who is valiant and strikes back, [should fight]."
"Come, Nāga, turn back! Why do you flee in fear?
Let the people of Aṅga and Magadha behold the prowess of both myself and you!
The meaning of this is: "You are a hero who, having encountered me, a hero, have displayed valor through your strength and courage, and possess the capability to deliver a blow."
"O elephant, for what reason do you depart without engaging in combat? Surely even a single blow ought to be given.
Therefore, come back, O elephant! Why do you flee in terror, being so stricken by the fear of death?
Let these people, dwelling within this boundary, witness the prowess of both myself and you; let Aṅga and Magadha behold it."
"Let both of you behold my prowess.
Having heard his words, the elephant pricked up his ears, turned back, approached him, and, seeking to appease him, spoke this second verse:
"I shall not kill you with my feet, nor with my tusks, nor with my trunk."
“I shall kill him with filth; let the putrid one be slain by the putrid.
This is its meaning: “I will not kill him with my feet or other limbs, but I shall kill him with filth suitable for you.
Having spoken thus, [he thought], “Let this worm in the putrid excrement be killed by the putrid itself,” and he placed a large lump of dung upon its head.
Having struck him down and released the water, he brought him to his death right there; then, letting out a cry like a heron, he entered the forest once more.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Koṇḍa was the dung-worm, the elephant was this monk, and the deity dwelling in that forest thicket was [myself] who had witnessed that event with my own eyes."
"But it was I myself who was he.
The seventh commentary, on the *Gūthapāṇa-jātaka*.
[228] 8. The commentary on the *Kāmanīta-jātaka*.
"Tayo giri" (Three Mountains): This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the brahmin named Kāmanīta.
The story, both in its present and past contexts, will be revealed in the *Kāmajātaka* of the Twelfth Nipāta.
Of those two princes, the elder came and became the king in Bārāṇasī, while the younger became the viceroy. Among them—

The king was insatiable regarding both sensual pleasures of the objects and sensual pleasures of the defilements, and he was greedy for wealth. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become Sakka, the King of the Devas, surveyed Jambudīpa;

perceiving that the king was unsatisfied in respect to both types of sensual pleasure, he thought, "I shall restrain this king and cause him shame. Assuming the guise of a brahmin youth, he came and saw the king, and by the king...

When he was asked, "For what purpose have you come, young man? he replied, "Great King, I see three cities that are secure, well-supplied with food, and abound in elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry;
they are filled with gold, silver, and ornaments, and it is possible to seize them with only a small force. I have come to give those to you. [The king asked: "When?"
When he said, "Let us go, young men," they replied, "Tomorrow, Great King. He said, "In that case, go; you should return early in the morning. "Very well, Great King;
prepare the army with haste," Sakka said, and having spoken, he returned to his own place.
On the following day, the king had the drum beaten, ordered the army to be readied, summoned his ministers, and [said] regarding the one from yesterday: "Yesterday..."
The Brahmin youth said, "I shall seize the sovereignty in these three cities—Uttarapañcāla, Indapatta, and Kekaka—and give it to you.
[The king replied,] "Take that youth and seize the sovereignty in those three cities; summon him quickly!
[The minister asked,] "Your Majesty, has a residence been assigned for him? [The king replied,] "No residence has been assigned for him. [The minister asked,] "What about his means of subsistence?"
"But was it given? "That too was not given. Then [the king asked], "Where shall we see him? "Look in the city streets," they replied.
While searching, they said, "We do not see him, Great King.
As the king did not see the young man, great sorrow arose in him, thinking, "Thus have we been deprived of such vast sovereignty! His heart grew hot.
His blood became agitated, and he was afflicted with dysentery; the physicians were unable to cure him.
Then, after three or four days had passed, Sakka, reflecting and perceiving that illness of his, thought, "I shall treat him.
Assuming the guise of a brahmin, he arrived, stood at the gate, and said, "A physician-brahmin has come for the purpose of treating you."
He had it announced. When the king heard this, he said, "The greatest of the royal physicians were unable to cure me;
give him a fee and send him away. Sakka, hearing this, said, "I have no need for clothing or a fee, nor will I accept any physician's reward; I shall cure him, so let the king see me again."
When the king heard this, he said, "In that case, let him come. Sakka entered, offered his greetings, and stood to one side.
The king said, "Are you going to treat me? "Yes, Your Majesty," he replied. "Then do so," said the king.
"Very well, Great King, tell me the symptoms of my illness; for what reason did it arise? What have I eaten, or..."
“Was it based on what was tasted, or rather on what was seen or heard? “My dear, my illness arose based on what was heard. “What did you hear?
“My dear, a young man came and said to me, ‘I will give you the sovereignty over three cities.
I did not provide him with a place to stay, nor did I grant him any means of subsistence.”
"Having become angry with me, he must have gone into the presence of another king.
Then, as I thought, 'I have been deprived of such great sovereignty,' this illness arose.
If you are able to treat my illness, which has arisen on account of a mind of sensual desire, then treat it. Thus he explained this matter.
He spoke the first verse:
“I desire the three regions between the mountains—Pañcāla, Kuru, and Kekaka;
even beyond that, O Brahmin, I desire it. O Brahmin, heal me, for I am afflicted by desire.”
In that context, *tayo girī* means "three mountains," or rather, this is the very reading [of the text].

Just as in the passage, "This is the gateway revealing the Sudassana mountain," where the city of the gods, Sudassana, is called "Sudassana mountain" because it is difficult to seize and difficult to traverse, so too here, the three cities are intended by the term "three mountains. Therefore, this is the meaning here:
“I desire three cities, and the threefold kingdom that lies between them—‘The Pañcālas, the Kurus, and the Kekakas.
These are the names of those kingdoms. Among them, ‘the Pañcālas’ refers to Uttarapañcāla;
there is a city named Kapila. ‘The Kurus’ refers to the kingdom of Kuru; there is a city named Indapatta. And ‘the Kekakas’ refers to [the kingdom of] Kekaya.”
This is a statement of purpose; by it, he shows the location of Kekaka. Therein, the city is simply the royal capital of Kekaka.
"Beyond that" means: having obtained from here the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, I desire a threefold sovereignty beyond that.
"Cure me, O Brahmin, who am led away by desires"—this refers to one who is led away, struck down, and overwhelmed by these sensual objects and by the defilements of desire.
“If you are able, O Brahmin, treat me.
Then Sakka said to him, “Great King, you cannot be cured by roots, herbs, and such things; you must be treated with the medicine of knowledge,” and spoke this second verse:
“For one bitten by a black snake, some wise men perform [the treatment]; for one possessed by a non-human spirit, the wise perform [the treatment].”
“No one treats one who is led by desire; for what is the cure for one whose semen has been discharged?

Regarding this, “some treat one bitten by a black snake”: some physicians indeed perform the treatment with mantras and medicinal herbs for one bitten by a black snake of terrible venom. “They treat one possessed by a non-human spirit”... [and so on].

Others say that "wise ones" are those who are true physicians; they provide medical treatment—by means of offerings, protective charms (*paritta*), and medicated herbs—for one who has been entered by, overcome by, or seized by non-human beings such as spirits (*bhūta*) or *yakkhas*.
But for a person led away by sensual desires, one who is under the sway of sensual pleasures, no one other than the wise can provide [such treatment].
No one provides medical treatment, and even if they did, there would be no one capable of doing so.

Why? Because for one whose semen has been emitted—meaning for a person who has transgressed the boundary of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), fallen away, and become established in unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*)—what kind of medical treatment could there be through mantras, medicines, and the like? It is not possible.
"to treat them with medicines.
Having shown this reason to her, the Great Being further spoke thus:
"Great King, even if you were to obtain those three kingdoms, while exercising rule over these four cities, could you do so all at once?"

"O Great King, even if you were to wear four pairs of garments, eat from four golden bowls, or lie upon four beds, it is not fitting to be one who is subject to craving; for this thing called craving is the root of misfortune.
As it increases, it causes the person who nourishes it to fall into the eight great hells and the sixteen [lesser hells]."

"He is cast into the Ussada hells, into various other types of hells, and into all remaining states of misery. Having thus threatened the king with the terrors of hell and other realms, the Great Being taught him the Dhamma.
Upon hearing his teaching, the king’s grief vanished, and he immediately attained freedom from disease.
Sakka, having given him this exhortation and established him in the precepts, returned to the world of the gods.
From that time forward, he too performed meritorious deeds such as giving and departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King was Kāmanīta the Brahmin, and Sakka was none other than myself.
This is the eighth commentary on the Kāmanīta Jātaka.
[229] 9. The Commentary on the *Palāyita-jātaka*.
"By the elephant herds and clouds"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a wandering ascetic who had fled.
It is said that he, having wandered throughout the whole of Jambudīpa for the sake of debate and having found no opponent, eventually...
Having gone to Sāvatthī, he asked the people, "Is there anyone capable of engaging in debate with me?

The people replied, "The All-Knowing One, the supreme among bipeds, the Lord of Dhamma, the crusher of the doctrines of others—the Great Gotama—is capable of debating even with a thousand such as you;
indeed, every doctrine of others that has arisen throughout all of Jambudīpa [is defeated by him]."

"There is no one capable of surpassing that Blessed One. For just as the waves of the ocean, upon reaching the shore, are shattered into fragments, so too all doctrines, upon reaching the feet of that Master, are reduced to dust. Thus they spoke in praise of the Buddha's qualities.
The wanderer asked, "But where is he now? and having heard that he was at Jetavana, he thought, "I shall now challenge him to debate."
Surrounded by a great multitude of people as he was going to Jetavana, he saw the gateway of Jetavana—
which Prince Jeta had caused to be built at a cost of ninety million pieces of gold— and asked, "Is this the palace where the ascetic Gotama dwells?
Upon hearing, "This is merely the gateway," he thought, "If even the gateway is such as this, what must the dwelling house itself be like?"
Having said this, when it was remarked that "the Gandhakuṭī is immeasurable," he fled from that very spot, thinking, "Who would engage in debate with such a recluse?
The people, raising a great clamor, entered Jetavana and, when asked by the Teacher, "Why have you come at an improper time?", they related what had occurred.
The Teacher said, "Lay followers, it is not only now; previously as well, he [fled] from my dwelling place."
"Having seen the gate-tower, he will surely flee," he said; and when requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, the Bodhisatta reigned in Takkasilā, while Brahmadatta reigned in Bārāṇasī.
Thinking, "I shall seize Takkasilā," he went with a great army and, having arrived not far from the city, stood there.
“Send forth the elephants by this method, the horses by this, the chariots by this, and the infantry by this;
thus, having charged, strike with your weapons! Thus, like thick rain-bearing clouds, let loose a shower of arrows! While instructing them in this way, he spoke these two verses:

“Surrounded on all sides by Takkasilā were the foremost elephants like clouds, the rows of excellent horses, chariots that stirred up the dust, and showers of arrows; with spears grasped and firm, powerful blows dealt,
and various sounds resounded from the neighing of the steeds, they rushed forward and pursued [the enemy].”
“Today a tumultuous roar arises, like the flash of lightning from a thundering cloud.

In this context, “by the foremost clouds of elephants” means by the foremost clouds of elephants; the meaning is: by the clouds that are excellent rutting elephants, roaring with the cry of the *koñca* crane.
“By the garlands of foremost horses” means by those possessing the foremost garlands of horses; the meaning is: by the cavalry divisions consisting of clans of excellent Sindhu horses.
"By those from whom dust-clouds arose" means by those from whom dust-clouds were produced, like the waters of the ocean when a surge has arisen;
the meaning is "by chariot-arrays. "By those raining showers of arrows" means by those very chariot-arrays raining showers of arrows like a dense rain-cloud.
"By those striking with firm blows while whirling their spears" means by those who, having whirled their spears here and there, struck with firm blows.
The meaning is: by infantry soldiers who, having turned around, seized their precious swords and stout staffs and struck out forcefully.
"Takkasilā was surrounded on all sides" means: act quickly so that this Takkasilā may be surrounded in such a manner.
"Run forward, run after, and run with great speed both forward and after! means:
"Be made to cry out variously together with the noble elephants; let there be various sounds through their trumpeting, roaring, and shouting"—this is the meaning.
"Let a tumultuous noise arise today" means: "Let a great, tumultuous sound like the roar of thunder arise today."

A sound. Just as lightning flashes from the mouth of a thundering cloud—just as the lightning issuing from the mouth of a thundering cloud moves about—so too, it says, "Wander about, surround the city, and seize the kingdom!
Thus that king, having thundered and marshaled his army, went near the city gate and saw the gateway.
Having asked, "Is this the king's residence? and being told, "This is the city gate-tower," he said, "If the city gate-tower is already like this, what must the king’s palace be like?
Upon hearing that it was "like the Vejayanta Palace," he thought, "We shall not be able to fight against a king so endowed with glory," and [he entered] the gate-tower.
Having seen this, he turned back, fled, and went back to Bārāṇasī itself.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was the runaway wanderer, and I myself was the King of Takkasilā.
This is the ninth commentary on the Palāyita Jātaka.
[230] 10. The Commentary on the Second Palāyita Jātaka. "The Banner is Unmeasured":
This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain runaway wanderer.
On this occasion, that wanderer entered Jetavana. At that moment, the Teacher—
Surrounded by a great multitude, seated upon a decorated Dharma-throne, he taught the Dharma like a lion cub letting out a roar upon a slab of emerald.
Upon seeing the Ten-Powered One’s form, which resembled the body of Brahmā, his face possessing the splendor of the full moon,
and his forehead like a golden plate, the wanderer thought, "Who could possibly defeat such a supreme person?"
He turned back, entered the surrounding crowd, and fled. The great multitude pursued him, turned back, and reported that occurrence to the Teacher.
The Teacher said, "It is not only now; in the past as well, upon seeing my golden-hued face, that wanderer fled," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, the Bodhisatta was ruling as king in Bārāṇasī, while there was a certain King of Gandhāra in Takkasilā.
Thinking, "I shall seize Bārāṇasī," he arrived with a fourfold army, surrounded the city, and stood at the city gate.
Surveying his own forces and vehicles, he said to his army, "Who will be able to defeat such a great host?"
Having praised him, he spoke the first verse:
“With a banner immeasurable and boundless, difficult for even vultures to overcome as if it were the ocean,
and as difficult to shake as a mountain by the wind— today I am ‘Difficult to Conquer’ (Duppasaha) against one such as you.”
In this context, "immeasurable banners" means that, having placed peacock-feather canopies upon my chariots, the banners raised aloft are immeasurable, vast, and numbering many hundreds.

"Boundless" means that even my army and vehicles—such as "this many elephants, this many horses, this many chariots, and this many foot soldiers"—are beyond the limit of calculation and thus boundless. "Invincible."
It is not possible for adversaries to withstand or overcome it. How so? Like the ocean by crows.
Just as the ocean is difficult to endure for many crows—either by their attempts to obstruct its current or by their crossing over—it is thus "difficult to endure" (*duppasaha*).
And like a mountain by the wind, it is "difficult to shake" (*duppasayha*); moreover, this army of mine is like a mountain because it cannot be shaken by the wind.
"Difficult to overcome; likewise, difficult to overcome by any other force.

"I am difficult to overcome today by one such as you"—this he says with reference to the Bodhisatta standing on the watchtower, meaning: "Today, I who am endowed with this power am difficult to overcome by anyone like you.

Then, showing his own face, which was as beautiful as the full moon, and intimidating him by saying, "Fool, do not prattle on! Now I shall scatter your army and vehicles like an elephant in rut destroys a thicket of reeds," he spoke the second verse:
“Do not lament out of folly, for such [a fate] is not for him; you are being consumed, for you find no one to restrain you.
You are attacking one who wanders alone like an elephant—one who will crush you with his foot as if you were a reed.
In this context, “do not lament out of folly” means do not prattle on about your own foolishness. “For such [a fate] is not for him” means—

Indeed, he would not be such; or rather, this is the reading. One who speculates in such a manner as, "My army and vehicles are boundless," would truly not be capable of seizing the kingdom—meaning he does not exist [as such].
You are burning, O fool; you are merely burning with the fever of lust, hatred, delusion, and conceit. For you do not obtain a restrainer.
"But you shall not yet obtain one who can forcibly overcome and restrain someone like me;
today I shall drive you away by the very path you have come. "Āsajjasi" means "you approach. "Like a solitary elephant" means like a solitary, intoxicated, noble tusker.
"He who shall crush you with his feet like a reed" means he who, just as an intoxicated noble tusker [crushes a reed] with his feet...
"It crushes and pulverizes the reed; it will crush you in the same way, for you have attacked it"—this he said, referring to himself.

When the King of Gandhāra heard this rebuke, he looked up and, seeing the king's great forehead which resembled a golden plate, became afraid of being captured. Turning back and fleeing, he returned to his own city.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King of Gandhāra was the runaway wanderer, and the King of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself."
The commentary on the Second Palāyita Jātaka is the tenth.
The eighth chapter, the Kāsāva Vagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
Kāsāva, Cūḷanandiya, Puṭabhatta, and Kumbhila;
Khantivaṇṇa, Kosika, Gūthapāṇa, and Kāmanīta;
and the two who fled.
9. The Chapter on Sandals [231] 1. The Commentary on the Sandal Jātaka:
"Just as a fly..."—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Devadatta. For in the Hall of Truth...
The monks started a discussion: "Friends, Devadatta, having renounced his teacher and become an adversary and opponent of the Tathāgata, has met with great ruin.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, about what discussion are you sitting here now? When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, it was not only now that Devadatta..."
"Having just now rejected his teacher and become my adversary, he has met with great ruin; indeed, he met with it even in the past," he said, and related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of elephant trainers and, upon reaching maturity, attained perfection in the science of elephants.
Then, a young man from a Kāsi village came and approached him.
He learned the craft in the presence [of the Bodhisatta]. For Bodhisattas, when teaching a craft, do not keep anything back as a "teacher's secret";

they instruct completely according to their own method of knowing. Therefore, that young man, having mastered the Bodhisatta’s knowledge of the craft without exception, said to the Bodhisatta: "Teacher, I shall attend upon the king."
The Bodhisatta said, “Very well, dear ones,” and having gone, he informed the king: “Great King, my pupil wishes to attend upon you.
“Very well, let him attend,” [the king replied]. “In that case, please determine his maintenance.
“Your pupil shall not receive what is equal to yours; when you receive a hundred, he shall receive fifty.”
“Of two who receive [the reward], one shall obtain it. Having gone home, he reported this news to his pupil.
The pupil said, “Teacher, I know the craft as well as you do. If I am to receive an equal fee, I will attend upon you;
if not, I will not attend upon you. The Bodhisatta related this occurrence...
He informed the king. The king said, "If he is equal to you, and is able to display his craft on exactly the same scale as you, he shall receive an equal share.
The Bodhisatta reported this matter to him; when the other replied, "Very well, I shall display it," he informed the king.
The king said, "In that case, let them both display their crafts tomorrow. "Very well," [he replied].
“We shall demonstrate it; have the drum beaten throughout the city! The king had the drum beaten, saying, “Tomorrow, it seems, both the teacher and his pupil will display their elephant-lore;
let those who wish to see them gather in the royal courtyard and watch.
The teacher thought, “My pupil does not know skill in means,” and taking an elephant, in a single night—

He trained him in reverse order. Having taught him to retreat when told "Go," to advance when told "Retreat," to lie down when told "Stand," to stand when told "Lie down," to set down when told "Take up," and to take up when told "Set down," he mounted that elephant on the following day and went to the royal courtyard.
The pupil also mounted a single pleasing elephant. A great crowd gathered. Both displayed their skills simultaneously.
Then the Bodhisatta made his own elephant act contrary to its nature:
when told "Go," it retreated; when told "Retreat," it ran forward; when told "Stop," it lay down; and when told "Lie down," it stood up.
When told, "Take it," he set it down; when told, "Set it down," he took it. The great crowd cried out, "You wicked pupil!
You are quarreling with your teacher; you do not know your own measure. You have the conceit that 'I know as much as the teacher'!
Having struck him with clods of earth, sticks, and other weapons, they brought about his death right then and there.
The Bodhisatta, having dismounted from the elephant, approached the king and said, "Great King, one learns a craft for the sake of one's own happiness;
however, for some, the craft they have learned brings only destruction, like a pair of ill-fitting shoes. Having said this, he spoke these two verses:
“Just as insects on a man’s sandals, for the sake of their own pleasure, might inflict pain upon him—
being scorched by the heat and crushed by his foot— they devour the very feet of that man;
even so, one who is of low birth and ignoble, though he takes up our knowledge and learning, [acts in the same way].”
"He chews that very thing there with his teeth; he is called ignoble, like one who drinks blood.
In this context, "udabbaheti" means "he would pull out. "Scorched by heat and crushed underfoot" means scorched by the heat and oppressed by the soles of the feet.
"Tasseva" (of that very person) refers to the one by whom those ill-fitting sandals were purchased for the sake of comfort and fastened upon his feet.
Of that very [person]. They devour him, meaning they bite his feet while inflicting wounds.
*Dukkulīno* means one of base birth, a son of no noble family. *Anariyo* means a non-noble person, a wicked man devoid of shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*).

Regarding the phrase *tammāka vijjañca sutañca ādiyāti*: here, because he esteems (*manati*) this and that, he should be called *tammo*; however, in the word *tammāko*, it refers to one who takes (*ādiyati*) this and that [knowledge and learning].
"Practices a craft" means he masters and turns it over; this is a name for a teacher (*ācariya*). Therefore, it is *tammāka*;
however, its short vowel form was made for the sake of metrical ease in the verse composition. "Knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to anything among the eighteen branches of knowledge.

"Learning" (*suta*) refers to any scriptural mastery. "Having taken up" (*ādāya*) means having acquired it. "He devours that very thing there with his learning" (*tameva so tattha sutena khādati*): "that very thing" (*tameva*) refers to himself.
"He" refers to one who, being of low birth and ignoble, receives both knowledge and learning from a teacher;

he is that person. In this context, "he eats by means of what was heard" means that in the presence of that [teacher], he devours his own self by means of what was heard. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, there is also the reading:
"By that very thing, he eats there by means of what was heard. Regarding that as well, "by that [means] by means of what was heard there, he [devours] his own self..."
"Eats" has this very meaning. "Un-Aryan" is said to be like a sandal; thus, "un-Aryan" means like a poorly made sandal, like a sandal that is ill-fitting.
For just as poorly made sandals eat away at a person's feet, so too he, while eating with his learning, eats himself by himself.
Alternatively, *pānadu* means "pain for the foot"; it refers to one whose feet have been scorched by a sandal or whose feet have been eaten away by a sandal.
This is the name. Therefore, he who devours himself with learning is called "ignoble" (anariya) because of being devoured by that learning;
he is said to be like one who drinks poison or like one whose feet have been scorched by sandals—this is the meaning here.
The king, being pleased, bestowed great glory upon the Bodhisatta.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, Devadatta was the pupil, while I myself was the teacher.
The First Exposition of the Sandalwood Clogs Jātaka [232].
2. The Second Exposition of the Lute-Pillar Jātaka.
"This is what was thought by one person"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain young girl.
It seems that this girl, the daughter of a merchant in Sāvatthī, having seen the honors being paid to Usabha the king in her own house, asked her nurse:
"Mother, who is this that receives such honor? "He is named Usabha the king," she replied.
“Mother! Then, one day, while standing on her palace and looking down the street, she saw a hunchback and thought:
“Just as there is a hump on the back of the leader among oxen, so too there must be something corresponding for the leader among men;
this one will be a bull among men. I shall become his handmaid.”
"It is right for her to be so. She sent a maidservant to inform him, saying, "The merchant’s daughter wishes to go with you;
go to such-and-such a place and wait there. Taking her valuables and disguised as a stranger, she descended from the palace and fled with him.
Later on, that deed became public knowledge throughout the city and within the Saṅgha of monks.
In the Hall of Truth, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, it is said that the daughter of such-and-such a wealthy merchant has run away with a hunchback.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what discussion are you sitting here having now?
When they replied, "This very one," the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that she lusts after the hunchback; in the past, too, she did so."
Having said, "Is it not for the sake of sensual pleasures?", he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a merchant family in a certain market town.
Having grown up and lived the life of a householder, increasing in the number of sons and daughters, [he looked after] his own son...
Having turned back the daughter of the merchant of Benares, he set a day for the ceremony.
When the merchant’s daughter saw the honor and hospitality being shown to the bull in her own house, she asked her nurse, "Who is this?
Upon hearing it was a "bull," she then saw a hunchbacked man walking along the street and thought, "This must be the bull among men," and taking a precious object, [she followed him].

He fled together with her. The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I shall bring the merchant’s daughter home," was traveling toward Bārāṇasī with a great retinue and set out upon that very same road. Both of them traveled the road all night long.
Then, because the hunchback had been chilled by the cold throughout the entire night, at the rising of the dawn, his bodily humors were disturbed, and a great...
Feelings arose within him. Stepping down from the path and overcome by those feelings, he lay down curled up like the neck of a lute;

the merchant’s daughter sat at his feet. Seeing the merchant’s daughter sitting at the hunchback’s feet, the Bodhisatta recognized her, approached her, and while conversing with the merchant’s daughter, he spoke the first verse:
“This matter was thought out by you alone; you are a fool and lack a guide.
Indeed, you ought not to unite with this hunchback.
In that passage, “this matter was thought out by you alone” means, mother, that which you have contemplated regarding this hunchback—
"Having fled, this must have been thought out by you alone. 'A fool and without a guide'—this one is a fool because he is a dwarf;
even though he is old, he is like a fool due to his lack of wisdom (*duppañña*); and because he is incapable of going when another is not taking him along, he is without a guide.
For with a dwarf who is left-handed, O lady, you ought not to associate. By this [he meant]:
"Indeed, because of your hunchbackedness or dwarfism, you are on the left side; you were born in a great family, you are beautiful and lovely to behold, so you do not deserve to go together with me.
Then, having heard those words of his, the merchant’s daughter spoke this second verse:
“Thinking him a bull among men, I desired the hunchbacked one;
yet here he lies contracted, like a pillar with its cord cut.
The meaning of this is: “Noble sir, having seen a certain bull, [I thought], ‘On the back of the leader of the herd is the hump...’”
"He possesses this [mark], and he must therefore be a bull among men"—thinking thus, and regarding the hunchback as a bull among men, I desired him.
He lay there shriveled up like a lute-neck with its strings cut and its skin removed.
The Bodhisatta, knowing that she had come forth in an unrecognized guise, bathed her, adorned her, placed her upon a chariot, and returned home.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, she was this very same merchant’s daughter, and the merchant of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself.
This concludes the second commentary, the Vīṇāthūṇa Jātaka.
3. The Commentary on the Vikaṇṇaka Jātaka.
"Go wherever you wish"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain dissatisfied monk.
For when that monk was brought before the Dhamma Hall and asked by the Teacher, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied? he replied, "It is true.
When the Teacher asked, "Why are you dissatisfied? he said, "On account of the strands of sensual pleasure."
The Teacher said: "Monk, these strands of sensual pleasure are like a poisoned arrow;
once they find a foothold in the heart, they bring about death, just as a poisoned arrow brings death to a porpoise that has been pierced. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while the Bodhisatta was ruling the kingdom of Bārāṇasī with righteousness, he went one day to a park and reached the bank of a lotus pond.
He arrived there. Those skilled in dance and song performed dances and songs;
the fish and turtles in the lotus pond, lured by the sound of the singing, gathered together and went along with the king.
Seeing a mass of fish as large as a palm tree trunk, the king asked his ministers, "Why is it that these fish are moving along right with me?"
The ministers said, "Your Majesty, these people are attending upon you.
The king, pleased at the thought, "It seems they are indeed attending upon me," established a regular meal for them. Every day he had rice and curry cooked.
However, at the time of the meal, some of the fish would arrive while others would not, and the food would go to waste. They reported this matter to the king.
The king said, "From now on, strike the drum at the seventh watch;

when the fish have gathered together at the sound of the drum, give them food. From then on, the cook had the drum struck and gave food to the fish who had assembled. They too, having gathered together at the sound of the drum, ate.
While they were thus assembled and eating, a crocodile came and devoured some fish.
The cook informed the king. Having heard this, the king said, "When the crocodile comes to eat the fish, pierce it with a spear and seize it.
Saying "Very well," he went and stood on the boat, and [aimed at] the crocodile that had come to eat the fish.
He struck him with a *vikaṇṇaka* (a type of arrow), and it entered deep into his back. Overcome by pain, he seized the man and fled.
When the cook realized he had been pierced, he spoke to him, reciting the first verse:
"Go wherever you wish, as you please; you have been struck in a vital spot by a *vikaṇṇaka*."
"Slain by well-prepared food, greedy as he pursued the fish.
Therein, "at will" means unreservedly. "Go wherever you wish" means go to whichever place you desire.
"In the vitals" means in the vital spot. "With a slanted arrow" means with a slanted-pointed shaft. "Slain by well-prepared food," etc.
"Greedy for fish while pursuing them": meaning that you, becoming greedy upon hearing the sound of drums and music while food was being distributed, pursued the fish for the sake of eating;
you were killed by that very food you tasted, and even at the place where you went, there was no life for you. Having gone to his own dwelling place, he met his end.
Having shown this reason, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke the second verse:
“Even thus, falling into the bait of the world, one who follows the dictates of the mind is tormented;
he is slain in the midst of his kinsmen and friends, like a crocodile following a fish.”
In this context, "worldly bait" (*lokāmisa*) refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*). For the world grasps these as desirable, lovely, and pleasing;

therefore, they are called "worldly bait. "Falling upon it" means that a person who pursues that worldly bait, following the power of the mind under the influence of the defilements (*kilesa*), is distressed and exhausted;
such a person is "slain" by his own kinsmen and friends.
"Like a crocodile pursuing fish, pierced in the middle by a harpoon, he who grasps the five strands of sensual pleasure as being 'pleasing' is slain, suffers, and indeed meets with great destruction.
Having thus delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, [the listeners attained realization].
The dejected bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, the fish were the Buddha’s retinue, and the King of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself.
This is the third commentary on the Vikaṇṇaka Jātaka.
[234] 4. The Commentary on the Asitābhū Jātaka:
"You alone are the one who made it so. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain young girl.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, in a family that served as supporters for the two Chief Disciples, there was a young girl who was beautiful.
Having attained great fortune and reached maturity, she entered a family of similar status.
Her husband, disregarding her in some matters, lived elsewhere under the influence of his own whims. She, however, did not take that lack of regard from him to heart;
instead, she invited the two Chief Disciples, gave them alms, and while listening to the Dhamma, she established herself in the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*). From that time forth...
Spending her time in the bliss of the fruits of the Path, she thought, "My husband does not desire me, and I have no further business with the household life;
I shall go forth. Having informed her parents and gone forth, she attained Arahantship.
Her conduct became well known among the monks. Then one day, the monks were discussing this matter in the Hall of Truth.
They raised the matter, saying: "Friend, the daughter of such-and-such a family was seeking her own welfare;

having learned that her husband was unwilling [to let her go], she heard the Dhamma from the Chief Disciples, established herself in the fruit of stream-entry, and then, having again asked permission of her parents, went forth and attained Arahatship.
Thus, friend, that young woman was one who sought her own welfare. The Teacher, having arrived, said:
“Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together here now? he asked.

When they replied, “For this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that this daughter of good family is a seeker of welfare; in the past, too, she was a seeker of welfare. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Having attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he took up residence in the region of the Himalayas.
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, having seen the excellence of his son Prince Brahmadatta’s retinue, became apprehensive and banished his son from the kingdom.
Taking his own queen named Asitābhū, he entered the Himalayas and [subsisted on] fish, meat, and various fruits.
While eating, he made his dwelling in a leaf-hut. Upon seeing a certain *kinnarī*, his mind became bound to her;
thinking, "I shall make her my wife," he disregarded Asitābhū and followed after her.
Seeing him following her, that *kinnarī* thought, "He disregards me and follows this *kinnarī*; what use have I for him? and her heart became detached from him.
Having made the offering, she approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and requested instruction on the preliminary practice for the *kasiṇas*.
While contemplating the *kasiṇa*, she attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).

Then, having paid homage to the Bodhisatta and returned, she stood at the door of her own leaf-hut. Meanwhile, Brahmadatta, following after the Kinnarī, wandered about, even along the path she had taken.
Seeing him, his hopes shattered, he returned toward the leaf-hut. Asitābhū, seeing him approaching, rose up into the air and,
standing in the sky which was the color of a jewel, said, "Noble son, it is by depending on you that I have obtained this bliss of meditation," and spoke this verse:
“Now you alone are the makara, O fisherman, since desire has departed from you;
it is now without rebirth, like dust blown away by a sharp wind.
In this passage, “Now you alone are the makara,” means: O noble son, you who have abandoned me and pursued the kinnarī—you yourself [are the makara].

"Now do this. "That desire which has departed from you": this indicates that the desire for me that had left you was abandoned through suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), and because of its abandonment, he demonstrates that he has attained this distinction.

"That desire is now without reconnection": furthermore, that desire has now become one that does not reconnect; it is no longer possible for it to reconnect. "Like dust on a surface cut by a rough [blade]."
"A saw" (*khara*) means a saw; "dust" (*renuka*) means an elephant's tusk.

"Just as an elephant's tusk, once cut by a saw, becomes disconnected and does not join together again in its former manner, so too there shall be no further joining of my heart with yours"—having said this, he flew up right before his eyes and departed elsewhere.
Then, while lamenting after she had gone, he spoke this second verse:
“Through excessive desire and through the intoxication of excessive greed,
one thus falls away from wealth, just as I have from my black-shouldered [buffalo].”
In this context, "immoderate desire" (*atriccha*) means desire that is boundless, characterized by craving for this or that;
"excessive greed" (*atilobha*) means greed that operates beyond its proper limits. And "by the intoxication of excessive greed" (*atilobhamadena*):

it is called the intoxication of excessive greed because it gives rise to human pride. This is what is meant: a person, through the influence of immoderate desire, being one who desires immoderately...
"By excessive greed and by the intoxication of excessive greed, just as I was deprived of the princess Asitābhū, so too does one's welfare perish.
Having lamented with this verse, he lived alone in the forest; and upon his father’s passing, he went and took over the kingdom.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the prince and the princess were these two people, while the ascetic was none other than myself."
The fourth is the commentary on the Asitābhū Jātaka.
[235] 5. The commentary on the Vacchanakha Jātaka:
"Happy are the homes of the bear-clawed ones. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Roja Malla.
It seems that this was a lay friend of the Venerable Ānanda. One day he sent a message to the Elder requesting his visit;
the Elder, having taken leave of the Teacher, went there.
After feeding the Elder with various kinds of choice food, he sat to one side and, having exchanged friendly greetings with the Elder, [addressed him] regarding the five household enjoyments.
Inviting him with the objects of sensual pleasure, he said, "Venerable Ānanda, in my house there is an abundance of treasures, both animate and inanimate;
having divided this in half, I shall give it to you. Come, let us both dwell together in the household.
The Elder, having explained the danger in the objects of sensual pleasure to him, rose from his seat and went to the monastery. Then the Teacher asked, "Ānanda, have you seen Roja?"
When asked, he replied, "Yes, venerable sir. When further asked, "What did you say to him? he said, "Venerable sir, Roja invited me to live the life of a householder;
I then spoke to him of the dangers inherent both in the household life and in the strands of sensual pleasure.
The Teacher said, "Ānanda, it is not only now that Roja the Mallian has invited those who have gone forth to live as householders; in the past, too, he invited them."
Having spoken thus, being requested by him, he related a past event:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a certain village of a market town into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he went forth as a seer (isipabbajjā); after dwelling for a long time in the Himalayan region, he [set out] for the sake of seeking salt and sour food."
Having reached Bārāṇasī and stayed in the royal park, on the following day he entered Bārāṇasī.

Then the merchant of Bārāṇasī, having gained confidence in his conduct and way of life, led him to his home, fed him, and after obtaining his promise to stay in the park, took care of him and had him reside there.
They developed mutual affection for one another.
Then one day, out of affection and confidence toward the Bodhisatta, the merchant of Benares thought thus:

“Renunciation is indeed suffering; let me cause my companion, the wandering ascetic Vacchanakha, to give up the homeless life, divide all my wealth in two, and give it to him, so that we both may live together in harmony. One day, at the conclusion of his meal—
Having exchanged pleasant greetings with him, he said, "Venerable Vacchanakha, renunciation is indeed painful, while life at home is pleasant;
come, let us both live together in harmony, enjoying sensual pleasures," and spoke this first verse:
"Pleasant are homes, Vacchanakha, Possessing wealth and provided with food; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
"Where, having eaten and drunk, you may sleep without anxiety.
In this context, "possessing gold" means endowed with the seven treasures.

"Possessing food" means having many kinds of hard and soft foods. "Where, having eaten and drunk" means in those houses possessing gold and food where one has partaken of various excellent flavors of meals.

"And having drunk various drinks, you shall lie down free from anxiety. "Those houses upon whose surfaces of magnificent, adorned couches you shall lie down free from anxiety—those are indeed exceedingly pleasant," [the merchant said].
Then, having heard this, the Bodhisatta said: "Great merchant, out of ignorance you have become greedy for sensual pleasures; as for the household life..."
Having said, "I have told you the virtues of going forth and the faults of it; now listen as I tell you the faults of the household life," he spoke the second verse:
"For one who does not long for the home, and for one who does not speak falsehoods from the home..."
“For one who does not take up the burden of the household, who does no harm to others—such a breach is difficult to overcome; who would enter such a household?
In this context, “for one who does not strive for the household” means for one who at all times does not exert effort or labor in activities such as plowing or cattle-herding.

"There is no such thing as a house" means that the household life does not find a firm footing. "There is no such thing as a house for one who does not speak falsely" means that even for one who speaks the truth for the sake of fields, lands, silver, gold, and so forth, there is no such thing as a house.
"For one who does not take up the rod and who does not deceive others":
"who does not take up the rod" means one who has not grasped the rod; for one who has laid down the rod and does not deceive others, there is no such thing as a house.

There is none. However, for one who, having taken up the rod of punishment, inflicts upon others—such as slaves and laborers—in accordance with their respective offenses punishments such as execution, imprisonment, mutilation, and flogging, it is precisely his household life that remains stable;
this is the meaning. Thus, "the house has a flaw that is difficult to overcome; who would enter such a home?"—this is now [said] regarding them.
If one fails to exert effort and so forth, there is a breach due to various forms of decline;

even if one does make such efforts, because it must be performed constantly, the household life is difficult to master and difficult to satisfy. Even for one who performs these duties constantly, it remains difficult to master and hard to fill.
Who, then, would undertake this, thinking, "I shall dwell in the household life free from anxiety"?
Thus the Great Being, having spoken of the faults of household life, went back to the park.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Roja the merchant of Bārāṇasī was Vacchanakha the Mallian, and I myself was the wandering ascetic Vacchanakha.
This is the fifth narrative, the Vacchanakha Jātaka.
[236] 6. The Commentary on the Bakajātakam:
"O, what a noble bird this is!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain hypocritical bhikkhu.
When the Teacher had him brought and saw him displayed, he said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past, too, this man was a hypocrite," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī,
the Bodhisatta lived as a fish with a great retinue in a certain lake in the Himalayan region. Then a certain crane, thinking, "I shall eat the fish," settled his head near the edge of the lake,
spread his wings, and stood there watching the fish very slowly, waiting for them to become careless.
At that moment, the Bodhisatta, surrounded by a school of fish, arrived at that place while seeking food.
Seeing the crane, the school of fish spoke this first verse:
“Ah, what a noble bird this is! A twice-born one resembling the kumuda lily!”
"With wings stilled, he meditates very gently.
Therein, "he meditates very gently" means that, becoming as if weak and powerless, he meditates all alone as if knowing nothing.
Then the Bodhisatta, having looked at him, spoke the second verse:
“You do not know his virtue; you praise him without knowing it.
This bird does not protect us; therefore, this winged one does not stir.
In this context, “without knowing” means not having understood. “This bird does not protect us” means that this bird neither guards nor protects us.
“Which of these shall I make into a morsel? he reflected. “Because of that, the bird does not stir”—meaning that for this reason the fowl did not move or tremble.
When this was said, the shoal of fish agitated the water and caused the crane to flee.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the deceitful crane was the monk, but the king of the fish was none other than myself.”
The Sixth: The Commentary on the Bakajātakavaṇṇanā.
[237] 7. The Commentary on the Sāketajātakavaṇṇanā.
"What indeed, Blessed One, is the cause?"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling in dependence on Sāketa, concerning a brahmin of Sāketa.
He spoke with reference to this. As for the background story here, it has already been told both in the past and in the present in the preceding Ekaka-nipāta (Single Chapter).
However, when the monks had gone to the dwelling place of the Tathāgata, they asked, "Venerable Sir, how does this thing called affection become established?
and they recited the first verse:
“What indeed, Blessed One, is the cause that for some individuals here, the heart becomes exceedingly cooled and the mind also gains confidence?
The meaning of this is: what indeed is the cause by which, upon merely seeing some individuals here, the heart becomes exceedingly [calmed]?
It is extinguished; it becomes cool like a well-perfumed vessel filled with cold water that has been sprinkled with a thousand jars of it;
yet some are not extinguished. Some find confidence in the mind at the mere sight [of the object]; it becomes pliant and, through the power of affection, adheres to it; while others do not adhere.
Then the Teacher, showing the cause of their affection, spoke this second verse:
“Whether through former association, or by benefit in the present,
Thus does that affection arise, like a lotus in the water.”
The meaning of this is as follows: Monks, this thing called affection arises from two causes.

If, in a previous existence, one has lived together with another—having been a mother, father, son, daughter, brother, sister, husband, wife, companion, or friend—in that very same place, then by virtue of that prior cohabitation, even in another life...
That affection, following along, does not abandon [the object]. Through what has been done in this present existence, or through benefit in the present, love (*pema*) arises in such a way.
Love arises by means of these two causes. How is this so? "Like a lotus in water" (*uppalaṃ va yathodake*).
The short vowel *vā* has been used; it is employed here in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), therefore [it means] "and the lotus."

The remaining meaning here should be understood as follows: just as a water-born flower, growing in water, arises dependent upon two causes—namely, the water itself and the mud—so too does affection arise through these two causes.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, the brahmin and the brahmin lady were these two people, while the son was none other than myself."
The seventh: The Commentary on the Sāketajātakavaṇṇanā.
[238] 8. The Commentary on the Ekapadajātakavaṇṇanā.
"Come now, dear one, even a single step!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain householder.
It is said that this was a householder living in Sāvatthī. One day, while his son was sitting on his lap, the boy asked him a question called "The Door of Wealth.
Thinking, "This question is within the domain of the Buddha; no one else will be able to explain it," he took his son and went to Jetavana.
Having paid homage to the Teacher, he said, "Venerable Sir, this boy of mine [was sitting] on my thigh..."
Seated there, he asked a question called "The Door to Meaning. Not knowing its meaning, I have come here;
please explain this question, venerable sir. The Teacher said, “Lay follower, this boy has not only now been a seeker of the goal;
in the past as well, having been a seeker of the goal, he asked this question of the wise, and the ancient sages explained it to him too.”
"However, because he had entered into a state of mental confusion, he did not perceive it," he said; and being requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of wealthy merchants.
Having reached maturity, upon his father’s passing, he obtained the position of the head merchant. Then, as his young son sat upon his lap, [the boy said]: "Father,..."
“Please tell me one word, dear father, which is based on many meanings and serves as a single cause,” he asked,
speaking the first verse: “Come now, dear father,
tell us some comprehensive single word, based on many meanings, by which we may accomplish our purpose.”
In this context, *iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of a request or an exhortation.
*Ekapadaṃ* means a single causal phrase, or a verbal expression associated with a single cause. *Anekatthapadassitaṃ* means dependent upon many phrases of meaning, that is, many causal phrases.
*Kiñci saṅgāhikaṃ brūsī* means: "Speak some single phrase that is inclusive of many phrases."
Or rather, this is the reading: “Tell me that single word, supported by many meanings, by which we might accomplish our own prosperity. Thus he asked.
Then his father, speaking to him, recited the second verse:
“O dear one, there is this single word ‘generosity,’ which is expressed with manifold meanings;
when it is conjoined with virtue and brought forth by patience,
it is sufficient to bring happiness to friends and suffering to enemies.”
In this context, "the single step of skill" (*dakkheyyekapada*) means a single step that is skillful.
"Skill" (*dakkheyya*) refers to energy associated with knowledge that is clever and proficient in producing gain. It is said to be "based on many words of meaning" (*anekatthapadassita*);
that is, the aforementioned kind of energy is supported by many words of meaning. By which ones? By virtue and so forth. For this very reason, he says: "And that is conjoined with virtue," and so on.

The meaning of this is as follows: Furthermore, this energy—endowed with conduct and virtue, and possessed of patience through endurance—is sufficient and capable of bringing happiness to friends and suffering to enemies.

For who indeed, being endowed with wholesome energy associated with the knowledge that produces gain, and perfected in conduct and patience, would not be able to bring happiness to friends or cause suffering to enemies?
Thus the Bodhisatta answered his son’s question. The son, too, having accomplished his own purpose according to the method explained by his father, departed according to his karma.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, both father and son were established in the fruit of Stream-entry. "At that time, the son was none other than this very son; the merchant of Bārāṇasī..."
"But it was I myself who was he.
The commentary on the Ekapada Jātaka is the eighth.
[239] 9. The commentary on the Haritamaṇḍūka Jātaka.
"Even a venomous snake is peaceful to me"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Veḷuvana concerning Ajātasattu.
For King Mahākosala, the father of the King of Kosala, when giving his daughter in marriage to King Bimbisāra, had given her the village of Kāsika as the dowry for her bath-money.
When she had been involved in the act of parricide by Ajātasattu, she soon [fell] through her affection for the king...
She passed away. Even after his mother had died, Ajātasattu continued to enjoy that village.
King Pasenadi of Kosala, thinking, "I will not give a village belonging to my family to a thief who has murdered his father," waged war against him.
Sometimes victory belonged to the maternal uncle, and sometimes to the nephew. But whenever Ajātasattu was victorious, he would be filled with joy.
Having hoisted his banner on the chariot, he would enter the city with great splendor.
But when he was defeated, he would enter in a state of dejection, having informed no one at all. Then one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
"Friends, Ajātasattu is satisfied when he defeats his maternal uncle, but when defeated, he becomes dejected."
“...is it? The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, this man was satisfied when he won and became overcome with dejection when he was defeated.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a blue frog.
At that time, people set snares here and there in rivers, caves, and other places for the purpose of catching fish.
Many fish entered one snare. Then, a water-snake, while devouring the fish, [encountered] that snare.
He entered [the trap], and many fish, having gathered together and devoured him, made him a single pool of blood.
Seeing no refuge and terrified by the fear of death, he forced his way out through the mouth of the trap and, overcome by pain, lay down on the edge of the water.
At that very moment, a blue frog leaped up and landed upon the tip of the trap's hook. The venomous snake went to the place of judgment.
Not finding [anyone], and seeing him lying there, he asked, "Friend Blue Frog, do you approve of the behavior of these fish?
and spoke the first verse:
"Though I am a venomous serpent, having entered the mouth of the basket;..."
“O son of the green frog, it pleases me that these little fish eat me.

Therein, “even though I am like a venomous snake with poison already risen” means even though I am one whose poison has manifested. “O son of the green frog, it pleases me that these little fish eat me”—he says this to mean, “This is what pleases you.
Then the green frog said to him, “Yes, friend, it does please me. “For what reason? “Because if you too—”
“You eat the fish that come into your domain, and the fish also eat you when you come into theirs;
for one who is in his own domain, his own place, his feeding ground, there is no such thing as being weak,” he said, and spoke this second verse:
“A man indeed plunders as long as it serves him;”
“And when others plunder, he who has been plundered plunders [in turn].
In this context, “the man indeed plunders as long as it serves him” means that for as long as that man’s power serves him—that is, as long as it succeeds and functions—he continues to plunder others.
There is also the reading, “as long as it serves him” (*yāva so upakappati*), which refers to however much...
The meaning is that the man is able to plunder at the right time.
"And when others plunder" means when other powerful persons, having become masters, plunder. "He, being plundered, plunders" means then that plunderer is plundered by others.
There is also a reading "vilumpate," which has the same meaning. They also read "vilumpanaṃ," but its meaning does not fit.
Thus, when the Bodhisatta had adjudged that "the plunderer shall meet with plunder," the schools of fish,
