knowing the water-snake's weakness and thinking, "We shall seize our enemy," emerged from the mouth of the trap and there brought him to his death before departing.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the water-snake was Ajātasattu, and the green frog was none other than myself.
This concludes the ninth narrative, the Commentary on the Harita-maṇḍūka Jātaka.
[240] 10. The Commentary on the Mahāpiṅgala Jātaka.
"Everyone," said the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, referring to Devadatta.
After Devadatta had harbored malice toward the Teacher, nine months later, he sank into the earth at the gateway of the Jetavana.
Then the residents of Jetavana and all the inhabitants of the kingdom exclaimed, "Devadatta, the thorn in the Buddha’s side, has been swallowed by the earth!"
“Now the Perfectly Enlightened One has become one who has struck down his enemies,” they said, filled with joy and delight.
Hearing their words, through the sound passed from one to another, all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa and the hosts of *yakkhas*, *bhūtas*, and deities likewise became filled with joy and delight.
Then, on a certain day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Dharma: “Friends, regarding Devadatta’s sinking into the earth...”
“The great multitude became joyful, thinking, ‘Devadatta, that thorn to the Buddhas, having been submerged, has been swallowed by the earth.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that the great multitude rejoices and laughs at Devadatta’s death.”
Having said, “And formerly too, he both sighed and laughed,” he related a story of the past:
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Mahāpiṅgala ruled the kingdom unrighteously and unjustly;
acting under the influence of desire and other passions, he committed evil deeds and, by seizing fines, taxes, forced labor, and coins, he squeezed the great multitude like sugarcane in a press.
He was harsh, cruel, and violent; he possessed not even a trace of compassion for others.

In his household, he was disliked and disagreeable to his wives, sons, daughters, ministers, brahmins, householders, and others, like dust fallen into the eye, like a pebble in a morsel of food, or like a thorn that has pierced the heel.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn as the son of Mahāpiṅgala. After Mahāpiṅgala had ruled the kingdom for a long time, he passed away.
When he had died, all the inhabitants of Bārāṇasī, joyful and delighted, laughed with loud laughter;
they cremated Mahāpiṅgala with a thousand carts of wood and extinguished the funeral pyre with many thousands of jars of water.
Having extinguished [the fire] and consecrated the Bodhisatta in the kingship, they were joyful and delighted, thinking, "We have obtained a righteous king.
They caused the festival drums to be beaten throughout the city, adorned the city with hoisted banners and flags, and erected pavilions at every gate.
Sitting in those decorated pavilions, whose floors were strewn with parched grain and flowers, they ate and drank.
The Bodhisatta also sat in the midst of a magnificent, elevated white canopy on a noble couch, enjoying great glory.
The ministers, brahmins, householders, provincial governors, gatekeepers, and others stood surrounding the king.
Then, one gatekeeper, standing not far away, wept, sighing and gasping for breath. The Bodhisatta—
Seeing him, he asked, “Friend gatekeeper, when my father passed away, everyone wandered about joyful, exultant, and celebrating a festival;
yet you stand here weeping. Is it that my father was dear and pleasing to you alone?
Thus he spoke the first verse:
“All the people were oppressed by Piṅgala; now that he is dead, they experience relief.
Was he dear to you, O dark-eyed one? Why do you weep, gatekeeper?
In this context, “oppressed” means afflicted by various kinds of punishments, taxes, and so forth. “By Piṅgala” means by the one with tawny eyes.
It is said that both his eyes were bloodshot and tawny, the color of a cat’s eye;
for that reason, they gave him the name “Piṅgala. “They experience conditions” means they experience raptures (*pīti*).
“Black-eyed” means tawny-eyed. “Why indeed do you weep? means for what reason do you weep? In the commentary, however, the reading is “kasmā tuvam.”
Having heard his words, he said: "Great King, it is not because 'Mahāpiṅgala is dead' that I weep out of sorrow;
rather, my head has become comfortable. For whenever King Piṅgala was descending from or ascending to the palace, he would strike my head eight times with each blow of a blacksmith's hammer;
even after going to the other world, he [continues] to strike my head."
“Even while giving, he would give a blow upon my head even to the guardians of hell or to Yama for the sake of virtue;
then they, thinking, ‘This man troubles us excessively,’ would bring him back here again and release him, and then he would give another blow upon my head.
It is out of fear of this that I weep,” saying this, he spoke the second verse to clarify this meaning.
“The one with black eyes was not dear to me; I fear his return.
For if he, having gone from here, should harm the King of Death, being harmed himself, he might bring him back here again.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him: “That king was burned by a thousand loads of wood and sprinkled with hundreds of water-pots;”

"Her funeral pyre has been dug out all around. Furthermore, those who have naturally departed to the other world do not return again with that very same body due to their destination elsewhere; do not be afraid. Thus, comforting him, he spoke this verse:
"He was burned by thousands of loads and sprinkled with hundreds of jars [of water];"
“That ground has been prepared; do not fear, it will surely come.

From that moment on, the gatekeeper regained his composure. Having ruled the kingdom with righteousness and performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, the Bodhisatta passed away according to his karma.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Mahāpiṅgala was Devadatta, but the son was none other than myself.”
The Tenth: The Commentary on the Mahāpiṅgala Jātaka.
The Ninth Chapter: The Chapter on Sandals.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is as follows:
Upāhana, Vīṇāthūṇa, Vikaṇṇaka, Asitābhu,
Vacchanakha, Baka, Sāketa, Ekapada,
and Piṅgala of Haritamātā.
10. The Chapter on the Jackal [241] 1. The Commentary on the *Sabbadaṭṭha-jātaka*:
"The jackal, stiff with pride"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta.
Devadatta was unable to make the gain and honor he had obtained by winning over Ajātasattu endure for long;
from the moment the miracle was witnessed during the incident at Nāḷāgiri, that gain and honor vanished from him.
Then one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth: "Friends, Devadatta’s gain and honor..."
“Having produced it, he was unable to make it endure for long. The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta causes the gain and honor that arose for himself to disappear;
in the past as well, he caused them to disappear. Having said this, he related the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his court chaplain, having reached the far shore of the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of learning. He knew the spell called *Pathavījaya*.
"Pathavījaya" is said to be a spell for summoning [spirits]. Then one day, the Bodhisatta thought, "I shall recite that spell," and in a certain...

Sitting upon a stone slab in the courtyard, he practiced his recitation. It is said that this mantra cannot be uttered unless one is composed in another manner and devoid of fear; therefore, he practiced it in such a place.
Then, while he was reciting, a jackal lying in a certain cave heard that mantra and mastered it. It is said that in the immediately preceding life...

There was a certain brahmin who was well-versed in the *pāguṇa* spell regarding the earth. After the Bodhisatta had finished his recitation and stood up, he said, "Ah, this spell is indeed well-mastered by me!
Then a jackal emerged from its den and, saying, "O brahmin, this spell is mastered even more thoroughly by me than by you," fled away. The Bodhisatta [thought], "This jackal is great..."
Thinking, “He will do something unwholesome,” he pursued him for a short distance, crying out, “Seize him! Seize him! The jackal fled and entered the forest.
Having gone there, he bit a female jackal slightly on her body. When she asked, “What is it, Master? he replied, “Do you know me or not?
She accepted his words, saying, “Yes, I know you. He then recited the Earth-Winner Spell (*pathavī-jaya-manta*).
Having commanded many hundreds of jackals, he brought all four-footed creatures—elephants, horses, lions, tigers, boars, deer, and so forth—into his presence.
Having done so, he became a king named Sabbadāṭha and made a female jackal his chief queen.
A lion stood upon the backs of two elephants, and upon the back of the lion sat the jackal king Sabbadāṭha.
He sat together with his chief queen, Siṅgālī, and great fame arose.
Having become intoxicated by that great fame and conceited, thinking, "I shall seize the kingdom of Bārāṇasī," he reached a place not far from Bārāṇasī surrounded by all four-footed creatures;
his retinue was twelve *yojanas* in extent. While still standing at a distance, he said: "Either give me the kingdom, or [fight]..."
Thus he sent a message to the king. The inhabitants of Bārāṇasī, terrified and trembling, stood with the city gates closed.
The Bodhisatta approached the king and said, "Do not fear, Great King;
the battle against Sabbadāṭhasiṅgāla is my responsibility. There is no one else capable of fighting him except for me."
Having reassured both the king and the citizens, he thought, "I shall ask Sabbadāṭha what he intends to do to seize the kingdom.
Ascending to the gate-tower, he asked, "Friend Sabbadāṭha, what will you do to take this kingdom?
[He replied: "By making him roar the lion’s roar and terrifying the great multitude with the sound..."
“I shall take it. The Bodhisatta, knowing that “it exists,” descended from the watchtower and caused a drum to be beaten, proclaiming:
“Let all the inhabitants of the city of Bārāṇasī, twelve leagues in extent, plaster their ear-holes with flour paste!

When the great multitude heard the command on the drum, starting even with the cats, all four-footed creatures as well as themselves plastered their ear-holes so that another’s [voice] could not enter.
The sound could not be heard; thus he was bribed with a month’s worth of flour.
Then the Bodhisatta, having climbed up to the watchtower again, said, “Sabbadāṭhā! “What is it, Brahmin?
“Having made what arrangement will you take this kingdom? “By making him roar his lion’s roar and terrifying the people, I shall bring about his destruction.”
“Having brought them here, I shall seize them. [The lion replied: “You will not be able to make them roar the lion’s roar.
For these lion-kings, endowed with noble birth and possessing deep-red hands and feet, will not carry out the command of a jackal like you in his old age.
The jackal, becoming arrogant with pride, said: “Let other lions be for now; I shall make even him roar upon whose back I sit!”
He said, “In that case, let him roar, if you are able. He gave a signal with his foot to the lion upon whom he was seated, saying, “Roar!
The lion pressed his face against the elephant’s frontal globe and let out an irreversible lion’s roar three times.
The elephant, overcome with terror, threw the jackal down at his feet and crushed his head with his foot.
Having attacked him, they ground him to pieces, and Sabbadāṭha met his death right there.
Hearing the lion’s roar, those elephants too, terrified by the fear of death, gored one another and met their end on that very spot.
With the exception of the lions, all other four-footed creatures—from deer and pigs down to hares and cats—met their destruction right there.
They reached the end of their lives. The lions fled and entered the forest, leaving behind a heap of flesh twelve yojanas in extent.
The Bodhisatta descended from his tower, had the city gates opened, and caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming:
"Let all those who desire meat bring it after removing the minced flesh from their own ears; let those seeking meat take as much as they need. Thus the people...
Having eaten all the meat, they dried the remainder and made it into jerky (*vallūra*). It is said that it was at that time that the making of jerky first came into being.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and spoken these verses of his own enlightenment, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
“The jackal, stubborn in pride, desiring a retinue...”
“He attained the great state, becoming the king of all tusked beasts.
In the very same way, among human beings,
he who possesses a retinue becomes great therein, like the tusked jackal.”
In that context, "stiff with pride" means stiffened by pride arisen on account of his retinue.
"Desiring a retinue" means desiring even further a retinue. "A great domain" means a great prosperity.
"You were the king of all tusked beasts" means he was the king of all those with tusks; for he was great among them. Thus, that man endowed with a retinue... [among] them.
"He was called 'Great' because of his retinue. 'Like a jackal among the tusked ones' means that just as the jackal was great among those with tusks, so he was great;
yet like that jackal, having fallen into negligence, he met his destruction by relying on that very retinue.
"At that time, Devadatta was the jackal, Sāriputta was the king, and I myself was the chaplain."
The First Exposition of the *Sabbadāṭha Jātaka*.
[242] 2. The Exposition of the *Sunakha Jātaka*:
"This dog is indeed a fool. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, in the assembly hall at the Ambaṇakoṭṭhaka.
He spoke concerning a dog that was fed the meal [left over]. It is said that from the time it was born, water-carriers took it and raised it there.
Later on, while eating the meal there, it became fat-bodied.
Then one day, a certain village dweller arrived at that place; seeing the dog, he [spoke] to the water-carriers.
Having given him an upper garment and a kahāpaṇa coin, he tied him with a leather thong, took him, and departed.
As he was being led away, the dog did not bark; instead, eating whatever was given to him, he followed right behind.
Then that man, thinking, "Now he loves me," released the leather thong. As soon as it was loosened, the dog rushed with a single bound straight to the dining hall.
He had gone. When the monks saw him and learned the reason for his departure, they raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall during the evening:
"Friends, a dog in the assembly hall that was skilled at escaping its bonds has returned as soon as it was let loose.
The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, what discussion are you sitting here having now?"
Having asked, "Is it by this [method]? and being told, "Yes, indeed," he said, "Monks, that dog was not only skilled in binding and releasing now;
he was skilled even in the past. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of great wealth in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Having been reborn, he reached maturity and entered the life of a householder. At that time, there was a dog belonging to a certain man in Bārāṇasī;
because it received alms-food, it became fat-bodied.
Then, a village dweller came to Bārāṇasī, and seeing that dog, he gave the man his upper garment and a kahāpaṇa coin, took the dog, and departed.
Having bound him with a leather thong and holding the end of the thong, he went along;
at the entrance to the forest, he entered a certain *sāla* tree, tied up the dog, lay down on a wooden plank, and fell asleep.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having set out for the forest on some business, saw the dog tied there with a thong and spoke the first verse:
“Foolish indeed is this dog, who does not bite the leather strap;
he might free himself from his bonds and, unsaddled, run back to his own home.

In this context, *pamuñceyya* means he would release himself; or rather, this reading (*pamoceyya*) is the correct one. *Asito ca gharaṃ vajeti*: having become unsaddled—that is, well-fed—he would go to his own dwelling place.
Having heard that, the dog spoke this second verse:
“It is fixed in my mind, and it is established in my heart;
I await the time until the people have fallen asleep.”
"In this regard, as for what you say, 'It is established in my mind, it is mine,' that has indeed been resolved by me; it is truly in my mind.
And furthermore, 'it is placed in my heart'—moreover, your words have indeed been taken to heart by me.
'And I await the time'—I am waiting for the time. 'Until the people fall asleep'—until this great multitude of people has fallen asleep."
"Let them fall asleep; meanwhile, I shall wait for the right time. Otherwise, the cry 'This dog is running away!
would arise. Therefore, when everyone is fast asleep during the night, I will chew through the leather thong and escape.
Having said this, when the great crowd had fallen asleep, he chewed the thong, and being well-fed, he escaped and went to his own place.
He went straight to his own master’s house.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, the dog was the very same dog as now; the wise man, however, was none other than I myself.
This is the second commentary on the Sunakha Jātaka.
[243] 3. The Commentary on the Guttila Jātaka.
"The seventy strings, so very sweet..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana grove concerning Devadatta.
At that time, the monks said to Devadatta: "Friend Devadatta, the Perfectly Enlightened One [is superior to you]..."
"Teacher, you mastered the Three Piṭakas by relying on the Perfectly Enlightened One and attained the four jhānas;
it is not fitting for a teacher to become an enemy to his own teacher. Devadatta replied, "But friend, was the ascetic Gotama my teacher?
Did I not master the Three Piṭakas and attain the four [jhānas] solely through my own power?"

“I have produced the jhānas,” he said, thereby rejecting his teacher. The monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, “Friends, Devadatta, having rejected his teacher and become an adversary to the Perfectly Enlightened One, has met with great ruin.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?”
When it was said, "Is his name indeed this?", [the Buddha] said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has met with destruction after rejecting his teacher and becoming my adversary;
he did so even in the past. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a family of musicians; his name was Guttila Kumāra.

They gave him a name. When he reached maturity, having attained perfection in the art of music, he became known as Guttila the musician, the foremost musician in all of Jambudīpa. Without taking a wife, he supported his blind parents.
At that time, merchants living in Bārāṇasī went to the city of Ujjenī for trade, and when a festival was announced, they offered a reward.

Having gathered together and taken much garlands, perfumes, ointments, and various kinds of food such as hard and soft edibles, they assembled at the place of entertainment and said, "Pay wages and bring us a musician.
At that time, there was a senior musician named Mūsila in Ujjenī; they summoned him and had him perform as their musician.
Mūsila, playing the lute, tuned it to the highest pitch and performed.
To those who were well-versed in the music of the Gandhabba Guttila, his performance appeared like the scratching of a cockroach on a palm leaf;
not even one of them showed a sign of delight. When they showed no sign of satisfaction, Mūsila thought, "I have played too harshly..."
"I shall sing," he thought; having become intoxicated by a moderate measure of intoxication, he sang in a moderate tone, and they remained indifferent even then.
Then, thinking, "I suppose these people know nothing," he himself acted as if ignorant and sang the verses with slackened tension, and they said nothing at all even then.
Then Mūsila said to them, "O merchants, why indeed..."
“When I was playing the lute, you were not pleased,” he said. “But what did you play on the lute?
For we had the perception that this person was merely tuning the lute.
“But do you know a teacher superior to me, or are you simply not pleased because of your own ignorance? The merchants replied, “In Bārāṇasī, there is the musician Guttila...”
"To those who have previously heard the sound of the lute, your lute's sound is like the voice of women coaxing their children," they said.
"In that case, well then, accept the travel expenses provided by you; I have no need for this.
However, as you go to Bārāṇasī, you should take me along. Having agreed, saying "Very well," they—
Taking him with them at the time of departure, they went to Bārāṇasī; having pointed out to him, "This is the dwelling place of Guttila," they each returned to their own residences.
Mūsila, having entered the Bodhisatta’s house, saw the Bodhisatta’s birth-lute hanging there.
Having taken it up, he played it. Then, because the Bodhisatta’s parents were blind and could not see him, they thought, "I suppose a mouse is eating the lute," and cried out, "Susu!
At that time, Mūsila set down the lute, paid homage to the Bodhisatta’s parents, and when asked, "Where have you come from? he replied, "In the presence of my teacher, I [studied] the craft..."
"I have come from Ujjeni to learn," he said. When [the teacher] replied, "Very well," he asked, "Where is the teacher?
Hearing, "My son, he is away; he will return today," he sat down right there.
Seeing the Bodhisatta arrive, he exchanged greetings with him and explained the reason for his own arrival. The Bodhisatta was a student of the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*).
Having recognized his unworthy character, he rejected him, saying, "Go, dear son;
you have no craft. He [the youth] grasped the feet of the Bodhisatta’s parents and, seeking to do them a favor and win their favor, entreated them, saying, "Teach me a craft.
Being urged again and again by his parents, the Bodhisatta, unable to refuse them, [taught] the craft.
He gave [it]. He went to the royal palace together with the Bodhisatta. When the king saw him, he asked, "Who is this, teacher?
"He is my pupil, Great King," he replied. Gradually, he became a trusted confidant of the king.
Without keeping anything back as a teacher's secret, the Bodhisatta taught him the entire craft according to his own method of understanding.
“Your craft is finished, my dear,” he said.
He thought: “My craft is mastered; and this city of Bārāṇasī is the foremost city in all Jambudīpa;
moreover, the teacher is advanced in years; it is fitting for me to live right here. He then said to the teacher: “Teacher, I—”
“I will attend upon the king. The teacher said, “Very well, dear one;
I shall inform the king,” and having gone there, he announced to the king, “Your Majesty, our pupil wishes to attend upon you;
please determine what gift he may receive. When the king replied, “He shall receive half of whatever gift is given to you,” the teacher reported that news to Mūsila.
Mūsila said, “I will attend upon you only when I receive the same [share] as you;
I will not do so when I do not. “For what reason? “Do I not know every craft that you know? “Yes, you do.
“That being the case, why do you give me only half? The Bodhisatta reported this to the king. The king said, “If it is so, then [you shall have] the same as you.”
"If you are able to demonstrate your craft, you shall receive an equal share," he said.

The Bodhisatta reported the king's words to him, and when he replied, "Very well, I shall demonstrate it," the Bodhisatta informed the king of that development. When the king said, "Very well, let him demonstrate;
on which day shall the discussion take place? he replied, "Let it be on the seventh day from now, Great King."
The king summoned Mūsila and asked, "Is it true that you will engage in a discussion with the teacher?
When he replied, "It is true, Your Majesty," the king said, "A dispute with the teacher is not appropriate; do not do it.
Although thus forbidden, Mūsila said, "Enough, Great King; let there indeed be a discussion between me and the teacher on the seventh day."
"Whose mastery shall we recognize? he asked. The king, accepting this with "Very well," had a drum beaten, proclaiming:
"On the seventh day from now, it is said, the teacher Guttila and his pupil Mūsila will display their craft after holding a discussion at the palace gate;
let the citizens assemble and witness the performance."
The Bodhisatta thought: "This Mūsila is young and vigorous, while I am old and my strength has declined;
it is said that an action undertaken by one who is old does not succeed. Even when a pupil is defeated, there is no distinction [in the teacher's status];
but if the pupil is victorious, death in the forest is better than having to undergo the shame one must incur. Thus he went to the forest.
Having entered, he would turn back out of fear of death, yet proceed out of fear of shame.
As he was thus making his journey back and forth, six days passed; the grass withered away, and a path for his legs was formed.
At that moment, Sakka’s palace manifested a sign of heat. Sakka, reflecting upon it, understood the reason and said: "The Gandhabba Guttila..."
“Out of fear for his pupil, he is undergoing great suffering in the forest; it is right that I should become his refuge.
Having gone there with haste, he stood before the Bodhisatta and asked, “Teacher, why have you entered the forest?
When asked, “Who are you? he replied, “I am Sakka. Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “As for me...”
"O King of Devas, out of fear of defeat by his pupil, he has entered the forest," she said, and recited the first verse:
"He recited the *Sattatanti*, so very sweet and delightful;
he calls me to the arena. Kosiya is my refuge."

The meaning of this is: "O King of Devas, I have taught my pupil named Mūsila, according to my own method of knowledge, the seventy-stringed lute that is exceedingly sweet and delightful; he now summons me to the arena.
Therefore, O Kosiya, may you be my refuge."
Having heard his words, Sakka said, “Do not fear; I shall be your protection and your refuge,” and spoke this second verse:
“O friend, I am your refuge; I am the one who honors the teacher.
The pupil shall not defeat you, O teacher; the teacher shall defeat the pupil.”
"In that regard, 'I shall protect you as your refuge' means: having become your refuge, support, and foundation, I shall protect you.
'Samma' is a term of endearment. 'O teacher, you will conquer the pupil' means: O teacher, while playing the lute, you will defeat the pupil.
Furthermore, while playing the lute, you should break one string and play with six; thus your lute—"
The word *pakati* will mean "natural. Mūsila too will break a string, and then there will be no sound from his lute.

At that moment, he will suffer defeat. Then, knowing his state of defeat, you should break a string for a second time, a third, a fourth, a fifth, and even a seventh time, and play only on the plain staff [the remaining strings], from the ends of which the strings have been broken.
“Having emerged from the lake, it will cover the entire city of Bārāṇasī, twelve yojanas in extent.
Having said this, Sakka gave three dice-cups to the Bodhisattva and spoke thus:
“But when the entire city is covered by the sound of the lute alone, you should throw one of these dice-cups into the air; then, before you—”
Having descended, three hundred celestial nymphs will dance. At the time of their dancing, you should throw the second [lot];
then another three hundred will descend and dance upon the neck of your lute. Then you should throw the third;
then another three hundred will descend and dance upon the stage. I too shall come into your presence.
"Go, do not be afraid," he reassured the Bodhisatta. At the time of forenoon, the Bodhisatta went home.
The citizens, having erected a pavilion near the palace gate, prepared a seat for the king.
The king descended from his palace and sat upon the couch in the center of the decorated pavilion, while twelve thousand adorned women, ministers, brahmins, householders, and others [attended him].
They surrounded the king, and all the citizens assembled; they erected tier upon tier of platforms and seat upon seat in the royal courtyard.
The Bodhisatta, having bathed and anointed himself and partaken of various choice foods, had his lute brought and sat down on the seat prepared for him.
Sakka, arriving in an invisible body, stood in the air; only the Bodhisatta could see him.
Mūsila also came and sat down on his own seat. The great multitude surrounded them, and from the very beginning, both played in perfect unison.
The great multitude, delighted by the playing of both, raised thousands of shouts of acclamation.
Sakka, standing in the sky, called out to the Bodhisatta alone, saying, "Cut one string! The Bodhisatta [cut] the string.
He cut it; although it was cut, it continued to emit sound from the severed end, vibrating like the music of gods and gandhabbas.
Musila also cut the string, but no sound emerged. The teacher cut it a second time... [and so on] ...until he cut it for the seventh time.
As he played the plain bamboo flute, the sound stood filling the entire city. Thousands of hand-claps and...
And thousands of shouts of acclamation arose. The Bodhisatta threw one die into the air; three hundred celestial nymphs descended and danced.
When he threw it a second and a third time, three hundred nymphs likewise descended each time and danced in the same manner described.
At that moment, the king gave a signal with his eyes to the great multitude;
the multitude rose up and rebuked Mūsila, saying, "Having come into conflict with the Teacher, you strive to act impartially, yet you do not know your own measure!
Having thus threatened him, they crushed him with whatever stones, staffs, and other objects they could lay hands on, bringing him to the end of his life, and [trampled] his feet...
Having taken it, he threw it away in a rubbish heap. The king, with a joyful heart, gave much wealth to the Bodhisatta as if raining down a thick shower;
the citizens did likewise. Sakka, having exchanged greetings with the Bodhisatta, said:
"O wise one, I shall have a chariot yoked with a thousand thoroughbred horses brought for you, and afterwards I will send Mātali."
Having said, "You should mount the excellent Vejayanta chariot yoked with a thousand [horses] and come to the world of the gods," he departed.
Then, having gone there, the daughters of the gods asked him as he sat upon the Paṇḍukambala stone, "Where have you been, Great King?
Sakka explained the matter to them in detail, recounting the Bodhisatta’s virtue and his qualities.
He praised him. The daughters of the gods said, “Great King, we too wish to see the teacher; bring him here.
Sakka addressed Mātali, saying, “Dear one, the celestial nymphs wish to see the Gandhabba Guttila;
go, have him seated in the Vejayanta chariot, and bring him back. Saying, “Very well,” he went and brought the Bodhisatta. Sakka—
Having exchanged greetings with the Bodhisatta, he said, “Teacher, it is said that these celestial maidens desire to hear a musical performance from you.
He replied, “Great King, we who are called Gandhabbas live by means of our craft; if we receive a fee, we shall perform.
“Perform then,” he said, “and I will give you the fee. “I have no need for any other fee; however, these daughters of the gods—”
“Let each of you speak of your own wholesome deeds; thus I shall cause you to teach.
Then the goddesses said to him, “We shall tell you of the wholesome deeds we have performed later; perform the music, Master.
For seven days the Bodhisatta performed music for the deities, and having surpassed that divine music—
[The narrative of] the occurrence. On the seventh day, starting from the beginning, he inquired about the meritorious deeds of the celestial maidens.

He asked a certain supreme cloth-giving goddess—born as a retainer of Sakka during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, surrounded by a thousand nymphs—“What deed did you perform in a previous existence to be reborn here? To her...
The manner of questioning and the answering are already found in the *Vimānavatthu*. For it is said there:
“O goddess, you who stand there with such exquisite beauty, illuminating all directions like a medicinal herb among the stars.”
“By what means is your complexion so radiant? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those riches arise for you that are dear to the mind?
I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: when you were a human being, what merit did you perform?”
“By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?
“The woman who gives the most excellent cloth becomes preeminent among men and women;
by giving such a pleasing and beautiful form, she attains a divine state upon reaching that place.”
“Behold my celestial mansion! I am a nymph of lovely form;
I am the most excellent among a thousand nymphs—behold the ripening of my merits.
It is because of this that I have such beauty, and it is because of this that I prosper here.”
“Riches arise for me, whatever is pleasing to the mind.
Therefore, my majesty blazes forth in this way,
and my complexion shines in all directions.”
Another gave flowers for the purpose of honoring a monk wandering for alms;
another gave scents, saying, "Give a five-finger-mark of perfume at the shrine"; another gave sweet fruits and various fruits; another gave sugarcane juice;
another gave a five-finger-mark of perfume at the shrine of the Dasa-balas Kassapa; and another [gave] to those traveling on the road.
One woman heard the Dhamma from the presence of monks and nuns who had come to stay at her family home;
another, standing in the water, gave water to a monk who had finished his meal on a boat that had arrived at the landing time;
another, living in the midst of a household, remained free from anger and performed her duties toward her mother-in-law and father-in-law; and yet another, even from her own allotted portion...
She enjoyed her food only after sharing it, and she was virtuous. Another woman, having been a slave in another's house, was free from anger and pride;
she shared whatever portion she received and was reborn as an attendant to the King of the Gods.
Thus, all thirty-six goddesses mentioned in the *Guttila-vimāna* were reborn there by performing such deeds.
Having been reborn there, the Bodhisatta questioned them all. They, in turn, recounted their own past deeds to him in verse.

Having heard this, the Bodhisatta thought: "It is indeed a gain for me, it is a great blessing for me, that having come here, I have heard of the divine attainments acquired through even minor kamma. From now on, [I shall go] to the world of humans..."
"Having gone, I shall perform only wholesome deeds such as giving," he said, and uttered this inspired utterance:
"Welcome indeed to me today! A truly auspicious dawn, well-awakened;
for I behold the deities, possessing the lovely forms of celestial nymphs."
“Having heard this Dhamma, I shall perform much that is wholesome:
through generosity, through even conduct, through self-restraint, and through self-mastery.
Thus I shall go to that place where, having gone, one does not grieve.”
Then, after seven days had passed, the King of the Devas commanded his charioteer Mātali to place him in the chariot and sent him back to Bārāṇasī.
Having arrived at Bārāṇasī, he explained to the people the reasons for what he had seen in the world of the devas.
From that time forth, people began to think with renewed enthusiasm about performing meritorious deeds.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time Mūsila was Devadatta, Sakka was Anuruddha, the king was Ānanda, and the musician Guttila was none other than myself.
This concludes the third narrative, the *Guttila-jātaka*.
[244] 4. The *Vigaticcha-jātaka* (The Story of One Free from Desire)
"He who sees something does not desire it"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain wandering ascetic who was fleeing.
It is said that, having failed to find an opponent anywhere in all of Jambudīpa, he came to Sāvatthī and asked, "Who is capable of engaging in debate with me?
Upon hearing that it was the Perfectly Enlightened One, he arrived surrounded by a great multitude.
Having gone to Jeta’s Grove, he asked a question of the Blessed One while he was teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly.
Then the Teacher, having answered him, asked the question, "What is 'one'?
Being unable to explain it, he rose up and fled. The assembled company said, "Venerable sir, that wanderer has been refuted by you with a single word."
The Teacher said, "Lay followers, it was not only now that I rebuked him with a single word; I have rebuked him even in the past," and having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Upon reaching maturity, he abandoned sensual pleasures, went forth as an ascetic, and lived for a long time in the Himālaya mountains. From those mountains...
Having descended, he took up residence in a leaf-hut at the bend of the Gaṅgā, near a certain market town.
Then a certain wanderer, having failed to find any opponent throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, arrived at that town and asked, "Is there anyone capable of engaging in debate with me?
To which [the people] replied, "There is," [describing] the power of the Bodhisatta.
Having heard this, surrounded by a great multitude of people, he went to the Bodhisatta’s dwelling place, exchanged greetings, and sat down.

Then the Bodhisatta asked him, “Will you drink the water of the Ganges, which is permeated with color and fragrance? The wanderer, attempting to evade the question with his own arguments, replied, “What is the Ganges?
Is the sand the Ganges? Is the water the Ganges? Is the near shore the Ganges? Is the far shore the Ganges?”

“[Where is] the Ganges? he asked. The Bodhisatta replied, “But you, wanderer, setting aside the water, the sand, the hither bank, and the further bank—where will you find the Ganges? The wanderer, rendered speechless, rose up and fled.
When he had fled, the Bodhisatta, teaching the Dhamma to the assembly seated there, spoke these verses:
“What one sees, one does not desire; what one does not see, one desires.
I think he will wander for a long time, for he shall not obtain that which he desires.
What he obtains, he is not satisfied with; and what he longs for, he despises when it is obtained.”
"Indeed, desire has an infinite range; we pay homage to those who are free from desire.
In this context, "whatever he sees" means that whatever water or other things he sees, he does not desire them to be the Ganges.

"And whatever he does not see" means that he does not see a Ganges apart from the water and so forth, yet he still desires it. "I think he will wander for a long time"—this refers to his continued wandering.
I think thus: "This wanderer, searching for such a Ganges as this, will wander for a long time.

Or, just as one might search for a Ganges apart from water and so forth, so too he who searches for a self apart from form and so forth will wander for a long time in saṃsāra. For even though he wanders for a long time, he shall not find that such a Ganges."
Or he desires for himself that which he does not obtain. "Whatever he obtains" means whatever water or forms and so forth he obtains, with that he is not satisfied.

And "whatever he longs for, having obtained it, he despises" means that being dissatisfied with what he has obtained, whatever success he longs for, having obtained each of those, he despises and disregards it, thinking, "What is the use of this? For desire has an infinite range.
Because one despises what has been obtained and desires another object, this desire is called craving (*taṇhā*), whose range is endless.
"We pay homage to those who have overcome desire": thus, we pay homage to those such as the Buddha who have overcome desire.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the wanderer was the wanderer of the present day, while the ascetic was none other than myself."
The fourth: The Commentary on the *Vigaticcha-jātaka*.
[245] 5. The Commentary on the *Mūlapariyāya-jātaka*:
"Time devours beings"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Subhagavana near Ukkaṭṭha, concerning the *Mūlapariyāya-sutta*.
He spoke with reference to this. At that time, it is said, five hundred brahmins who had mastered the three Vedas entered the religious life within the Teaching;
having learned the Three Piṭakas, they became intoxicated with pride and conceit, thinking, "Even the Perfectly Enlightened One knows only the Three Piṭakas, and we too know them.
Such being the case, what difference is there between him and us? and thus they did not attend upon the Buddha.
They go about acting as adversaries.
Then one day, while they were sitting near him after having approached him, the Teacher, having adorned his discourse with the eight stages, preached the Mūlapariyāya Sutta;
yet they did not perceive anything therein. Then this thought occurred to them: "We..."
"We once harbored the conceit that there were no wise men equal to us; but now we know nothing at all.
Truly, there is no wise man equal to the Buddhas—oh, how great are the qualities of the Buddhas!

From that time forth, having humbled their pride, they became like snakes with their fangs extracted, devoid of all venomous intent. The Teacher, having dwelt at Ukkaṭṭhā for as long as he pleased, departed.
Having gone to Vesālī, he preached the discourse known as the Gotamaka Sutta at the Gotamaka Shrine;
the ten-thousandfold world-system quaked, and upon hearing it, those bhikkhus attained arahantship.
However, at the conclusion of the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, while the Teacher was staying at Ukkaṭṭhā, the bhikkhus initiated this discussion in the Dhamma Hall:
“Friends, oh, the power of the Buddhas! Those brahmin renunciants, so intoxicated by pride and arrogance, have been humbled by the Blessed One through the teaching of the *Mūlapariyāya*.
When the Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now? and they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now.”
"Even in the past, when they were wandering about with their heads held high by pride, I indeed humbled them," he said, and related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family;
having reached maturity, he became a world-renowned teacher who had mastered the three Vedas and was instructing five hundred young students.

He taught them the mantras. When those five hundred had completed their training and applied themselves to the craft, they became arrogant and conceited, thinking, "Whatever we know, the teacher knows exactly that much;
there is no distinction. Consequently, they did not go to the teacher's presence nor did they perform their duties of service.
One day, while the teacher was sitting at the foot of a jujube tree, [they failed to attend upon him].
Desiring to mock him, they struck a jujube tree with their fingernails and said, "This tree is without pith.
The Bodhisatta, realizing he was being mocked, said to his pupils, "I shall ask you a question. They were delighted and joyful, saying, "Ask it;
we shall answer. As the teacher asked the question, he spoke the first verse:
“Time devours all beings, including itself;
and he who has become a devourer of time devours the cooker of beings.
In this context, “time” refers to such periods as the time before the meal and the time after the meal. “Beings” is a designation for sentient creatures.
Time does not devour living beings by plucking away their skin, flesh, and so forth;
rather, it is said that it "devours" and "eats" them by exhausting their lifespan, beauty, and strength, crushing their youth, and destroying their health.
And while devouring in this way, it spares nothing—it devours everything. It is not only living beings that it consumes, but also the world together with its inhabitants.
It devours even itself; it does not reach the time after the meal from the time before the meal. This same principle applies to the time after the meal and so forth.
And as for the phrase "he has become one who devours time," this is a designation for one whose taints are destroyed.

For he is called "one who has become a devourer of time" because, by means of the Noble Path, he has consumed and exhausted the time of future rebirth and stands [therein]. He cooks that which cooks beings.

“This craving which cooks beings in the states of misery—that he has cooked and burnt with the fire of knowledge, reducing it to ashes; therefore, he is called ‘the Cooker of Beings’ (*bhūtapacaniṃ paci*).
There is also a reading, “*pajaniṃ*,” meaning “the progenitor” or “the producer.
Upon hearing this question, not a single one among the young brahmins was able to understand it. Then the Bodhisatta—
"Do not form the perception that 'this question exists within the three Vedas.
Thinking, 'I know everything that I know,' you treat me as if I were a jujube tree;
you do not realize that there is much more that I know which is unknown to you. Go; I shall give the answer on the seventh day. By this much time—"
“Reflect upon this question. Having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, they each returned to their own dwellings;
yet even after reflecting for seven days, they could see neither the end nor the limit of the question.
On the seventh day, they went into the presence of the teacher, paid homage, and sat down. When he asked, “My dear friends, have you understood the question? they replied, “No.”
"We know," they said. Then the Bodhisatta, reproaching them, spoke this second verse:
"Many are the heads of men, hairy and large, Hung around their necks; yet here, perhaps, is one who has ears."
The meaning of this is as follows: Many heads of men are seen;
all of them are hairy, and all are fixed upon necks that are large, not held in the hand like a palm fruit. There is no difference between them in these respects.
However, in this context, someone says "I am one with ears" (*kaṇṇavā*) referring to himself. "One with ears" means one who possesses wisdom (*paññavā*).
"But there is no one who lacks ear-holes. Having thus reproached those young men, saying, "O fools, you possess nothing but ear-holes;
you have no wisdom," he answered the question. Upon hearing this, they thought, "Oh, how great indeed are these teachers!
They asked for forgiveness, cast aside their pride, and waited upon the Bodhisatta.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the five hundred young brahmins were these very monks, and the teacher was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Jātaka, the fifth.
6. Commentary on the Bālavāda Jātaka.
"Having slain, having cut, and having struck"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Gabled Hall near Vesālī, concerning the General Sīha.
For after he had gone for refuge to the Blessed One and invited him, he provided a meal of equal portions of meat on the following day.
When the Nigaṇṭhas heard this, they became angry and displeased, desiring to harass the Tathāgata.
“The ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared specifically for him,” they reviled. The monks raised this discussion in the Hall of Dharma:

“Friends, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta wanders about with his assembly, reviling [the Buddha], saying, ‘The ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared specifically for him. Having heard this, the Teacher said, “No, friends...”
“Monks, it is not only now that the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta censures me for eating meat prepared specifically for me;
he has censured me even in the past,” he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
Having reached maturity and gone forth into the ascetic life, he went from the Himalayas to Bārāṇasī for the purpose of subsisting on salt and sour gruel.

On the following day, he entered the city for alms. Then a certain householder, thinking, "I shall harass this ascetic," invited him into his home, had him sit on a prepared seat, served him with fish and meat, and at the conclusion of the meal, [stood] to one side.
Having sat down, he said, "This meat was prepared by killing living beings specifically for you; let this unwholesome karma not fall upon us alone, but be yours as well.
Having spoken thus, he recited the first verse:
"Having killed, having cut, and having slaughtered, the unrestrained man gives a gift;..."
“Eating such food, he is defiled by evil.
In this context, “having struck” means having hit; “having cut” means having tormented; “having killed” means having caused death.

“The unrestrained one gives a gift” means that one who is unrestrained and immoral gives a gift after having acted in such a manner. “Eating such food, he is defiled by evil” means: *Edisaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjamāno, sa pāpena upalippati.* [He who eats such food is smeared with evil.]
“Even that ascetic who eats food prepared specifically for him is defiled by evil and becomes bound by it.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
“Even if one gives a gift after having killed his own children and wife, if he is unrestrained;”
“Even while eating, the wise man is not defiled by evil.

In this regard, “even while eating, the wise man”: let alone other meat, even if he eats what has been given by an immoral person after that person has killed his own children and wife, the wise man—endowed with qualities such as patience and loving-kindness—is not defiled by evil.
Having thus spoken the Dhamma to him, the Bodhisatta rose from his seat and departed.
Having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time the householder was Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, but the ascetic was none other than myself.
This is the sixth commentary, the Bālavāda Jātaka.
[247] 7. The Commentary on the Pādañjali Jātaka.
"Surely all with palms joined..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyī.
For one day, the two Chief Disciples were deciding upon a question; the monks, listening to the question, [honored] the Elders...
They praised them. But the Elder Lāḷudāyī, sitting within the assembly, snapped his lips, thinking, "What do these fellows know that is equal to what we know?
Seeing this, the elders rose and departed, and the assembly was split.
In the Hall of Truth, the monks initiated a discussion: "Friends, Lāḷudāyī has snapped his lips in disparagement of the two Chief Disciples."
Having heard this, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, Lāḷudāyin knew nothing beyond the breaking of an elephant's tusks.
Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his advisor in matters of welfare and righteousness.
He became a minister. The king had a son named Pādañjali, who was drooling and slow in his movements.
Later, the king passed away. After the ministers had performed the funeral rites for the king, they deliberated, saying, "We shall consecrate him in the kingdom," and spoke to Prince Pādañjali.
However, the Bodhisatta [the future Buddha] thought, "This prince is drooling and slow in his movements..."
“Having taken possession of it, we shall consecrate him,” he said. The ministers prepared the court of justice and, having seated the prince nearby, they proceeded to decide a lawsuit;
however, they did not judge it correctly. Having made one who had no owner the owner, they asked the prince, “Prince, how do you think we have judged the case well? He bit his lip.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I suppose this prince is wise; he must have recognized the state of being unjustly judged," spoke the first verse:
"Surely all those with palms joined in reverence surpass him in wisdom."
“For he bites his lip; surely he sees something further.
The meaning of this is: “In every way, Prince Pādañjali surpasses us all in wisdom. For he bites his lip; surely he perceives some other, further reason.
On the following day as well, they prepared a legal case and, having thoroughly adjudicated another lawsuit, [asked]: “Of what kind is it?”
"Your Majesty, he has judged it well," they asked. He, however, broke his lip once again.
Then, knowing his state of blind folly, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
"He does not distinguish between Dhamma and non-Dhamma, nor does he understand what is beneficial and what is harmful."
"Except for the opening of his lips, he knows nothing at all.
When the ministers realized that Pādañjali was merely a child, they consecrated the Bodhisatta in the kingdom.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Pādañjali was Lāḷudāyī, and the wise minister was none other than myself."
The Seventh: The Commentary on the Pādañjali Jātaka.
[248] 8. The Commentary on the Kiṃsuka-upama Jātaka:
"The Kiṃsuka tree was seen by all"—this was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Kiṃsuka-upama Sutta.
He spoke. For four bhikkhus had approached the Tathāgata and requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*);
the Teacher taught them a meditation subject. Having taken that meditation subject, they went to their respective night-quarters and day-quarters.
Among them, one attained Arahantship by comprehending the six bases of contact (*phassāyatana*), and another [attained it] by [comprehending] the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*).
One [had attained] the four great elements; another, the eighteen elements. They each reported to the Teacher the specific distinction they had realized.
Then, a reflection arose in one bhikkhu: "The meditation subjects of these men are diverse, yet Nibbāna is one;
how is it that all have attained Arahantship? He asked the Teacher. The Teacher said, "What do you think, bhikkhu?"

"What difference is there between us and those who have seen the *kiṃsuka* tree? Having said this, when the monks requested, "Venerable sir, please tell us the reason for this," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, he had four sons. One day, they...
Having summoned the charioteer, they said, "Friend, we wish to see the *kiṃsuka* tree; show us the *kiṃsuka* tree.
The charioteer replied, "Very well, I shall show it," but instead of showing all four of them at once, he first had the eldest prince sit in the chariot.
Leading him into the forest, he showed him the *kiṃsuka* when it was merely a stump, saying, "This is the *kiṃsuka*."
At one time it was the season for thick foliage, at another for flowering, and at another for fruiting.
Later on, the four brothers sat together and initiated a discussion: "What is this thing called a *kiṃsuka* like?
Then one said, "It is just like a charred pillar. The second said, "It is just like a banyan tree (*nigrodha*). The third said, "It is just like..."
The fourth said, "It is just like a *sirīsa* tree. Unsatisfied with one another's descriptions, they went into the presence of their father and asked, "Your Majesty, what is a *kiṃsuka* tree like?

When he replied, "What did you yourselves say?", they each related the manner in which they had described it to the king. The king said, "All four of you have seen the *kiṃsuka* tree; [yet you describe it differently]."
"O charioteer, it was simply because you did not ask me to distinguish, 'At this time, what is the *kiṃsuka* tree like? At that time, what is it like?
while showing us the *kiṃsuka*, that doubt arose in you. Having said this, he spoke the first verse:
"All have seen the *kiṃsuka*; why then do you have doubt about this?"
"For the charioteer has not been questioned in all instances.
Regarding this, "For the charioteer has not been questioned in all instances" means: "Have you all seen the *kiṃsuka* tree?
Why then do you have doubt about this? In all instances it is a *kiṃsuka*, yet by you [it was not so seen] in all instances."
“O charioteer, you were questioned regarding these points; therefore, doubt has arisen in you.

Having shown this reason, the Teacher said, “Bhikkhu, just as those four brothers gave rise to doubt concerning the *kiṃsuka* tree because they had asked for a division [of it], so too have you given rise to doubt regarding this Dhamma. Having spoken thus, he became perfectly enlightened (*abhisambuddho*).
Having offered the second verse, he said:
“Thus, those by whom all phenomena have not been known through all forms of knowledge,
they indeed harbor doubts regarding those phenomena, like the brothers regarding the *kiṃsuka* tree.”
The meaning of this is as follows: Just as your brothers were in doubt because they had not seen the *kiṃsuka* tree in all those places,

so too, for those by whom all phenomena— comprising the six bases of contact, the aggregates, the primary elements, and the derivative elements— have not been known through all the knowledges of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*),
and have not been penetrated because the path of stream-entry has not been attained, they indeed [remain in doubt] regarding those phenomena such as the bases of contact and so forth.
“They are in doubt, as were the four brothers over a single *kiṃsuka* tree.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī.
This concludes the eighth commentary, the *Kiṃsukopama-jātaka*.
[249] 9. The Commentary on the Sālakajaṭaka.
"You shall have but one son"—this the Teacher spoke while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain great elder.
It seems that this elder, having ordained a young boy, lived there while oppressing him. The novice monk was oppressed...
Unable to endure it, he went forth into homelessness. The Elder went to him and consoled him, saying, "Young man, your robe shall remain yours, and your bowl too;
even the bowl and robe belonging to me shall become yours. Come, go forth!
Although he replied, "I will not go forth," he was told this again and again until he finally did go forth. Then, from the day he had gone forth...
From that time on, the elder harassed him again. Unable to endure the oppression, he left the order once more;
yet even though he entreated him many times, the elder said, "You cannot endure me, nor can you live without me; go, I will not let you be ordained," and thus did not ordain him.
The monks raised this discussion in the Hall of Truth: "Friends, how compassionate that man must be!"
“Having understood the dwelling-place of the Great Elder, the boy did not go forth.

The Teacher, having arrived, asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that this man is kind-hearted;
in the past he was also kind-hearted. Having seen his fault once, he did not approach him again. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of householders;

having reached maturity, he made his living by selling grain. There was also a certain snake-charmer who, having trained a monkey and had it take medicinal herbs, made his living by performing with the snake. When a festival was proclaimed in Benares, he [went there].
Desiring to enjoy the festival, he placed the monkey in the hands of that grain merchant, saying, "Do not let him escape," and went to enjoy the festival.
On the seventh day, having returned to his presence, he asked, "Where is the monkey?
Hearing his master's voice, the monkey quickly emerged from the grain shop. Then, with a bamboo scraper—
Having struck him on the back and taken him away, he went to the garden, bound him in a secluded spot, and fell asleep.

The monkey, perceiving that he was asleep, freed himself from his bonds, fled, climbed an *āmra* tree, ate some mango fruit, and dropped the stone onto the snake-charmer’s body. When the man woke up and looked upward, he saw—
Seeing him, [the hunter] thought, "I will deceive him with sweet words, bring him down from the tree, and seize him," and while coaxing him,
he spoke the first verse: "You shall have an only son, and you shall be the master in our family."
“Descend from the tree, Sālaka; come now, let us go to our home. The meaning of this is:
“You shall be my only son, and you will be the master of wealth in my family. Descend from this tree; come, we shall go to our home. He spoke thus, addressing him by the name Sālaka.
Having heard that, the monkey spoke the second verse:
“Do you not consider me to be kind-hearted, even though you strike me with a bamboo staff?
We take delight in the Pakkamba forest; go to your own home as you please.
Therein, “do you not consider me to be kind-hearted? means: do you not indeed consider me to be “kind-hearted”? “Kind-hearted” [means...]
The meaning is: "You think thus. And as for [the words] "and you strike me with a bamboo staff," he indicates:
"Because you despise me in this way, and because you strike me with a bamboo scraper, I do not come.
Then, having said to him, "We take our delight in this mango grove; you may go to your own home as you please," he sprang up and entered the forest. The snake-charmer also—
Displeased, he went to his own home.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, the monkey was the novice, the snake-charmer was the Elder Mahāthera, and the grain merchant was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Sālakajātakaya, the ninth.
[250] 10. The Commentary on the Monkey Jātaka (*Kapi-jātaka-vaṇṇanā*).
"This seer delights in tranquility and self-restraint"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain hypocritical monk.
For that monk’s hypocrisy had become well known among the monks. The monks, in the Hall of Dharma...
How did they originate [the report]? "Friend, such-and-such a monk, having gone forth in the Buddha’s liberating teaching, fulfills the practice of a hypocrite.
When the Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, with what conversation are you sitting here gathered now?
and they replied, "With this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that this monk is a hypocrite; in the past, too, he was a hypocrite."
"Because of a mere spark of fire, having become a monkey, he practiced deceit," he said, and then related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi.
When he had grown up and his son was running about and playing, the brahmin wife died; [the Bodhisatta] then took the son..."
Taking him on his hip, he entered the Himālaya mountains and, having gone forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isipabbajjā*), he made that son a young ascetic and took up residence in a leaf-hut.
During the rainy season, while the rain fell in unbroken torrents, a certain monkey, afflicted by the cold, wandered about gnashing its teeth and trembling. The Bodhisatta [saw] great logs of wood...
Having brought fire and prepared it, he lay down upon a couch; his son sat beside him, massaging his feet.

That monkey, having put on the bark garments belonging to a deceased ascetic and draped them over himself, slung a deerskin over his shoulder, and taking a goatskin water-pot, approached in the guise of an ascetic and performed a deceptive act for the sake of the fire at the entrance of the leaf-hut.
Having done so, he stood there. Seeing him, the young ascetic said to his father, addressing him with the first stanza as a request:
“This seer, who delights in tranquility and self-restraint, stands here trembling, afflicted by the fear of the cold; please call him here, and he will warm himself.”
"Come now, enter this little hut to dispel the cold and all distress.
In this context, "delighting in tranquility and self-restraint" means delighting in the pacification of defilements such as lust and in the self-restraint of virtue.
"He stands" means he remains there. "Out of fear of the cold" means out of fear of the chill produced by wind and rain. "Afflicted" means oppressed.
"Let him enter," he said, "let him enter this place. "Entirely" means whole and without remainder.
Having heard his son’s words, the Bodhisatta rose and looked; perceiving that it was a monkey, he spoke the second verse:
"This is no sage who delights in tranquility and self-restraint; this is a monkey whose domain is the branches of the excellent tree."
"Thus he is a defiler and a vexer, and base, if he should defile even a flower.
In this context, "having the branches of excellent trees as his range" means having the branches of excellent trees as his domain. "He is a defiler and a vexer, and base" means:
he is a *dūsaka* (defiler) because he defiles every place he goes to; he is a *rosaka* (vexer) because of his abrasive nature; and he is *jammo* (base) because of his lowly character.
"If he enters," [the Bodhisatta thought], "if he should enter this leaf-hut, he will defile it all with his excrement and urine and by setting fire to it.
Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta took a torch, terrified him, and drove him away. He, having leapt up—
Having entered the forest, he remained there as one who had truly entered; he did not return to that place again.

The Bodhisatta, having realized the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), instructed the young ascetic in the preliminary practice of the meditation objects (*kasiṇaparikamma*). He too produced the higher knowledges and the meditative attainments.
Both of them, without falling away from their jhānas, became destined for the Brahma-world.
The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now; from ancient times this one has been a hypocrite.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, he identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some attained Arhatship. “At that time, the monkey was the hypocritical monk.”
“Rāhula was my son, and I myself was his father.
This concludes the commentary on the Kapi Jātaka, the tenth.
The tenth chapter, the Siṅgāla Vagga, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Sabbadāṭhī and the dog, Guttila and Vigaticchā;
the Mūlapariyāya and the instruction to the fool, Pādañjali and the simile of what is like a well.
The monkey gave ten *sālaka* fruits.
Now, the summary verse of the sections (*vagguddāna*):
The Section on Firmness (*Daḷhavagga*), Intimacy (*Santhava*), and those like Kalyāṇadhamma.
Rūhaka, Daḷhavagga, Bīraṇathambha, Kāsāva, Upāhana,
and Siṅgāla— these ten chapters would each consist of two [sections].
The commentary on the Book of Twos (Dukanipāta) is concluded.

3. The Third Collection (Tikanipāta) 1. The Chapter on Intentions (Saṅkappavagga) [251] 1. The Exposition of the Saṅkapparāga Jātaka The intention of one who has not seen the Truths is like a ship upon the great ocean; it is carried away by the current of craving and does not reach the further shore. But for one who has seen the Truths, that very same intention becomes like a ship with a favorable wind, swiftly reaching the further shore. This was said by the Blessed One when he spoke of the difference between the intentions of those who have seen the Truths and those who have not. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was seated nearby. Having heard the Blessed One’s words, he recited them in verse: “Just as a ship upon the great ocean is carried away by the current of craving and does not reach the further shore, so too is the intention of one who has not seen the Truths. But for one who has seen the Truths, that very same intention becomes like a ship with a favorable wind, swiftly reaching the further shore. Having thus spoken, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat and approached the Blessed One. Having paid homage to him, he sat down at one side and reported to the Blessed One exactly what he had said. The Blessed One, having understood the meaning of this, spoke these verses: “The intention of one who has not seen the Truths is like a ship upon the great ocean; it is carried away by the current of craving and does not reach the further shore. But for one who has seen the Truths, that very same intention becomes like a ship with a favorable wind, swiftly reaching the further shore. Thus did the Blessed One speak. Having delighted the Venerable Sāriputta with these words, he rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta, reflecting on the Blessed One’s teaching, thought: “It would be good if I were to explain this matter in detail to the monks. Accordingly, he assembled the monks and, having gathered them together, delivered this discourse: “Friends, the intention of one who has not seen the Truths is like a ship upon the great ocean; it is carried away by the current of craving and does not reach the further shore. But for one who has seen the Truths, that very same intention becomes like a ship with a favorable wind, swiftly reaching the further shore. At that time, a certain monk approached the Venerable Sāriputta, paid homage to him, and sat down at one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed him with these verses: “Just as a ship upon the great ocean is carried away by the current of craving and does not reach the further shore, so too is the intention of one who has not seen the Truths. But for one who has seen the Truths, that very same intention becomes like a ship with a favorable wind, swiftly reaching the further shore. Then that monk, having heard the Venerable Sāriputta’s words, reflected: “It would be good if I were to explain this matter in detail to the Blessed One. Accordingly, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down at one side. Having sat down, he reported to the Blessed One exactly what the Venerable Sāriputta had said. The Blessed One, having understood the meaning of this, spoke these verses: “The intention of one who has not seen the Truths is like a ship upon the great ocean; it is carried away by the current of craving and does not reach the further shore. But for one who has seen the Truths, that very same intention becomes like a ship with a favorable wind, swiftly reaching the further shore. Thus did the Blessed One speak. Having delighted that monk with these words, he rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. At that time, the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of that monk, addressed the monks: “Monks, the intention of one who has not seen the Truths is like a ship upon the great ocean; it is carried away by the current of craving and does not reach the further shore.

But for one who has seen the Truths, that very same intention becomes like a ship with a favorable wind, swiftly reaching the further shore. This is the first sutta in the Saṅkappa-vagga of the Tika-nipāta. It is known as the Saṅkapparāga-jātaka. The detailed account of its past lives is as follows: In the past, in the city of Benares, there lived a king named Saṅkappa-rāga. He was a righteous ruler who governed his kingdom according to the Dhamma. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy family in that same city. When he grew up, he became a master of all branches of knowledge and was renowned for his wisdom. One day, King Saṅkappa-rāga, desiring to test the Bodhisatta’s wisdom, devised a riddle. He summoned the Bodhisatta and said: “O wise man, I have a riddle. If you can solve it, I shall grant you a boon. The Bodhisatta asked: “What is the riddle? The king replied: “I am like a ship upon the great ocean, carried away by the current of craving and unable to reach the further shore. Tell me, how may I cross over? The Bodhisatta answered: “O Great King, if you would listen, I shall tell you. You must abandon the five hindrances and cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment. By practicing the Noble Eightfold Path, you will cross over the flood of existence and reach the further shore. The king, having heard these words, was filled with joy. He accepted the Bodhisatta’s advice and set out to practice the Dhamma. Through his diligent effort, he eventually attained the fruit of stream-entry. Thus, through the power of the Bodhisatta’s teaching, the king crossed over the great ocean of saṃsāra. This is the story of the Saṅkapparāga Jātaka, illustrating how the intention of one who has seen the Truths leads to liberation, while that of one who has not remains bound by the currents of craving. [End of the Exposition of the Saṅkapparāga Jātaka]
"By washing away the passion of intention"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a dissatisfied bhikkhu.

It is said that a son of good family living in the city of Sāvatthī, having placed his heart in the Dispensation and gone forth, one day while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, saw a woman fully adorned and prepared.
Upon seeing her, lust arose within him, and he wandered about discontented.
When his teachers, preceptors, and others saw him, they asked him the cause of his dissatisfaction;

having understood his desire to leave the order, they said, "Friend, the Teacher—having removed the defilements of those oppressed by the taints such as sensual lust, and having revealed the Truths—bestows the fruits of stream-entry and the rest.
Come, let us take you into the presence of the Teacher. And so, they took him and went. By the Teacher...
And when [the Buddha] asked, "Monks, why have you come taking hold of a monk who clearly does not wish it?", they reported the matter to him.

The Teacher asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied? When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher asked, "For what reason? He reported the matter to him. Then the Teacher said to him, "Women..."
"Bhikkhu, these [defilements] have brought about defilement even for pure beings whose defilements were previously suppressed by the power of jhāna;
why then would they not defile such a hollow person?
Pure beings become defiled, and even those possessing supreme glory fall into disgrace, let alone those who are impure. [This is like] the wind that shakes Mount Sineru."
"Will this defilement not agitate even one who has sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree and attained full enlightenment, having shaken off the tangle of withered leaves?
Having said this, when requested by them, he related a story of the past:
'In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy brahmin family possessing eighty crores of wealth.'"
Having been reborn and reached maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkaśilā.
Returning to Bārāṇasī, he took a wife, and upon the passing of his parents, he performed their funeral rites.
While carrying out the business of examining his wealth, he reflected: "This wealth is visible, but those by whom it was accumulated are not seen."
He became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, and sweat broke out from his body.
Having lived long in the household life, he gave a great gift, abandoned sensual pleasures, and, casting off his tearful circle of kinsmen, entered the Himalayas.
There, having gone forth as an ascetic, he built a leaf-hut in a delightful place and sustained himself by the practice of gleaning, subsisting on forest roots, fruits, and the like.
Before long, having aroused the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and having lived for a long time sporting in the play of jhāna, he thought:
"I shall go to the realm of men and partake of salt and sour food;
thus my body will become firm, and the practice of walking meditation (*jaṅghavihāra*) will be accomplished. And those who give alms to a bhikkhu like me, endowed with virtue—"
"Or if they see me, or perform such acts as salutation and so forth, they shall fill the city of heaven.
Having descended from the Himālayas and wandering by stages on his journey, he reached Bārāṇasī;
at the time of sunset, looking for a place to stay, he saw the royal park and thought, "This is suitable for seclusion; I will dwell here."
Having entered the park, he sat at the foot of a certain tree and spent the night in the bliss of *jhāna*.
On the following day, after tending to his body, in the morning he adjusted his matted hair, antelope skin, and bark garments;
taking his alms-bowl, with senses calmed, mind tranquil, and endowed with perfect deportment, looking only a yoke’s length ahead, he proceeded with all aspects of his conduct perfected.
Drawing the eyes of the world toward him with the splendor of his own form, he entered the city and, while wandering for alms, arrived at the gate of the king’s palace.
As the king was walking upon the great terrace, he saw the Bodhisatta through a window;
becoming inspired with faith by the very posture of the Bodhisatta, he thought: "If there is such a thing as the True Dhamma, let it be within this man."
Thinking, "It must be so," he commanded a minister, "Go, bring that ascetic here.
The minister went, paid his respects, took the bowl for alms, and said, "Venerable sir, the king summons you.
The Bodhisatta said, "O one of great merit, the king does not know us. [The minister replied,] "In that case, venerable sir, until I return..."
"Come right here! Having gone there, he informed the king. The king said, "We have no ascetic who is our family preceptor;
go, bring him here. He himself, stretching out his hand through the window while paying homage, said, "Come this way, venerable sir.
The Bodhisatta placed the alms-bowl in the minister's hand and ascended to the great terrace.
Then the king, having paid homage to him and seated him upon the royal couch, served him with the rice-gruel, snacks, and meals prepared for himself.

When the Elder had finished his meal, the king asked him a question. Being even more deeply satisfied by the Elder’s answer to the question, he paid homage to him and asked, "Venerable sir, where do you dwell? From where have you come? "We are dwellers of the Himalayas," he replied.
When he said, "Great King, we have come from the Himalayas," and was asked again, "For what reason?
and replied, "Great King, during the rainy season, it is necessary to obtain a fixed residence," [the king said], "In that case, venerable sir, stay in the royal park;
you shall not lack for the four requisites, and I too shall gain merit conducive to heaven."
