Having obtained his promise, saying, "I shall attain [it]," he ate his morning meal and went with the Bodhisatta to the park.
There, he had a leaf-hut built, constructed a walking path (caṅkama), and prepared the remaining requisites such as a night-quarters and a day-quarters.
Having set out the requisites for one who has gone forth, he entrusted the park-keeper with the words, "Dwell here at ease, venerable sir."
From that time forth, the Bodhisatta dwelt in that very place for twelve years.
Then one day, the king’s frontier region rose in revolt. Desiring to go there to pacify it, he addressed the queen, saying, "My dear lady, it is fitting for you to remain behind in the city.
"On what grounds do you say this, my lord? "On account of one who is virtuous."
“An ascetic, my lady? “Your Majesty, I shall not neglect him; the care of our noble lord is my responsibility.
You may go without any anxiety. The king departed and left, and the queen likewise attended upon the Bodhisatta with great care.
However, when the king had gone, the Bodhisatta would come at his regular time.
Having gone to the royal palace at his own chosen hour, he performed his meal duties.
Then one day, while the Bodhisatta was delaying excessively, the queen prepared all manner of hard and soft foods;
having bathed and adorned herself, she arranged a low couch and, waiting for the Bodhisatta’s arrival, put on her smooth, fine cotton garment.
Having loosened her garment and put it on, she lay down.
The Bodhisatta, having observed the time, took his alms-bowl and, arriving through the air, reached the door of the great window. Hearing the sound of his bark-garment, the queen rose up suddenly;
the smooth cloth from her body fell away. Seeing this disagreeable object, the Bodhisatta’s faculties—
Having broken through [the hindrances], he looked with a state of sublime beauty.
Then, by the power of his jhāna, even though the defilement was suppressed, it rose up spreading its hood like a venomous snake placed in a basket; it was as if an axe had struck a milk-tree.
Simultaneously with the arising of the defilement, the factors of jhāna declined, and the faculties became incomplete.
He became like a crow with its wings clipped. Unable to sit down and perform his meal as he had before, he would not sit even when being urged to do so.
Then the queen placed all the solid and soft food into the alms-bowl itself.
And just as before, having finished his meal, he would go out through the lion-window and travel through the air.
Thus, he was unable to go that day. However, taking his food, he descended by the great staircase and went to the park.

The queen also perceived that his heart was bound to her. Having gone to the park, he did not eat the food but placed it on a lower couch, saying, "The queen has such beauty of hand and such beauty of foot; such..."
Lamenting such things as, "The end of the thighs reaches to the waist; such was the mark of my thighs," he lay prostrate for seven days, and his food became putrid and swarming with blue flies.
Then the king, having pacified the border regions, returned and circumambulated the city, which was fully adorned and prepared for his arrival.
Having prepared the royal residence, he went to the park without even going there first, thinking, "I shall see the Bodhisatta.
Seeing that the hermitage grounds were in disarray, he thought, "He must have departed," and opening the door of the leaf-hut, he entered.
Seeing him lying there, he thought, "He must be suffering from some ailment," and having had putrid food discarded and the leaf-hut cleaned, he attended to him.
“Venerable sir, what is troubling you? he asked. “I have been pierced, Great King,” he replied.
The king thought, “My enemies, finding no opening against me, must have come thinking, ‘We shall weaken his position,’ and it is likely they have pierced him.
Turning his body around and looking at the place where he had been pierced, the king did not see any wound.
“Where were you pierced, venerable sir? he asked. The Bodhisatta replied, “I was not pierced by another, Great King;
rather, I pierced myself in the heart. Having said this, he rose up, sat down, and spoke these verses:
“By the cleansing of intention from passion, and sharpened by reflection;”
“Not by one adorned with beauty, nor by one fashioned like an arrow-maker;
not by one with long ears, nor even by one who frequents peacocks—
by him I have been pierced in the heart, he who burns all my limbs.”
“I see no wound from which blood might flow, so long as my mind is not improperly directed; it is by myself that suffering has been brought upon me.
In this context, “washed by the passion of intention” means washed by the passion associated with sensual thoughts. And “sharpened by reflection” means...
By that very water of passion, sharpened on the stone of discursive thought (*vitakka*). "Neither adorned nor auspicious" means neither adorned and auspicious, nor unadorned and hideous;
the sense is that it is not [either]. "Nor even fashioned by fletchers" means not even fashioned by fletchers.
"Not drawn back to the right ear-tip and released" means not having been pulled back as far as the right ear-lobe and then released. Nor is it "served by peacocks."
By not employing [the arrows] made from peacock feathers, vulture feathers, and so forth.
"I was pierced in the heart by that"—by that arrow of defilement (*kilesakaṇḍa*), I was pierced in the heart. "Burning all my limbs"—capable of burning all the limbs.
O Great King, from the moment I was pierced in the heart by that arrow of defilement, all [my faculties] were as if set ablaze by fire.
It shows that "the limbs are burning.
"And I see no wound" means that I do not see a scar at the place where I was pierced.
"From which blood might flow" means that I do not see that [place] from which blood would stream out due to being pierced. Regarding the phrase "as long as the mind is unmethodical": here—
The particle *yāvāti* has the sense of "exceedingly firm"; the meaning is that he developed his mind in an improper way with extreme firmness.
"I myself have brought this suffering upon myself" means that I, by my own self, have brought this suffering upon myself.
Thus, having taught the Dhamma to the king with these three verses, the Bodhisatta [dismissed] the king from the leaf-hut.
Having performed the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa*, having restored the lost *jhāna*, and having emerged from the leaf-hut,
he sat in the air and exhorted the king, saying, "Great King, I shall go back to the Himālaya.
Although he was told, "Venerable Sir, it is not possible for you to go," he replied, "Great King, while dwelling here, such a misfortune befell me."
"Now it is no longer possible for me to live here," he said, and even as he was thus entreating the king, he sprang up into the air and went to the Himālaya.
There he remained for the duration of his lifespan and passed away to the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, [The identification follows: "The one who was the king at that time was Ānanda. The ascetic was myself."
The monk who was weary of the world established himself in Arahatship. Some became Stream-enterers, some Once-returners, some Non-returners, and some became Arahats.
"At that time, King Ānanda was [the king], but the ascetic was none other than myself.
This is the first commentary on the *Saṅkapparāgajātaka*.
[252] 2. The Commentary on the *Tilamuṭṭhi-jātaka* (The Handful of Sesame Birth Story).
"Even today, that [thought] is still in my mind. The Teacher related this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain angry bhikkhu.
It is said that a certain bhikkhu was prone to anger and full of agitation; even when spoken to only slightly...
Being thus provoked, he became angry and resentful, manifesting anger, hatred, and dissatisfaction.
Then one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth: "Friends, such-and-such a monk is wrathful and full of vexation;
he wanders about making a sizzling sound like salt thrown into a hot pan. In this Dhamma and Discipline of the Buddha, which is free from anger—"
“Having gone forth, he is not even able to restrain his anger.
When the Teacher heard their conversation, he sent for a monk, summoned that monk, and asked him, “Is it true, monk, that you are prone to anger?
When he replied, “It is true, venerable sir,” the Teacher said, “Monks, this man was prone to anger not only now, but in the past as well.”
Having said, "It was thus," he related a story of the past:
"In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, he had a son named Prince Brahmadatta.
And the kings of old [would train] their sons thus: 'In this way they shall have their pride and arrogance subdued, endure cold and heat, and understand the ways of the world...'"
Thinking, "They will become such [masters]," even though there were world-renowned teachers in their own city,
they sent them far away across foreign lands for the purpose of learning crafts; therefore, that king also summoned his son,
who was sixteen years of age, gave him single-layered sandals, a leaf parasol, and a thousand kahāpaṇas, and said, "Dear son, to Takkasilā..."
“Go and learn a craft,” he sent him off. Saying, “Very well,” he paid homage to his parents, departed, and in due course reached Takkasilā.
Having inquired for the teacher’s house, he went there while the teacher was walking at the door of the house after rising from teaching the crafts to his young students.
At the very spot where he stood and saw the teacher, [he left] his sandals...
Having set aside his sunshade and removed his turban, he paid homage to his teacher and stood before him.

The teacher, perceiving that the youth was weary, offered him hospitality as a guest. After eating his meal and resting for a short while, the prince approached his teacher, paid homage, and stood there.
When the teacher asked, "From where have you come, dear boy? he replied, "From Bārāṇasī. "Whose son are you? he asked.
“Of the King of Bārāṇasī,” he replied. “For what purpose have you come? “To learn a craft.
“Have you brought a teacher’s fee, or do you wish to be a student of the Dhamma?
He said, “I have brought a teacher’s fee,” and placing a purse of a thousand pieces at the teacher’s feet, he paid homage.
The students of the craft (dhammantevāsikā) perform work for their teacher during the day and learn the craft at night;
those who provide the teacher’s share live like eldest sons in the house and learn the craft alone.
Therefore, that teacher also began the prince's training on an auspicious day under a favorable constellation. And as the prince was learning the craft, one day—
He went with his teacher to bathe. Then an elderly woman sat there, having spread out sesame seeds that she had husked and keeping watch over them.
Seeing the white sesame seeds, the prince, desiring to eat them, took a handful of sesame and ate them.
The elderly woman, thinking "this one is greedy," said nothing and remained silent. On the following day, he [again] by her...
At that time, he did exactly as before, and she said nothing to him. On the third day, he did the same again;
then the old woman, raising her arms, cried out, "A world-renowned teacher is having his own pupils plunder me!
The teacher turned back and asked, "What is this, mother? [She replied,] "Sir, your pupil—by me..."
“He ate one handful of white sesame seeds today, one yesterday, and one the day before; surely, by eating in this way, he will exhaust everything belonging to me.
“Mother, do not weep; I will give you back the cost,” [the teacher said].
“I have no need for the cost, Master, but please instruct the boy so that he does not act like this again. The teacher—
“Now then, look at him, mother! he said, and having had the two boys seize the prince by both hands and take up a bamboo cane, he struck him thrice on the back, saying, “Do not do such a thing again!
The prince, enraged with his teacher, rolled his eyes red with anger and glared at him from the soles of his feet up to the crown of his head. He, too, being provoked, [glared back].

He understood his intention. Having completed his training, the prince thought, "Once he has been granted leave, he must be killed by me," and keeping the harm done by him in his heart, he paid homage to his teacher at the time of departure.

He then made a promise as if with affection, saying, "Teacher, when I have attained the sovereignty of Bārāṇasī and send for you, you should come then," and having thus secured his consent, he departed.
Thus, having reached Bārāṇasī and paid homage to his parents, he displayed his craft.
The king, thinking, "I have seen my son alive; while he is still living, I shall see him enjoy the glory of sovereignty," installed his son in the kingdom.
While enjoying the glory of sovereignty, remembering the wrong done by his teacher, he became angry and, intending to have him killed, set out to summon him.
He sent a messenger to the teacher. The teacher thought, "I will not be able to convince him while he is young," and so he did not go.
When the king reached middle age, [the teacher] thought, "Now I will be able to convince him," and having gone there, he stood at the palace gate and had it announced:
"The teacher from Takṣaśilā has arrived. The king was delighted and had the brahmin summoned. Then...
Seeing him approach him, he gave rise to anger; with bloodshot eyes, he addressed his ministers, saying:
"Sirs, even today the place where I was struck by my teacher still aches. My teacher has come with Death upon his forehead, thinking 'I shall die';
today this man's life is at an end. Having said this, he spoke the first two verses:
“Even today I remember that, when you seized me by the arm with a handful of sesame seeds and struck me with a staff.
Did you not take no pleasure in life, that you came here as a brahmin?”
"Since you seized me by the arm and thrice struck me.
In this context, the accusative case in both instances of "yaṃ maṃ bāhāya" (me by the arm) is dependent upon the acts of striking and seizing.
Since you struck me for the sake of three handfuls of sesame, and while striking me you seized me by the arm and struck me.
"That slapping [of my back] is still in my mind even today"—this is the meaning here. "Do you not take delight in life?"—I think that you do not find pleasure in your own life.
"Because you have come here, O Brahmin"—since you, O Brahmin, have come here into my presence.
"Having seized me by the arm"—having grasped my arm; having [seized] me by the arm.
"Having taken [it]," is also the meaning. "He struck it three times" means he struck it with the bamboo staff on three occasions;
saying, "Now receive the fruit of that today," he spoke thus, threatening him with death.
Having heard that, the teacher spoke the third verse:
“The noble one who restrains with punishment the ignoble one who acts ignobly—this is instruction, not enmity; thus do the wise understand.
In this context, “noble” (*ariya*) is a designation for what is beautiful. Furthermore, that noble one is fourfold: the noble one in conduct, the noble one in vision, and so forth.
The noble one by mark and the noble one by penetration. In this context, whether one is a human or an animal, if one stands firm in noble conduct, one is called "noble by conduct.
And this has been said:
"O Vakkaṅga, whoever honors almsfood while abiding in the way of the noble ones..."
"I release you from that husband; may you both go as you please.
Now, he was endowed with a beautiful form and a graceful, lovely deportment, and was thus known as Dassana-ariya (Noble to Behold). And this has been said:
"You have the appearance of a nobleman, with eyes full of serenity; I think, sir, you have gone forth from a family of high standing."
“How indeed did the wise one, having abandoned wealth and thoughts, go forth and renounce the home?

Furthermore, one who wanders about like a recluse by adopting the dress, the robes, and the outward signs, even if he is immoral, is called a “noble in sign” (*liṅga-ariya*). With reference to such a person it was said:
“Having put on the disguise of those of good vows, the lecherous defiler of families, the impudent one;”
“A deceiver, unrestrained, and hollow, walking in disguise—he is a defiler of the path.

The Buddhas and others, however, are called “noble ones through realization” (*paṭivedha-ariya*). Thus it is said: “The noble ones are called the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha. Among these, here the “noble one by conduct” (*ācāra-ariya*) alone is intended.
“Ignoble” (*anariya*) refers to one who is immoral and of evil nature. “Practicing” (*kubbantaṃ*) refers to the fivefold work of immorality, such as the taking of life and so forth.
One who is performing this single unwholesome act, namely a person committing an ignoble, base, and contemptible deed involving the fivefold fear of enmity.
"Whoever" (yo) refers to anyone among the kṣatriyas and so forth. "With a rod" (daṇḍena) means with whatever weapon.
"Restraints" (nisedhati) means he wards him off by striking him, saying, "Do not do such a thing again. That is instruction; it is not enmity.

"Great King, when one’s sons, daughters, or pupils are doing what ought not to be done, striking them in this way to restrain them is indeed instruction, guidance, and admonition in this world; it is not enmity.
Thus do the wise understand it. Therefore, Great King, you too should know this: one should not harbor enmity in such a situation."

"You ought to do so. For if you, Great King, had not been thus instructed by me, then as time passed, while carrying cakes, flour-cakes, and the like, as well as various fruits, you would have become addicted to thievery;

gradually committing such acts as housebreaking, highway robbery, and the plundering of villages, you would have been caught with the stolen goods and declared, 'This man is a thief who has offended against the king.'"
Having seized him, he was presented to the king [with the words], "Go, inflict upon him a punishment appropriate to his offense. [The teacher thought:
"If he were to fall into the fear of such punishment, from where would you have obtained such prosperity? Is this sovereignty not something you received by depending on me?
In this way, the teacher made the king understand. When the ministers standing around him heard these words, they said, "It is true..."
“Your Majesty, this sovereignty belongs to your teacher alone,” they said.
At that moment, the king, perceiving the teacher’s virtue, said, “Teacher, I give you all this sovereignty;
accept the kingdom. The teacher refused, saying, “Great King, I have no need for the kingdom. The king—
Having sent him to Takkasilā, he had the teacher’s wife and children brought back, granted him great authority, appointed him as his own domestic priest, and established him in his father’s position.
Abiding by his advice, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and became destined for heaven.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths—
The angry monk was established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and many people became stream-enterers (sotāpanna), once-returners (sakadāgāmin), and non-returners.
“At that time, the king was the angry monk, but the teacher was none other than myself.
This is the second commentary on the *Tilamuṭṭhi-jātaka*.
[253] 3. The Commentary on the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka.
"My food and drink"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at the Aggāḷava Cetiya near Āḷavī, concerning the training rule on building huts.
For the monks of Āḷavī, while having huts built by means of solicitation, were excessively begging and excessively making requests.
They lived there saying such things as, "Give us a man! Give us a man who performs the work of a man!
The people, distressed by these entreaties and alarmed by the requests, were terrified, agitated, and fled upon seeing the monks.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa approached Āḷavī and entered for alms; and the people, seeing even the Elder, [were likewise terrified].

They did exactly so. After returning from his almsround following the meal, he addressed the monks, asking, "Friends, formerly this Āḷavī was easy to obtain alms in; why has it now become difficult to obtain alms?
Having heard the reason for this, when the Blessed One had arrived at Āḷavī and was staying at the Aggāḷava Shrine, he approached the Blessed One.
He reported this matter. On account of this, the Teacher had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks of Āḷavī:
"Is it true, monks, that you are having huts built by means of begging?
When they replied, "It is true, venerable sir," he rebuked those monks, saying: "Monks, this so-called 'begging' is like [the theft of] the seven treasures."
"Even for the Nāgas dwelling in the Nāga-abode, this is disagreeable, let alone for humans;
for those who earn even a single kahāpaṇa, it is like the time when their flesh is torn from a stone," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of great wealth among the brahmins.
He was reborn there. While he was wandering about, running hither and thither, another meritorious being was also reborn in his mother’s womb.
When both brothers had reached maturity, their hearts were filled with agitation at the passing away of their parents;
they went forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isipabbajjā*), and having constructed leaf-huts on the bank of the Ganges, they dwelt there. Of them, the elder lived by the upper Ganges.

A leaf-hut was established for the younger brother at Adhogaṅgā. Then one day, a Nāga king named Maṇikaṇṭha, having emerged from his Nāga abode, wandered along the bank of the Gaṅgā in the guise of a young brahmin student.
He went to the younger brother’s hermitage, paid homage, and sat down to one side. After they had exchanged friendly greetings with one another, they became intimate friends.
They were unable to live without him. Maṇikaṇṭha would frequently come into the presence of his younger brother ascetic;

after sitting and engaging in conversation, at the time of departure, out of affection for the ascetic, he would cast off his own form, envelop the ascetic with his coils, embrace him, and holding a great hood over the ascetic’s head, [he would stay] for a short while.
Having satiated that affection, dispelled it, and disentangled his body, he paid homage to the ascetic and returned to his own place.
Due to fear of him, the ascetic became thin, haggard, discolored, pale, and his limbs were covered with visible veins.
One day, he went into the presence of his brother, who then asked him: "Why, sir, are you thin?"
“Wretched, ill-favored, pale and sallow, with veins showing all over his body.
Having reported that news to him, when asked, “But sir, do you wish for the arrival of that Nāga king, or do you not?
he replied, “I do not wish it. [The other continued,] “But as that Nāga king approaches you, what kind of ornaments will he be wearing?”
When he said, "He is coming," [the king] replied, "It is the jewel-treasure. [The sage said:

"In that case, as soon as that Nāga king comes into your presence, you must request him, even before he has sat down, saying, 'Give me the jewel. Then that Nāga will depart without encircling you with his coils.
On the following day, standing at the entrance of the hermitage, you should request it from him as soon as he arrives; on the third day..."
"Standing on the bank of the Ganges, you should beg him for it just as he is emerging from the water; in this way, he will not come back to you again.
Having agreed, saying "Very well," the ascetic went to his own leaf-hut.
On the following day, as soon as the Naga king arrived and stood there, he begged him, saying, "Give me this jewel that adorns you. Without even sitting down, the Naga fled.
Then, on the second day, standing at the entrance of the hermitage as he was approaching, he said, "Yesterday you did not give me the jewel-treasure;
today it is right for you to give alms. Without even entering the hermitage, the nāga fled.
On the third day, as soon as he emerged from the water, [the man] said to him, "Today is the third day of my begging; give now!"
"This is my jewel-treasure," he said. Standing in the water, the Naga king spoke two verses in rejecting the ascetic:
"Abundant and excellent food and drink arise for me because of this jewel;
I will not give it to you, for you are an excessive beggar, nor will I come to your hermitage."
“Just as Susu, with hands washed clean of gravel, terrified this rock while pleading;
so too, I will not give it to you, for you are an excessive beggar, nor will you come to my hermitage.
In that context, “my food and drink” refers to my divine food, such as rice porridge and boiled rice, and my divine drink, consisting of the eight kinds of beverages.
"Vipula" means much. "Uḷāra" means excellent and refined. "Taṃ te" means that jewel of yours. "Atiyācako si" means you have been asking excessively;
having transgressed both the proper time and the proper measure, for these three days you have been begging me for my dear and pleasing jewel-treasure—you have asked too much.
"Na cāpi te" means not only will I not give it to you, but I shall not even come to your hermitage.
"Susū" means just as a young man, a youth. "Sakkharadhotapāṇī" means one whose hands have been washed with sand;
it refers to one who has washed his sword-blade on a stone with oil.
"Tāsesimaṃ selaṃ yācamāno" means that while begging for this gem, you frightened me like a young man who, having drawn the tip of a golden-sheathed sword, says, "I shall cut off your head."
Having spoken thus, the Nāga king submerged himself in the water, returned to his own Nāga abode, and did not come back.
Then, because he could no longer see that beautiful Nāga king, the ascetic became even more emaciated, haggard, discolored, and pale;
his body was covered with a network of veins. Then the elder ascetic [said to] the younger...
Thinking, "I shall learn his way of life," he went into his presence;
seeing that he had become even more afflicted with jaundice, he asked, "Sir, why have you become so much more afflicted with jaundice?
Having heard the reply, "Because of not seeing that beautiful Nāga king," [he thought], "This ascetic is unable to live without the Nāga king."
Having observed this, he spoke the third verse:
“One should not beg from one whom one wishes to please; excessive begging makes one a stranger.
When the elephant was asked for his jewel by the brahmin, it simply vanished from sight.”
In this context, "he does not beg for that" means he should not ask for that merchandise. "He seeks what is dear to him" means he should know which merchandise is dear to that person.
"He becomes unlovely" means he becomes unpleasant. "By excessive begging" means by asking for choice merchandise beyond the proper measure;
because of that excessive begging, "he met with nothing but invisibility," meaning from that point on...
"He has gone to the state beyond sight.
Having spoken thus, and having comforted him by saying, "From this day forward, do not grieve," the elder brother returned to his own hermitage.
Thereafter, both brothers developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
"They became intent upon the Brahma-world.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching—"Bhikkhus, even for Nāgas dwelling in a Nāga abode complete with the seven treasures, a request is indeed unpleasant;
how much more so for humans?"—then identified the Jātaka.
“At that time, Ānanda was the younger brother, while I myself was the elder.
This concludes the third commentary, the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka.
[254] 4. The Commentary on the Kuṇḍakakucchisindhava Jātaka.
"Having become one who grazes on grass," the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Sāriputta.
For on one occasion, when the Fully Enlightened One had spent the rains retreat at Sāvatthī and returned after wandering on tour,
people, thinking, "We shall perform hospitality for the newcomers," prepared a great almsgiving for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
They gave. They appointed a single monk named Dhammaghosaka to the monastery; he would select whichever monks were desired by whoever came and give them to those people.
Then, a certain poor old woman prepared only one portion of food and, among those people [who were distributing] to the monks—
When the alms had been distributed after she had made her selection, she returned to Dhammaghosaka at sunset and said, "Give me one bhikkhu.
He replied, "I have already selected and given away all the bhikkhus; however, the Elder Sāriputta is still in the monastery, so you should give him your alms.
Delighted, she said, "Very well," and stood at the gateway of the Jeta Grove.
When the Elder arrived, [the people] paid homage to him, took the bowl from his hand, led him to their house, and had him sit down.
Many faithful families heard the report: "It is said that the Dhamma-Senāpati has been invited to sit in his own house by a certain elderly woman.
Among them, King Pasenadi Kosala, having heard this news, [sent] her a garment and a purse containing a thousand [pieces].
He sent [the gifts] together with food vessels, saying: "When serving my noble lady, let her put on this cloth and, using these kahāpaṇas, serve the Elder.
Just as the King did, so too did Anāthapiṇḍika, Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika, and the great female lay follower Visākhā send [gifts].
Furthermore, other families also sent [gifts] by way of one hundred, two hundred, and so forth, according to their own means.
They sent coins according to their own means. In this way, in a single day, that elderly woman obtained about one hundred thousand.

The Elder, however, drank only the gruel given by her, ate only the snacks and cooked rice she had prepared, and after giving a blessing of thanksgiving, established that elderly woman in the fruit of stream-entry and returned to the monastery.
In the Hall of Truth, the monks initiated a discussion on the virtues of the Elder:
"Friends, the General of the Dhamma rescued the elderly housewife from her state of poverty and became her support; he partook of the food she gave without feeling any disgust.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?"

Having asked, "Is it indeed she?", and being told "It is she," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta has become a refuge for this old woman, nor is it only now that he partakes of the food given by her without revulsion; in the past, too, he partook of it.
Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of horse-dealers in the northern region (Uttarāpatha).
Five hundred horse-dealers from the northern country brought horses to Benares for sale.
One particular horse-dealer, taking five hundred horses, set out on the road to Benares. On the way,...
And not far from Bārāṇasī there was a certain market town; formerly, there had been a very wealthy merchant there.
His residence was vast, but that family gradually fell into ruin until only an old woman remained, who lived in that house.
Then that horse-dealer, having reached that market town, [thought: "Wages..."
“I will give it,” he said; taking up residence in her house, he tethered the horses in a secluded spot.

On that very day, one of his noble mares went into foal. Having stayed for two or three days and having allowed the horses to regain their strength, he set out with the horses, thinking, “I shall see the king. Then the old woman said to him, “The house-fee—”
Having said, "Give it," when he replied, "Very well, mother, I shall give it," she said, "Father, while giving me my wages, please deduct this colt from my wages and give it to me.
The merchant did so and departed. She, having established a motherly affection for that colt, cared for him by providing him with fodder, firewood, food scraps, and grass.
Then, at a later time, the Bodhisatta arrived leading five hundred horses and took up residence in that house.
Having caught the scent from where the young Sindhava horse named Kuṇḍakakhādaka stood, not even a single horse was able to enter the house.
The Bodhisatta asked the old woman: "Mother, is there a horse in this house?"
“There is,” he said. “Dear father, there is no other horse; however, having adopted him as my son, I am rearing a young colt, and he is here.
“Where is he, mother? “He has gone out for a walk, dear father. “At what time will he return, mother?
“In the evening, dear father. The Bodhisatta, awaiting his arrival, left the horses outside and remained waiting.
He sat down. The young colt, too, having wandered about, returned at the very time [of the meal].
The Bodhisatta, seeing the young colt in Kuṇḍaka’s belly and comparing his marks, thought: “This colt is priceless; it is fitting to purchase him by paying a high price.
The young colt, having entered the house, stood right in his own stall.
At that moment, those horses were able to enter the house.
After staying for two or three days and having satisfied the horses, the Bodhisatta was departing and said, "Mother, give me this young horse for its price.
"What are you saying, dear? Are there people who sell their own children?"
“Mother, what do you feed him and look after him with? “Father, I look after him by feeding him rice-gruel, burnt rice, and fodder-herbs, and by giving him to drink a mash of broken rice.
“Mother, having obtained this, I shall feed him choice food fit for alms; I will spread a cloth canopy over his standing place and, upon a carpeted surface—”
“I shall set them aside. “Dear son, that being the case, let my son enjoy his happiness; take him and go.

Then the Bodhisatta, having placed one thousand pieces of gold at the base of each of the horse’s four feet, its tail, and its mouth—making six thousand bags in total—and having had the old woman dressed in new clothes, [he gave her] to the young Sindhava horse.
He placed it before him. The horse opened its eyes, looked at its mother, and shed tears.
She, having rubbed its back, said, "I have received the means to raise my son; go now, dear one," and then he departed.
On the following day, the Bodhisatta prepared a meal of milk-rice for the young colt and thought, "I shall first test him."
“Does he know his own strength, or does he not? Thinking thus, [the king] had gruel mixed with broken rice poured into a trough and offered it to him.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, “I will not eat this food,” did not wish to drink that gruel.
To test him, the Bodhisatta spoke the first verse:
“Having eaten grass for fodder, having eaten the scum of rice and broken grains—this was your food; why do you not eat it now?
In this context, “having eaten grass for fodder” means that formerly you ate what remained after various [members of the household] had eaten, which was given by the elder woman.
Having grown up by eating what is known as "scavenger-grass" (vighāsa-tiṇa), which is mere refuse;

and having eaten "rice-scum and broken rice"—here, "rice-scum" (ācāma) refers to the remains of cooked rice, and "broken rice" (kuṇḍaka) refers simply to broken grains—it is shown that you grew up by eating even this.
"This was your food formerly": why do you not eat it now? Even I [shall provide] for you...
“That very gift was given; why do you not eat it now?
Having heard this, the young Sindhava horse spoke these two verses:
“Where people know nothing of a person, either by birth or by discipline;”
“There is much there for you, Great Brahmā, even the scrapings of rice-water.
You yourself know what this supreme horse is like;
knowing this, and having understood it, I will not eat your scrapings.”
In that context, *yattha* means "in which place. *Posanti sattaṃ* means they nourish a being. Regarding *jātiyā vinayena vā*:
they do not know [him] in this way—“Is he endowed with noble birth or not? Is he fit in conduct or not? He spoke thus, addressing him with the respectful address “Mahābrahmā.
*Yādisāyaṃ*: “Of what sort this one is”; he speaks referring to himself. *Jānanto jānamāgamma*: knowing, having come by means of his knowledge.
"Knowing my own strength, how could I come to you and depend upon you to eat broken rice?
Indeed, it was not out of a desire to feed me broken rice that you gave six thousand [pieces of gold] and took me.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta comforted him, saying, "I did that for the purpose of testing you; do not be angry."
Having fed him with excellent food and taken him along, he went to the royal courtyard; there, having stationed five hundred horses on one side,
he surrounded another side with a variegated screen, spread a rug beneath it, fastened a cloth canopy above,
and placed the young Sindhava horse therein.
The king came and, while inspecting the horses, asked, "Why has this horse been set apart?
Having heard, "Great King, this Sindhava horse will cause these other horses to be released," he asked, "Is this Sindhava horse excellent, sir?
The Bodhisatta replied, "Yes, Great King," and when the king said, "In that case, we shall see his speed," [the Bodhisatta consented].
Having prepared that horse and mounted it, he said, "Behold, Great King," and after clearing away the people, he sent the horse galloping across the royal courtyard.
The entire courtyard became as if surrounded by a continuous mass of whirling horses.
Then the Bodhisatta said, "Behold, Great King, the speed of this young thoroughbred," and released it; not even a single person could see it.
Again, he wrapped a red cloth around his belly and released it; they saw only the red cloth.
Then he released it onto the surface of the water in a park lotus pond within the city;
as it ran across the surface of that water, even its hooves were not wetted. Once more, running upon lotus leaves, not even a single leaf was—
He did not cause it to sink in the water. Having thus demonstrated its possession of speed, he dismounted, struck his hand, and extended his palm.
The horse approached, placed all four feet together, and stood upon the palm of his hand.
Then the Great Being said to the king: "Great King, if the full extent of this young horse’s speed were to be displayed in every way, it would reach the very limits of the ocean."
“It is not enough,” he said. The king, being pleased, gave half his kingdom to the Great Being. He also consecrated the young Sindhu horse and made it a state ceremonial steed.
It became dear and pleasing to the king, and great honor was shown to it.
Indeed, its dwelling place was like the king’s own decorated bedchamber; they smeared the ground with the four kinds of fragrant scents.
They hung down garlands of perfumes and garlands of flowers; above, there was a cloth canopy inlaid with golden stars; it was surrounded on all sides by variegated curtains;
fragrant oil lamps burned constantly; even for his place of excrement and urine, they provided a golden basin;
and he always ate food fit for a king. From the time of his arrival...
From that time on, the entire kingdom of Jambudīpa came into the hands of the king alone.
Standing upon the Bodhisatta’s advice, the king performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and became destined for heaven.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, [the identification was made].
Many became stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arahants. [The Buddha said: “At that time, the old woman was this very same old woman;
the Sindhava horse was Sāriputta; the king was Ānanda; and I myself was the horse-dealer.
This is the fourth commentary on the Kuṇḍakakucchisindhava Jātaka.
[255] 5. The Commentary on the Sukajātaka:
“As long as he did not know moderation,” the Teacher related this while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a monk who had died from indigestion after eating too much.
It is said that when he had thus passed away, the monks were discussing it in the Hall of Truth.

They initiated a discussion regarding his faults, saying, "Friends, a certain monk named so-and-so, not knowing the capacity of his own stomach, ate too much; being unable to digest it, he has passed away.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, for what conversation are you sitting here gathered now? When they replied, "For this one," he said, "No, monks..."
"Monks, it was not only now; in the past as well, this one died because of overeating. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Himālaya region in the womb of a partridge.
He became the king of many thousands of partridges who lived in the Himalayan regions along the seashore."
There was. He had one son; when that son reached maturity, the Bodhisatta became weak of sight.
It is said that parrots possess a swift speed, and for that reason, their eyesight becomes weak first when they reach old age.
One day, the Bodhisatta’s son, having placed his parents in their nest, brought back food from the feeding ground and nourished them. On that occasion...
Having gone to his feeding ground and standing upon the mountain peak, he looked out over the ocean and saw an island.
On that island there was a mango grove with golden-colored, sweet fruit.
On the following day, at the time for seeking food, he flew up, descended into that mango grove, drank the juice of the mangoes, took some ripe mangoes, and returned to give them to his parents.
While eating it, the Bodhisatta recognized its flavor and said, "Father, was this not mango fruit from such-and-such an island?
When his father replied, "Yes, dear," he said, "Father, there are no parrots that live a long life while traveling to that island;
do not go to that island again. But he did not heed his words and went anyway.
Then one day, having drunk much mango juice and taking ripe mangoes for the sake of his parents, he was traveling along the edge of the ocean;
due to extreme exhaustion, his body was overcome by sleep. Even as he slept, he continued on his way, but the ripe mango held in his beak fell.
Gradually leaving the path of travel, he began to sink, moving only upon the surface of the water.
As he was coming back, he fell into the water. Then a fish seized him and ate him.
At the time of his departure, the Bodhisatta had known that he would fall into the ocean and die because he did not return.
Consequently, his parents, unable to obtain food, withered away and died.
The Teacher, having brought this past event to mind and having attained full enlightenment, spoke these verses:
“As long as that bird knew moderation in eating,
for so long did he reach his destination and nourish his mother.”
“But when he consumed food in excess,
it settled right there within him, for he was one who lacked moderation.
Therefore, moderation is good, and lack of greed regarding food is likewise.”
"For those who do not know the proper measure sink down, while those who know the proper measure do not sink.
In this context, "as long as he" means as long as that bird knew the proper measure in eating.

"He reached such a duration" means he reached a certain period of the duration of life; he attained his lifespan. "And his mother" is merely a figure of speech for the teaching; it refers to both his mother and father.
The meaning is "he ate. And from that time (*yato ca kho*) means at which time indeed. "He swallowed the food" means he took in the essence of the mango.
"From there" means at that time. "He sank right there" means he settled and submerged in that very ocean, becoming food for fish.

"Therefore, moderation is good": because the foolish man who lacked moderation in food perished after sinking into the ocean, therefore the state of being moderate—which consists in freedom from greed for food—is good; the meaning is that knowing the proper measure is excellent.
Alternatively: "Reflecting wisely, he takes food neither for amusement nor for intoxication... [but] for the maintenance and support of this body, and for its easeful living."
“Even while eating all kinds of food, one would not be fully satisfied;
a mindful bhikkhu should wander with a moderate stomach and measured food.
Having eaten only four or five morsels, he should drink water.”
“It is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute:
for a person who is always mindful and knows the proper measure regarding food obtained, his pains become thin; he ages slowly, preserving his life.”
Thus, moderation in eating is also praised as excellent:
"Just as one eats the flesh of one's own son in the wilderness, or like oil for the axle of a cart,
so should one take food for the sake of sustenance, remaining free from infatuation."
Thus, non-greediness is also rightly praised. However, in the *Pāḷi* it is written as "one who is not greedy" (*agiddhimā*);
therefore, this reading from the *Aṭṭhakathā* is indeed superior. For those who lack moderation sink;

that is, those who do not know the measure in eating commit evil deeds through the power of craving for flavors and sink into the four states of misery. And those who possess moderation do not sink; that is, those who know the measure in eating.
“They do not sink in either this present life or in the future life.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*), the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, many became stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), and arahants. “At that time, the son of the boar-king...”
“The monk was one who lacked moderation in eating, while I myself was the king of the swine.
This concludes the commentary on the *Sukajātakaya*, the fifth.
[256] 6. The commentary on the *Jarūdapānajātakaya*.
"Digging a well at Jarūdapāna"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning some merchants from Sāvatthī.

It is said that when they had taken goods in Sāvatthī, filled their carts, and were setting out on a journey for trade, they invited the Tathāgata, took refuge, and established themselves in the precepts. Having paid homage to the Teacher, they said: "We..."
“Venerable sir, we shall travel a long distance for the sake of trade;
once we have disposed of our goods, achieved success, and returned safely, we shall pay you homage,” they said, and then set out on their way.
On the desert road, seeing an old well, they thought, “There is no water in this well, yet we are thirsty; we shall dig it. And so they began to dig.

In succession they obtained much gold... pe ... and beryl. Being satisfied with that alone, they filled carts with those jewels and returned safely to Sāvatthī. Having stored the wealth they had brought back, they thought, "We have achieved our goal;
we shall give a meal," and having invited the Tathāgata, given the gift, and paid homage, they stood to one side.

Seated there, they reported to the Teacher how they had acquired their wealth. The Teacher said, "Lay followers, because you were content with that wealth and knew its proper measure, you have obtained both wealth and life;
however, those of old, being discontented and lacking measure, failed to act upon the words of the wise and met with the destruction of their livelihood. Having said this to them, he...
Being requested, he related a past event.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a merchant family in Benares;
having reached maturity, he became the chief caravan leader. Taking goods in Benares, he filled his wagons and set out.
Taking many merchants with him, he set out upon that very same wilderness and saw that very same well.
There, those merchants, thinking, "We shall drink water," dug into that well one after another and obtained much iron and other metals.
Having obtained much treasure, they were not satisfied with that and thought, "There will surely be something even more beautiful than this here."
They dug even more deeply. Then the Bodhisatta said to them, “O merchants, this greed is indeed the root of destruction.
We have already obtained much wealth; be satisfied with just this much and do not dig further.
Although they were thus forbidden by him, they continued to dig. That well was protected by a nāga, and beneath it—
When his own palace was being shattered and bricks and dust were falling, the Nāga King Vasu became enraged;
setting aside the Bodhisatta, he struck all the others with the wind from his nostrils, bringing them to their deaths.
Then, departing from the Nāga realm, he yoked carts, filled them with all kinds of jewels, and placed the Bodhisatta upon a comfortable carriage.
Having seated him and having had the wagons yoked by the young nāgas, he led the Bodhisatta to Bārāṇasī,
brought him into his home, settled him there, and then returned to his own nāga-abode. The Bodhisatta,
having distributed that wealth and made all of Jambudīpa free from the burden of taxes, gave gifts, undertook the precepts, and performed the Uposatha observances.
Having done so, at the end of his life, he filled the city of heaven.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke these verses:
“Like merchants seeking water who dig a well at Jarūdapāna, ... [the rest of the verse follows] ...”
The merchants obtained tin, copper, lead, and zinc;
silver and gold, and many pearls and beryl gems.
Yet, not satisfied with those, they sought more and more.
"Therefore, a fierce, venomous serpent will destroy him with its fiery power by means of his own fire.
Thus, one should not dig too little, nor should one dig too much;
for digging too little is evil, while wealth gained by digging is lost by digging too much."
In this context, *ayasa* means black iron; *loha* means copper; *muttā* means pearls.
"And they were not satisfied with that" means those merchants were not content with that wealth. "There" refers to those merchants at that well.

*Tejassī* means one endowed with piercing splendor (*visateja*). "He struck them with splendor" means he killed them with piercing splendor. "Lost through excessive digging" means by digging too deeply.
And both that wealth and his life were lost.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Nāga king was Sāriputta, while the chief caravan leader was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Jarūdapāna Jātaka, the sixth.
[257] 7. The Commentary on the Gāmaṇicanda Jātaka:
"This one is not skilled in household life. This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the praise of wisdom.
For in the Hall of Truth, the monks were sitting together praising the wisdom of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, saying: "Friends, the Tathāgata..."
“Possessing great wisdom, broad wisdom, laughing wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom, he surpasses the world with its devas by means of his wisdom.
The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, the Tathāgata—”
Having said, "Only one possessed of wisdom," he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Janasandha reigned. The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen.
His face was as pure as the surface of a well-polished golden mirror.
Because he had attained such extreme beauty, on the day of his naming they gave him the name Ādāsamukhamāra.
Within seven years, however, his father instructed him in the three Vedas and everything in the world that ought and ought not to be done;
then, when he was seven years old, the father passed away. The ministers performed the funeral rites for the king with great honor.
Having performed the funeral offerings and given gifts, on the seventh day they assembled in the royal courtyard and said, “The prince is too young;
it is not possible to consecrate him to the kingdom. We shall test him and then consecrate him.
One day, having had the city decorated, the court of justice prepared, and a throne set out, they went into the presence of the prince.

Having arrived, they said, "Your Majesty, it is fitting to go to the place of legal adjudication. The prince said, "Very well," and having gone with a great retinue, he sat down cross-legged on a throne.
While he was seated, the ministers brought a monkey that moved about on two legs, dressed in the guise of a teacher of the science of site-selection (*vatthuvijjā*).

Having had him arrested and brought before the court of justice, they said, "Your Majesty, this man was a master of the science of site-selection (*vatthuvijjā*) during the time of his father, the Great King;
he was proficient in the science and could perceive the merits and defects within a space of seven cubits underground.

It is only by his selection that the sites for the residences of royal families have been established. May Your Majesty favor him and appoint him to an official position. The prince [acted accordingly].
Looking down and up, and realizing, "This is no human; this is a monkey," and reflecting,
"Monkeys indeed know how to destroy what has been done, but they do not know how to do or deliberate upon what has not been done," he spoke the first verse to his ministers:
“This one is not skilled in household matters; this monkey is fickle.
Whatever has been done, he would surely spoil it; such is the nature of this family.
Therein, “this one is not skilled in household matters” means that this being is not skilled in managing households, or in investigating domestic affairs.
Or he is not skillful at doing it. "Lol" means one who is by nature lustful. "Valīmukha" means one who has wrinkles (*valī*) on his face;
thus he is "Valīmukha. "Thus this is a family of Dhamma" means that this so-called monkey family is of such a nature that whatever is done must be defiled and destroyed.
Then the ministers said, "It shall be so, Your Majesty," and having removed him, after the lapse of one or two days, they adorned him once again.
They brought him to the place of legal judgment and said, "Your Majesty, this man was a minister of justice during his father, the Great King’s time;
the legal codes were well-administered by him. It would be fitting to retain him and have him carry out the work of judgment.
The prince looked at him and thought, "A person possessed of consciousness does not have body hair such as this; he is a mindless monkey."
Knowing that he would not be able to perform the act of adjudication, he spoke the second verse:
“This is no hairy beast, nor is this a deer that breathes with ease;
it has been taught to me by the multitude of men, yet it understands nothing at all.”

In this context, "this is not the hair of one who possesses consciousness" means that the coarse hair on his body does not belong to one possessed of a mind associated with investigative wisdom (*vicāraṇa-paññā*). However, there is no animal whatsoever that is devoid of ordinary consciousness (*pākatika-citta*).
"This is not one who can provide comfort" means that he is incapable of either being a refuge or of giving instruction in order to comfort another.
"It is not reassuring. By "deer," he means a monkey. "It was told to me by Janasandha" means: "This was told—that is, spoken—by my father Janasandha:
'A monkey, it is said, does not know what ought to be done and what ought not to be done'; thus was the instruction given. "He knows nothing at all":
therefore, one must reach the conclusion that this monkey knows nothing whatsoever.
In the Pāḷi, however, it is written: “He would not defile anything at all,” but that is not found in the Aṭṭhakathā.

Having heard this verse as well, the ministers said, “It shall be so, Your Majesty,” and having removed him, on another day they again adorned that very man, brought him to the court of justice, and said, “Your Majesty, this man [belonged to] his father, the Great King...”
"One who serves his mother and father at the proper time, and one who performs the duties of honoring the elders in the family—such a person is fit to be supported," they said.
The prince looked at her and thought, "Monkeys are by nature fickle-minded; they are not capable of performing such a task.
Having reflected thus, he spoke the third verse:
“Such a person as I am would not support mother or father, nor brother or sister, as has been taught to me by Daśaratha.
In this context, “brother or sister” means one’s own brother or sister. However, in the canonical text (pāḷiyaṃ), it says “sakhaṃ.”
It has been written; furthermore, this has already been discussed in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "When 'kinsman' (*saka*) is said, one's own brothers and sisters are understood;
when 'friend' (*sakha*) is said, a companion is understood. "He would support" means he would nourish.
"Such a person"—meaning a being of the monkey species such as this one is seen—would not support such a person. "I was well-reared by Daśaratha"—thus [it was said].
"I was instructed by my father. For his father is called "Janasandha" because he binds people together with the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*);
and he is called "Dasaratha" because he performs, by means of his own single chariot alone, what should and should not be done that is to be performed by ten chariots.
It was because he had heard such advice from him that he spoke thus.
The ministers said, “So be it, Your Majesty,” and having removed the monkey, they thought, “The prince is wise; he will be able to rule the kingdom.
They consecrated the Bodhisatta in the kingship and caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming, “This is the command of King Ādāsamukha!
From that time forth, the Bodhisatta ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma, and his reputation for wisdom spread throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa.
Furthermore, these fourteen instances have been brought forward for the purpose of illustrating the nature of a wise man:
“The ox, the son, and the horse, the reed-worker and the village headman;
The courtesan, the young woman, the snake, the deer, the partridge, and the deity.”
“A nāga, an ascetic, and furthermore, a brahmin student.

Herein, this is the sequential account: When the Bodhisatta had been consecrated in the kingdom, a certain attendant at the feet of King Janasandha named Gāmaṇicanda thought thus: “This kingship truly shines when shared with those of equal age.”
“I am old and will not be able to attend upon a young prince; I shall live by performing agricultural work in the countryside.
Having traveled three *yojanas* from the city, he made his dwelling in a certain village.
However, he had no oxen for the sake of farming; when it rained, he requested two oxen from a friend.
Having plowed all day and fed the oxen grass, he went home to hand them over to his master.
At that moment, he was sitting with his wife in the middle of the house eating his meal.
The oxen, out of habit, entered the house; as they were entering, the husband lifted up his bowl, and the wife moved her bowl away.
Gāmaṇicanda, looking out with the thought, "They might invite me for a meal," departed without handing over the oxen.
That very night, thieves broke into the pen and carried off those same oxen. Early in the morning, the owner of the oxen entered the pen;
not seeing the oxen and knowing they had been stolen by thieves, he nevertheless approached Gāmaṇicanda, thinking, "We shall take his life."
“O oxen, give it back to me,” he said. “But the oxen have already entered the house.
“Then were they handed over to me? “They were not handed over. “In that case, here is your royal messenger; come! he said.
For in those regions, if anyone picks up even a pebble or a shard of a potsherd and says, “This is your royal messenger; come!”, whoever does not go—
The king gave him an order; therefore, as soon as he heard he was a "royal messenger," he set out.
While traveling with him toward the royal palace, he reached a village where a friend lived. He said, "Friend, I am very hungry;
stay right here until I enter the village, attend to my meal, and return. Having said this, he went to his friend's house.
He entered. However, he had no companion in the house. His wife, seeing him, said, "Master, there is no cooked food;
please wait a moment, and I will give it to you after cooking it right now.
As she was quickly climbing the ladder to the rice storehouse, she fell to the ground, and at that very instant, her seven-month-old fetus miscarried. At that moment, for her—
The husband returned, saw her, and said, "You struck my wife and caused her to miscarry;
here is the king’s messenger for you—come along! Taking her with him, he departed. From then on, the two people walked with the village headman in the middle.
Now, at a certain village gate, a horse-herder was unable to turn his horse back, and the horse [refused to go] by their side.
He was going along. Seeing the village headman Canda, the horse-herder said, "Uncle Canda, please turn this horse back by striking it with something.
He took a stone and threw it; the stone struck the horse's foot and shattered it like a castor-oil stalk. Then the horse-herder said to him, "You have broken my horse's foot; this..."
Saying, "He is a royal messenger," they seized him.
As he was being led away by the three men, he thought: "They will present me to the king;
I cannot even afford the price for an ox, let alone the fine for causing an abortion. But where shall I find the price for a horse? Death is better for me."
As he was going along, on the way, in the middle of a forest near the path, he saw a solitary mountain precipice.
In its shade, two basket-makers, father and son, were weaving a mat together. Gāmaṇicanda said, "Sirs, I wish to attend to the needs of my body;
stay right here for a short while until I return," and having spoken, he climbed the mountain to the edge of the precipice.
As he was falling, he landed on the back of his father, the reed-worker, who died instantly from the blow.
Gāmaṇi stood up. The son of the reed-worker said, “You are a thief who has murdered my father;
this is the king’s messenger for you,” and seizing him by the hand, he emerged from the thicket. When [Gāmaṇi] asked, “What is this? he replied, “A thief who has murdered his father.”
Thus he spoke. From then on, four men surrounded him, placing the village headman in their midst, and led him away.
Then, at another village gate, a village overseer saw Candā the village headman and asked, "Uncle Candā the village headman, where are you going?
When he replied, "To see the king," the overseer said, "Surely you will see the king; as for me—"
“I wish to give a message to the king; will you carry it? he asked. “Yes, I shall carry it,” [the other] replied. [The first man said:
“By nature I was handsome, wealthy, renowned, and healthy; but now I am both destitute and afflicted with jaundice.
Ask the king what the reason for this is—for the king is said to be wise and will explain it to you—and then you should report his message back to me.”
"So be it," he consented.
Then, at a certain village gate ahead, a courtesan saw him and asked, "Uncle Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?
When he replied, "To see the king," she said, "The king is reportedly wise; please carry my message to him."
Having spoken thus, he said: “Previously I received a large wage, but now I do not receive even as much as a betel leaf;
no one at all comes near me. Ask the king what the reason for this is, and having returned, tell it to me.”
Then, at a certain village gate ahead, a young woman saw him and asked him the same question.
He said to her, "I am unable to live either in my husband's house or in my parents' home;
having gone there and asked the king what the reason for this is, please return and tell me."
Then, later on, a snake living in an anthill near the main road saw him and asked, "Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?
When he replied, "To see the king," the snake said, "The king is reportedly wise; bring him my message. [The man thought:
"At the time I set out for grazing, I was hungry, distressed, and my body was withered as I emerged from the anthill."
"Having filled the cave with my body, I emerge with great difficulty while dragging my frame along;
but when I have returned from foraging, well-fed and stout of body, I enter so swiftly that I do not even touch the sides of the cave.
What is the reason for this? You should ask the king and tell me. Thus he spoke.

Then, a certain deer, seeing him from the front, asked him the same question and said, "I am unable to eat grass anywhere else; I can do so only at the foot of a single tree. You should ask the king what the reason for this is.

Then, further along, a certain partridge, seeing him, asked him the same question and said, "I am able to rain pleasantly only while sitting at the base of a single termite mound; sitting in other places, I am not able to do so."
"In that case, you should ask the king, 'What is the reason for this? he said.
Then, a tree deity who saw him from ahead asked, "Canda, where are you going?
When he replied, "To the presence of the king," she said, "The king is reportedly wise; formerly I was one who received honors, but now [I have not even] so much as a handful of sprouts."
“I do not obtain it; what is the reason for that? you should ask the king.
Later on, a certain Nāga king saw him and asked him the same thing, saying: “The king is said to be wise.
Formerly, the water in this lake was clear and the color of jewels; now it is turbid, covered with leaves and moss.”
“Why is that? he said, “you should ask the king.

Then, when some ascetics living in a monastery near the edge of the city saw him, they asked him the same question and replied, “The king is indeed wise; formerly, in this monastery, the fruits were sweet.”
"Now they have become sapless and bitter; ask the king what the reason for this is," they said.
Then, having gone before him, some young brahmins saw him in a certain hall near the city gate and asked, "Where are you going, sir Canda?
When he replied, "To the presence of the king," they said, "In that case, take a message from us..."
"Go," they said, "for previously the places where we took [the treasure] were clearly visible;
but now, like water in a cracked jar, it does not remain nor is it perceived—it has become like darkness.
You should ask the king what the reason for this is."
Having received these ten instructions, Gāmaṇicanda went into the presence of the king.
The king was seated at the place of judgment. The owner of the oxen took Gāmaṇicanda and approached the king.
Upon seeing Gāmaṇicanda and recognizing him, the king said, "This man was the attendant of our father; he raised us and cared for us. Where indeed..."
Having thought, "He has lived here for such a long time," he said, "Ho, Village Headman Canda! Where have you been living all this time?
You have not been seen for a long period; for what purpose have you come? [Canda replied:
"Yes, Your Majesty, ever since our lord passed away to heaven, I went to the countryside and have lived by performing agricultural work. Then, from there..."
“This man, for the sake of half a cow, showed himself as a royal messenger and dragged you here.
“If he had not been dragged, he would not have come,” [the other replied]. “The very fact that he was dragged is excellent; now I may see him. Where is that man?
“He is here, Your Majesty. “Is it true, sir, that he showed himself as our messenger to Canda?”
“It is true, Your Majesty. “For what reason? “Because, Your Majesty, this man will not give me the two oxen. “Is it true, Canda?
“In that case, Your Majesty, please listen to my words as well,” she said, and related the entire account.
Having heard this, the king asked the owner of the oxen: “Sir, did you see the oxen entering your house? “I did not see them.”
"O King! [The man replied. "Sir, have you never heard before when people say, 'He is named King Ādāsamukha'?
Speak with confidence. "I saw him, Your Majesty. "Sir Canda, because the oxen were not returned, the oxen are your debt;
furthermore, this man, having seen them, said, 'I do not see them,' and thus spoke a conscious lie. Therefore, you alone—"
“Having become the overseer, gouge out the eyes of both this man and his wife, and give me twenty-four kahāpaṇas for the price of the ox yourself.
When this was said, they sent the owner of the ox outside. He thought, “What shall I do with twenty-four kahāpaṇas once my eyes have been gouged out?
and falling at the feet of Candā the village headman, he said, “Master Candā,…”
“Let the ox and the mūlaka-kahāpaṇas be yours alone; take these as well,” he said, giving him more kahāpaṇas and fleeing.
Then the second one said, “Your Majesty, this man struck my wife and caused her to miscarry. “Is it true, Canda?
“Listen, Great King,” Canda replied, and he related everything in detail. Then the king asked him, “What—”
“But you struck his wife and caused her to miscarry,” he asked. “I did not cause it to miscarry, Your Majesty,” she replied.
“Well then, my friend Canda, will you be able to prove that this miscarriage was brought about by him? “I cannot, Your Majesty. “What will you do now?
“Your Majesty, it is necessary for me to obtain a son. “In that case, my friend Canda—”
“Make her your wife in your own house; when she has given birth to a son, then take her back and give her to him.
He too fell at Gāmaṇicanda’s feet, saying, “Do not destroy my home, master,” and having given the coins, he fled.
Then the third man came and said, “Sire, this man struck me and broke my horse’s leg. “Is it true? [he asked.]
“Canda! [the king said]. “Listen, Great King,” Canda replied, and he related the matter in detail.
Having heard this, the king said to Assagopaka, “Is it true that you said, ‘Strike the horse and turn back’?
“I did not say so, Your Majesty,” he replied. When questioned a second time, he said, “Yes, I did say so. The king then addressed Canda:
“Ho, Canda! This man speaks a lie, saying ‘I will not speak’ after having already spoken;
cut off his tongue, take a horse’s hoof from us, and give us a thousand [pieces]. Having said this, Assagopaka gave him other coins as well and fled.
Then the son of the reed-worker said, “Your Majesty, this man is my father-murdering thief. “Is it true, Canda?
“Listen, Your Majesty,” Canda replied, and he related the matter in detail. Then the king addressed the reed-worker and asked, “What are you doing now?
“Your Majesty, I must recover my father. “Well then, Canda, for this man—”
"It seems one ought to obtain a father, but it is impossible to bring back one who is dead.

Bring this man's mother, place her in your own house, and become his father. Naḷakāraputta said, "Do not, Master, destroy the home of my deceased father," and having given the village headman Candana a kahāpaṇa coin, he fled.
Having achieved victory over the half-month, Gāmaṇicanda, with a joyful heart, said to the king:
"Your Majesty, there is a message sent by certain people; shall I tell it to you? "Tell me, Canda," he replied.
Canda related each statement one by one in reverse order, beginning with the message of the young Brahmin students. The king answered them in their proper sequence.
How so? First, having heard the report: "Formerly, in their dwelling place, there was a cock that would crow at the proper time;
by its sound they would rise, take up their mantras, and perform their recitations, and only then would the dawn break, so that whatever they had learned was never lost.
But now, in their dwelling place, there is a cock that crows at the wrong time."
“There is,” he said, “when it rains either too late at night or too early in the morning.
When it rains too late at night, they wake up to the sound of it, take up their mantras, and being overcome by sleep, do not perform their recitation and fall back asleep.

When it rains too early in the morning, they wake up to the sound of it and do not get the opportunity to recite. Because of this, what they have learned and mastered does not become manifest. Thus he spoke.
Having heard the second [account], he thought: "Formerly, when they were practicing the duty of a recluse, they were devotedly engaged in the preliminary exercises of the *kasiṇas*.
But now, having abandoned the duty of a recluse, they are devotedly engaged in what should not be done;

having given the fruits and flowers grown in the monastery to their supporters, they maintain their livelihood through wrong livelihood by means of scraps of alms-food. Therefore, these fruits and flowers..."

"They have not become sweet. However, if they apply themselves once again to the duties of a recluse as they did before, their fruits will become sweet again. Those ascetics do not know the wisdom of royal families;
tell them how to perform the duties of a recluse," he said.

Having heard the third [report], he said: "Those two Nāga kings are quarreling with one another; because of that, the water has become turbid. If they become reconciled as they were before, it will become clear again.
Having heard the fourth [report], he said: "That tree deity used to protect people traveling through the wilderness;
therefore, she received various kinds of offerings. But now she no longer provides protection; therefore, the offerings..."
"She does not obtain it. If she provides protection as she did before, she will once again reach the pinnacle of prosperity.
She does not know of the presence of kings; therefore, tell her to provide protection for the people who have entered the forest," he said.

Having heard the fifth [instruction], he said, "Beneath that termite mound, at the foot of which the partridge sits and sings its pleasing song, there is a large pot of treasure. Dig it up and take it."
Having heard the sixth [story], he said, "At the foot of whichever tree that deer is able to eat grass, there is a large honeycomb of bees above that tree;
being infatuated with the grass smeared with honey, he is unable to eat anything else.
You, having taken that cluster of honey, send us the finest honey, and you may enjoy the remainder yourself."
Having heard the seventh [verse], he thought: "Beneath the anthill where that snake dwells, there is a large jar of treasure.
While living there guarding it, when it is time to come out, out of greed for wealth it relaxes its body and comes out clinging;
but having taken its prey, out of attachment to the wealth, it enters suddenly with speed without clinging."
"Having lifted up that treasure-pot, you must take it," he said.
Having heard this eighth [dream], she thought: "Between the village where the husband of that young woman lives and the village of her parents, there is a lover in a certain small village.
Remembering him and out of affection for him, she was unable to remain in her husband's house."
Being unable [to remain], thinking, "I shall see my mother and father," she stays for a few days in her lover's house and then goes to her parents' house;
staying there for a few days, she remembers her lover again and, thinking, "I will go to my husband's house," she goes back once more to her lover's house.
Having informed the kings of that woman's situation, [he says], "To her husband alone..."
“Tell her: ‘Stay in the house. If the king has you seized, there will be no life for you; it is necessary to practice heedfulness.
Having heard this ninth [instruction], she thought: “That courtesan, having previously received wages from one man, failed to digest them and [took wages] from another...”
She does not take [food] from the hand [of one person], for because of that she previously had much [income].

But now, having abandoned her own proper nature, she takes from the hand of another even before she has digested what was taken from the first; she makes no room for the former and makes it for the latter.
Because of this, her wages do not arise, and no one approaches her. If she... [her own]...
"He will abide by the Dhamma; he will become just as he was before. Speak to him so that he may abide in his own Dhamma," he said.
Having heard this tenth [instruction], [the king thought]: "In the past, that village headman adjudicated legal cases with justice and equity;
because of that, he was dear and pleasing to the people. Being fond of him, the people brought many gifts for him, and because of that, he became handsome..."
"He was once wealthy and possessed of fame. But now, having become a taker of bribes, he adjudicates lawsuits unjustly;
consequently, he has become poor and destitute, overcome by jaundice. If he would adjudicate lawsuits justly as he did before, he will once again become like his former self.
He does not know that the King is present; tell him to adjudicate lawsuits justly. Thus he spoke.
Thus Gāmaṇicanda reported these matters to the king. The king, through his own wisdom, explained them all just as an omniscient Buddha would;
he gave much wealth to Gāmaṇicanda, made the village where he lived a royal grant (*brahmadeyya*), and having given it to him, sent him away.
Having departed from the city, [he delivered] the message given by the Bodhisatta.
Having informed the brahmins, the young students, the ascetics, the king of the nagas, and the tree deity, he took the treasure from the partridge’s dwelling place;
having taken the bee-honey from the tree at the spot where the deer grazed on grass, he sent the honey to the king;
and having dug up the anthill at the serpent’s dwelling place, he took the treasure from there for the young woman.
Having delivered the message to the courtesan and the village headman exactly as it had been told to the king, he returned to his own village with great honor;
there he lived out his lifespan and departed according to his karma.
King Ādāsamukha, too, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, departed at the end of his life filling the city of heaven.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata is of great wisdom; even in the past he was indeed of great wisdom.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, he identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, many became stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arahants. "At that time, Gāmaṇicanda was Ānanda, and Ādāsamukha was the King."
"But I myself was he.
The seventh: The Commentary on the Candagāmaṇi Jātaka.
[258] 8. The Commentary on the Mandhātu Jātaka.
“As far as the moon and sun,” this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain dissatisfied monk.
It is said that while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a woman fully adorned and prepared, and became dissatisfied.
Then the monks brought him to the Hall of Truth and said, “Venerable Sir, this monk is dissatisfied.”
They presented them to the Teacher. The Teacher asked, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are dissatisfied?
When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Bhikkhu, when living as a householder, when will you ever be able to fulfill your craving?
For this craving for sensual pleasures is as difficult to fill as the ocean. Even the kings of old, [ruling] over the two thousand minor islands that surround [Jambudīpa]..."
