Having exercised the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch over the four great continents, having ruled the kingdom in the world of the Four Great Kings with the very manner of a human being,
and even having exercised divine sovereignty in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven— the dwelling place of the thirty-six Sakkas—
they nonetheless passed away without being able to satisfy their craving for sensual pleasures; but when will you ever satisfy this craving?
Having said, "Will you be able? he related a story of the past.
In the past, among those of the first eon, there was a king named Mahāsammata.
His son was named Roja; his son was named Vararoja; his son was named Kalyāṇa; his son was named Varakalyāṇa; his—
His son was named Uposatha, and his son was Mandhātā.
Endowed with the seven treasures and the four supernormal powers, he ruled as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-rājā*).
When he rubbed his left hand and clapped it with his right hand, a rain of the seven treasures fell from the sky like a divine cloud, reaching down to the knees; such was he.
He was a marvelous man. For eighty-four thousand years he played as a youth;
for eighty-four thousand years he exercised the office of viceroy; for eighty-four thousand years he ruled as a universal monarch (cakravartin);
and his lifespan was incalculable.
Thus, one day, being unable to satisfy his craving for sensual pleasures, he showed signs of weariness.
Then the ministers asked, "Why is it, Your Majesty, that you are weary? He replied, "When I consider the power of my merit, what will this kingdom do for me?
What place, indeed, is most delightful? "The world of the gods, Great King," they said. Thereupon, the Wheel-Treasure...
Having showered him with offerings, he went together with his retinue to the Cātumahārājika heaven.
Then the Four Great Kings, surrounded by hosts of gods and carrying divine garlands and perfumes in their hands, went out to meet him;

taking him with them, they went to the Cātumahārājika heaven and bestowed upon him the sovereignty of the gods. While he was exercising that sovereignty, surrounded by his own retinue, [the following occurred].
A long period of time has passed.
Even there, being unable to satisfy his craving, he showed signs of weariness.
The Four Great Kings asked him, "Why, O Lord, are you weary? He replied, "Which place is more delightful than this divine world?"

“Your Majesty, we are the retinue of attendants for others; the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is delightful. Mandhātā, having sprinkled the wheel-treasure with water, set out toward the Tāvatiṃsa heaven surrounded by his own retinue.
Then Sakka, the king of the gods, with celestial garlands and perfumes in hand and surrounded by a host of deities, went out to meet him, took him by the hand, and said: “From here—”

"Come, Great King," he said. At the time of the King’s departure, surrounded by his host of gods, the Counsellor-treasure took the Wheel-treasure and, descending to the path of men along with the assembly, entered his own city.
Sakka led Mandhātā to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, divided the deities into two portions, and shared his divine sovereignty in the middle between them.
He gave it away. From that time on, the two kings ruled the kingdom together.
As time passed in this manner, Sakka exhausted his lifespan of thirty-six million and six hundred thousand years and passed away; another Sakka was reborn.
He too, having exercised divine sovereignty, passed away at the end of his life. In this way, thirty-six Sakkas passed away, as did Mandhātā.
Nevertheless, he continued to exercise divine sovereignty with the same human care.
As time passed in this manner, an even greater craving for sensual pleasures arose within him, and he thought: "What use is half a kingdom to me?
I shall kill Sakka and rule as a sole monarch. It was impossible to kill Sakka; thus, craving—
This was the root of his misfortune; consequently, his life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) declined, and old age assailed his body.
Since a human body does not perish in the world of the gods, he fell from that celestial realm and descended into the park.
The park keeper reported his arrival to the royal court. Having come to the palace, [the king] had a couch prepared right there in the park. The king—
He lay down on a bed of non-exertion. The ministers asked, "Your Majesty, what shall we say after you?
He replied, "After me, you should tell this message to the great multitude:

'The Great King Mandhātu, having exercised the sovereignty of a Wheel-turning Monarch over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand minor islands, and having ruled for a long time among the gods of the Four Great Kings...'"
“Having exercised sovereignty in the deva-world for the lifespan of thirty-six Sakka-devas, he passed away without having fulfilled his craving.
Having spoken thus, he died and departed according to his karma.
The Teacher, having brought forth this past event and attained full enlightenment, spoke these verses:
“As far as the sun and moon revolve, illuminating the quarters with their radiance—
every living being established upon the earth was a servant of Mandhātā.
There is no satiety found in sensual pleasures, even by a rain of gold coins.”
"Sensual pleasures have little flavor and are suffering"— having understood this,
the wise person does not find delight even in celestial sensual pleasures.
The disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One delights in the destruction of craving.
In this context, *yāvatā* is a term denoting a limit. *Pariharanti* means that they encompass Sineru by whatever extent of limit.
*Disā bhanti* means they shine and radiate light in the ten directions. *Virocanā* means having the nature of shining because of producing illumination.
"All the servants of Mandhātā, whatever beings dwell upon the earth"—this refers to all those beings who depend upon the earth within such an area.
The people living in the countryside—all of them, because they had submitted with the thought, "We are the slaves of King Mandhātu;
King Mandhātu is our grandfather"—were indeed slaves, even though they were actually free men.
"Not by a rain of kahāpaṇas" refers to that which Mandhātu, having clapped his hands, [rained down] for the benefit of those people who had become his slaves.
He causes a rain of the seven treasures to fall; this is what is referred to here as a "rain of kahāpaṇas. Regarding "no satiety in sensual pleasures":
even by that rain of kahāpaṇas, there is no such thing as satiety in either sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) or sensual defilements (*kilesakāma*);

thus, this craving is difficult to fill. "Sensual pleasures have little relish and are suffering": sensual pleasures, which are like a mere dream, have little relish and offer only trifling happiness; they are nothing but suffering.
There is much more here, which should be illustrated by way of the *Dukkha-khandha Sutta*. "Thus having understood" means having known in this way.
"In celestial things" means among the forms and other objects of enjoyment belonging to the deities.

"He finds no delight" means that even when invited by celestial sensual pleasures, that meditator on insight does not find delight in them, just like the Venerable Samiddhi. "One who delights in the destruction of craving."
"Delighting in Nibbāna. For it is by coming to Nibbāna that craving is exhausted; therefore, it is called "the destruction of craving.
One delights therein, being thoroughly delighted. "A disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One" refers to a learned practitioner born within the hearing of the Buddha.
Having thus brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma and revealed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths—
The weary bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry, while many others attained the fruits of stream-entry and the higher stages.
"At that time, I myself was King Mandhātu.
This concludes the eighth commentary, the Mandhātujātaka.
[259] 9. The Commentary on the Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka:

"This knowledge does not belong to him. This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the occasion when the Venerable Ānanda received a thousand pieces of cloth—five hundred from the hands of the women of the Kosalan king and five hundred from the hands of the king himself.
He related [the story]. The background of the tale has already been explained in detail in the Guṇa Jātaka of the Second Book (Dukanipāta).
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi;
on the day his name was given, he was named Tirīṭavacchakumāra, and having gradually reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā.
Having mastered all the arts, while living as a householder, his heart was moved by the passing away of his parents;
he went forth, entered the ascetic life of an *isi*, and made his dwelling in a forest region, subsisting on roots and fruits.
While he was living there, the border regions of the King of Bārāṇasī rose in revolt, and the king went there to engage in battle.
Defeated and terrified by the fear of death, he fled on one side while mounted upon the back of an elephant and wandered into the forest.
In the morning, when Tirīṭavaccha had gone out for the sake of fruits and roots, he entered that hermitage.
Thinking, "This is a dwelling place for ascetics," he dismounted from the elephant; exhausted by the wind and heat and parched with thirst, he [sought] a water-jar.
Looking about and seeing nothing at all, he saw a well at the end of the walking path.
Not seeing a rope and jar for drawing water, and being unable to endure his thirst, he took the cord bound to the elephant’s belly,
placed the elephant on the edge of the well, tied the cord to its foot, and [lowered it] into the well with the cord.
Having descended, he could not reach the rope; having climbed back up, he tied his upper robe to the end of the rope and descended again, yet even so, it was still not enough.

Touching the water with the tips of his toes, being extremely thirsty, he thought, "Even death is better than enduring this thirst," and fell into the well. Having drunk his fill, he prepared to climb out.
Being unable to proceed, he stood right there. The elephant, too, because of its excellent training, did not go elsewhere but stood right there, looking toward the king.
In the evening, the Bodhisatta, having gathered fruits, saw the elephant and thought, "The king must have arrived;
yet only the armored elephant is visible—what could be the reason? He then approached the elephant.
He approached. The elephant, perceiving his intention to approach, stood to one side.
The Bodhisatta went to the edge of the well, and seeing the king, reassured him, saying, "Do not fear, Great King.
He then constructed a ladder, helped the king down, massaged his body, anointed it with oil, bathed him, and fed him various fruits.
He removed the elephant’s armor. After resting for two or three days, the king took a promise from the Bodhisatta to come into his presence and departed.
The royal army remained stationed, having pitched camp not far from the city.
Seeing that the king was approaching, they surrounded him, and the king entered the city.
The Bodhisatta, too, having reached Bārāṇasī after the lapse of half a month and staying in the park, went to the palace gate on the following day while wandering for alms.
The king, having opened a large window and looking out over the royal courtyard, saw the Bodhisatta;
recognizing him, he descended from the palace, paid homage, and led him up to the upper floor, where [the king sat] upon his royal couch beneath a raised white parasol.
Having had him seated and fed the food he had prepared for himself, and having eaten as well, he led him to the park;

there, having had a dwelling place constructed for him with a walking path and other requisites, and having provided all the articles necessary for the life of a renunciant, he entrusted him to a park-keeper, paid his respects, and departed.
From that time forth, the Bodhisatta resided and took his meals solely within the royal palace.
There was great honor and respect [shown to him]. Unable to endure this, the ministers said, "What would even a single soldier not do for such honor?
and approaching the viceroy, they said, "Your Majesty, our king is excessively infatuated with a certain ascetic; what—"
“Indeed, he has seen it; you too should consult with the king,” they said. He consented, saying, “Very well,” and approaching the king together with his ministers, he spoke the first verse:
“He possesses no knowledge whatsoever derived from science, neither is there any kinsman nor any friend of his.”
"Now, for what reason does Tirīṭavaccha, the bearer of the triple staff, eat the first alms-offering?
In this context, "he has no work consisting of knowledge" means that this ascetic has no work whatsoever consisting of knowledge (*vijjāmaya*).
"Neither a kinsman" means among the various types of kinsmen—namely, kinsmen by sons, kinsmen by craft, kinsmen by clan, kinsmen by lineage, and kinsmen by blood—he is none of these.
"He has none" means that he has no companion who plays with him in the dust.

"For what reason? means for what cause. "Tirīṭavaccha" is his name. "A bearer of the triple staff" (tedaṇḍika) refers to one who wanders about carrying a triple staff for the purpose of holding a water-pot (kuṇḍika).
"The finest alms-food" (aggapiṇḍa) refers to the best food, endowed with flavor and fit for a king.
Having heard that, the king addressed his son, saying, "Dear son, do you remember how I was defeated in battle at the frontier and had not returned for two or three days?
When the prince replied, "I remember," the king said, "At that time, it was by relying on him that I regained my life," and after recounting the entire account,
he said, "Dear son, when he who gave me my life comes into my presence, [give him] the kingdom..."
"Even though he gave [me this], I am not able to do anything in return that is commensurate with the merit he has performed," he said, and spoke these other two verses:
"When I was defeated in battle and alone in a terrible wilderness, he stretched out his hand to me who had fallen into distress;
thus, though overwhelmed by suffering, I crossed over."
“Because of this duty, he has arrived here from the realm of the Vessāyins in the world of the living;
O dear one, Tirīṭavaccha is worthy of gain. Give him wealth and let him perform sacrifice.
Therein, *āpāsū* means in times of distress. *Ekassa* means of one who is without a second. *Katvā* means having shown compassion and having generated affection.
"In a forest devoid of water" means in a wilderness lacking drinking water. "Terrible" means dreadful. "He extended his hand to me who had fallen into distress":
having fashioned a ladder and lowered it into the well, he extended his hand—connected with effort—for the sake of rescuing me who was beset by suffering.
"By that I crossed over, though overwhelmed by pain": for that reason, although I was surrounded by suffering, I emerged from that well.
"By his service, I have arrived here": by the service of this ascetic, by the power of the service performed by him, I have arrived here.
"The domain of Vesāyī": Vesāyī is said to be Yama; it is his domain. "In the world of the living" (*jīvaloke*): in the world of humans.
For while I was standing in this world of the living, I was as if gone to the domain of Yama, the domain of Death, the other world.
"It is for this reason that I have come here once again"—this is what is meant. "Worthy of gain" (*lābhāraho*) means he is worthy of gain;

he is one who is a fit recipient for the four requisites of gain. "Give him wealth" (*deth' assa bhogan*): give to him the wealth consisting of the four requisites for a recluse, which are to be used by him.
"And you yourself perform the sacrifice" (*yajathañca yaññaṃ*): both you, the ministers, and the citizens—all of you together.
“Give him wealth and perform a sacrifice for him. For when a gift is given to him, it becomes his wealth because he is to enjoy it;
for others, however, it is a sacrifice because of its nature as a gift and an offering. Therefore he said: “Give him wealth and perform a sacrifice for him.
Thus, when the Bodhisatta’s virtues were proclaimed by the king, as if causing the full moon to rise in the vault of the sky, [to him...]
His virtue became manifest everywhere, and his gain and honor increased even further.
From that time on, neither the viceroy, nor the ministers, nor anyone else was able to say anything against the king.

Abiding by the Bodhisatta’s counsel, the king performed meritorious deeds such as giving and filled the city of heaven. The Bodhisatta, too, [cultivated] the higher knowledges and meditative attainments.
Having generated that [state], he became one whose ultimate destination was the Brahma-world.

The Teacher, having brought forward this Dhamma teaching, saying, "Even the ancient wise ones acted out of a sense of gratitude," concluded the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the king, but the ascetic was none other than myself.
This is the ninth narrative, the Commentary on the Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka.
[260] 10. The Commentary on the Messenger Jātaka (*Dūtajātaka*).
"For whose sake messengers come from afar"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain greedy monk.
The story will be revealed in the *Cakkavāka Jātaka* in the *Navaka Nipāta*. However, the Teacher addressed that monk...

Having addressed him, [the Buddha] said, "Monk, it is not only now; in the past as well you were greedy, and for the very reason of your greed, you received the cutting off of your head with a sword," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as his son and reached maturity.
Having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and established himself in the kingdom upon his father’s passing, he became a "purifier by food.
Thus, the name *Bhojanasuddhikarāja* (King Purifier by Food) arose for him.
It is said that he ate his meal according to such a method that the value of a single bowl of rice reached one hundred thousand pieces of gold. While eating, he...

However, he did not eat at home; desiring to cause the great multitude—who were watching his own arrangements for the meal—to perform meritorious deeds, he had a jeweled pavilion constructed at the palace gate.

At the time of the meal, having had it decorated and seated upon a royal throne adorned with a raised white parasol made of gold, surrounded by noble maidens, he [ate] from a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces].

He was eating food containing every kind of flavor. Then a certain greedy man, having observed his manner of eating and desiring to eat that same food, being unable to endure his thirst, thought, "There is a stratagem.
He put on his upper garment tightly, raised his hands, and approached the king, crying out in a loud voice, "O King, I am a messenger! I am a messenger!"
At that time, people in that country did not stop anyone who said, "I am a messenger. Therefore, the great multitude split into two groups and gave him passage.
He went with speed, took a morsel of food from the king’s bowl, and placed it in his mouth.
Then the sword-bearer drew his sword, intending to cut off his head, but the king cried out, "Do not strike!"
He stopped him, saying, "Do not fear; eat," and having washed his hand, he sat down.
At the conclusion of the meal, after having water for drinking and betel leaf provided for himself, he asked, "O man, you say, 'I am a messenger'; for whom are you a messenger? [The man replied:
"Great King, I am a messenger of craving, a messenger of the belly. Craving has sent me, saying: 'You..."
Having sent a messenger with the words, "Go!", he spoke these two preceding verses:
"To whom people go even a long distance to beg, even from an enemy—of him I am the messenger to his stomach.
Do not be angry with me, O bull among charioteers."
“Whose power young men yield to, by day and by night— I am but a messenger to his belly;
do not be angry with me, O bull among chariot-warriors.

In this context, “whose purpose they follow even to a distance” means that for whose sake these beings, being enslaved by craving, go even far away. “O bull among chariot-warriors” means the foremost of those who fight from chariots.
Having heard his words, the king thought, "This is true; these beings wander about as messengers of their own bellies, driven by craving;
it is craving indeed that directs these beings. Delighted with that man, thinking, "How pleasingly this has been said!", he spoke the third verse:
"I give you, O Brahmin, a thousand Rohiṇī cows together with a bull!"
"For how could a messenger not give the message to another messenger? We too shall become his messengers.
In this context, "O Brahmins" is merely a form of address. "Of the rohis" means of those that are red in color.
"Together with the bull" means together with the leader of the herd, the ox who protects them from calamities. "We too" refers to myself and the rest.
"All beings are messengers of that very belly; therefore, since I am a messenger of the belly, why should they not give to you, who are also a messenger of the belly?
Having spoken thus, thinking, "Ah, this man has indeed spoken a reason never heard before," he was delighted in heart and bestowed great honor upon him.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that greedy monk was established in the fruit of a Once-Returner (Sakadāgāmi), while many others became Stream-Enterers (Sotāpanna) and so forth.
"The greedy man of that time was the greedy monk of the present, and the King who purified his food was none other than I myself."
The commentary on the Dūta Jātaka is the tenth.
The first chapter, the Saṅkappa Vagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
Saṅkappa, Tilamuṭṭhi, Maṇi, Sindhavāsuka;
Jarūdapāna, Gāmaṇi, Mandhātā, and Tirīṭadūta. 2.
The Chapter on the Lotus (Paduma-vagga).
[261] 1. The Commentary on the Paduma Jātaka.
The story beginning with “Just as the hair and the beard,” was told by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the monks who offered garlands at the Ānanda Bodhi tree.
The narrative will be made clear in the Kāliṅgabodhi Jātaka. That [tree], however, was planted by the Elder Ānanda...

Because it was planted by him, it became known as the "Ānanda Bodhi. Indeed, the fact that the Elder had planted the Bodhi tree at the gateway of the Jeta Grove spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

Then, some monks living in the countryside, thinking, "We shall perform a floral offering at the Ānanda Bodhi," came to the Jeta Grove, paid homage to the Teacher, and on the following day entered Sāvatthī.
Having gone to the lotus grove and returned without having obtained any garlands, they reported to the Elder Ānanda:
"Friend, we went to the lotus grove thinking, 'We shall offer a garland-worship at the Bodhi tree,' but we did not obtain even a single garland.
The Elder said, "Friends, I will bring some for you," and going to the lotus grove, he had many bunches of blue lotuses lifted up.
Having approached them, he had it given to them; they took those flowers and made an offering to the Bodhi tree.
Hearing of this occurrence, the monks in the Dhamma Hall initiated a discussion on the Elder’s virtues: "Friends, the country monks are of little merit;
having gone to Uppalavīthi, they did not obtain any garlands, yet the Elder went there and had them brought back. The Teacher, having arrived, [asked]: "What [was the subject of your conversation]?"
"Monks, for what discussion have you sat down here now? he asked.

When they replied, "For this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that those who are clever in speech and skilled in conversation receive honor; in the past as well, they received it. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was the son of a merchant. Inside the city...
In a certain lake, lotuses were in bloom. A man with a severed nose was guarding that lake.

Then one day, when a festival had been proclaimed in Bārāṇasī, three sons of merchants, wishing to wear garlands and enjoy the festivities, thought, "We will ask for the garlands by speaking falsely in praise of this man whose nose has been cut off," and as he was gathering the lotuses—
Having approached Sāriputta, they stood to one side.
One among them addressed him and spoke this first verse:
"Just as the hair of the head and the beard grow back again and again once they have been cut off,"
"May your nose thus grow back; give the lotus, as you have been asked.
He, becoming angry with him, did not give the lotus.
Then his second [companion] spoke this second verse:
“As a seed sown in the field grows in the autumn season,
so may your nose grow back, since you have been asked for a lotus.
Thereupon, he became angry even at him and did not give the lotus.
Then he spoke this third verse for a third time:
“Both of them are merely prattling on, ‘She will even give us lotuses.
Whether they speak rightly or whether they do not speak rightly, there is no growing of a nose.”
“Give me, good sir, the lotuses; I beg you, I am asked.
In this regard, “both of them prattle” means these two speak falsely.
“Perhaps he will give us the lotuses”—thinking thus, they speak in this way. “Whether they say it or not, let your nose grow! [is said] so that your nose may heal.
Whether they should speak thus or not, their word is not authoritative; in every respect, there is no growing [of flowers] from the nose.
However, I say nothing regarding your nose; I simply entreat you: "My good man, give those lotuses to me who has asked for them."
Having heard this, the guardian of the lotus pond thought, "These two have spoken falsehoods, whereas you have spoken the truth;
these lotuses are worthy of you. Taking a great bundle of lotuses, he gave them to him and returned to his own lotus pond.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, I myself was the merchant’s son Padumalābhin.
The First Exposition of the Paduma Jātaka.
2. The Exposition of the Mudupāṇi Jātaka.
“If one’s hand is soft,” etc.—the Teacher spoke this while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was disenchanted with the religious life.
The Teacher had him brought before the Dhamma Hall and asked, “Is it true, monk, that you are disenchanted?
When he replied, “It is true, Bhante,” the Teacher said, “Monk, these women are so called because they move according to the power of the defilements.”
"Even the ancient wise men were unable to protect their own daughters;
though she stood with her father’s hand grasping hers, she did not inform her father and fled with a man out of defilement," he said, and related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta [was conceived] in the womb of his chief queen.
Having been reborn and reached maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkaśilā. Upon his father’s passing, he was established in the kingdom and ruled according to the Dhamma.
While supporting both his daughter and his nephew within his own household, one day, sitting together with his ministers, he said: "After my passing, my nephew shall be king; as for my daughter—"
Having said, "I shall become his chief queen," at a later time, when his nephew had reached maturity, he sat again with his ministers and said:
"We shall bring a daughter of another king for my nephew, and we shall give our own daughter to another royal family; in this way, our kinsmen will become more numerous."
The ministers consented.
Then the king had his nephew’s quarters assigned outside the palace and forbade him from entering within. However, their hearts were bound to one another.
The prince thought, “By what means might I have the princess led outside?”
Thinking, "There is a way," he gave a bribe to the nursemaid. When she asked, "What is it, noble son?
he said, "Mother, how might we find an opportunity to get the king’s daughter out of here? She replied, "I will speak with the king’s daughter and let you know.
"Very well, mother," he said. She went and said, "Come here, mother; I will remove the lice from your head."

Having made her sit on a low seat while she herself sat on a high one, and having placed the princess’s head upon her own thighs, she scratched lice and pierced the princess’s head with her fingernails. The princess, realizing, “This person is not piercing me with her own nails;
it is the nails of my paternal uncle’s son, the prince,” said, “Mother, you [are doing this] to the prince...”
“Has he come into your presence? she asked. “Yes, mother,” he replied. “What message did he deliver?
“Mother, he asks for a means to cast you out. The princess, thinking, “Being wise, he will understand,” composed the first verse and said, “Mother, learn this and tell it to the prince.”
“If his hand were soft, and he were a well-trained elephant, and it were raining in the dark—then indeed, at that time, [it would be possible].
Having learned this, she went to the prince. When asked, “Madam, what did the princess say? she replied, “Noble son,…”

“Without saying anything else, she sent this verse,” he said, and recited that verse. The prince, having understood its meaning, dismissed her, saying, “Go, mother. The meaning of the verse is as follows:
If the hand of even one of your junior attendants were as soft as my own hand, if—
Furthermore, let there be for you a well-trained elephant as the cause for its immovability;
and suppose that on that day there were an exceedingly dense darkness accompanied by the four factors, and the rain were to fall.
"Then indeed it would happen"—in such a time, by means of these four conditions, your desire would certainly reach its fulfillment.

The Prince, having understood this matter as it truly is, prepared a handsome young attendant with supple hands as his personal servant; he gave a bribe to the keeper of the auspicious elephant and had the elephant trained for the purpose of being irresistible.
Then, waiting for the appointed time, he remained there. On a certain day of the dark fortnight, during the middle watch of the night, a thick black cloud rained down.
Thinking, "This is now the day appointed for the princess," he mounted the elephant, taking his young attendant with supple hands along.
Having seated her upon the back of an elephant and traveled [to the palace], he had the elephant lean against a great wall at a spot facing the courtyard of the royal residence;

then, having tethered it near a window, he stood there. The king, too, not wishing to let his daughter sleep elsewhere for fear of protecting her, had her lie down on a small couch by his own side. She, thinking, "The prince will come today,"...
Realizing this, she did not even descend into sleep, but while lying there said, “Father, we wish to bathe.

The king said, “Come, mother,” took her by the hand, led her near the window, and saying, “Bathe, mother,” lifted her up, placed her at the opening on the outside of the window, and stood there holding her by one hand. While she was bathing, [she spoke] to the prince...

She extended her hand; he removed the ornaments from her hand and placed them upon the hand of the attendant, then lifting her up, he set her down in front of the princess. She took her hand and placed it in her father’s hand;
he took her hand and released his daughter’s hand, and she [released] the other hand as well.
Having removed her ornaments and fastened them upon the girl’s second hand, she placed it in her father’s hand and went along with the prince.
The king, perceiving "this is indeed my daughter," had the girl laid to rest in the bedchamber at the conclusion of her bath;
he closed the door, sealed it, assigned guards, and then went to his own bed and lay down.
Thus, when the night had turned to dawn, he opened the door and, seeing that girl, asked, "What is this?
She told him how she had gone with the prince. The king, feeling remorseful, thought, "Even by holding her hand while walking, one cannot protect a woman;
thus, women are not to be protected," and spoke the other two verses:
“Flaming yet soft-spoken, difficult to satisfy like rivers;
knowing them thus, one should sink down [in indifference] and avoid them from afar.
Whatever these women pursue, whether by desire or by wealth;”
"Like fire, they quickly burn up one's standing place.
In this context, "analā mudusambhāsā" means that even with gentle words they cannot be won over; the meaning is that it is not possible to win them over with soft speech.
Alternatively, they are called *analā* because men do not find satisfaction (*ala*) in them. They are called *mudusambhāsā* because, even when their hearts are hard, there is only outward speech.
They are soft and speak softly. They are as difficult to fill as a river:

just as a river is difficult to fill because it flows with water that comes again and again, so too they are difficult to fill because they are never satisfied by successive acts of sexual intercourse and the like. Therefore it was said:
"Bhikkhus, unsatisfied and insatiable in three things, women pass away. Which three?"
"Of three things: sexual intercourse, childbirth, and adornment. Indeed, monks, it is with an insatiable and unrelenting desire for these three things that women pass away.
"They sink" means they plunge into the eight great hells and the sixteen subsidiary hells. "Nan" is merely a particle.
"Having known" means having understood thus. "One should avoid them from afar" means:
knowing that "these women, unsatisfied by sexual intercourse and other such acts, sink into these hells after death;
how can these women, who are themselves sinking in this way, bring happiness to anyone else?", a wise person avoids them from a distance—this is what is being illustrated. By desire...

Or by means of wealth, or by their own will, preference, or affection, or by wealth obtained through the power of service—those women attend upon and consort with whichever man [they choose]. *Jātavedo* is fire;
for as soon as it is born (*jāta*), it is felt (*vediyati*), known, and made manifest, thus it is *jātavedo*. Just as that [fire] consumes its own place, cause, and location, so too do these [women].

Whomever they attend upon—even if that person is endowed with wealth, fame, virtue, and wisdom—they quickly burn and consume him, rendering him incapable of ever arising again in those same attainments by destroying all his wealth and other virtues. As it is said:
"The strong become weak, and even the powerful decline."
Those with vision become blind when they have fallen under the power of women.
The virtuous become devoid of virtue, and even those possessed of wisdom decline.
The heedless lie in bondage, having fallen under the power of women.
“Study, austerity, virtue, truth, generosity, mindfulness, and wisdom—
these they snatch away from one who is heedless, just as highway robbers seize the traveler’s goods.
Fame, reputation, steadfastness, heroism, erudition, and discernment— ”
"They consume the heedless one, just as fire consumes a heap of wood.

Having spoken thus, the Great Being, thinking, "My nephew must also be supported by me," gave his daughter to him with great honor and established him in the position of viceroy. He, too, after the passing of his maternal uncle, was established in the kingdom.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. "At that time, I myself was the king."
The second commentary: The Story of Mudupāṇi.
[263] 3. The Commentary on the Cūḷapalobhana Jātaka: "When the water was not yet flowing...
This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who had become disenchanted with the religious life.
The Teacher spoke concerning this matter. Having brought him before the Dhamma Assembly, he asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are weary of the religious life?
When he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, these women cause defilement even in pure beings of old," and then related a story of the past.
In the past, in Benares, King Brahmadatta, being childless, said to his women, "Make a vow for a son.
They made vows for sons. When a long time had passed in this way, the Bodhisatta, descending from the Brahma-world, was reborn in the womb of the chief queen.
As soon as he was born, they bathed him and gave him to a nurse to suckle.
They gave it to him. While being nursed, he cried; then they gave it to another woman. When it was in the hands of a woman, he would not remain silent.
Then they gave it to a certain man who served at his feet; as soon as it was taken by him, he became silent.
From that time on, men alone carried him about. When they were nursing him with milk, they would nurse him after having him cry, or through a screen of hemp cloth.
Or they would place it in his mouth. Therefore, they gave him the name Anitthigandha Kumāra (The Boy with Unpleasant Odor).

Even as he grew from one stage to another, it was impossible for them to show him a woman. Consequently, the king had separate places for sitting and so forth, as well as a meditation chamber, built specifically for him.
Thus, when he was sixteen years old, [the king] thought: "I have no other son;
yet this prince does not enjoy sensual pleasures and will not desire even the kingdom. Alas, what a poor lot my son has!
Then, a young dancing girl, skilled in song, dance, and instrumental music, who was capable of bringing men under her influence by attending upon them, [approached him].
Having approached him, she asked, "Your Majesty, what are you thinking about? The king explained the reason to her. She said, "Very well, Your Majesty;
I shall entice him and make him experience the flavor of sensual pleasure.
"If you can entice my son, Prince Anitthigandha, he shall become king and you shall be his chief queen. She replied, "This burden is mine."
"Do not worry," she said, and having approached the guards, she spoke to them:
"I shall come at dawn, stand outside the meditation hall where the noble son lies, and sing.
If he becomes angry, you must inform me and I will depart; if he listens, you must speak my praises. They...
They accepted, saying, “Excellent.

She too, standing in that place at dawn, sang with a sweet voice, matching the sound of the lute strings to the melody of her song and the melody of her song to the sound of the lute strings without overstepping them;
the prince lay down while listening, and on the following day, in a nearby spot...
He ordered him to sing while standing [at a distance]; on the next day, he ordered him to sing while standing in the meditation hall; on the following day, he ordered him to stand near him.

In this gradual manner, having aroused desire and indulged in worldly pleasures, and having experienced the taste of sensual desire, he thought, "I shall not give women to others," and taking a sword, he went down into the middle of the street and [attacked] the men.
He wandered about, following her. Then the king had him seized and had him led out of the city together with that young woman.

Both of them entered the forest, went down along the Ganges, and having established a hermitage between the two—with the Ganges on one side and the ocean on the other—they took up residence there. The young woman stayed in a leaf-hut.
Having sat down, she cooked the roots, tubers, and other provisions, while the Bodhisatta brought fruits and nuts from the forest.
Then one day, when he had gone out for the sake of fruit and nuts, a certain ascetic from an island in the ocean was traveling through the air on his alms-round;
seeing smoke, he descended at the hermitage. Then she said to him, "Sit down, while [the food] cooks."
Having seated him and enticed him with feminine wiles, she caused him to fall from his meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and made his holy life (*brahmacariya*) disappear.
Like a crow with clipped wings, being unable to abandon her, he remained right there all day long;
then, seeing the Bodhisatta approaching, he fled swiftly toward the ocean. Then [the Bodhisatta] said to him, "O enemy..."
Thinking, "This shall be mine," he took his sword and pursued him. The ascetic displayed the appearance of leaping into the air and fell into the ocean.
The Bodhisatta thought, "This ascetic must have come through the air; having fallen away from his meditative absorption (jhāna), he has fallen into the ocean.
It is fitting that I should become his support. Standing on the shore, he spoke these verses:
“Though the waters were not overflowing, you came yourself by means of psychic power;
having gone to the woman who was mingled with others, you sank into the great ocean.
‘The Great Illusion is alluring, a subverter of the holy life.’”
Knowing this, they sink down; one should avoid them from afar.
"Whatever these women pursue, whether by desire or by wealth, they quickly burn him up, like a fire consuming its own place."
In that context, "when the water was undisturbed" means when this water was not moving or shaking;

having arrived through the air by means of psychic power (*iddhi*) without touching the water. "Intercourse with women" refers to becoming mixed with women due to the influence of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
"The Enchantress, the Great Illusionist": these women are called "the Enchantress" because they entice by means of the lure of sensual desire.
She was named Mahāmāyā because she was endowed with infinite feminine wiles (itthimāyā). For this has been said:
“Deceit and mirages, grief and disease, calamity;
These are harsh bonds, the snare of Death dwelling in the cave.”
“The man who places his trust in them is the lowest among men.
“The subversion of the holy life” (*brahmacariyavikopana*) means the subversion of the supreme practice, the holy life characterized by abstinence from sexual intercourse. “Sinking” (*sīdanti*):
women indeed sink into the states of misery (*apāya*) through the subversion of the holy life of the seers (*isī*). The remainder should be construed in the same manner as previously explained.

Having heard these words of the Bodhisatta, the ascetic, while still standing in the midst of the ocean, re-aroused his lost meditative absorption (jhāna) and departed through the air for his own dwelling place. The Bodhisatta thought:
"Even though this ascetic was so heavy, he has gone through the air like a tuft of *simbali* cotton; I too shall arouse meditative absorption just as he did."
"It is fitting to travel through the air. Having gone to the hermitage, he led that woman to a human settlement and dismissed her, saying, "Go now.
Then, entering the forest, he established a hermitage on a delightful spot of ground.

Having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, he performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and became destined for the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. "At that time, I myself was the youth Anitthigandha.
This concludes the third narrative, the Cūḷapalobhana Jātaka.
4. The Mahāpanāda Jātaka Narrative.
"He was the king named Panāda"—this the Teacher spoke while seated on the bank of the Ganges, concerning the power of the Elder Bhaddaji.

For at one time, after spending the rains retreat in Sāvatthī, the Teacher—thinking, "I shall provide for the young man Bhaddaji"—set out on a journey surrounded by the community of monks; having reached the city of Bhaddiya, he stayed in the Jātiyā Grove.
He dwelt there for three months, awaiting the ripening of the Prince’s wisdom.
Prince Bhaddaji was the only son of the wealthy merchant Bhaddiya, whose fortune amounted to eight hundred million. For him, there were three palaces suited to the three seasons.
He would dwell in each one for four months; having stayed in one, surrounded by his theatrical troupe and great splendor, he would move on.
He went to another palace. At that moment, thinking, "We shall see the glory of the prince," the entire city was stirred;
they constructed tier upon tier of platforms and level upon level of galleries within the palace.
After staying for three months, the Teacher announced to the city-dwellers, "We are going. The citizens said, "Venerable Sir,..."

“May you come tomorrow,” they invited the Teacher. On the following day, having prepared a great almsgiving for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, they erected a pavilion in the center of the city, adorned it, arranged seats, and announced that the time had come.
The Teacher, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, went there and sat down; the people then presented the great almsgiving.
When the Teacher had finished his meal, he began the expression of thanks with a sweet voice.

At that moment, Prince Bhaddaji was going from palace to palace; on that day, no one went with him to see his splendor, for he was surrounded only by his own attendants. He asked his men: "At other times, when I go from palace to palace..."
"As they go about, the entire city is thrown into agitation; they are setting up wheel-against-wheel and couch-against-couch.
But today, apart from my men, there is no one else here. What could be the reason?
"Master, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having stayed near this city of Bhaddiya for three months, will depart this very day. He has finished his meal."
Having finished his meal, he taught the Dhamma to the great multitude, and all the inhabitants of the city listened to his discourse on the Dhamma.
[The king] thought, "In that case, come along; we too shall listen. Adorned with all his ornaments and accompanied by a large retinue, he approached and stood at the edge of the assembly.
While listening to the Dhamma, even as he stood there, he eradicated all defilements.
He attained the fruit of the highest path, Arhatship.
The Teacher addressed the merchant Bhaddiya: "Great merchant, your son has established himself in Arhatship while listening to the Dhamma discourse, still fully adorned and prepared;
therefore, it is fitting for him either to go forth this very day or to attain final Nibbāna."
[The Blessed One] said, “Or so. [The man replied,] “Venerable Sir, there is no further need for my son’s parinibbāna; let him go forth.
Having let him go forth, please take him with you and visit our home tomorrow.
The Blessed One accepted the invitation, took the young man of good family to the monastery, granted him the going-forth, and had him receive full ordination. To him—
The parents performed great honors for seven days. Having stayed for seven days, the Teacher took the young man with him and, while wandering on his journey, arrived at Koṭigāma.
The people dwelling in Koṭigāma gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher began the expression of thanks. At the time when the expression of thanks was being made, the young man—

Having gone outside the village, he thought, "I shall rise up at the very moment the Teacher arrives," and so he sat down at the foot of a tree near the Ganges ford, having attained meditative absorption (jhāna). Even when the elder monks were approaching, he did not rise;
rather, he rose only at the moment the Teacher arrived. The ordinary monks (puthujjana) [said], "This man, having gone forth as before, [disregards] the great elders..."
They became angry, saying, "Even seeing him approaching, he does not rise.
The people living in Koṭigāma moored their boats together in a fleet. The Teacher stood upon the moored boats and asked, "Where is Bhaddaji?
"He is right here, Bhante," they replied. "Come, Bhaddaji, [board] the same boat as us."
"Come aboard! The Elder also leaped up and stood upon the same boat.
Then, when they had reached the middle of the Ganges, the Teacher said, "Bhaddaji, where is the palace you inhabited during the time of King Mahāpanāda?
"It is submerged at this spot, Bhante," he replied. The ordinary monks said, "The Elder Bhaddaji is explaining something other than what he knows."
The Teacher said, “In that case, Bhaddaji, dispel the doubt of your fellow celibates.

At that moment, the Elder paid homage to the Teacher, went by means of his power of psychic potency, and taking the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe, he lifted the twenty-five-league palace and rose into the air.
Having risen, he shattered the palace for those standing below it.
It became visible. He lifted the palace out of the water to the height of one league, two leagues, three leagues, and so on up to twenty leagues.

Then his kinsmen from a previous existence—who, out of greed for the palace, had been reborn as fish, turtles, nāgas, and frogs in that very palace—turned over and over again and fell back into the water as the palace rose up. The Teacher...
Seeing them falling, he said, "Bhaddaji, your kinsmen are suffering. Having heard the Teacher's words, the Elder released the palace;
the palace settled back in its original place, and the Teacher went to the further bank of the Ganges.
Then they prepared a seat for him right there on the bank of the Ganges, and upon that excellent Buddha-seat thus prepared, he sat like the rising sun with its rays.
He sat down, letting [the water] flow out. Then the bhikkhus asked him, "Venerable sir, at what time did the Elder Bhaddaji dwell in this palace?
The Teacher said, "During the time of King Mahāpanāda," and related the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Videha, in Mithilā, there was a king named Suruci; his son was also named Suruci. Of him—
Furthermore, his son was named Mahāpanāda, and they obtained this palace.
As for the prior karma for its acquisition: two father and son built a leaf-hut for a Paccekabuddha using reeds and udumbara wood.
In this Jātaka, the entire background story will be revealed in the Suruci Jātaka of the Pakiṇṇakanipāta.
The Teacher, having brought this past event to mind, spoke these verses while being the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“That king was named Panāda, whose sacrificial post was made of gold;
it was sixteen spans across and, they say, a thousand spans in height.”
“With a thousand shafts and a hundred joints, adorned with banners and made of gold,
six thousand gandhabbas danced there in seven groups.
Thus it was then, Bhaddaji, just as you have described.”
"I was Sakka at that time, your attendant.
In this context, "the sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) refers to the palace. "Sixteen spans across" means it was sixteen *kaṇḍapāta* in width.
"They say it was a thousand high" means it was as tall as a thousand *kaṇḍa*-lengths; by the calculation of a thousand *kaṇḍa*-lengths, it was exceedingly lofty.
It was twenty-five yojanas in height, while its width was eight yojanas.
As for the phrase "sahassakaṇḍo satageṇḍu," that palace had a thousand pillars and was ten stories high;
it was "dhajālū" (possessing banners), meaning it was well-equipped with banners; and "haritāmayo" means it was surrounded by green gems. However, in the commentary, it says "samāluharitāmayo."
The meaning is that it was furnished with door-panels and windows made of green gems.
*Samālū* is said to be the name for door-panels and windows. "Gandhabbas" refers to actors;
six thousand of them, having divided into seven groups, danced in seven locations within that palace for the sake of producing delight for the king.
This is the meaning. Although they danced in this manner, they were unable to make the king laugh. Then Sakka, the King of the Devas, sent celestial dancers and held a festival;
at that time, Mahāpanāda laughed.
Regarding the words "As you say, Bhaddaji," it was by the Elder Bhaddaji that [it was said]: "Bhaddaji, during the time of King Mahāpanāda..."
When it was asked, "Where is the palace you inhabited?", he replied, "It has sunk into this place, Bhante.
By saying this, he spoke of how, at that time, he had caused that palace to be built for his own sake and held the status of King Mahāpanāda.
Taking that up, the Teacher said: "Bhaddaji, just as you say, so it was exactly like that at that time."
“At that time, Sakka, the lord of the gods, was your personal attendant,” he said. At that moment, the monks who were still ordinary worldlings became free from doubt.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, King Mahāpanāda was Bhaddaji, and Sakka was none other than myself.
This is the fourth commentary on the Mahāpanāda Jātaka.
[265] 5. The Commentary on the Khurappa Jātaka.
Having seen the arrow-head: This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who had slackened his energy.
For the Teacher, having asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you have slackened your energy? and he having replied, "It is true," said:
When he had said, "Venerable sir," [the Buddha] replied, "Monk, why have you slackened your energy after going forth in this teaching that leads to liberation?
Even ancient wise men exerted their energy in matters that do not lead to liberation. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of forest-protectors in a certain wilderness.

Having been reborn and reached maturity, he became the senior leader among five hundred forest guards with a retinue of five hundred men, and he made his dwelling in a village at the entrance of the forest.
Taking wages, he escorted people across the forest.
Then one day, the son of a caravan leader from Bārāṇasī arrived at that village with five hundred wagons.
Having summoned him, he said, "Friend, take a thousand pieces of money and escort me across the forest. He replied, "Very well," and took the thousand from his hand;
even as he was receiving the wage, he surrendered his own life for him.
Taking him, he entered the forest. In the middle of the forest, five hundred bandits rose up; seeing the bandits, the remaining men—
They lay down for the night. Only the chief guard, shouting, roaring, and striking out, drove away even the five hundred bandits and enabled the caravan leader’s son to cross the wilderness safely.
Having established camp in the foreign wilderness, the caravan leader’s son [provided] the chief guard with various foods of exquisite flavor.
Having fed him and having himself finished his morning meal, sitting comfortably and conversing with him,
he asked, "Friend, when you were attacking those most cruel thieves while grasping their weapons,
for what reason did not even a slight tremor of fear arise in your mind? and spoke the first verse.
“Having seen the arrows impelled by the force of the bow, and the sharp swords grasped and polished with oil;
when that terror of death was arrayed, why indeed did you not experience paralysis?
In this context, *dhanuveganunne* means discharged by the force of the bow. *Khagge gahīte* means firmly grasped by the hilt-handles.
"Khagge" means at the time of death; "viyūḷhe" means when death has presented itself. "Kasmā nu te nāhu" means for what reason indeed were you not [afraid]?
"Chambhitattaṃ" means trembling of the body.
Having heard that, the chief guardian recited the other two verses:
“Having seen the arrows impelled by the force of the bow, and the sharp swords grasped and polished with oil;
when that terrifying death was arrayed, I attained vast and sublime knowledge.
Born of that knowledge, I overcame my enemies; even before this, my life had already been surrendered.”
"For one who makes no attachment to life, a hero will never fail to perform his heroic duty.
In this context, "I obtained joy" means I attained satisfaction and gladness. "Vipula" means abundant.
"Uḷāra" means supreme. "Ajjhabhaviṃ" means I overcame [all fear] by relinquishing my life. "Even before, my life was already abandoned" means...
"Even while receiving wages from your hand, I previously gave up my life.
For one who makes a dwelling in life—that is, one who forms an attachment to life—never performs his manly duty.
Thus, because he had abandoned attachment to life while the rain was falling in torrents, he [perceived] that he himself had performed the task of a hero."
Having made this known and sent away the caravan leader’s son, he returned to his own village, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and departed according to his karma.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who had slackened his energy was established in Arahatship. “At that time, I myself was the chief guard.
This is the fifth narrative, the Khurappa Jātaka.
[266] 6. The Commentary on the Vātaggasindhava Jātaka.
"By whom you were made thin and pale"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain householder in Sāvatthī.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a beautiful woman who, upon seeing a handsome householder, [fell in love with him].
Her mind became bound [to him], and as if her entire body were burning, the fire of the defilements arose within her.
She obtained neither physical satisfaction nor mental satisfaction; even food no longer appealed to her, and she simply lay down, clutching the frame of her bed.
Then her attendants and companions asked her: "What is the matter with you?"
“With a trembling heart, she took hold of the bedpost and lay down; what is it that makes you unwell?
Without speaking once or twice, she was told again and again until she related the matter.
Then, having comforted her, they said, “Do not worry; we shall bring him to you,” and having gone there, they consulted with the householder, who refused.
Though she was told again and again, she consented.
They took her leave, saying, "Come on such-and-such a day at such-and-such a time," and having gone, they informed her. She prepared her bedchamber, adorned herself, and sat upon the bed.
When he arrived and sat down on one side of the bed, she thought: "If I..."
“Without treating this as a serious matter, I shall grant permission right now; otherwise my authority will diminish.
Granting permission on the very day one arrives is improper; today I shall not cause him distress, but will grant permission on another day.
Then, as he began to play with her by taking her hand and so forth, [the other] took his hand and said, “Go away, go away! Do not—”
“I have no need for you,” she rebuked him. He, shrinking back in shame, rose up and went straight to his own home.
When the other women learned what she had done, they approached her after the householder had departed and spoke to her thus:
“You lay down there, refusing food, because your heart was bound to him; then we [pressed him] again and again...”
“We requested her and brought her here; why did you not grant her an audience? She explained the matter to them.
The other woman said, “In that case, you shall be known,” and they departed. The householder, however, did not even look back when he turned away.
Failing to obtain him, she died right there from lack of food. When the householder learned of her death, he...
Taking many garlands, perfumes, and ointments, he went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.

When the Teacher asked him, "Upāsaka, why have you not been seen for some time?", he explained the matter and said, "Venerable Sir, out of shame I did not come to attend upon the Buddha for all this time. The Teacher said, "Upāsaka, it is not so..."
"Now, by means of her defilements, she summoned him and, when he had arrived, she put him to shame by giving him no place [to stay].
But previously also, having fixed her heart on the wise man, she summoned him and, when he had arrived, gave him no place and sent him away after making him suffer.
Having said this, being requested by him, she related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī,
the Bodhisatta was reborn in a Sindhu horse family and became a horse named Vātagga-sindhava, serving as his state charger. When the grooms led him to bathe in the Ganges,
a she-donkey named Bhaddalī saw him and, her heart becoming bound to him, out of the power of defilement—
Trembling, she neither ate grass nor drank water; having withered away, she became mere skin and bone.
Then her son, the young donkey, seeing his mother wasting away, said:
"Mother, why is it that you neither eat grass nor drink water? Having withered away, you lie here and there trembling?"
“What is it that makes you unwell? he asked. Without speaking at first, she was eventually made to tell him the matter after being questioned again and again.
Then her son, having comforted her, said, “Mother, do not worry; I shall bring you [him].
When the horse Vātaggasindhava returned from bathing, he approached him and said, “Father, my mother’s heart is bound to you, and she has gone without food.”
"She will die from dehydration; give her the gift of life," he said. "Very well, dear one, I shall give it.
The horse-keepers will bathe me and release me for a short while to wander along the bank of the Ganges;
you take your mother and go to that place. He went, brought his mother, released her in that spot, and stood concealed to one side.
The keepers of the horses also released the noble Sindhu horse at that spot. He looked toward the she-ass and approached her.
Then, as he drew near and was sniffing her body, the she-ass thought:
"If I grant him access right now, without showing him respect, my reputation and my authority will diminish."
Thinking, "It is better to act as if I do not wish for this," she struck the hind ankle of the Sindhava horse with her foot and fled;
the roots of his tusks broke and it was as if he had already departed. The Wind-Swift Sindhava, thinking, "What use have I for her?
and feeling ashamed, fled from that very spot. She, filled with remorse, fell down right there and lay weeping.
Then her son approached her and, asking, spoke this first verse:
“By whom you have become thin and pale, by whom food is no longer pleasing—here is that husband come; why do you flee now?”
In that context, "by which" means by reason of that state of having a mind bound [to him].
Having heard her son's words, the she-ass spoke this second verse:
"But if intimacy indeed arises from the very first moment;..."
“Fame declines for women; therefore, dear one, flee from them.

In this regard, “from the very beginning” means right at the start, first of all. “Intimacy” refers to intimacy with friends by way of association through sexual intercourse. Regarding the phrase “fame declines for women”:
dear one, for those women who do not treat [the husband] with respect and instead cultivate intimacy from the very outset, fame declines.
“Her reputation declines, and her pride in power and status diminishes. Thus she explained the true nature of women to her son.
But after he had attained full enlightenment, the Teacher spoke the third verse:
“She who does not welcome one born into a family of renown when he has arrived—”
"She grieves for a long night, like a *bhaddalī* cow struck by the wind.

In this context, "renowned" (*yasassim*) means endowed with fame. "She who does not desire him" refers to that woman who does not desire such a man. "For a long night" (*cirarattāya*) means for a long time, for a long duration; this is the meaning.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and proclaimed the Truths (*saccāni*), the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths...
The householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the female donkey was that woman, and I myself was the noble stallion Vātaggasindhava.
This concludes the sixth discourse, the Vātaggasindhava Jātaka.
[267] 7. The Commentary on the Kakkaṭaka-jātaka (The Crab Birth Story).
"The deer with horns"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain woman.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain householder took his wife and went to the countryside to clear up a debt. Having cleared the debt, he...
While returning after having purified himself, he was seized by bandits along the way. His wife, however, was beautiful, charming, and lovely to behold;
out of affection for her, the chief of the bandits began to kill the householder. But that woman was virtuous, endowed with good conduct, and devoted to her husband;
she fell at the feet of the chief of the bandits and said, "Master, if you have affection for me..."
"There is a way; do not kill my husband. If you kill him, I too shall die by taking poison or by suffocating myself with the breath of a snake, but I will not go with you.
Do not kill my husband for no reason," she entreated, and thus she had him released. Both of them reached Sāvatthī safely, and [resided] at the Jetavana Piṭṭhivihāra.

As they were going along, thinking, “We shall enter the monastery and pay homage to the Teacher,” they went to the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side. When the Teacher asked them, “Where have you been coming from, lay followers?
they replied, “To clear up our debts. When he asked, “Did you come along the way in good health? the householder said, “Along the way—”
"No, venerable sir, the thieves seized me; there, while I was being led to execution, she entreated the chief thief and set me free.
It is by depending on her that I have obtained my life. The Teacher said, "Lay follower, it was not only now that she gave you your life in this way;
in the past as well, she gave life even to wise men. Having been requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a great lake of water in the Himalayas.
There lived a great golden crab, and because it resided there, the lake became known as "Kuḷīradaha" (the Crab Lake). The crab was enormous, the size of a threshing floor;
it would seize elephants, kill them, and eat them. Out of fear of him, the elephants did not descend there to graze.
They were unable to do so. At that time, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a female elephant by depending upon the leader of a herd of elephants living near the Kuḷīra Lake.
Then his mother, thinking, "I shall protect the fetus," went to another mountain region; having protected the fetus there, she gave birth to her son. He gradually reached the age of discretion.
Having attained a great body, endowed with strength, and reached the height of fortune, he became like a mountain of añjana.
Having lived in union with a single female elephant, thinking, "I shall seize the crab," he took his wife and mother and approached that herd of elephants;
seeing his father, he said, "Father, I shall seize the crab."
He said. Then his father, having restrained him who was speaking again and again with the words, "You will not be able to do it, dear son," said, "You yourself shall know.
He gathered all the elephants living near the crab pond and went with them all to the vicinity of the pond, [inquiring]:
"Does that crab catch him at the time of descending, or at the time of gathering food, or at the time of ascending?"

Having asked him, and hearing that it was "time to cross," he said, "In that case, you all should descend into the crab-pool, take as much fodder as you need, and cross first; I will follow behind. The elephants did accordingly.
As the Bodhisatta was crossing behind, the crab seized him with its great pincers, just as a blacksmith seizes an iron rod with his large tongs.
With his two claws, as if with iron, he seized the Bodhisatta’s foot firmly; the female elephant, not abandoning the Bodhisatta, stood right nearby.
The Bodhisatta tried to pull the crab away but could not move it, while the crab, pulling him toward itself, turned him face-to-face.
Terrified by the fear of death, he let out a piercing cry, and all the elephants were likewise struck with the fear of death.
Letting out a cry like a peacock and discharging urine and dung, they fled; his female elephant, unable to remain, also began to flee.
Then, making her aware that he was bound, he spoke the first verse in order to prevent her from fleeing: 49.
"There, the golden deer..."—in this context, *siṅgī* means a deer of golden color. By means of two antlers, he performed the function of horns.
The meaning of *siṅgī* is "yoked" (*yuttatāya*). As for the term "deer" (*miga*), it is used here to refer to the crab (*kuḷīra*) in the sense of including all living beings.
Regarding the phrase "with long eyes and eyelashes" (*āyatacakkhunetta*): here, "eye" (*cakkhu*) is in the sense of seeing, and "eyelash" (*netta*) is in the sense of leading.
Thus, one whose eyelashes—which are designated as "eyes"—are long is "one with long eyes and eyelashes"; the meaning is "one with long eyes. His shell alone performs the function of skin.
"Bone and skin": "Overpowered by that" means being overpowered, overwhelmed, and rendered motionless by that deer.
"I weep piteously" means, having fallen into a state of compassion, I weep and cry out. "Do not indeed abandon me" means:
do not indeed forsake me, your own dear husband who is like your very life, now that I have met with such calamity.
Then that female elephant, having turned back and consoling him, spoke this second verse:
“Noble sir, I will not abandon you, the sixty-year-old elephant;
for you, Suppiya, have been my very own throughout the four quarters of the earth.”
In this context, "sixty years" means that at the age of sixty, elephants decline in their physical strength.
Thinking, "I shall not abandon this one who has reached such a calamity and is thus deprived of strength;
do not fear," she said, "For among this four-cornered earth which reaches the ocean in its four directions, you are very dear to me."
Then, having steadied her, she said, "Noble sir, now I shall cause you to release him by engaging you in a brief conversation," and requesting the crab, she spoke this third verse:
"Of all the crabs in the ocean, in the Ganges, and in the Yamunā, you are the best of those born in water;
release the husband of this weeping woman."

The meaning of this is as follows: "Of all the crabs in the ocean, or in the Ganges, or in the Yamunā, you alone are the best and most excellent by virtue of your perfect color and your great size. Therefore, I entreat you: release my husband while I am weeping.
As she was speaking, the crab, perceiving the sign in her feminine voice, became drawn toward her;
while withdrawing his claws from the elephant's foot, he did not realize anything, thinking, "Once released, she will do such-and-such. Then—
One elephant, lifting his foot, stepped on him on the back; at that very moment, his bones shattered.
The elephant let out a cry of joy. All the elephants gathered together, pulled the crab out, placed him upon the ground, and trampled him until he was reduced to powder.
Two of his claws broke off from his body and fell to one side. And so it was with Kuḷīradaha.
The *gaṅgā-ekābaddha* is as follows: when the Ganges is full, it is filled with Ganges water; when the water subsides, the burning [fire] descends into the Ganges.
Then those two *aḷā* floated away and were carried by the current of the Ganges. Of these, one entered the ocean;
the other the ten brothers, the kings, while playing in the water, caught and made into a drum called an *āḷiṅga*.
When the ocean had entered its bed, the asuras took it and fashioned a drum called Ālambara.
Later, having been defeated by Sakka in battle, they abandoned it and fled; then Sakka had it seized for his own use.
It is with reference to this that people say, "He thunders like the Ālambara-cloud."
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:

“At that time, the female elephant was this female lay disciple, and the male elephant was I myself. At the conclusion of the Truths, both husband and wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The seventh is the Commentary on the *Kakkaṭaka-jātaka*.
[268] 8. The Commentary on the *Ārāmadūsaka-jātaka*:
"He who indeed is equal toward all... This was spoken by the Teacher concerning a certain son of a park-keeper in the Dakkhiṇāgiri country.
He spoke concerning this. It is said that after the Teacher had completed his rains retreat, he departed from Jetavana and wandered on a journey through the country of Dakkhiṇāgiri.
Then a certain lay follower invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, seated them in a park, and having satisfied them with rice gruel and solid food, said:
"Venerable sirs, if you wish to go for a stroll in the park, [you may do so] together with this park-keeper."
Having said, "Let them wander," he commanded the park-keeper: "You should give fruits to the noble ones.
As the bhikkhus were wandering, they saw a spot that was bare and with sparse trees, and they asked, "This place is bare and has thin foliage;
what could be the reason for this? Then the park-keeper explained to them: "It seems there was a son of a park-keeper who, regarding the planted trees..."
“While pouring water, thinking, ‘I will pour it up to the level of the roots,’ he uprooted [the tree] and poured the water up to the level of the roots;
by that means, that spot became a hole. The monks went into the presence of the Teacher and reported this matter.
The Teacher said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past as well, that boy was a destroyer of groves,” and he related a story of the past.

In the past, while King Vissasena was ruling in Bārāṇasī, when a festival had been proclaimed, the park-keeper, thinking, "I shall enjoy the festival," said to the monkeys living in the park: "This park is of great benefit to you;
I shall enjoy the festival for seven days, so you must water the plants for seven days. They...
“Very well,” they replied and accepted. He gave them leather water-bags and departed.
As the monkeys were pouring water, they poured it onto the upper parts of the plants. Then the elder monkey said to them: “Wait a moment;
water is indeed difficult to obtain at all times, so it must be preserved. One should pull out the plants, determine the depth of their roots, and [pour] it upon those with long roots.”
"In the case of many [plants] with short roots, it is necessary to pour only a small amount of water.
They replied, "Very well," and some went away after uprooting the young plants, while others planted them and poured water on them.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was the son of a certain family in Bārāṇasī; he, for some business or other...
Having gone to the park and seeing those monkeys acting in such a manner, he asked, "Who is making you do this?
When they replied, "The leader of the monkeys," he said, "Such is the wisdom of your leader; but what will yours be like?
And explaining that matter, he spoke this first verse:
“He who was esteemed as the best among all those who were equal—such is his wisdom; what then can be said of other folk?

In this context, “among all those who were equal” means among all these of the same kind. “Ahuvā” means he was. “What then can be said of other folk? refers to those other inferior people among them; one wonders what kind of wisdom they possess.
Having heard his words, the monkeys spoke this second verse:
“Just so, O Brahmā, you revile us without knowing anything;
how can one know that a tree is firmly established without having seen its roots?”
In this context, "O Brahmin" is merely a form of address. This, however, is the summary of the meaning here:
"O man, you revile us in this manner without knowing what is right and what is wrong. For how can one know whether a tree is 'planted deep' or not without first uprooting it?
Therefore, we shall uproot it and water it according to the extent of its roots."
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:
“I do not reproach you, nor those other monkeys in the forest;
But one who has planters of trees for his own benefit is indeed to be censured.”

"In this matter, Vissasena alone is to be blamed" means that here it is King Vissasena of Bārāṇasī who is to be censured. "For whose sake you plant trees" means for whose sake people like you have become tree-planters.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the elder monkey was the prince who ruined the park, while the wise man was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka, the eighth.
[269] 9. The Commentary on the Sujāta Jātaka.

"For one endowed with beauty..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Sujāta, the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya, the sister-in-law of Anāthapiṇḍika, and the younger sister of Visākhā. It is said that she...
Filling the house of Anāthapiṇḍika with great splendor, she entered; yet, being stiff with pride, thinking, "I am the daughter of a great family," she was irascible, fierce, and harsh.
She did not perform her duties toward her mother-in-law, father-in-law, or husband, and she lived about threatening and striking the members of the household.
Then one day, the Teacher, surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus, [arrived at] Anāthapiṇḍika’s...
Having gone home, he sat down. While listening to the Dhamma, the Great Merchant sat close to the Blessed One;
at that moment, Sujātā was quarreling with the slaves and laborers. The Teacher paused his discourse on the Dhamma and asked, "What is this noise?
"Venerable Sir, this daughter-in-law of our family is disrespectful; she does not perform her duties toward her mother-in-law, father-in-law, or husband."
“There are those who are faithless and lacking confidence, who spend their days and nights quarreling. “In that case, summon her,” [the Teacher said].
She came, paid homage, and stood to one side.
Then the Teacher asked her, “Sujātā, there are these seven kinds of wives for a man; which of them are you?”
“Venerable sir, I do not understand the meaning of what was spoken in brief; please explain it to me in detail.
The Teacher said, “In that case, listen with an attentive ear,” and spoke these verses:
“One whose mind is corrupted, who lacks compassion, who is devoted to others and treats her husband with contempt—”
A wife who, for the sake of killing her husband, is eager to acquire wealth—
such a woman as this is called both a murderer and a wife.
Whatever wealth a husband acquires through his wife— whether by means of a craft, trade, or agriculture, or by exerting himself— [it belongs to her].
She even wishes to steal away his wealth; such a wife as this is called a wife who is a thief.
[2] “One who is unwilling to work, lazy, gluttonous, harsh, fierce, and a speaker of evil words—”
She who prevails over those who rise up [against her], such a wife of a man is called both "mistress" and "wife.
[3] She who at all times is benevolent and compassionate, protecting her husband as a mother protects her son—
Then she protects the wealth he has accumulated. A wife of such a kind for a man is called both "mother" and "wife.
