One who is well-behaved, virtuous, and devoted—such a wife as this is called both a friend and a wife.
[6] “When threatened with violence or punishment, she remains free from anger;
with a mind devoid of malice, she endures her husband.”
“Free from anger, obedient to her husband—such a wife as this is called both a slave and a wife. [7] These, Sujātā, are the seven kinds of wives for a man.
Among them, those who are like executioners, like thieves, and like mistresses—these three are reborn in hell; the other four are reborn in the Nimmānarati deva world.
“Those women here who are called ‘murderers,’ or who are called ‘thieves’ and ‘noble ladies,’ being immoral in nature,
harsh, and disrespectful— they go to hell after the breakup of the body.
Those women here who are called ‘mother,’ ‘sister,’ ‘friend,’ or who are called ‘slave’ and ‘wife’— ”
“Because they were established in virtue and long restrained, at the breaking up of the body, they go to a happy destination.
While the Teacher was thus showing these seven wives, Sujātā became established in the fruit of stream-entry.
When asked, “Sujātā, which of these seven wives are you? she replied, “I am like a slave-girl, Bhante.”
Having paid homage to the Tathāgata, she asked for his forgiveness. Thus, having subdued Sujātā, his daughter-in-law, with a single exhortation, the Teacher finished his meal and went to Jetavana.
When the Bhikkhu Saṅgha had performed the customary duties, he entered the Fragrant Chamber.
And in the Hall of Truth, the Bhikkhus raised a discussion on the virtues of the Teacher: "Friends, with a single exhortation..."
“Having tamed Sujātā, his daughter-in-law, the Teacher established her in the fruit of stream-entry.
When the Teacher returned and asked, “Monks, with what discussion are you gathered here now? and they replied, “With this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, I tamed Sujātā with a single instruction. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered all arts at Takkaśilā; after his father’s passing, he established himself on the throne and ruled the kingdom with righteousness and equity.
His mother, however, was prone to anger, fierce, harsh, abusive, and insulting.
Thus, although he wished to give his mother advice, thinking it improper to speak without a basis, he wandered about looking for a simile to instruct her.
Then one day he went to a pleasure grove, and his mother went along with him.
On the way, a partridge bird cried out; the Bodhisatta’s retinue, hearing that sound, [covered] their ears.
Having closed [the door], he said, "O you of fierce speech, you of harsh speech, do not make a sound!
But while the Bodhisatta was wandering in the park with his mother, surrounded by a theatrical troupe, a single cuckoo perched upon a *sāla* tree in full bloom uttered its cry in a sweet voice.
The great multitude, captivated by that sound, raised their joined palms and said, "O you of gentle speech..."
With gentle and soft words, saying, "Rain, rain! he stood there with his neck uplifted, listening intently and looking about.

Then the Great Being, seeing those two reasons, thought, "Now I shall be able to persuade my mother," and said, "Mother, on the way we heard the cry of a quail, and the great multitude cried out, 'Do not make a sound! Do not make a sound! covering their ears..."
“Shut your mouth! Harsh speech is not dear to anyone,” he said, and spoke these verses:
“For those who are endowed with beauty, sweet-voiced, and pleasant to look upon— Even they do not become dear if their speech is harsh, neither in this world nor in the next.”
“Do we not see this Kālī, so ill-favored and covered in moles?
Yet the cuckoo, by its sweet voice, is dear to many living beings.
Therefore, one who speaks kindly, who speaks with measured words and is composed, [is likewise beloved].”
“He illuminates the goal and the Dhamma; his speech is sweet.

This is the meaning for them: “O mothers, these beings, though endowed with a bodily complexion like that of the *piyaṅgu* flower and so forth, and being sweet-voiced through the sweetness of their speech, and lovely to behold due to their beauty—even while they are thus, they [behave] toward even their own parents by means of abuse, revilement, and the like.”
Because one who is endowed with harsh speech is so possessed, such a person is not beloved in this world or the next;
like a harpy (*kikī*) with harsh speech on the road, they are disliked.
But those who speak gently, endowed with smooth and sweet speech, are beloved even if they are ugly. Therefore I say this to you: do you not see this Kāḷī, who is ill-favored?
Even a cuckoo, though struck by dark spots that make it darker in color than its body, becomes dear to many despite being so ill-favored in appearance because of its sweet-sounding voice.

Thus, since a being with harsh speech is disliked even by his own parents in this world, a person who desires to be dear to the multitude should be gentle in speech, possessing a soft, smooth, and mild voice. By means of wisdom, which is termed *manta*...

One who speaks with deliberation (*mantabhāṇī*) is so called because they speak after having made a thorough assessment; one who is not agitated (*anuddhata*) is so called because they speak with moderation, free from restlessness.
When such a person elucidates both the text (*pāḷi*) and the meaning (*attha*), their speech is called "sweet" (*madhura*) because it is based on reason and spoken without reviling others.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma to his mother with these three verses, made her understand; from that time forth, she became endowed with proper conduct. The Bodhisatta, too, having rendered his mother free from reproach with a single word, departed according to his karma.
The Teacher, having brought forward this teaching of the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Sujātā was the mother of the King of Bārāṇasī, but the King was none other than myself.
This is the ninth narrative of the Sujāta-jātaka.
[270] 10. The Commentary on the Ulūka-jātaka:
"By all their kinsmen," it is said—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a quarrel between crows and owls.
At that time, the crows were devouring the owls during the day, while the owls [were devouring them] there starting from sunset.
There, they would cut off the heads of the crows lying there and bring them to their death.
Now, one day, while a certain bhikkhu was dwelling in a small cell on the outskirts of Jetavana, seven or eight, or even more, crow-heads had to be discarded by him from a tree as he was sweeping.
He reported this matter to the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus...
In the Dhamma Hall, they raised this discussion: "Friends, it is said that in the dwelling place of such-and-such a bhikkhu, as many crow-heads as these must be discarded day after day.
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you gathered here now? The bhikkhus replied, "About this very one."
“Venerable sir, from when did the mutual enmity between crows and owls arise? they asked.
The Teacher replied, “From the time of the first world-age,” and related a story of the past.
In the past, during the first world-age, humans gathered together and [elected] one who was handsome, possessed of great beauty, and endowed with virtuous conduct.
Having taken a man endowed with all excellent qualities, they made him their king; even four-footed animals gathered together and made a lion their king;
in the great ocean, the fish made a fish named Ānanda their king.
Then, the flocks of birds gathered on a flat rock in a region of the Himalayas and said, "Among humans, a king is known."
"Likewise, among the four-footed animals and the fish, there is no one who is our king;
it is not right for us to live without a lord. We too must obtain a king. Know that one worthy to be established in the position of king must be found.
Looking about for such a bird, they chose an owl and said, "This one pleases us."
They said: "Then one bird, in order to ascertain the inclinations of them all, made the proclamation three times.
While he was proclaiming it, after two proclamations had been endured, at the third proclamation a crow rose up and said: 'Wait!
At this time of his royal consecration, such as is this face of his; what will it be like when he is angry? For by him, when angry—'"
To make this point clear— that we shall break apart right there and then, like salt thrown into a small pot— he spoke the first verse: “Indeed,
it seems that by all our kinsmen, Kosika has been made the lord.”
“If I am permitted by my kinsmen, I shall speak with a single utterance.
This is its meaning: having heard this proclamation that is being made, I say this.
For it is said that when all these kinsmen have assembled, they have made this Kosiyarāja. However, if I were permitted by my kinsmen, then what must be said here is as follows:
"Let him say something with a single utterance.
Then, granting him permission, the birds spoke this second verse:
"Speak, friend, for you are permitted; speak the meaning and the Dhamma in its entirety."
“There are indeed young birds who are wise and radiant.
To this he replied: “Speak, friend, you are permitted. “Friend, crow, you are permitted by all of us;
speak whatever you have to say. And as you speak, let it be entirely for the sake of the goal and the Dhamma, providing both the reason and that which has come down through tradition.”
"Speak without abandoning your words. "The wise who possess radiance"—there are indeed young birds who are both endowed with wisdom and bearers of the splendor of knowledge.
Having been thus permitted, he spoke the third verse:
“I do not approve of this, may it be well with you; the consecration of the owl.
Behold the face of one who is not yet angry—how could he act when he is enraged?
The meaning of this is: “May it be well with you regarding this threefold proclamation of the words for the consecration of the owl.”

"It is being done; this does not please me. Look at his face now—his mind is satisfied and he is not angry—but I do not know how he will act when he is provoked to anger; in every respect, this does not please me.
Having said this, crying out "It does not please me! It does not please me! he leapt into the air, and the owl too—
He rose and followed him. From that time on, they harbored mutual enmity.
The birds departed, making the golden swan their king.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, many became stream-enterers and others. "At that time, I myself was the young swan who was consecrated to the kingship."

The second chapter: The Lotus Section (Paduma-vagga).
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
Paduma, Mudupāṇi, Palobhana, Panādaka, Khurappa, Sindhava, Kakkaṭa, Rāmadūsaka,
Sujāta, and Ulūka— these are the ten.
3. Udapānavagga [271] 1. Udapānadūsakajātakavaṇṇanā:
“Of the forest-dwelling seer... This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning a jackal who had fouled a well.

He related the story: "It seems that once a jackal, having defiled a water well belonging to the community of monks with excrement and urine, departed. Then one day, when he came near the well, the novices struck him with clods of earth and harassed him; from that time on, he did not even look back at that place again. When the monks learned of this occurrence, [they asked: The Buddha said: "Monks, do not harass that jackal. If you harass him, he will become angry; being angry, he will harbor a grudge; harboring a grudge, he will seek out a weakness; seeking out a weakness, he will cause harm; causing harm, he may even take the life of one of you. Therefore, monks, you should not harass that jackal. At that time, there was a certain monk who was a forest-dweller, one who lived on alms-food, one who wore rag-robes, and one who used a three-legged stool. He was a man of few desires, contented, detached, energetic, and possessed of great power. He went to the Blessed One, paid homage with his head at his feet, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One addressed him: "Monk, have you seen that jackal? "Yes, venerable sir," he replied. "Monk, what do you think? If that jackal were to come here, would you be able to recognize him? "If I saw him, venerable sir, I would certainly be able to recognize him. "Monk, it is because of such qualities as these—being a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, a wearer of rag-robes, a user of a three-legged stool, one of few desires, contented, detached, energetic, and possessed of great power—that you would be able to recognize that jackal if you were to see him. However, monks, there are other qualities even more excellent than these by which one recognizes a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata. What are they? They are: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the five spiritual faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well has the Blessed One stated this: 'Monks, there are other qualities even more excellent than these by which one recognizes a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata. "So it is, Ānanda, so it is! It is exactly as you have said. Thus the Blessed One spoke, and the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then the Venerable Ānanda, rising from his seat after the Blessed One had gone into his dwelling, approached the Venerable Sāriputta and said: "Friend Sāriputta, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well has the Blessed One stated this: 'Monks, there are other qualities even more excellent than these by which one recognizes a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata. "Friend Ānanda, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well has the Venerable Ānanda grasped the meaning of what was stated by the Blessed One. For what the Blessed One briefly stated in brief, the Venerable Ānanda has explained in detail. [End of the Discourse] The Teacher, having related this Jātaka, identified the births: "At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, and the forest-dwelling monk was myself. Thus he spoke. [End of the Commentary] The Teacher then preached the Dhamma: "Monks, do not harass that jackal. If you harass him, he will become angry; being angry, he will harbor a grudge; harboring a grudge, he will seek out a weakness; seeking out a weakness, he will cause harm; causing harm, he may even take the life of one of you. Therefore, monks, you should not harass that jackal. Then the monks asked the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, how long has it been since that jackal has not looked back at that place? "Monks, it has been seven years since that jackal has not looked back at that place. The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, what discussion are you gathered here for now? When they replied, "For this very one," he said, "Monks, no..."
"Just now, in the past as well, this jackal was nothing but a defiler of the well," he said, and related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, this very place of the sages (Isipatana) and this very well existed.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been born into a noble family in Bārāṇasī, reached maturity, went forth into the ascetic life, and dwelt at Isipatana surrounded by a company of sages.
He made it his dwelling place. At that time, a certain jackal would defile this very well and then depart.
Then one day, the ascetics, having surrounded him, captured him by a certain stratagem and brought him into the presence of the Bodhisatta.
As the Bodhisatta conversed with the jackal, he spoke the first verse:
“How did you cause the well dug with great hardship by the forest-dwelling seer, who has practiced austerities for a long time, to overflow? The meaning of this is:
because he dwells in the forest, he is a forest-dweller (*āraññika*); because he has sought spiritual qualities, he is a seer (*isi*); and because he has relied upon austerity for a long time...
"O jackal, why have you caused this well— which has been established by one who has practiced austerities for a long time, and which was produced with hardship and suffering—
to be filled and defiled with urine and excrement? Or rather, why did you pour that urine and excrement into it and cast it down there?"
Having heard that, the jackal spoke this second verse:
“This is the law of jackals, that having drunk, we vomit;
this is the law of our fathers and grandfathers—you ought not to reproach us for that.”
"In this matter, 'this is our custom' means this is our nature. When he says, 'Friend, that which we drink for water, that very thing we also vomit and spit out,' he shows:
'This is our custom, we jackals. 'From father and grandfather' means: 'This is our custom from our fathers and grandfathers.
'You ought not to find fault with that' means: 'with that which has come down through our lineage.'"
"You ought not to abandon the nature of the Dhamma; it is not fitting for you to be angry in this matter.
Then the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse to him:
"Such is your Dhamma; but what is your 'non-Dhamma' like?"
“May we never at any time see you as either Dhamma or non-Dhamma.
Therein, “May we not” means: “We have never at any time seen you as either Dhamma or non-Dhamma.
Having thus given him this advice, the Bodhisatta said, “Do not come back again. From that time forth, he did not turn back nor even look behind him.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the one who defiled the well was none other than this jackal; as for the leader of the troop, he was I myself.
The first explanation: The Udapānadūsaka Jātaka. 2.
The Explanation of the Byaggha Jātaka.
"By whatever friend one is associated with..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Kokālika.

The story of Kokālika will be revealed in the Takkarīya Jātaka in the Thera-nipāta. Now, Kokālika, thinking, "I shall go after having seized Sāriputta and Moggallāna," came from the country of Kokālika to Jetavana;
having approached and paid homage to the Teacher, he [addressed] the Elders.
Having approached him, he said, "Friend, the people of the Raṭṭha country are summoning you, Kokālika; come, let us go. "Go yourself, friend;
we are not coming," he replied. Refused by his companions, he went by himself.
Then the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, Kokālika [has been rejected] by Sāriputta and Moggallāna..."
“He is unable to exist either with them or without them; he cannot endure union, nor can he endure separation.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has been unable to endure Sāriputta and Moggallāna; formerly, too, he was unable to do so.”
Having said, "It cannot exist without [the other]," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a certain forest region.
Not far from his celestial mansion (vimāna), in a certain pre-eminent lord of the forest...
Another tree deity dwells there. In that forest grove, a lion and a tiger also dwell.
Out of fear of them, no one cultivates fields there, nor does anyone cut down trees; indeed, there is no one capable of even turning back to look.
Those lions and tigers kill various kinds of wild animals and eat them, and [they leave] the remains of what has been eaten.
Leaving that very spot, they departed. Consequently, that forest grove became foul with the stench of impure corpses.
Then, on one occasion, another tree deity—foolish and ignorant of what was right and wrong—said to the Bodhisatta:
"Friend, because of these lions and tigers, our forest grove has become foul with the stench of impure corpses; I shall drive them away. The Bodhisatta said: "Friend..."
"Depending on these two, our celestial mansions are protected; if they flee, our mansions will perish.
Not seeing the tracks of lions and tigers, humans will cut down the entire forest, clear it into a single open space, and establish fields there.
Do not let this happen," he said, and spoke the first two verses:
“From association with whatever friend security from bondage is lost,
a wise person should guard against that even before it occurs, as they would their own eyes.
From association with whatever friend security from bondage increases...”
“A wise person should conduct themselves with equality toward all tasks.
In this context, “by association with whatever friend” means by reason of association, by cause of association, with whatever evil friend— namely,
association through seeing, association through hearing, physical association, association through conversation, and association through shared enjoyment.
The meaning is: "by having committed these five kinds of association. "Security from bondage" (yogakkhema) refers to physical and mental happiness;
for that is intended here as "security from bondage" because it is secure from the yoke of suffering. "Is ruined" means he falls away.

"A wise man should guard against his overbearing nature as he would his own eyes" means that he should protect himself against the overbearing nature of that evil friend, by which he might be overcome.
A wise person should protect their own gain, fame, and livelihood even before others do, guarding them as one would one's own eyes, so that another does not overwhelm them.
Regarding the second verse, "by whom" means by which spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) through association with whom; "the security from bondage increases" means it flourishes.
Physical and mental happiness increases. Regarding the phrase "one should act as an equal":

in all matters concerning that spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*), a wise person should perform everything exactly as they would for their own livelihood and their own conduct regarding enjoyments and possessions;
they should do even more than that, but never less.
Although the Bodhisatta had explained the reason in this way, that foolish deity, without reflecting, one day displayed a terrifying form as an object and caused those lions and tigers to flee.

When the people did not see their tracks and footprints, they realized, "The lions and tigers have gone to another forest grove," and they cleared away one side of the forest grove. The deity [then spoke to] the Bodhisatta...
Having approached him, he said, "Friend, I did not do as you told me and caused them to flee;
now that I have learned they have gone, people are cutting down the forest grove—what indeed should be done? Being told, "They are now living in such-and-such a forest grove;
go and bring them back," he went there, stood before them, and with palms joined in reverence...
Having recited the third verse, he said:
“Come, tigers, turn back; go back to the great forest.
Do not cut down the forest that is now tigerless; O tigers, do not leave the forest without its tigers.”
In this context, "byagghā" means that they both addressed one another by the name "tiger. "Nivattavho" means "turn back.
"Paccupetha mahāvanaṃ" means "go back to that great forest," or "return once more"; this is the reading itself. "Mā vanaṃ chindi nibyagghaṃ" means:
"Do not cut down the forest; for now, due to your absence, our dwelling-forest grove has become 'without tigers' (nibyagghaṃ)."
"May humans not cut them down. May the tigers not become forestless"—that is, may tiger-kings like you not become *nibbana*, deprived of the forest that serves as their dwelling place.
Even though they were thus entreated by that deity, they simply refused, saying, "Go yourself; we will not come."
The deity returned alone to the forest grove. Within just a few days, the people had cleared the entire forest, established fields, and begun the work of plowing.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time..."
"The foolish deity was Kokālika; Sāriputta was the lion; Moggallāna was the tiger;
but I myself was the wise deity.
This concludes the second commentary, the Byaggha Jātaka.
[273] 3. The Commentary on the Tortoise Jātaka.

"Who is this whose meal has been served?"—the Teacher related this while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the pacification of a quarrel between two high ministers of the King of Kosala. The present-day account has already been told in the Dukanipāta.
In the past, however, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Having been reborn, he reached maturity and, having mastered all arts at Takkaśilā, renounced sensual pleasures and went forth as an ascetic.

Establishing a hermitage on the banks of the Ganges in the Himalayan region, he dwelt there, developing the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), living his life sporting in the play of *jhāna*. In this Jātaka, it is said, the Bodhisatta was supremely impartial.

He fulfilled the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhāpārami*). While he was sitting at the door of his leaf-hut, a certain shameless and immoral monkey came and inserted its male organ into his ear-cavities like a stick; yet the Bodhisatta did not prevent it, but remained sitting there with complete equanimity.
Then one day, a tortoise emerged from the water onto the bank of the Ganges.
Having opened his mouth and basking in the sun, he fell asleep. Seeing him, that greedy monkey inserted a stick into his mouth.
Then the tortoise woke up and bit him as if thrusting his organ into a casket;
a powerful pain arose. Unable to endure the pain, he thought, "Who indeed might deliver me from this suffering? To whom [should I go]?"
Thinking, "I shall go into his presence," and further reflecting, "There is no one else capable of releasing me from this suffering except for the ascetic;
it is fitting that I go to him alone," he lifted the tortoise with both hands and went into the presence of the Bodhisatta.
Meanwhile, the Bodhisatta was amusing himself with that immoral monkey.
He spoke the first verse:
“Who is this who, like one with food already served, or like a brahmin with his bowl full, has wandered for alms? To which family did he approach?”
In that context, "Who indeed is like one with overflowing food?
means: who is this coming along as if he were one whose alms-food has increased, as if holding in his hands a bowl of alms-food filled to the brim? Or, "Like a brahmin with a full hand":
just as a brahmin who, having received a recitation in the month of Kattika, comes with a full hand of gifts—so too, who indeed is this? [He said this] regarding the monkey.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Where, O monkey, did you wander for alms? means: "In which place did you wander for alms today?

"Which faithful one (*saddha*) did you approach? indicates: "To which meal prepared for the ancestors (*pubbapeta*) did you go, or which faithful individual (*puggala*) did you approach? From where was this gift (*deyyadhamma*) obtained by you? Thus he explains.
Having heard that, the immoral monkey spoke this second verse:
“I am a foolish monkey, O Kapī, who touched what should not be touched.
Deliver me, may it be well with you; once freed, I shall go to the mountain.”
"In that regard, 'I am dull-witted in Kapila' means: 'Blessings upon you; I am dull-witted, fickle-minded, like a monkey.
'I touched what should not be touched' means: I touched places that ought not to be touched. 'O blessed one, release me, blessings upon you! means:
'O compassionate and merciful one, release me from this suffering; may it be well with you. 'Once freed, he would go to the mountain.'"
"By your power, I have been delivered from this calamity; I shall go back to the mountain itself and will not show myself again within the range of your sight.
Speaking thus with compassion to the tortoise, the Bodhisatta uttered the third verse:
“Tortoises are of the Kassapa clan, monkeys are of the Koṇḍañña clan;
release Koṇḍañña, Kassapa! You have committed an act of sexual intercourse.
The meaning of this is: those called tortoises are of the Kassapa lineage, and monkeys are of the Koṇḍañña lineage; and as for the Kassapas and Koṇḍaññas...
"There exists a mutual relationship of marriage between you two.

Surely this act of sexual intercourse—consisting of unwholesome conduct on the part of you, the lustful and immoral monkey, and on the part of this immoral monkey with you—is appropriate for the union of those sharing a common lineage; therefore, release him, Kassapa Koṇḍañña!"
Having heard the words of the Bodhisatta, the tortoise was inspired with faith by the reason given and released the monkey’s organ.
As soon as it was released, the monkey paid homage to the Bodhisatta and fled; even when returning to that place, he did not look back.
The tortoise also paid homage to the Bodhisatta and went back to his own place. The Bodhisatta, too, remained with his meditative absorption unimpaired.
He became one whose ultimate goal was the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the tortoise and the monkey were the two chief ministers, while the ascetic was none other than myself.
This is the third narrative, the Kacchapa-jātaka.
[274] 4. The Exposition of the *Lolajātakavaṇṇanā*.
"The crane with the crest on its body..."—the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a certain greedy monk.
Having brought that monk before the Dhamma assembly, the Teacher said: "Monk, you were not greedy only now; even in the past, you were indeed greedy."
"Having reached the end of his life as if through greed itself, even the ancient wise men were driven out from their own dwelling places because of him.
Having said this, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there was a cook in the kitchen of the chief merchant of Benares."
For the sake of merit, he set out a nest-basket. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been reborn in the womb of a pigeon, made his dwelling there.
Then, a certain greedy crow, while passing over the kitchen, saw various kinds of fish and meat preparations;
overcome by thirst, he thought, "By relying on whom might it be possible for me to obtain a place? and so he reflected.

Having seen the Bodhisatta and forming the conviction, "I shall be able [to achieve my goal] by relying on him," he followed closely behind him as the Bodhisatta went into the forest for his alms-round.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him, "Crow, our feeding grounds are different, and yours are different; why then do you follow me? "Master, your deeds are pleasing to me."
“I too, having become one who shares the same range as you, wish to attend upon you. The Bodhisatta consented.

Moving along with him as if sharing a single feeding ground, he would retreat, scatter heaps of cow dung, eat the insects therein until his belly was full, and then approach the Bodhisatta, saying, “For so long a time you have...”
"Come now, surely it is right to know the proper measure in eating; come, let us go before it is too late," he said.
The Bodhisatta took him and went to his dwelling place. The cook, thinking, "Our friend the pigeon has returned with a companion," set out a basket of chaff even for the crow.
And the crow lived there for four or five days according to that same routine.
Now one day, a great quantity of fish and meat was brought for the merchant. Seeing this, the crow, overcome by greed, lay down groaning from the time of dawn onwards.
Then on the following day, the Bodhisatta said to him, "Come, friend, let us set out for our food.
"You go," he replied, "I have a suspicion that my food has not been digested."
“Good man, there is no such thing as indigestion for crows; for only a small amount, about the size of a lamp-wick, remains in your stomach, while the rest is digested as soon as it is swallowed.
Do as I say; do not act thus upon seeing this fish-meat. “Master, what are you saying? I have no suspicion of indigestion at all. “In that case—”
Having exhorted him, saying, "Be diligent," the Bodhisatta departed.
The cook, having prepared various dishes of fish and meat, stood at the door of the kitchen wiping the sweat from his body.
The crow, thinking, "Now is the time to eat meat," went there and perched upon the rim of the sauce-pot.
Hearing the sound "kirī," the cook turned back and looked; seeing the crow, he entered, seized it, and plucked all the feathers from its entire body.

Having placed a crest upon its head and ground ginger, black pepper, and other spices, he mixed them with buttermilk and said, "You have made our merchant's fish and meat into leftovers," and [he applied this] to its entire body.
Having smeared it and thrown it into the nest-basket, she caused intense pain to arise.
The Bodhisatta, returning from his feeding ground, saw her groaning and, expressing his displeasure, spoke the first verse:
“O crested crane, you thief, the granddaughter of Laṅghī! What is this body [of yours]?”
“Come here, Balākā! My friend the crow is fierce.

Therein, “Who is this crested Balākā?”—he addresses the crow thus, calling her “Balākā” because her body is white in color, being smeared with his thick fat, and she is called “crested” because of the crest placed upon her head. “A thief! [he says].
Because she entered the family home without the permission of the family, or because she entered the basket against the crow’s will, he calls her a "thief.
Regarding "grandfather of the leaper": a "leaper" (*laṅghī*) refers to a cloud, so called because it leaps through the sky;
and since the crane (*balākā*) conceives by the sound of the cloud, the sound of the cloud is the father of cranes, and the cloud is the grandfather. Therefore, he says, "grandfather of the leaper."
"Come here, Balāka! O Balāka, come from here. My friend Yasa, the crow who is the master of my back, is fierce and cruel;
he has arrived, and upon seeing you, he will strike you with his beak like a spear and bring about the end of your life.
Therefore, before the crow arrives, descend from my back and come here."
"Fly away quickly! he said.
Hearing that, the crow spoke the second verse:
"I am not a crested crane; I am Lolos, a crow."
“See, having disregarded your word, I have returned shorn.
Therein, “I have returned” means: you have now returned from the pasture ground; see me shorn—this is the meaning.
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:
“O friend, you will surely experience suffering again, for your conduct is such as this;
indeed, human enjoyments are not fit to be enjoyed by a bird.
In this context, “O friend, you will surely experience suffering again” means: O friend crow, you will certainly encounter such suffering once more.
"There is no liberation for you by such means alone. Why is that? For your morality is indeed so evil, since your conduct and character are only suited to the attainment of suffering.
For humans are not called 'greatly meritorious'—animals do not possess such merit—and therefore human enjoyments are not to be consumed by an animal bird."
Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta thought, "From this moment on, it is no longer possible for me to dwell here," and flying up, he departed elsewhere. The crow, groaning, died right there.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka:

at the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy monk was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). "At that time, the greedy crow was the greedy monk, while the pigeon was none other than myself."
The Fourth: The Commentary on the Lolaja Jātaka [275].
5. The Commentary on the Rucira Jātaka.

"Like a crane, beautiful of body"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain greedy bhikkhu. Both the introductory narratives are similar to those previously related; the verses are also the same.
“A beautiful crane seeks her body’s rest within the crow’s nest;
the fierce crow is my friend, for whom this little nest was made.
Do you not know me, O twice-born one who feeds on *sāmāka* grain?”
“See, I have returned shorn, having failed to follow your word.
You will surely obtain another, my friend, for such is your character;
for human enjoyments are not fit to be enjoyed by a bird.”
The verses here are indeed interspersed.
In this context, "beautiful" (*rucirā*) is said with reference to its white color due to its body being smeared with lime; the meaning is that it is beautiful, lovely to behold, and pure.
"In a crow’s nest" (*kākanīḷasmin*) means in a crow’s nest. There is also a reading, "in a crow’s nest" (*kākaniḍḍhasmin*). "Birds" (*dijā*)—
The crow calls out to the pigeon: "O you who feed on *sāmāka*! Here, by the mention of *sāmāka*, all kinds of grass seeds are intended.
In this instance as well, the Bodhisatta, thinking, "It is no longer possible for me to dwell here from now on," flew up and went elsewhere.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:

at the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy monk was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). “At that time, the greedy crow was the greedy monk, while the pigeon was none other than myself.
This is the fifth commentary on the Rucira Jātaka.
[276] 6. The Commentary on the *Kurudhamma Jātaka*.
"Your faith and virtue..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was a swan-killer.
Two friends from Sāvatthī, having gone forth as monks and received full ordination, for the most part...
They wandered about together. One day, having gone to the Aciravatī River, they bathed and stood on the sandy bank basking in the sun, engaged in friendly conversation.
At that moment, two swans were traveling through the air.
Then, one young bhikkhu took a pebble and said, "I shall strike out the eye of one of these young swans."
The other said, "You will not be able to do it. [The swan replied,] "Let an eye remain on this side; I shall strike an eye on the opposite side.
[The other said,] "You will certainly not be able to do even this. [The swan said,] "In that case, hold it steady.
Taking a pebble the size of a third part, he threw it at the back of the swan. Hearing the sound of the pebble, the swan turned around and looked; then [the other struck him].
The other took a round pebble, struck him in the eye from the opposite side, and made it come out through the other eye.
The swan, crying out and turning around, fell right at their feet.
Seeing him there, the monks who were standing here and there came forward and said, "Friends, having gone forth in such a teaching that leads to liberation, you have done what is unbecoming."
Having said, "By those who commit the taking of life," they took him and presented him to the Tathāgata. The Teacher asked, "Is it true, as it seems, that you, monk, committed the taking of life?
When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Monk, why did you do such a thing after going forth in this liberating dispensation?
In former times, when no Buddha had appeared, even the ancient wise men, while living in the midst of the household life..."
"Those who lived in a defiled dwelling were full of remorse even over minor matters;
yet you, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, did not commit even a trace of remorse. Should a bhikkhu not indeed be restrained in body, speech, and mind?
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Dhanañjaya Koravya was reigning in the city of Indapatta in the kingdom of Kuru, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of his chief queen.

Having gradually reached the age of discretion and mastered all arts at Takkasilā, he was established by his father in the position of viceroy; subsequently, upon the passing of his father, he ascended the throne.
Having attained the ten royal duties, he lived conducting himself without violating the Kurudhammas. The so-called Kurudhamma consists of the five precepts;

the Bodhisatta, having made them perfectly pure, guarded them. And just as the Bodhisatta did, so too did his mother, the chief queen, his younger brother, the viceroy, the chaplain, the brahmin, the rope-bearer, the minister, the charioteer, the guild-leader, and the granary-manager.
The high minister, the gatekeeper, and the courtesan Nagarasobhinī—these are such [examples].
"The king, the mother, the chief queen, the viceroy, the chaplain;
the tax-collector, the charioteer, the guild-leader, the granary-keeper, and likewise the gatekeeper;"
“Eleven people, including Gaṇikā, were established in the Kurudhamma.
Thus, all of them, having purified themselves, observed the five precepts.
The king, having caused six halls of giving to be built—at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the door of his own residence—gave six hundred thousand [pieces of money] every day.
Distributing his wealth, he gave alms until the entire land of Jambudīpa was left with no one remaining to receive them;
indeed, his inclination toward giving and his delight in charity overwhelmed the whole of Jambudīpa. At that time, King Kāliṅga reigned in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kāliṅga.
Because the rain did not fall in that kingdom, and while it remained unfallen, throughout the entire realm—
A drought occurred, and due to the failure of food supplies, a disease broke out among the people;
thus, three fears arose: the fear of poor rainfall, the fear of drought, and the fear of disease. The people, driven by necessity, took their children in their hands and wandered here and there.
All the inhabitants of the kingdom gathered together, went to Dantapura, and raised a clamor at the king’s gate. The king—
Standing by the window, he heard that sound and asked, "For what reason are these people crying out?
"Great King, three fears have arisen throughout the entire kingdom: the rain does not fall, the crops have failed, and a drought has occurred.
People, deprived of food and overcome by disease, wander about in distress, even seizing their children by the hands."
“Make it rain, O Great King. “What did the kings of old do when the rain did not fall?

“When the rain did not fall, Great King, the kings of old gave gifts, observed the Uposatha, undertook the precepts, entered the inner chamber, and lay down upon a layer of kusa grass for seven days; then the rain would fall. The king said, “Very well.”
Having accepted [the request], he acted accordingly. Even so, the rain did not fall.
The king asked his ministers: "I have performed the duties that ought to be done, yet the rain does not fall;
what shall we do? "Great King, in the city of Indapatta, King Koravya Dhanañjaya has a state elephant named Añjanavaṇṇa."
“There is one; we shall bring it, and when that is done, the rain will fall. “That king is powerful, well-equipped with forces, and difficult to overcome;
how shall we bring his elephant? “Great King, there is no need for war with him.
That king is inclined toward giving and delights in charity; when he is asked, he would even cut off his own decorated hair and his gracious eyes.”
“Even if he were to uproot the entire kingdom and hand it over as a gift, there would be nothing at all that could be said regarding the elephant;
he will certainly give it when asked. “But who is capable of asking him? “The brahmins, Great King.
The king summoned eight brahmins from a brahmin village, honored them with hospitality and respect, and [sent them] for the purpose of requesting the elephant.
He sent them off. Taking their travel expenses and assuming the guise of travelers, they proceeded with haste, staying only one night everywhere along the way.
After spending a few days at the alms-halls by the city gates, eating and refreshing their bodies, they asked, "When will the king come to the head of the distribution of gifts?
The people replied, "On three days of the fortnight: the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and..."
"He comes on the eighth day, but tomorrow is the full moon; therefore, he will come tomorrow," they said.
On the following day, the brahmins went early in the morning and stood at the eastern gate.
Early in the morning, the Bodhisatta bathed, anointed his limbs, adorned himself with all ornaments, and, mounted upon the back of a magnificent decorated elephant, set out with a great retinue.
Having gone to the hall of giving by the eastern gate and descended, he personally gave food to seven or eight people;
saying, "Give in this very manner," he mounted his elephant and went to the southern gate.
Because the protection at the eastern gate was so strong, the brahmins found no opportunity there and went instead to the southern gate, where they saw the king approaching.
Standing on a high spot not far from the gate, they watched him and, raising their hands, hailed the arriving king, saying, "Victory to you, Great King!
The king, having turned back the elephant with his adamantine hook, went into their presence and asked, "O brahmins, what do you desire? The brahmins [praised] the virtues of the Bodhisatta.
Praising him, they spoke this first verse:
“Having recognized your faith and virtue, O lord of men,
we have fashioned a likeness of you in Kalinga with the color of collyrium.”

In this context, "faith" (*saddhā*) refers to the faith of conviction (*okappaniya-saddhā*), by way of believing in the results of kamma. "Virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the virtue of restraint (*saṃvara-sīla*) and the virtue of non-transgression (*avītikkama-sīla*).
"Gold" (*vaṇṇa*): at that time, in that region, it was called "gold" (*suvaṇṇa*); this is merely a synonym for the teaching.
However, by this term, all wealth and grain, such as bullion and gold, are included. "With the color of collyrium" (*añjana-vaṇṇena*).
"By this elephant of yours, whose color is like a heap of collyrium, we [exchanged] in the presence of the King of Kāliṅga—at the side of the Kāliṅga king.
‘Nimimhasa’ means we took it by way of exchange, or else we placed it in our bellies by way of consumption; ‘se’ is a mere particle.
This is what is meant: O Lord of Men, having understood your faith and virtue, we thought, ‘Surely for us...’"
"Thus, a king endowed with faith and virtue will give the elephant of the color of collyrium when requested.

Having said this, we thought, "We shall bring the elephant to the King of Kalinga as if it were our own," and so we collected much wealth and grain, bartered for it, and stored it in our bellies. Carrying it thus, we have come here.
"Let the King know what must be done there.

Another method: Having heard of your faith and your reputation for virtue, [Kāliṅga] thought, "The King possesses such sublime qualities that he would give even his own life if asked, let alone an animal like this elephant," and thus, in the presence of Kāliṅga, by means of this ointment-colored [elephant].
“We have praised your virtues; we have praised them and weighed them, and for that reason we have come here.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta comforted them, saying, “If you brahmins have consumed and enjoyed wealth by exchanging this nāga, do not worry;
I shall give you back the nāga exactly as he was adorned,” and he spoke the other two verses:
“Whether it be Annabhāra or Bhāradvāja, whoever goes for the sake of these [offerings], all of them are not to be refused;
this is the word of the former teachers.
‘O Brahmins, I give to you this elephant, worthy of a king, fit for a king’s enjoyment, and renowned.’”
“Go where you wish with the charioteer, [this chariot] adorned and covered with a golden net.
In this context, those who are supported by a man for their livelihood, being sustained by food such as rice-gruel and solid meals, are called *annabhaccā* (food-eaters);
the others, because they are not so sustained, are called *abhaccā*. Furthermore, here, due to the grammatical euphonic combination (*sandhi*), [the form is *annabhaccā*].

The elision of the vowel *a* should be understood. Up to this point, all beings—whether depending on a self or not depending on a self, and whether living or not—have been shown by dividing them into two groups.

Regarding the phrase "he who goes for the sake of someone here": among those beings in this world of the living, whichever being goes for the sake of some person with the expectation of some kind of service. All...
"They are not to be refused" means that even if there are many people going out specifically for that purpose, nevertheless, all of them must not be refused by that man;
the meaning is that one should not refuse them by saying, "Go away, I will not give to you.
"This is the word of the former teachers" refers to the fact that parents are called "former teachers," and this is their word. Thus I...
He indicates that he was instructed by his parents.
"I give this Naga to you, O Brahmins"—because this is the word of our ancient teachers, therefore, O Brahmins, I give this Naga to you.
"Worthy of a king" means suitable for a king. "The enjoyment of a king" means the possession of a king.

“Yasassin” means one endowed with a retinue; the meaning is: “I give you that elephant together with those five hundred families—namely, the elephant-keepers, elephant-doctors, and so forth—who, it is said, live by depending on that elephant.
“Alaṅkataṃ” means adorned with various kinds of elephant ornaments. “Hemajālābhichannaṃ” means covered with a golden net. “Sasārathiṃ” means together with the driver.
"However, I give him together with his charioteer and his elephant-keeper, who is his teacher;
therefore, having taken this elephant along with its charioteer, you may go wherever you wish with your retinue.
Having thus given by word while still seated upon the back of the noble elephant, the Great Being then descended from the elephant's back and said: "If..."
"There is a place that has not yet been adorned; having adorned it, I shall give [the elephant]. Having said this, he circumambulated him three times, searching for a spot that was unadorned.

Finding no such spot, he placed the elephant's trunk in the hands of the brahmins, poured water scented with flowers and perfumes from a golden pitcher, and gave him away. The brahmins, together with their retinue, accepted the elephant.
Seated upon the back of an elephant, they went to Dantapura and presented the elephant to the king; yet even when the elephant had arrived, the rain did not fall.
The king, asking what the cause might be, inquired further: "King Dhanañjaya Koravya observes the Kurudhamma;
therefore, in his kingdom, it rains every half-month and every ten days. [What is the reason for this in the case of our] king?"
Hearing that this was indeed the power of his virtues, [the king thought], "But how great could the virtues of this animal be?
He then dispatched brahmins and ministers, saying, "In that case, send back the elephant together with its retinue exactly as it was adorned, give it to the king,
and having written down that *kurudhamma* which he observes upon a golden plate, bring it here."
Having gone there and presented the elephant to the king, they sent word: "Your Majesty, even though this elephant has come, it does not rain in our kingdom.

It is said that you observe the Kurudhamma; our king also wishes to observe it, so please write it down on this gold plate and bring it here. [The king replied: "Give us the Kurudhamma. [They said: "Sirs,..."
“Truly, I do observe this Kurudhamma; however, I now have scruples regarding it, and that Kurudhamma does not satisfy my mind. Therefore, I am unable to give it to you.
But why did that virtue not satisfy the king? It is said that at that time, for kings, every third year—
In the month of Kattika, there occurs what is called the festival;

during that festival, kings adorned with all ornaments and assuming the guise of deities stand before a yakṣa named Cittarāja and cast flower-adorned discs in the four directions toward the lake of Cittasara.
This king also, playing at that moment, [cast one] from the bank of a certain pond toward Cittarāja.
Standing before the yakkha, he shot four arrows into the four directions;

seeing the three arrows that had struck the remaining directions, he did not see the arrow shot upon the surface of the water. The king felt remorse, wondering, "Has the arrow I shot perhaps fallen upon the body of a fish?
This arose from the violation of his virtue due to the act of taking life; therefore, he did not attain purity of virtue.
So he spoke thus: "Sirs, I have a qualm regarding the Kurudhamma; however, my mother guards it well-protected.

Receive it from her. [The others replied: "Great King, you have no intention to take life, and without that, there is no such thing as the destruction of life. Give us the Kurudhamma that you yourself protect. "Therefore..."
He had it inscribed on a golden plate: "No living being is to be killed; what is not given is not to be taken;
one must not engage in sexual misconduct; one must not speak falsehood; intoxicants are not to be drunk.
Having had this written, he said: "Even though this is so, she does not please me; take her from my mother's presence."
The messengers, having paid homage to the king, went into her presence and said, "Queen, it is said that you observe the Kurudhamma;
give that to us. She replied, "Sirs, it is true that I observe the Kurudhamma, but now remorse has arisen within me regarding it;
that Kurudhamma does not satisfy me, therefore I am unable to give it to you. To her—
It is said that he had two sons: the elder was king, and the younger was viceroy.
Now, one king sent to the Bodhisatta a block of choice sandalwood worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and a golden garland worth a thousand.
He, thinking, "I shall honor my mother," sent it all to his mother. She thought: "Neither do I anoint myself with sandalwood, nor do I wear the garland; [it is for] my daughters-in-law..."
"I shall give it. Then this thought occurred to her: "My eldest daughter-in-law is the mistress, established in the position of chief queen;
I will give the golden garland to her. But my youngest daughter-in-law is in a poor state; I will give the choice sandalwood to her.
Having given the golden garland to the king’s queen, she gave the choice sandalwood to the junior queen, and having given it, she—
Then she felt remorse, thinking: "I am observing the *kurudhamma*; the fact that these women have fallen from good fortune to even worse misfortune is no concern of mine.
It is only fitting for me to perform the duty of honoring my elder sister.
Could it be that because I failed to do so, my virtue has been broken? It was for this reason that she spoke thus. Then the messengers said to her: "That which belongs to oneself..."
"It is given according to your pleasure; even if you feel remorse over this much, what other evil could you possibly do?
Morality is not broken by such a thing as this. Give us the Kurudhamma! Having said this, they took it from her as well and inscribed it upon a golden plate.
“Dear ones, even though this is so, she does not satisfy me; however, my daughter-in-law protects me well.
Receive it from her,” she said. Having been told this, they approached the chief queen and, in the same manner as before, requested the Kurudhamma.
She too spoke in the same manner as before and said, “Now my virtue no longer satisfies me; therefore, I am unable to give it to you.”
It is said that one day, while standing at the lion-window as the king was circumambulating the city, she saw the viceroy seated on the back of an elephant behind him.
A sense of lust arose in her, and she thought, "If I were to form an intimacy with him, he would support me once he is established in the kingdom upon my brother's passing. Then, for her—
“I was observing the custom of the Kurus; though I had a husband, I looked upon another man out of defilement.
Since my virtue must have been broken,” she felt remorse, and therefore she spoke thus. Then the messengers said to her:
“A transgression, noble lady, does not occur by a mere arising of thought; you are feeling remorse even for this much, yet there has been no violation.”
"What will you do? One's virtue is not destroyed by this much; give us the Kurudhamma.
Having said this, they took it from her as well and wrote it down on a golden plate.
"Dear ones, even though this is so, she does not please me at all, but the Viceroy protects it very well; let us take it from him."
When they were told, "Take them," they approached the viceroy and requested the Kurudhamma in the same manner as before.

Now, when he went to attend upon the king in the evening, having reached the royal courtyard by chariot, if he intended to eat in the presence of the king and sleep right there, he would discard the reins and the goad inside the chariot box. By that [act]...
Having perceived this, the people departed and, returning early the following morning, stood waiting while looking for his departure.
The charioteer also kept the chariot hidden and, returning early the next morning, stood at the palace gate with him.
If he wished to depart at that very moment, he would go to attend upon the king, leaving the reins and the goad within the chariot.
Because of that perception, the great multitude stood right at the palace gate thinking, "He will depart this very moment.
One day, having acted thus, he entered the royal residence; as soon as he had entered, it began to rain.
The king, saying, "It is raining," did not allow him to leave. He ate there and lay down. The great multitude thought, "He will depart now."
He stood there, wetted throughout the entire night. On the second day, the viceroy went out and saw the great multitude standing there, drenched with water.
He thought, "While protecting the Kurudhamma, I have caused so many people to suffer; surely my virtue must have been broken," and he was filled with remorse.
Because of that, he said to those messengers: "Truly, I do protect the Kurudhamma; however, now for me—"
“There is remorse; therefore, it is not possible for you to give [the requisites],” he said, and explained the matter to him.
Then the messengers said to him, “Your Majesty, you have no thought that ‘these people are suffering’; an action performed without intention does not constitute a deed.
How could there be an offense against you for those who feel remorse even to this extent? Having said this, they [reported it] in his presence as well.
Having received the precepts, they wrote them down on golden plates.
"Even so, he does not please me; however, the chaplain protects them well, so receive them from him," she said.
Thus addressed, they approached the chaplain and made their request. One day, as he was going to attend upon the king, he—
One king, seeing a chariot with the color of the rising sun sent by that other king on the road, asked, "Whose chariot is this?

Upon hearing, "It was brought for the king," he thought, "I am old; if the king would give me this chariot, I could travel about comfortably riding upon it. Having thus reflected, he went into the presence of the king. After the king had caused him to win [the contest],...
When it was time for the king to depart, they showed him the chariot. Upon seeing it, the king said, "This chariot is exceedingly beautiful; give it to my teacher.
The chaplain did not wish to accept it, and even though he was asked again and again, he still refused.
For what reason? It was because he thought to himself: "While observing the Kurudhamma, I have felt greed for another's property; if I were to break this principle..."
“I must be possessed of virtue. Having explained this matter, he said, “Sirs, I have scruples regarding the Kurudhamma;
that practice does not satisfy me, therefore it is not possible for me to give [the girl]. Then the messengers said to him, “Noble sir, virtue is not broken by the mere arising of greed;
why do you feel such scruple even over this much? What transgression [have you committed]?”
Having said, "I shall do so," they received the precepts from him as well and wrote them down on golden plates.
"Even though this is so, he does not please me; however, the minister Rajjugāhaka protects [the precepts] very well, so receive them from him.
Being thus addressed, they approached him and made their request. On one occasion, he was in the countryside at a field...
Measuring out the rope, he tied it to a wooden stake; having had one end taken by the field-owner, he took the other himself.
The stake bound to the end of the rope taken by him reached the middle of a crab's burrow.
He thought: "If I push the stake into the burrow, the crab inside will perish. If..."
"But if I do it from the other side, the king's property will be ruined. If I do it from this side, the householder's property will be ruined.
What indeed should be done? Then it occurred to him: "There must be a crab in the hole;
if there were one, it would be seen. I shall let it down right here. And he let the stick down into the hole.
The crab let out a "kirī" sound. Then this thought occurred to him: "Daṇḍaka must have fallen upon the back of the crab;
the crab will die, and I am observing the Kurudhamma. Because of that virtue, I must be separated from my life.
Having explained this matter, he said: "For this reason, I have scruples regarding the Kurudhamma."
"It exists, therefore it is not possible for you to give it," he said. Then the messengers said to him, "It is not that you have no intention that 'the crab should die';
indeed, there is no such thing as an unconscious action. Since you feel remorse even over this much, what transgression could you possibly commit?
Having spoken thus, they took the precepts from him as well and inscribed them upon a golden plate.
“Even though this is so, he does not please me; however, the charioteer protects me well, so learn it from him.
Having been told this, they approached him and made their request. One day, he drove the king in a chariot to the pleasure garden.
After the king had sported there during the day and departed in the evening, he mounted the chariot; even before he had reached the city—
At the time of sunset, a cloud arose. Out of fear that the King might become wet, the charioteer gave the signal with the whip to the horses.

The horses galloped away with speed. From then on, whether going to the pleasure garden or returning from it, whenever they reached that spot, they would go and come back with speed. For what reason? It is said that this thought occurred to them:
“There must have been some danger in this place; that is why the charioteer then gave the signal with the whip.
It occurred to the charioteer as well: “Whether the King was drenched by the rain or not, it is not my fault.
However, I gave the signal with the whip to the well-trained Sindhava horses in an improper place; therefore, they are now galloping back and forth.”
“They become exhausted; yet I am observing the Kurudhamma, so it must be that my virtue has been broken.
Having explained this matter, he said, “For this reason, there is scruple regarding the Kurudhamma; therefore, you are not able to give [the horses].
Then the messengers said to him, “It was not your intention that ‘the Sindhava horses should become exhausted’; they are insentient beings...”
"Kamma does not cease merely by this; and even while you are feeling remorse for this much, what transgression could you possibly commit?
Having said this, they took the precepts from him and wrote them down on a golden plate.
"Even so, he does not please me; but the merchant protects them well—take them from him."
Furthermore, they approached him and made their request.
One day, after going to his own rice field and returning while reflecting upon the heads of rice that had emerged from the ground, he thought, "I shall have a row of rice planted.
He had a handful of rice heads brought and had them tied to a pillar. Then it occurred to him: "From this field..."
“I must give my share to the king; yet, even though I have not given my share, I have been made to take a handful of rice from my field.
Since I am observing the Kurudhamma, my virtue must be broken by this.
Having explained this matter, he said, “For this reason, I have scruples regarding the Kurudhamma; therefore, it is not possible for you to give [it to me].”
The messengers said to him: "You have no intention to steal; without that, it is impossible to define what is called 'taking what is not given.
Even with such a degree of conscientiousness, how could you take another's property?
Having spoken thus, they took the precepts from him as well and inscribed them upon a golden plate.
“Even though this is so, he does not satisfy me; however, the great official Doṇamāpaka protects [the grain] very well, so take it from him.
Having been told this, they approached him as well and made their request.
It is said that one day, while sitting at the door of the storehouse measuring out rice for the king’s portion, he took some rice from a heap of immeasurable rice.
He set up a tally mark, and at that moment it rained. The chief minister, having counted the tallies, said, "The measured grains of rice amount to this much.

He gathered the tallies of rice, threw them into the heap of measured rice, and went quickly to stand at the gatehouse, where he thought: "What indeed have I done by putting the tallies of rice into the heap of measured rice?"
“Were they placed in my measured heap of grain, or rather in the immeasurable heap? Then this thought occurred to him:
“If they were placed in my measured heap of grain, then for no reason at all the king’s property has increased while the householders’ property has been lost;
and since I am observing the Kurudhamma, my virtue must have been broken by that. Having explained this matter, he said: “By this...”
He said, "Because of this reason, there is remorse (*kukkucca*) regarding the duty of the Kurus; therefore, it is not possible for me to give it to you.
Then the messengers said to him, "You have no intention of theft; without that, it is impossible to define what is called 'taking what is not given.
Even while feeling such remorse, would you take what belongs to another? Having said this, [they spoke] in his presence as well.
Having received the precepts, they wrote them down on golden plates.
"Even so, he does not grant them to me; however, the gatekeeper guards them well, so receive them from him," she said.
Having been told this, they approached him and made their request. On one occasion, at the time when the city gate was being closed, he—

He caused the sound to be proclaimed three times. Then a certain poor man, who had gone to the forest with his younger sister to gather wood and leaves, heard that sound as he was returning; taking his sister with him, he arrived at the gate in great haste.
Thereupon the doorkeeper said to him, "Do you not know that there is a king in the city?"
“You do not know that the gates of this entire city are being closed;
instead, you spend the day wandering about in the forest with your own wife, sporting in sensual pleasures,” he said.
When the other replied, “Sir, she is not my wife; she is my sister,” he thought to himself: “Alas, I have done a wrong in thinking my sister was my wife!”
"By speaking thus, 'I am observing the Kurudhamma, therefore my virtue must remain unbroken,' he explained this matter and said, 'For this reason I have scruples regarding the Kurudhamma;
therefore, it is not possible for you to give [it]. Then the messengers said to him, 'This was spoken by you under such a misconception; herein there is a breach of your virtue.'"
"There is no [fault], but even with this much, what will you do by committing intentional lying under the name of 'the Dharma of the Kurus' while feeling remorse?
Having said this, they took the precepts from him as well and wrote them down on a golden plate.
"Even so, he does not please me; however, the courtesan Suvaṇṇadāsī protects [the precepts] very well. Take them from her."
Furthermore, they approached her and made the same request, but she refused in the same manner as before. For what reason?

It is said that Sakka, the lord of the devas, thinking, "I shall test her virtue," came in the guise of a young brahmin, gave her a thousand pieces of gold, saying, "I will return," and having gone back to the world of the devas, did not come for three years.
Out of fear of breaking her own virtue, she did not accept even so much as a leaf of betel from the hand of another man for three years.
Gradually falling into poverty, she thought: "I have become destitute because the man who took my thousand coins has not returned for three years; I am unable to maintain a livelihood."
“From now on, it is proper for me to report the matter to the judges and receive a maintenance allowance.
Having gone to the court, she said, “Sir, three years have passed since my husband left with a maintenance allowance;
I do not even know if he is dead, and I am unable to support myself. What shall I do, sir?”
“What will you do if he does not come for three years? From now on, take his travel expenses.
As she was leaving the court after receiving this decision, a man presented her with a bundle worth a thousand pieces of money.
Just as she was reaching out her hand to take it, Sakka revealed himself. Upon seeing him, she said, “For me...”
At the end of three years, a man who was a donor of a thousand coins arrived and said, "Dear father, I have no need for your kahāpaṇas," and he withdrew his hand.
Sakka, having manifested his own body, stood in the sky blazing like the rising sun, and the entire city gathered together. In the midst of the great crowd, Sakka said, "I am her..."
Having given her this instruction, saying, "By way of investigation, I gave a thousand [pieces of gold] at the conclusion of three years;

you who guard your virtue must likewise guard it in such a manner," he filled her residence with the seven kinds of jewels and, having exhorted her, saying, "From now on, be diligent," he departed for the world of the devas. For this reason, she [said], "I have received my wages..."
She refused, saying, "I extended my hand for wages being given by another without having even digested [the previous meal];
for this reason, virtue does not reach fulfillment in me, and therefore it is not possible for me to give to you.
Then the messengers said to her, "There is no breach of virtue merely by extending one's hand; indeed, virtue is the supreme purity," and they received the precepts from her as well.
Having taken it, they inscribed it upon a golden plate.

Thus, having recorded the protective code of these eleven persons on the golden plate, they went to Dantapura, gave the golden plate to the Kāliṅga king, and reported the matter to him. The king, conducting himself according to that Kurudhamma, remained steadfast.
He fulfilled the five precepts. At that moment, rain fell throughout the entire kingdom of Kāliṅga;

the three fears were pacified, and the kingdom became secure and well-supplied with food. Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving for as long as he lived, the Bodhisatta, together with his retinue, filled the city of heaven.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths...
“Some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some became arahants. However, in the *Jātakasamodhāna* it is said:
“The courtesan was Uppalavaṇṇā, Puṇṇa was the gatekeeper then;
Kaccāyana was the rope-holder, and Moggallāna was the measurer of grain.”
“Sāriputta was then the merchant, and Anuruddha the charioteer;
the elder Kassapa the brahmin was the viceroy Nanda-paṇḍita.
Mahesī was Rāhula’s mother, Māyādevī the mother of the Birth-giver.”
"The Bodhisatta was the King of the Kurus; thus you should remember this Jātaka.
The sixth commentary on the Kurudhamma Jātaka is concluded.
[277] 7. Commentary on the Romaka Jātaka.
“Over fifty years” refers to what the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning an attempt to kill the Blessed One. The present-day account is clear enough.
In the past, however, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, having become a pigeon, lived with a large retinue of pigeons in a mountain cave in the forest.
There was also a certain ascetic endowed with virtue who [lived near] those pigeons...
Having established a hermitage near a frontier village not far from his dwelling place, he made his home in a mountain cave.
From time to time, the Bodhisatta would come into his presence and listen to what was worth hearing.
After that ascetic had lived there for a long time, he departed; then another fraudulent matted-hair ascetic came and took up residence there.
Surrounded by his pigeons, the Bodhisatta approached him, paid homage, and exchanged friendly greetings.
He wandered about in the hermitage, took his food near a mountain cave, and returned to his own dwelling place in the evening.
The ascetic Kūṭa lived there for more than ninety thousand years.
Then one day, people living in a frontier village prepared and gave him the meat of a pigeon.
Becoming attached to it through craving for its flavor, he asked, "What kind of meat is this?
Upon hearing that it was "pigeon meat," he thought, "Many pigeons come to my hermitage; I shall kill them and eat their meat."

“It is fitting,” he thought. He then brought rice, ghee, curd, milk, pepper, and other such items, set them aside in a corner, and concealing his club with the hem of his robe, sat at the door of the leaf-hut watching for the arrival of the pigeons.
The Bodhisatta, surrounded by his flock of pigeons, arrived; having observed the wicked deed of that fraudulent ascetic, he said: “This—”
The wicked ascetic was sitting in a different posture; [the king thought], "Could it be that he has eaten the flesh of one of our own kind?
I shall investigate him. Standing upwind and smelling his body odor, [the king realized], "This man intends to kill us and eat our flesh;
it is not right to go near him. Taking the pigeons, he retreated.

He wandered about. Seeing that he was not coming, the ascetic thought, "It is fitting to kill those who have approached me with confidence after conversing sweetly with him, and eat their flesh. Having thought this, he spoke the first two verses:
"O Romaka, we have lived for more than fifty years in the cave of the rock; ... [the rest of the verse follows] ..."
“In the past, those born from eggs would come into my very hands because they were unable to move about due to their state of being fully extinguished [in the womb].
Why now, Vakkaṅga, do these birds eagerly seek out another mountain cave?
Surely they do not think of me as they did before, or perhaps they are not those same ones who have been away for so long.”
In this context, "possessing concentration" means those who have attained concentration. "Romaka" means produced in Rumā;
she addresses the Bodhisatta as a "pigeon" because his eyes and feet were the same color as well-polished coral.

"Without fear" means that while we have lived in this mountain cave for more than fifty years, these egg-born creatures have not shown even a single day’s suspicion toward me, remaining with their minds entirely tranquil.
"Previously they came within my hands, into the reach of my outstretched arms"—this is the meaning.
"Now they" (*tedāni*) means "they now. "Vakkaṅgā" is an address to the Bodhisatta;
however, all birds are called "vakkaṅgā" because they stretch their necks (*vakaṃ*) when taking flight. "What purpose" (*kimatthaṃ*) means "perceiving what reason?"
"Longing" means being in a state of yearning. "A mountain cave" means another mountain cleft distinct from the mountain itself.
"As before" means that just as these birds formerly held me in high regard and regarded me with affection, they surely do not so regard me now;
for they think, "The ascetic who lived here before was one, this one is another"—thus they must perceive me.
He illuminates this: "They have been gone for a long time, or perhaps they are not these. He asks:
"Is it because these [birds] have returned after being away for a long time, at the end of a long duration, that they do not recognize me, thinking 'this is he indeed'?
Or rather, are those whose minds were extinguished among us not these? Are these others, birds who have arrived as newcomers? Why do they not approach me? Thus he questions.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta stepped forward and, standing there, spoke the third verse:
“We know you; we are not deluded. You are indeed that very person, and we are those others, no different.
Your mind is corrupted toward these people; it is because of that livelihood that we are afraid of you.”
"In this matter, 'we are not utterly deluded' means that we are neither confused nor negligent.
'And your mind is corrupted toward these people' means that you—and no one else; you alone—have a mind corrupted toward these people, an intent arisen to kill us.
'Ājīvika' refers to a corrupted ascetic who has gone forth for the sake of a livelihood."
“Because of that we are terrified; for that reason we are afraid and do not approach him.
The ascetic Kūṭa, thinking, “I am well-known to these people,” threw a club, but missed his mark. He said, “Go away for now; I have missed you.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “Indeed, you have missed me, but you will not miss the four states of misery.”
"If you remain here, I shall report to the village dwellers that 'this man is a thief' and have him seized; flee quickly!
Having thus threatened him, he departed. The false ascetic was unable to stay there and went elsewhere.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka: "At that time..."
"The false ascetic was Devadatta; the former virtuous ascetic was Sāriputta; and I myself was the elder pigeon.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Romaka-jātaka.
8. The Commentary on the Mahimsa-rāja-jātaka.
"For what purpose was this said?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain greedy monkey.

It is said that in a certain family in Sāvatthī, there was a pet monkey who would go to the elephant stable, sit upon the back of a virtuous elephant, and defecate and urinate on its back. On the back...
He paced back and forth. Because of his own possession of virtue and perfection of patience, the elephant did nothing at all.
Then one day, another wicked young elephant took the place of that elephant. The monkey, perceiving "This is he indeed," climbed onto the back of the wicked elephant.
Thereupon, the elephant seized him with its trunk, set him down on the ground, and [struck him] with its foot.
Having stepped upon it, he crushed it to pieces. This incident became known throughout the community of monks.

Then one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth: "Friends, it is said that a greedy monkey, perceiving a virtuous elephant to be a wicked one, climbed onto the back of that wicked elephant, and then the elephant brought about his death. The Teacher approached and...
