"Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? he asked. When they replied, "For this very discussion," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that this greedy monkey is of such a character;
from of old he has been of just such a character. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born in the species of buffalo in the Himalayan region.
Having been born, he reached maturity, possessing great strength and a massive body.
Wandering among mountain slopes, foothills, inaccessible peaks, and forest thickets, he saw a pleasant spot at the foot of a tree; having taken his food, he stood by that tree root during the day.
Then a certain greedy monkey descended from a tree, climbed onto his back, and discharged excrement and urine upon him.
Having seized him by the horns, he played while dangling him; having seized him by the tail, he played while swinging him about.
Through his perfection of patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, the Bodhisatta did not take that misconduct of the monkey to heart, yet the monkey continued to do so again and again.
Then one day, a deity dwelling in that tree, standing upon the trunk of the tree, said to him: "O King of Elephants, why [do you tolerate this]?"
Having said, "Endure the insult of this wicked monkey; do not restrain him," she spoke these two preceding verses to clarify the matter:
"For what purpose, with what intention, do you endure this suffering from one of fickle mind and treacherous nature, even though he is like a granter of all desires?"
“Kill him with a horn, and trample him with your feet;
the fools will only become even more enraged, and there would be no one to restrain them.
In this regard, with what purpose does he intend this? What indeed is the reason, depending upon what, seeing what? [He says] “the treacherous ones” (dubbhino).
"Of one who betrays a friend. "Like the master of the Giver of All Desires" means like the owner of the Giver of All Desires.
"You endure" means you tolerate. "And you stand upon with your foot" means step upon it with the sharp edge of your hoof so that he dies right there.
"Even more, O fools" means that if there were no one to restrain them, these foolish, ignorant beings would [act] again and again.
He indicates that they might become angry, strike him, or harass him.

Upon hearing this, the Bodhisatta thought: "Tree deity, if I, being superior to him in birth, lineage, strength, and so forth, do not endure his offense, how will my own aspiration reach fulfillment? But as for him..."
"Thinking that he might do such an improper act as if it were something else, those fierce lions to whom he does this will surely kill him.
His death at the hands of others will be my liberation from suffering and from the taking of life.
Having said this, she spoke the third verse:
“Thinking, ‘He is just like me,’ others will act in this same way;
they will kill him there, and that shall be my deliverance.
After a few days had passed, the Bodhisatta went elsewhere. Another fierce buffalo arrived at that place and stood there.
The wicked monkey, perceiving that it was indeed he, climbed onto his back and behaved with the same impropriety as before.
Then, shaking him off, the bull threw him to the ground, pierced him in the heart with his horn, and crushed him to pieces under his feet.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka: “At that time...”
"That wicked buffalo was this wicked elephant; that wicked monkey is this present monkey;
and the virtuous king of the buffaloes was none other than I myself.
Thus ends the eighth narrative, the Commentary on the Mahiṃsarāja Jātaka.
[279] 9. The Commentary on the Jātaka of the Hundred-Footed One (Satapattajātakavaṇṇanā).
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this concerning Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
For two of the group of six, Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, lived in dependence upon Rājagaha, as did the two, Assaji and Punabbasuka.
They lived depending on Kīṭāgiri; however, these two, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, lived at Jeta’s Grove depending on Sāvatthī.
They reopened legal cases that had been settled according to the Dhamma.
Even those who were their close associates and friends acted as their supporters, saying: "Friends, you should not [be judged] by these matters of birth, clan, or virtue..."

"Or they will become even more inferior. If you would relinquish your own adherence, these others will overcome you all the better," and so saying, they did not allow them to relinquish their adherence. Consequently, quarrels, disputes, strife, and contention arose.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One...
Having caused the monks to assemble and summoned Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, he asked, “Is it true, monks,
that you yourselves reopen legal cases and do not allow others to release their holdings?
When they replied, “It is true, Venerable Sir,” he said, “Since this is so, monks, your conduct is like that of the young brahmin Satapatta.”
Having said, "It is like a mere action," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a certain family in a village of Kāsī.
Upon reaching maturity, instead of making his living through farming, trade, or other such means, he [joined] about five hundred bandits...
Having taken them, he became their leader and made his living by performing such acts as highway robbery and housebreaking.
At that time in Bārāṇasī, a certain householder gave a thousand kahāpaṇas to a countryman and then passed away without ever reclaiming them.
Later, when his wife fell ill and lay upon her deathbed, she addressed her son:
“Father,” she said, “your father died after giving one thousand [kahāpaṇas] to a man but without having them brought back; if I too were to die, he would not give them to you.
Go while I am still alive and have him bring them back and take them.
He agreed, saying, “Very well,” went there, and obtained the coins. Then his mother, having passed away, out of affection for her son—
On the path by which he was to come, she was reborn as a spontaneously born female jackal.
At that time, the chief of the bandits, together with his followers, stood on that path intending to plunder those who had entered it.
Then, when her cubs reached the entrance of the forest, the jackal said, "Dear ones, do not enter the forest; there are thieves standing here."
“Having killed him, they will take his kahāpaṇas,” she said, repeatedly blocking the path to prevent him from proceeding.
Not understanding the reason for this, he thought, “This ill-omened jackal is blocking my way.
Taking up a clod of earth and a stick, he drove his mother away and set out into the forest. Then a hundred-winged bird [said], “Of this man...”
Crying out, "I have a thousand kahāpaṇas in my hand; kill this man and take that money! he lunged toward the thieves.
The young man, unaware of the reason for his actions, thought, "This is an auspicious omen;
now I shall be safe," and raising his joined palms, he cried, "Rain down, Master! Rain down, Master!"
The Bodhisatta, who knew the cries of all creatures, observed the actions of these two and thought:
"This female jackal must be the mother of this one; she is forbidding him out of fear that he will kill her and take the coins.
"But this hundred-petaled lotus must be an enemy; therefore, he says, 'Kill this one and take the coins.'"
He reported this to us. But he, not knowing this matter, having threatened his mother who desired his welfare, caused her to flee;
and with the perception that "he is one who desires my welfare," he offers salutation with joined palms to Sata-patta, who does not desire his welfare.
"Oh, how foolish this man is! Indeed, even for Bodhisattas who are Great Beings, the taking of another's property occurs by way of an unfavorable rebirth-linking.
Some say it was due to the fault of the stars.
The young man arrived and reached the border of the thieves' territory. The Bodhisatta had him seized and asked, "Where do you live?
He replied, "I am a resident of Bārāṇasī. "Where have you been? [He answered,] "In a certain village, a thousand [pieces of gold] were to be obtained."
“There is; he has arrived there. “But did you receive anything? “Yes, I received it. “By whom were you sent?
“Master, my father is dead and my mother is ill; thinking, ‘He will not obtain this when I am dead,’ she sent me.
“Do you know now what has become of your mother? “I do not know, Master. “Your mother—”
When you had departed, she died and, out of affection for her son, became a female jackal;
terrified by the fear of your death, she blocked your path and tried to stop you. You threatened her and drove her away. As for the hundred-winged bird, he was your enemy.
He informed us, saying, "Kill this man and take his coins. Yet, through your own foolishness, you [trusted] him who wished you well.
"You think, 'My mother desires my harm,' yet you think of the hundred-petaled lotus, which desires your harm, as one who 'desires my welfare.
You have no merit whatsoever toward her, whereas your mother possesses great merit; take the coins and go," he dismissed him.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke these verses:
“Just as a young man on the road might think that a jackal roaming the forest,
who wishes him well and speaks for his benefit, desires his harm;
or think that a hundred-feathered bird, who desires his harm, wishes him well.”
“In just the same way, there is a certain person here who,
when addressed with words for his welfare, receives them as if they were from the left.
And those who praise him do so out of fear or to elevate him.”
"For he considers that person a friend, just as the young man [considers] the hundred-petaled lotus.

In this context, "by those seeking welfare" means by those desiring well-being and growth (*vuddhi*). "Spoken to with words" means addressed with instruction and admonition that brings about welfare and happiness.
"Accepts with hostility" means one who does not accept the instruction thinks, "This does not bring me benefit; it brings me harm."
"Taking it as 'this is mine,' he receives it from the left side; this is what is meant by 'receiving.
And those who say 'ye ca kho nan'ti—those who, having taken that person standing with their own grasp, praise them, saying:
'Those like you must indeed be people who stand having taken up the legal case (*adhikaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "they exalt out of fear": of this...
They expel them by showing fear caused by dismissal, saying: "Because of your dismissal from this household, such and such dangers will arise for you;
do not dismiss them! These [qualities] are not attained by you through mere erudition, noble lineage, or retinue. Having thus shown the fear caused by dismissal, they expel them.
For he considers those who are like this to be friends; among such people, he [relies on] anyone whatsoever.
A certain foolish person, due to his own folly, considers someone to be a friend; he thinks, "This person is a friend who wishes for my welfare.
Just as the young man Sata-patta—though that youth was actually one who wished him harm—the foolish man, because of his own ignorance, considers him to be "one who wishes for my welfare.
But a wise person, not taking such a person to be a "friend who speaks only pleasant words," [recognizes him for what he is].
One avoids such a person from afar. Therefore it was said:
“A friend who takes for his own ends, a friend who is merely words, one who speaks only what is pleasing, and one who is a companion in states of woe.”
“These four are enemies,” thus understanding, the wise man should avoid them from afar, just as one would a dangerous path.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, I myself was the chief of the thieves.”
The ninth is the commentary on the Satapatta-jātaka.
[280] 10. The commentary on the Puṭadūsaka-jātaka:
"Surely you are indeed the king of beasts," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain grain-spoiler.

He related the story: It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain minister invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, seated them in a park, and while giving alms-food, said, "Let those who wish to wander in the park go for a walk between meals.
The bhikkhus went for a stroll in the park. At that moment, the park-keeper climbed a tree laden with fruit.
Taking very large leaves, they made bags, thinking, "This one will be for flowers;
this one for fruits," and set them down at the foot of the tree. A young boy, his son, tore open every bag that was set down.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past, too, he was a destroyer of bags," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a certain brahmin family in Benares.
Having grown up and living as a householder, one day he went to a park on some business.
Many monkeys lived there. The park-keeper used this very method to drop [food] into leaf-baskets.

The senior monkey was destroying whatever had already been destroyed by the garden-keeper. The Bodhisatta addressed him, saying, "I suppose the garden-keeper wishes to make it even more beautiful by destroying what has already been destroyed," and spoke the first verse:
"Surely this king of beasts must be skilled in the art of basket-making."
"For he spoils the bundle; surely he will make another.
In this context, "king of beasts" is said while praising the monkey. "Of the bundle-work" means of the making of flower garlands.
"Skilled" means clever. This, however, is the summary of the meaning here: "I think this king of beasts is certainly skilled in the work of making bundles."
"For indeed, having dropped one bundle, he defiles it, thinking, 'Surely I shall make another even more pleasing than that.
Having heard this, the monkey spoke the second verse:
"Neither my mother nor my father is skilled in the work of making bundles."
"We shall surely ruin what has already been done; such is the custom of this family.
Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:
"What kind of conduct is yours, and what kind is unrighteousness?"
"May we never, at any time, see what is Dhamma as Adhamma.
Having spoken thus, he rebuked the troop of monkeys and departed.

The Teacher, having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the monkey was the child who spoiled the bundle; the wise man, however, was none other than myself."
The tenth: The Exposition of the Puṭadūsaka Jātaka.
The third chapter: The Chapter on the Well.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
The excellent well, the forest tiger, the monkey, the crested crane, and the beautiful swan;
the lord of good people, Romaka, Dūsa, and again, the hundred-leaved lotus and the work on the leaf-cup—these are the ten.
4. The Internal Chapter.
[281] 1. The Commentary on the Abbhantara Jātaka.
Regarding the statement "The tree named Abbhantara," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the gift of mango juice by the Elder Sāriputta to the Therī Bimbādevī.
For when the Wheel of the Sublime Dhamma had been set in motion by the Perfectly Enlightened One at Vesālī...
While [the Buddha] was dwelling in the Gabled Hall, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī went there with five hundred Sākiyan women, requested the going-forth, and received both the going-forth and full ordination.
Later on, those five hundred bhikkhunīs, having heard the Nandakovāda discourse, attained arahantship.
Furthermore, while the Teacher was dwelling in dependence on Sāvatthī, Rāhulamātā...
Queen Bimbā thought, "My husband has gone forth and attained omniscience; my son too has gone forth and dwells in his very presence.

What shall I do remaining in the midst of the household? I too shall go forth, go to Sāvatthī, and dwell there constantly seeing both the Perfectly Enlightened One and my son. Having thus reflected, she went to the nunnery.

Having gone forth and traveled with her preceptor and teacher to Sāvatthī, she took up residence in a certain nunnery while visiting the Teacher and her beloved son. The novice Rāhula came and saw his mother.
Then one day, the elder nun’s abdominal wind became disturbed; wishing to see her son who had come to visit her, she—
He was unable to leave; others came and reported his state of discomfort.
He went to his mother and asked, "What do you need? She replied, "Dear son, when I drink mango juice mixed with sugar while living at home, my abdominal wind is pacified.
Now that we are making our living by wandering for alms, where shall we get it?"
The novice said, "I will bring it when I get it," and departed.

Now, that venerable one’s preceptor was the Dhammasenāpati, his teacher was Mahāmoggallāna, his younger father was the Elder Ānanda, and his father was the Perfectly Enlightened One—thus he possessed great fortune.
Nevertheless, instead of going to another, he went to his preceptor, paid homage, and with a dejected expression...
Having offered the oblation, he stood there. Then the Elder said to him, “Rāhula, why do you look so dejected?
“Venerable sir, my mother’s elder sister has a wind disorder in her stomach,” he replied. “What is required to cure it?
“It is said, venerable sir, that she will feel better with mango juice mixed with sugar. “Very well, I shall obtain it; do not worry.”
Then, on the following day, taking him with him and entering Sāvatthī, he had the novice sit in the hall of seats and went to the king’s gate.
When the King of Kosala saw the Elder, he had him sit down; at that very moment, a park keeper brought a basket of sweet mangoes prepared for a meal.
The king removed the skin from the mangoes, added sugar, and...
Having crushed it himself, he filled the elder’s bowl and gave it to him.
The elder, having departed from the royal palace, went to the refectory and gave it to the novice, saying, "Take this and give it to your mother. He took it and gave it;
as soon as the elder nun had consumed it, her abdominal wind was stilled. The king also sent a messenger, saying, "The elder sat here but did not consume the mango juice."
“Go and find out whether he has been given away to anyone. He went together with the Elder, learned of that occurrence, and having returned, told the king.
The king thought: “If the Teacher had lived as a householder, he would have become a Wheel-turning Monarch;
the novice Rāhula would have been the Jewel of the General; the Elder nun would have been the Jewel of the Woman; and the entire realm of the world-system would have been his.”
"This would have been for them alone. While we were attending to them, we should have practiced [virtue];
now that they have gone forth and are living depending on us, it is not fitting for us to be negligent.
From then on, he had mango juice regularly given to the Elder Nun. The Elder informed the Elder Nun Bimbādevī that mango juice had been given to her.

He became well-known within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then one day, the bhikkhus initiated a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying, "Friends, it is said that the Elder Sāriputta satisfied the Elder Nun Bimbā with choice food.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered here now? When they replied, "For this very discussion," he said:
“Monks, it is not only now that Rāhula’s mother was satisfied by Sāriputta with ambrosia; in the past, too, he satisfied her in this very way.
Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family in a village of Kāsi.
Having reached maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā; after establishing a household life, upon the passing of his parents, he went forth as an ascetic.
Having attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) in the Himalayan region, he became a teacher of a group, surrounded by a company of seers.
After a long period had elapsed, he descended from the mountain slopes in order to partake of salt and sour food.
While wandering on his alms-round, he reached Bārāṇasī and took up residence in a park.

Then, by the power of the ascetics' virtue, Sakka’s celestial abode trembled. Sakka, reflecting upon this, understood the cause and thought: "I shall strive to prevent these ascetics from dwelling here;
then, with their residence disrupted and being troubled, they will not attain one-pointedness of mind."
Thinking, "In this way, I shall find comfort," and investigating, "What indeed might be the means?

he saw this method: immediately after the middle watch of the night, having entered the bedchamber of the king’s chief queen and standing in the air, he said, "Bhadde, if you were to eat a mango fruit that has ripened inside [the tree], you will obtain a son; he will be a Wheel-turning Monarch."
“I shall declare: ‘It will happen. When the king hears the queen’s words, he will send her to the park for mangoes;
then I will make the mangoes disappear. They will report to the king the absence of mangoes in the park.
When he asks, ‘Who has been eating them? they will say, ‘The ascetics have been eating them. Upon hearing this, the king will beat the ascetics and have them expelled.”
"Thus they will be afflicted.

Then, immediately after the middle watch of the night, he entered the inner chamber and, standing in the air, made known his status as a king of the devas. Speaking with her, he uttered these first two verses:
"The tree within is indeed a tree, from which this divine fruit has come;..."
“Having experienced her pregnancy-longing, a woman gives birth to a Wheel-turning Monarch.
‘You too, my lady, are the chief queen, and you are dear to your husband;
the King will bring for you this fruit from within.’”

In this context, by the phrase "the tree within," he refers first of all to a single mango tree (*ambavṛkṣa*) located within—without specifying it as being inside a village, town, district, mountain, or the like.
"Whose divine fruit" refers to the divine fruit of that mango tree which is fit for the enjoyment of the deities. As for the word "this":
It is merely a particle. "Dohalinī" means one who has conceived a longing. "Tvampi, bhadde, mahesīsī" means you, O beautiful lady, are the chief queen.
In the commentary, however, there is also the reading "mahesī ca.
"Sā cāpi patino piyā" means that she, as the chief queen among the sixteen thousand ladies, is dear to her husband. "Āharissati te" [means he will bring for you...]

"O King, this shall bear fruit within; the King will cause this fruit of the kind I have described to be brought for that beloved Queen, your chief consort. Having consumed it, she will conceive a Cakkavatti embryo.
Having spoken these two verses to the Queen, Sakka said, "Be heedful; do not be dilatory. Tomorrow..."
Having thus instructed him, saying, "Inform the king," he went back to his own dwelling place.
On the following day, she showed herself as if ill, gave instructions to her attendants, and lay down.

The king, seated upon a lion-throne beneath a raised white parasol, watching the performances, did not see the queen and asked his attendants, "Where is the queen? "She is ill, Your Majesty," they replied.
So, having gone to her presence and sitting down at the side of her bed, he massaged her back and asked, "What is it that makes you uncomfortable, my lady?
"Your Majesty, there is nothing else that is uncomfortable; a pregnancy craving has arisen in me.
"What do you desire, my lady? "The fruit of an inner mango, Your Majesty. "And where is this so-called 'inner mango'?"
“Is there one? “I do not know, Your Majesty, whether there is an inner mango tree;
however, for me, life exists if I obtain its fruit, but it does not exist if I do not. “In that case, I shall have one brought; do not worry,” the king said, comforting the queen.
Having risen and gone, he sat upon his royal couch, summoned his ministers, and [said]: “Regarding the queen’s inner mango tree…”
A pregnancy craving arose in her, and she asked, "What should be done? [The ministers replied: "Your Majesty, there is a mango tree standing between two other mango trees called the 'inner mango.
Send someone to the garden, have fruit brought from that inner mango tree, and give it to the Queen.
The King said, "Very well, bring such a mango," and sent them to the garden. By means of his own supernatural power, Sakka [prepared the fruit] in the garden.
Having made the mangoes look as if they had been eaten, he caused them to disappear. People who had gone for the sake of mangoes searched throughout the entire park;
finding not even a single mango, they went and informed the king of the absence of mangoes in the park.
"Who is eating the mangoes? "The ascetics, Your Majesty. "Drive the ascetics out from the park!"
The people, having replied, "Very well," carried her out. Sakka’s wish reached its fulfillment.

The queen lay down, having made a vow for the sake of mango fruit. Seeing no further duty to be performed, the king convened his ministers and brahmins and asked, "Do you know whether there are any mangoes within [the palace]? The brahmins—
They said, “Your Majesty, the ‘Internal Mango’ is the enjoyment of the deities;
it is said to exist within the Golden Cave in the Himalayas—this is our traditional oral report. “But who will be able to bring a mango from there?
“No human being can go there; it would be proper to send a young son of a bird.”
At that time, in the royal palace, there was a young parrot with a large body, as big as the hub of a prince’s chariot wheel, endowed with great strength, wise, and skilled in means.
The king had him brought and said, "Dear young parrot, I have been very kind to you;
you dwell in a golden cage, you eat honeyed parched rice from a golden platter, and you drink sugar-water."
"You drink [this], yet you must also help us accomplish one task," he said. "What is it, Your Majesty?
"Dear father, the Queen has conceived a longing for the fruit of the inner mango tree. That mango is located on the Golden Mountain in the Himālayas and is the enjoyment of the deities;
it is not possible for a human being to go there. Therefore, you must [bring] a mango fruit from there..."
“It is fitting to bring it. “Very well, Your Majesty, I shall bring it. Then the king had him eat honeyed parched rice from a golden platter and drink sugar-cane juice;

he smeared the bird’s wings with oil refined a hundred times, took hold of it with both hands, and standing at the lion-window, released it into the air. Having shown his profound respect to the king, the bird—

Leaping into the air and passing beyond the path of men, he went into the presence of the green pigeons dwelling in the first mountain range of the Himālayas and asked, "Where is the place called Abbhantara-amba? Tell me that location.
"We do not know," they replied, "the pigeons in the second mountain range will know."
Having heard their words, he flew up from there and went to the second mountain range;
likewise, he went to the third, the fourth, the fifth, and the sixth. There too, the partridges said to him, "We do not know;
the partridges in the seventh mountain range will know. Having gone there as well, he asked, "Where is the one called Abbhantara-amba?"
He asked. They replied, "In such-and-such a place, within a mountain of gold. He said, "I have come for the sake of its fruit;
lead me there and give me the fruit from it. The group of *Sukas* said, "Friend, that is the property of the Great King Vessavaṇa;
it is not possible to approach it. The entire tree, from its very roots, is covered with seven nets of iron."
"It is surrounded and guarded by a thousand *kumbhaṇḍa* demons; for one seen by them, there is no life.
It is a place like the world-ending fire or the great Avīci hell; do not make a wish for it.
"If you will not go, then tell me of another place. "In that case, by such-and-such a place and such-and-such a place..."
"Go! Following exactly what they had instructed him, he carefully examined the path and went to that place.

Hiding himself during the day, he approached the interior of the mango tree at the time of the middle watch, when the rākṣasas were falling asleep, and began to climb slowly through one of the root openings. The iron net made a "kirī" sound.
The rākṣasas woke up, saw the young parrot, and thinking, "This is a mango-thief," they seized him and deliberated upon how to execute their punishment.
One said, "I shall put it in my mouth and swallow it. Another said, "I shall crush it with my hands, form it into a ball, and scatter it about.
Another said, "I shall split it in two, roast it over coals, and eat it. Such was their deliberation regarding his execution.
Even after hearing this, not being at all afraid, he addressed the rakkhasas and said, "Ho, rakkhasas!
Whose subjects are you? "Of the Great King Vessavaṇa. "Ho, you too are the subjects of a king, and I am also the subject of a king;
the King of Bārāṇasī sent me for the sake of some inner mango fruit, and so I was right there—my own..."
"Having given my life to the king, I have returned. For he who sacrifices his life for the sake of his own parents and his master is reborn in the world of the gods;
therefore, I too, having passed away from this animal womb, shall be reborn in the world of the gods.
Having said this, he spoke the third verse:
“The brave man who, sacrificing himself, strives for the sake of his master and reaches whatever state [is required], shall become a lord. In this context,
“master” (*bhattu*) refers to those who support and nourish one with food and so forth— namely, the father, the mother, and the husband.
Thus, for the sake of his husband who had perished in these three ways. "Exerting himself" means making effort, striving.
"The state he attains" means that he attains whatever cause of happiness, glory, gain, or heaven he reaches.
"A hero" means one who is fearless and endowed with valor. "One who sacrifices himself" means being regardless of both body and life.
"By sacrificing myself for the sake of my husband, who is of these three kinds:
'If he should obtain [a reward], may I too obtain it'—if such a hero as he obtains the excellence of gods or the excellence of humans, may I too obtain that;
therefore, there is only joy for me here, not fear. Why do you try to frighten me?"
Thus he taught them the Dhamma with this verse. Having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, they were filled with confidence and said, "This man is righteous;
it is not possible to kill him. Let us release him. Having released the young parrot, they said, "O young parrot, you are free; go safely from our hands. "My coming..."
"Do not treat me with contempt; give me one mango fruit. "O young parrot, it would indeed be no burden for us to give you one mango fruit;
however, the mangoes on this tree were gathered after they had fallen. If even a single fruit is missing, our lives will cease to exist.
For when Vessavaṇa becomes angry and casts a single glance, it is like sesame seeds being thrown into a heated pan."
“Like a thousand *kumbhaṇḍa* spirits, it breaks apart and scatters; therefore, we are unable to give it to you.
However, we shall tell you where it can be obtained. “Let anyone give it; I have need only of the fruit itself. Tell me where it can be obtained.
“Between this Golden Mountain, there is an ascetic named Jotirasa who offers oblations into the fire using a golden bowl.”
"There dwells one named Paṇṇasālā, a devotee of Vessavaṇa; Vessavaṇa regularly sends him four mango fruits.
Go to him. Having agreed, saying "Very well," he went to the ascetic, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
Then the ascetic asked him, "Where have you come from? "From the presence of the King of Bārāṇasī," he replied. "For what purpose have you come?
"Sir, a craving for ripe mangoes from within our king's inner garden has arisen in our queen; it is for that purpose that I have come.
However, the Rakkhasas, instead of giving me the ripe mangoes themselves, have sent me to you. "In that case, sit down."
“You shall obtain it. Then Vessavaṇa sent him four fruits. The ascetic ate two of them and gave one to the young parrot to eat.
When the parrot had eaten that, the ascetic placed one fruit in a pouch, tied it around the young parrot’s neck, and released the young parrot, saying, “Now go! It [flew away].
Having brought it, he gave it to the queen. She ate it, and her craving was appeased; however, because of that, she had no son.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the queen was Rāhula’s mother; the parrot was Ānanda; the ascetic who gave the mango fruit was Sāriputta; and the ascetic living in the garden was none other than myself.
This is the first commentary on the Abbhantara-jātaka.
[282] 2. The Commentary on the Seyyāsa Jātaka.
"He who is better becomes even better. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a minister of the King of Kosala.
It is said that he was of great service to the king and accomplished all his tasks. The king thought, "He is of great service to me..."
Thus he bestowed great honor upon him. Unable to endure this, others brought slander against him to the king and caused his downfall.
The king, believing their words and without even investigating the fault, had that virtuous and blameless man bound with iron shackles and cast into prison. There, he remained all alone.
Vasanta, relying on his perfection of virtue, attained one-pointedness of mind; with a concentrated mind, he comprehended conditioned phenomena and reached the fruit of stream-entry.
Later, when the king realized that he was innocent, he had his shackles broken and bestowed upon him a greater honor than he had previously enjoyed.
He thought, "I shall pay homage to the Teacher," and prepared many...
Taking garlands, perfumes, and other offerings, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Tathāgata, and sat down to one side.
The Teacher, exchanging greetings with him, said: "We have heard that a misfortune has befallen you.
"Yes, venerable sir, it has befallen me; however, through that misfortune, I have achieved a benefit, for by sitting in prison—"
“He attained the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher said, “Lay follower, it is not you alone who have brought about benefit through what was not beneficial;
even the ancient wise ones brought about benefit through what was not beneficial for themselves. Having said this, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
“In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta [was conceived] in the womb of his chief queen.”
Having been reborn and reached maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā. Upon his father’s passing, he was established in the kingdom;
there, without violating the ten duties of a king, he gave alms, observed the five precepts, and performed the Uposatha rites.
Then, one of his ministers became corrupt within the inner palace. When the footmen and others learned of it, they reported: "Such-and-such a minister has become corrupt within the inner palace."

They informed the king. The king, investigating and understanding the matter as it truly was, summoned him and, saying, "Do not attend upon me from this time forth," deprived him of his position. He went and attended upon a certain neighboring king;
the entire account is exactly as told below in the Mahāsīlava Jātaka. Here too, that king [summoned him] three times...
Having reflected on it and trusted the words of that minister, he reached the border of the kingdom with a vast retinue,
thinking, "I shall seize the sovereignty of Bārāṇasī. When the seven hundred great warriors of the King of Bārāṇasī heard this news,
they said, "Your Majesty, it is said that a certain king named so-and-so, intending to seize the sovereignty of Bārāṇasī, is breaking through the countryside..."
“He is coming; let us go right there and seize him,” they said.
“I have no need for a kingdom obtained through the injury of others; do not do anything,” [the king replied].
The robber-king arrived and surrounded the city. Again, the ministers approached the king and said, “Sire, do not—”
They said, "Do this, and we shall take [him]. The king said, "Nothing can be done;
open the city gates," and having spoken, he himself sat upon the royal couch on the great terrace, surrounded by his assembly of ministers.
The king of thieves, striking down people at the four gates, entered the city, ascended the palace, and [approached] the one surrounded by ministers.
Having had the king seized and bound with chains, he had him cast into prison.

While sitting in the prison, the king directed loving-kindness toward the robber-king and attained the meditative absorption of *mettā*. Through the power of that loving-kindness, a burning heat arose in the body of the robber-king;
his entire frame became as if it were being consumed by twin fires. Overwhelmed by great suffering, he—
“What, indeed, is the cause? he asked. “Because you cast a virtuous king into prison, this suffering has arisen for you.
He went and apologized to the Bodhisatta, saying, “Let your kingdom be yours alone,” and having handed over the kingdom to him, [said], “From now on, you are my adversary...”
Having said, "Let this be my burden," and having issued a royal command against the corrupt minister, he went back to his own city.
Seated upon the royal throne on the decorated great terrace beneath a raised white parasol, the Bodhisatta, conversing with his ministers, spoke these first two verses:
"He becomes more excellent, indeed more excellent, who attends upon what is excellent; ... [the rest of the verses follow]"
"Having made peace with one, I released those who were to be executed.
Therefore, having made peace together as one with the entire world, one may go to heaven after death; listen to this, O people of Kāsi!"
In this regard, "he who associates with the superior becomes more superior" means:
one whose portion (*aṃsa*) or part (*koṭṭhāsa*) consists of the blameless and supreme Dhamma is "one whose portion is superior" (*seyyaṃso*), that is, a person who relies upon wholesome states.

Furthermore, he who repeatedly associates with that superior person—whether it be through the cultivation of wholesome states or by delighting in what is wholesome—becomes more superior and more praiseworthy.
And he is even superior. Having formed an alliance with one, he released a hundred men condemned to death;

this should also be understood by this means: "For while I was practicing the sublime meditation on loving-kindness, having formed an alliance and intimacy with one king of thieves through that meditation on loving-kindness, I released you, a hundred people, from execution."

The meaning of the second verse is as follows: Since I, by establishing a connection through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*) with a single individual, liberated you hundred people who had reached the point of execution, therefore this must be understood:
consequently, by establishing a connection through the cultivation of loving-kindness with the entire world, a person would go to heaven in the next world after death.
"For while the access stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*) bestows rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), absorption (*appanā*) bestows rebirth in the Brahma-world.
Listen all of you, inhabitants of the kingdom of Kāsi, to these words of mine.
Thus did the Great Being, having praised the virtue of the cultivation of loving-kindness to the great multitude, [speak] in the city of Bārāṇasī, which measured twelve yojanas.
Having abandoned his white parasol and entered the Himalayas, he went forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isi*).
When the Teacher had become the Perfectly Enlightened One, he spoke this third verse:
“Having said this, the great king Kaṃsa, the ruler of Bārāṇasī...”
"Having laid aside his bow and arrow, he entered upon self-restraint.
In this context, "a great king" means a *mahārāja*. *Kaṃsa* is his name. Because he took possession of and resided in Bārāṇasī, he is called "the Taker of Bārāṇasī.
Having spoken these words, that king laid aside his bow and his arrow, which is to say, his shaft.

"Having abandoned and cast aside his moral restraint, he entered the life of a wanderer; and having gone forth, he developed meditative absorption (jhāna) and, without falling away from that absorption, was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, the king of thieves was Ānanda, while the king of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself."
The second *Seyyajātaka* commentary.
[283] 3. The *Vaḍḍhakīsūkarajātaka* commentary:
"Choose, choose indeed..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Dhanuggahatissa.

He related the story: "King Pasenadi’s father, Mahākosala, when giving his daughter Vedehikā—known as Kosala-devī—to King Bimbisāra, gave her a village in Kāsī called Satasahassuṭṭhāna, which yielded a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] for the cost of her bathing powder.
But when Ajātasattu had killed his father, Kosala-devī, overcome by grief, passed away. Thereupon, King Pasenadi of Kosala thought:"
“Father was killed by Ajātasattu; my sister also passed away because her husband died, and out of grief for him.
I will not give the village of Kāsī to a thief who has murdered his father. Thus, he did not give that village to Ajātasattu.
Dependent upon that village, there were occasional battles between those two: Ajātasattu was young and capable, while Pasenadi was already old.
Thus he was frequently defeated; for the most part, even the people of Mahākosala were vanquished.
Then the king asked his ministers, "We are constantly being defeated; what indeed should be done? They replied, "Your Majesty, those called 'noble ones' (ayya) are experts in counsel;
it would be well to listen to the discourse of the bhikkhus in the Jetavana monastery. The king said, "In that case..."
“Listen to the conversation of the bhikkhus at that time,” he commanded his scouts, and from then on they did so.
At that time, however, two elder monks were living in a leaf-hut on the outskirts of the monastery: the Elder Datta and...
And there was the Elder Dhanuggaha-Tissa. Among them, the Elder Dhanuggaha-Tissa, having slept during both the first watch and the middle watch, woke up during the last watch;
he straightened his arrows, kindled a fire, and while sitting there, said, "Venerable sir, Elder Datta!
"What is it, venerable sir, Elder Tissa? "Why are you sleeping, venerable sir? he asked.
“‘If we do not sleep, what shall we do? ‘Then stand up and sit,’ he replied. Having stood up and sat down, he said to the Elder Datta:
‘Venerable Elder Datta, this greedy Mahodarakosala here makes even a mere bowl of rice go bad;
he knows nothing at all of the conduct of war, yet when defeated, he only causes others to say, "He is defeated!"’”
"But what is it proper to do? At that moment, those scouts stood listening to their conversation.

The Elder Dhanuggahatissa considered the battle: "Venerable sir, there are three kinds of battle arrays—the lotus array (*padumabyūha*), the wheel array (*cakkabyūha*), and the cart array (*sakaṭabyūha*).
For one who wishes to capture Ajātasattu, [one should position them] in such-and-such a mountain valley..."
Having stationed men on two mountain walls and displayed a weak force in front, and having ascertained that they had entered between the mountains,
he blocked the path of entry; then, roaring and shouting from both mountain walls in front and behind,
he treated them like a fish fallen into a net or like a young mouse caught inside a closed fist.
"It would be possible to capture him. The scouts reported this message to the king.
Upon hearing it, the king had the war drums beaten, went forth, and having formed his troops into a wagon-array, he captured Ajātasattu alive.
He gave his own daughter, Vajirakumāri, to his nephew, and made the village of Kāsi her bathing-grounds.
Having given [the gift], he sent her away. This report became well known among the community of monks.
Then one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, it is said that the King of Kosala has defeated Ajātasattu through the mediation of the Elder Dhanuggahatissa.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, with what conversation are you sitting here gathered now?"
Having asked, "Is it indeed she? and being told that it was, he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
even in the past, Dhanuggahatisso was skilled in the art of warfare," and he related a story of the past.
Long ago, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in the forest.

He was reborn. At that time, a carpenter from a village of craftsmen living near Bārāṇasī went into the forest for a pillar and saw a young boar that had fallen into a pit; he brought it home and cared for it.
When it grew up, it became large-bodied with curved tusks and was well-behaved. Because it was raised by the carpenter, it was known simply as "the carpenter’s boar."
He was discovered. While the carpenter was stripping bark from a tree, the snake would turn the tree with its snout;
having bitten him with its mouth, it would fetch the axe, the adze, the chisel, and the mallet, and seize the end of the black cord.
Then that carpenter, fearing that someone might eat it, led it away and released it in the forest. It too, having entered the forest, [sought] a secure and comfortable place.

While looking about, he saw a great mountain glen within the mountains, a comfortable place to dwell, abundant in roots and fruits, and crowded with many hundreds of wild boars. When those boars saw him, they approached him.
He said to them: "I have been wandering about looking for you; indeed, I have seen you, and this is the place."
“It is delightful; I too shall dwell right here now. “This place is indeed delightful, but there is danger here.
“I too, upon seeing you, understood this: since you dwell in such a place endowed with excellent provisions, there is no flesh or blood in your bodies;
what, then, is your fear here? “A tiger comes here every morning.”
“Having come, he takes whatever he sees and goes away. “But does he take them regularly, or only occasionally?
“He takes them regularly. “But how many tigers do you have? “Only one. “You are not able to fight against so many with just one tiger, are you? “Yes, we are not able. “I shall capture him for you.”
"Do you simply do as I say? Where does that tiger live? "On this mountain.

Having sent the pigs out during the night, he deliberated on the battle, saying, "A battle is of three kinds: by way of the lotus array (*padumabyūha*), the wheel array (*cakkabyūha*), and the chariot array (*sakaṭabyūha*).
He then arranged them in the lotus array, for he knew the terrain. Therefore—
Thinking, “It is fitting to deliberate on the battle in this place,” he placed the mothers of the young piglets in their midst.
Having passed them by, he placed the middle-aged sows; having passed them by, the young piglets;
having passed them by, the old sows; having passed them by, the long-tusked sows; and having passed them by, the stronger sows capable of fighting.
He stationed ten, twenty, or thirty men at each respective place, forming a troop of soldiers.
In front of his own position, he had a circular pit dug; behind him, he had one dug in the shape of a ploughshare, sloping gradually like a mountain slope.
Taking sixty or seventy fighting boars, he [placed them] at those various spots, saying, "Do not..."
As he was reflecting on his deed, thinking, "I am afraid," the dawn broke.
The tiger arose, realized it was time, and having gone there, stood upon a mountain slope directly in front of them;
opening his eyes, he looked at the boars. The carpenter-boar gave a signal to the other boars, saying, "Look back!"
They stared back at him. The tiger opened his mouth and roared;
the pigs did likewise. The tiger discharged urine; the pigs did the same. Thus, whatever he did, they did the very same thing in return.
He thought: "In the past, when the pigs were merely looked upon by me, they were unable even to flee; yet today—"
"Without fleeing, they have become my adversaries and are merely repaying what I myself did.
Standing upon this very spot of ground, there is even one among them acting as their coordinator; today, as I have gone forth, victory is not apparent.
Having said this, he turned back and went to his own dwelling place. However, there was a certain fraudulent ascetic there who ate the meat taken by him.
Seeing him approaching with empty hands, he spoke to him and recited the first verse:
"Previously you wandered from place to place seeking choice boar's flesh,
having overcome the wild boars in this very region."
"Now you sit meditating alone, having gone off by yourself;
O tiger, is it that your strength no longer exists?
"In this place, you used to roam about slaying the best of boars one after another, having overcome them. "O friend..."
"O tiger, formerly in this place you used to roam about, having overcome all the boars and slaying the very best, the most excellent among these boars.
But now, having left one behind, you meditate; you have gone away alone and are meditating, brooding. This is your strength."
"Now there is no tiger for you today"—what does that mean to you, O tiger? "Is it that today you have no physical strength?
Hearing this, the tiger spoke the second verse:
"These many [beings] were indeed going here and there in the past, driven by fear and seeking a refuge."
"Now they dwell together, gathered in one place, where they stand difficult for me to overcome.
In this context, *sudam* is a particle. This, however, is the summary of the meaning:
previously, upon seeing me, these pigs were terrified, oppressed, and seeking a shelter; they went in various directions, scattered and separate, here and there.

They were fleeing toward every direction; but now they have all come together and are staying, dwelling as one, having reached that headland where, standing firm, they think, "Today these men are difficult for us to overcome, difficult to subdue.
Then, generating enthusiasm in him, the false ascetic said, "Do not fear! Go! When you roar and leap into the water, all of them—"
"Terrified, they will break apart and flee," he said. Encouraging him thus, the tiger became courageous and went back again, standing on the mountain slope.
The carpenter-pig stood between the two pits.
The pigs said, "Master, the great thief has come back! [The tiger replied,] "Do not be afraid; now I shall seize him. The tiger—
Having roared, he fell upon the carpenter-pig; at the moment the pig was falling upon him, he turned over and fell with great force straight down into the pit dug for him.
Unable to sustain his momentum, the tiger went upward and fell into the extremely narrow entrance of the pit dug across the mouth of the boar-trap, becoming like a heap of tangled matter.
The boar emerged from the pit and, moving with the speed of a thunderbolt, struck the tiger between the ribs with his tusk.
He tore him open down to the region of the kidneys, wrapped the five-fold sweet flesh around his tusk, and brandished it over the tiger’s head, crying out, "Take this, your enemy!
He then lifted him up and threw him outside the pit.
Those who arrived first received the tiger meat, while those who arrived later wandered about sniffing at their faces, wondering, "What does tiger meat smell like?
The pigs were not yet satisfied. Seeing their behavior, the carpenter-pig thought, "Why is it that you..."
“Be silent,” he said. “Master, what is the use of killing this tiger? There is indeed another fraudulent ascetic (*kūṭajaṭila*) capable of commanding tigers.
“Who is he? “A certain immoral ascetic. “The tiger has been killed by me;
what power does he have over me? Come, let us seize him! And so he set out with his herd of pigs. The fraudulent ascetic—
While the tigers were lingering, thinking, "Could it be that the pigs have captured the tiger?", the man went out to meet them.
Seeing the pigs approaching, he took his belongings and fled;
pursued by them, he abandoned his gear and quickly climbed an udumbara tree. The pigs cried out, "Master, we are lost now! The ascetic—"
"Having fled, he climbed a tree," they said. "What kind of tree is it? "An udumbara tree.
He gave these instructions: "Let the female pigs bring water; let the piglets dig the earth; let the long-tusked pigs cut the roots;
and let the rest surround and guard [the tree]. While they were doing so, he himself—
Just as one striking the straight, thick root of an udumbara tree with an axe, he felled the udumbara tree in a single blow.
The pigs that were standing around threw the fraudulent ascetic to the ground, tore him into pieces, and devoured him until only the bones remained.
Then, having made the carpenter-pig sit right upon the trunk of the udumbara tree, [they left him there] for the fraudulent ascetic.
Having brought water by means of three shells, they consecrated him and made him king;
and they made a young sow his chief queen. From that time until the present day, it is said, kings have been seated upon the auspicious Udumbara throne and consecrated with the three shells.
The deity dwelling in that grove, having seen that marvel, stood facing the boars from within the fork of a branch and spoke this third verse:
“Homage to the Saṅghas who have come together! Having seen this myself, I declare it a wonder:
that where tusked tigers were defeated by deer, they were released through harmony even against the strength of those tusks.”
"May there be homage to that Saṅgha"—this homage of mine be for the assembled herds of swine.
"Having seen this, O friends, I say it is wonderful"—having myself seen this friendship and state of intimacy, which was unprecedented and marvelous in the past, I speak thus.
"Where the tusked deer have conquered the tiger"—for indeed, where the tusked ones...
"The pigs and deer defeated the tiger," or rather, this is the reading: "By means of harmony, they were released from the fanged beasts.

The meaning is: that harmony among the pigs—their single-minded intent—which existed toward those fanged beasts, by means of that harmony, having seized their enemies, those fanged beasts were today released from the fear of death.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Dhanuggahatisso was the carpenter-pig, and the tree deity was none other than myself.
This concludes the third narrative, the Vaḍḍhakīsūkara-jātaka.
4. The Commentary on the Sirijātaka.
"Those who strive and gather [it]"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain Brahmin named Siricora.
In this Jātaka, the story of the present has already been explained in detail in the Khadirangāra Jātaka below.
Here, however, it concerns the deity of wrong view who lived at the fourth gate-tower of Anāthapiṇḍika’s house.
While performing penance, she brought forty-four crores of gold and filled the storehouses, becoming a companion to the merchant.
Then, taking her with him, he went into the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher taught her the Dhamma;
having heard the Dhamma, she became a stream-enterer. From that time forth, the merchant’s reputation returned to its former state.
Then a certain brahmin living in Sāvatthī, who was skilled in interpreting bodily marks, thought:
"Anāthapiṇḍika, having been poor, has become a lord once again; what if I were to go as if desiring to see him, steal some of his fortune from his house, and then return?
He went to his house, and after being honored and treated with hospitality by him, while they were engaged in friendly conversation, he said:
When he was asked, "For what purpose have you come? he looked about, wondering, "Where indeed is prosperity established?
Now, the merchant had a pure white cock, with a luster like a polished conch shell, which he had placed inside a golden cage;
prosperity settled upon its crest. As the brahmin looked on, he perceived that prosperity was established there.
Having understood this, he said: "Great merchant, I teach the mantras to five hundred young brahmins;
because of one cock that crows at the wrong time, both they and I are exhausted. It is said that this cock crows at the right time;
I have come for its sake. Give this cock to me. "Take it, brahmin; I give you the cock. And at the very moment he said, "I give," [the merchant gave it].
The goddess Sirī withdrew from his head and settled upon the cluster of jewels placed at his pillow.
When the brahmin realized that the goddess had settled upon the jewels, he asked for the jewels as well.
At the very moment it was said, "I shall give you the jewels," Sirī withdrew from the jewels and settled upon the protective staff placed at his pillow. The brahmin [realized] the goddess...

Knowing that it had settled there, he asked for it as well. At the very moment he was told, "Take it and go," the Glory (Sirī) moved away from its standing place and settled upon the head of the chief queen of the merchant named Puññalakkhaṇādevī.
Knowing that it had settled there, the Brahmin Siricora thought, "This is property that must not be surrendered; even to ask for it..."
Thinking, "It is not possible," he said this to the merchant: "Great merchant, I came to your house thinking, 'I shall steal the fortune and depart.
But your fortune became established upon the crest of your cock;
when it was given to me, it moved away from that and became established upon the jewel. When it was given to me on the jewel, it became established upon the protective staff."
Having been given for the purpose of protection, it moved away from there and settled upon the head of Queen Puññalakkhaṇā.
Then [the thief] rose from his seat and departed, saying: "This, moreover, is an inviolable treasure; even this was not taken by me. It is impossible to steal your glory;
let what belongs to you remain yours. Anāthapiṇḍika [reported] this matter to the Teacher...
"I shall tell you. Having gone to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and bowed down, he sat to one side and related everything to the Tathāgata.
Upon hearing this, the Teacher said: "Householder, it is not only now that the glory of others departs elsewhere;
in the past as well, the glory produced by those of little merit went only to the feet of those possessed of merit."
Having spoken thus, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered his arts at Takkasilā; then, while living as a householder, his parents passed away."

Filled with spiritual urgency, he went forth and, having taken up the ascetic life of a seer (*isi*) in the Himalayan region, he developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
After a long period had passed, he went to the countryside to seek salt and sour food;
staying in the king’s park at Bārāṇasī, on the following day, while wandering for alms, he came to the door of the elephant trainer’s house.
Thus, having gained confidence in his conduct and way of life, he gave him alms-food, had him dwell in the park, and looked after him constantly.
At that time, a certain wood-gatherer, bringing firewood from the forest, was unable to reach the city gate by the appointed hour.
In the evening, he placed his bundle of wood at the head of his bed and lay down in a temple; many [creatures] were released in that temple.

Cocks were sleeping in a tree not far from him. Among them, the cock sleeping on top, while voiding excrement at the time of dawn, let it fall upon the body of the cock sleeping below. When asked, "By whom was excrement dropped on my body?
he replied, "By me. When asked, "For what reason? he said, "Without reflecting," and then dropped it again.
Then both of them, angry with one another, quarreled, saying, "What is your strength? What is your strength?
Thereupon, the cock lying on the bottom said, "If you kill me and eat my meat roasted on coals, you will obtain a thousand kahāpaṇas at dawn.
The cock lying on top said, "Hey, do not boast so much! My meat is fat..."
“If one eats [my] flesh, one becomes a king; if a man eats my outer flesh, he obtains the position of commander-in-chief; if a woman, she obtains the position of chief queen.
But if one eats my bone and flesh, if they are a householder, they obtain the position of treasurer;
if they have gone forth, they obtain the status of one who attends upon the royal family.”
Having heard their words, the wood-gatherer thought, "Now that he has attained the kingdom, there is no need for a thousand pieces of money.
He climbed up slowly, seized the cock lying on top, killed it, and placing it in his lap, he went forth thinking, "I shall become king.
Entering the city through the very gate that was open, he stripped the cock of its feathers and cleaned out its belly.
“Prepare this chicken meat very well,” he said, and gave it to Pajāpatī.
She prepared both the chicken meat and the rice, and presented it to him, saying, “Eat, my lord. He replied, “Bhadde, this meat is of great power;
by eating this, I shall become king and you shall become the chief queen. [Take] that rice and the meat...”
"Let us take [the food], go to the bank of the Ganges, bathe, and eat," they said; so, having set down the food vessel on the bank, they descended into the water to bathe.
At that moment, the water, stirred up by the wind, came forward, took the food vessel, and carried it away.
As it was being swept along by the river current, a certain elephant trainer, a high official, who was bathing an elephant in the lower reaches of the river, [saw it].
Having seen it, he had it lifted up and opened, and asked, "What is there?
"It is rice and chicken meat, master," they replied. He had it covered and sealed, and sent it to his wife with the instruction, "Do not open this rice until we return.
That wood-gatherer, meanwhile, [was affected] by the sand-water that had entered his mouth.
With his belly bloated, he fled.
Then, a certain ascetic possessing the divine eye, who was a family friend of that elephant trainer, reflected with his divine eye: "My attendant does not leave the elephant stables;
when indeed will he attain prosperity? and he observed that man.
Having seen him and understood the reason, he went ahead and sat down in the elephant trainer’s residence.
When the elephant trainer arrived, he paid homage to him and, sitting to one side, had a bowl of food brought and said, "Serve the ascetic with rice and meat.
The ascetic took the rice, but when the meat was being served, he did not take it and said, "This meat..."
Having said, "I shall investigate," when [the king] replied, "Investigate, venerable sir," he had the large pieces of meat and so forth divided into individual portions;
he gave the large meat to the master of the elephant-riders, the outer meat to his wife, and he himself consumed the bone-meat.
As he was departing at the conclusion of the meal, he said: "On the third day from now, you shall become king."
Having said, "Be heedful," he departed. On the third day, a neighboring king arrived and besieged Bārāṇasī.
The King of Bārāṇasī had his elephant trainer assume royal attire and commanded him, "Mount the elephant and fight.
He himself, moving about the army in the guise of a stranger, was pierced by a powerful arrow and at that very moment—
He died. Knowing that he had passed away, the elephant trainer had many kahāpaṇa coins brought out and caused the drum to be beaten, proclaiming:
"Let those who desire wealth come forward and fight! In a mere moment, the army brought the neighboring king to his end.
The ministers, having performed the funeral rites for the king, deliberated, "Whom shall we make king? and [said], "Our..."
While the king was still alive, he gave his own insignia to the elephant trainer, thinking, "This man alone shall wage war and seize the kingdom;
we shall give the sovereignty to him. Thus they consecrated him with the royal inauguration, and they also made his wife the chief queen.
The Bodhisatta became a member of the royal household.
The Teacher, having recalled the past and attained full enlightenment, spoke these two verses:
“Whatever great wealth those unfortunate ones,
whether skilled in arts or unskilled, strive to accumulate, one who possesses good fortune enjoys it.”
“Everywhere, for a living being who has performed merit,
abundant wealth arises— even in remote places. In this context,
“who have exerted themselves” means those who have applied effort and conceived a desire for the accumulation of wealth, [obtaining] much with difficulty.

“They amass wealth. There is also the reading “ye ussukā,” meaning those men who are eager in the accumulation of wealth—both those possessing crafts such as elephant-training and those without crafts, even including those who amass great wealth by performing work for wages.
“The fortunate one enjoys them” means that the meritorious person [enjoys] those riches which were called “great wealth” for himself.
While enjoying the fruit of merit, one enjoys it even without performing any further action.
"Exceeding other beings indeed" (*aticcaññeva pāṇino*) means exceeding other beings indeed. The particle *eva* should be construed with the preceding word;

the meaning is that in all cases, one exceeds other beings who have not performed merit, while oneself has performed merit. "Even in the spheres of absorption" (*appanāyatanesupi*) means even in those that are not spheres [of absorption].
In places that are not mines of gems, gems appear; in places that are not sources of gold, gold and the like appear;
and in places that are not abodes for elephants, elephants and so forth appear. Thus, many possessions—both animate and inanimate—arise.
In this regard, concerning the arising of pearls, jewels, and the like where there are no mines, the story of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya should be told.

But the Teacher, having spoken these verses, said: "Householder, there is no other sphere for these beings equal to merit; for indeed, in the dominions of those possessed of merit, treasures arise of their own accord. Having said this, he taught this Dhamma:
"This is the treasure that grants all desires to gods and humans;
whatever they aspire to, all that is obtained by means of this."
“Golden complexion, a beautiful voice, an excellent form, and a handsome appearance;
sovereignty and a retinue—all this is obtained by means of this [merit].
Local kingship, lordship, and even the cherished happiness of a wheel-turning monarch.”
Even sovereignty over the gods— all this is obtained by means of this.
"Both human prosperity and whatever delight there is in the world of the gods,
as well as the attainment of Nibbāna— all this is obtained by means of this."
“By relying on a virtuous friend and applying oneself with proper method,
one attains mastery over true knowledge and liberation— all this is obtained through this means.
The analytical knowledges, the liberations, and whatever perfection of a disciple there may be— ”
“Paccekabuddhahood and the stage of a Buddha—all this is obtained by means of this.
Thus great is the benefit of this, namely, the perfection of merit;
therefore, the wise and the learned praise the performance of meritorious deeds.”
Now, in order to show those jewels upon which Anāthapiṇḍika’s glory was established,
he said: “The cock, the gem, the staff, and women with auspicious marks—
these appear for a person who is free from evil and has performed meritorious deeds.”
In this context, "staff" is said with reference to the staff of protection; "woman" refers to the merchant’s wife, the queen Puññalakkhaṇā.
The rest here is self-evident. Having spoken the verse, he then identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the king, but I myself was the ascetic who visited families;
the Perfectly Enlightened One was [the other ascetic]."
The fourth commentary on the Siri-jātaka.
[285] 5. The commentary on the Maṇi-sūkara-jātaka:
"For seven years in the wilderness"—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the killing of Sundarī.
Now at that time, it is recorded in the *Udāna* that the Blessed One was honored and esteemed;

this is the summary of the matter: when gain and honor arose for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus like the great flood of the five great rivers, the followers of other sects, deprived of gain and honor, were like fireflies at the rising of the sun.

Having become as if devoid of splendor, they gathered together and deliberated: "Since the time the ascetic Gotama appeared, we have been deprived of gain and honor; no one even acknowledges our existence.
With whom, then, can we join together to raise up dispraise of the ascetic Gotama so that his gain and honor may vanish?"
Then it occurred to them: "We shall be able [to speak with her] if we stay together with Sundarī.
One day, having entered the monastery of the sectarians and paid their respects, they stood there without speaking to Sundarī.
Although she spoke to them again and again, receiving no reply, she asked: "Venerable ladies, have you perhaps been troubled by someone?"
“Sister, do you not see that the ascetic Gotama is wandering about having harassed us and deprived us of our gains and honor?
She replied, “What can I possibly do in this matter? [He said: “Sister, you are beautiful and have attained the pinnacle of fortune;
by attributing infamy to the ascetic Gotama, you should turn the great multitude toward your side.”
“Having had her taken in, deprive her of her gains and honor! She accepted this, saying, “Very well,” and having paid homage, she departed.

From that time on, taking flowers, perfumes, ointments, camphor, long pepper, and other such items, she would go toward Jetavana every evening when the great multitude, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, was entering the city. “Where? [she asked.]
When asked, "Where are you going? she replied, "To the presence of the ascetic Gotama; for I am living with him in the same fragrant chamber.
Having stayed in a certain monastery of the non-Buddhist sects, she descended onto the path to Jetavana early in the morning and proceeded toward the city.
When asked, "What is it, Sundarī? Where have you been? she said, "With the ascetic Gotama..."
"Having lived together in the same fragrant chamber and having caused her to delight in the pleasure of the defilements, we have returned," she said.

Then, after a few days had passed, they gave money to some ruffians and said, "Go, kill Sundarī, place her among the flower refuse near the fragrant chamber of the ascetic Gotama, and then come back. They did accordingly.
They did so. Then the heretics, crying out in a great clamor, "We do not see Sundarī," informed the king.
When asked, "Where is your apprehension? they replied, "She has been staying at Jetavana during these days; we do not know her whereabouts there.
Thereupon, permitted by the king with the words, "In that case, go and search for her," they took their own attendants and departed.
Having gone to Jetavana and searching, they saw her among the floral refuse; they placed her on a litter, brought her into the city, and reported to the king:

"The disciples of the ascetic Gotama, thinking 'we shall conceal the evil deed committed by our Teacher,' have killed Sundarī and buried her among the floral refuse. The king said: "In that case, go!..."
“Roam through the city,” he said. They roared out in the streets of the city, “Behold the deed of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans!
and so forth, and then they returned once more to the gate of the king’s residence.
The king had Sundarī’s body placed upon a funeral pyre in the raw charnel ground and had it guarded. The residents of Sāvatthī, with the exception of—

The rest of the noble disciples for the most part said, “See the work of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans,” and so forth, as they wandered about, reviling and abusing the bhikkhus both inside and outside the city.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Tathāgata. The Teacher said, “In that case, you too should counter-accuse those people in this way.”
“The speaker of untruth goes to hell, as does he who, having done a deed, says ‘I did not do it.
Both of them, having passed away, become equal in the next world—those men of base deeds.
Thus he spoke this verse.
The king sent men, saying, "Find out whether Sundarī was killed by others.
Those rogues, meanwhile, were drinking liquor with those kahāpaṇas and quarreling with one another. There, one of them said:
"You killed Sundarī all at once, threw her among the floral refuse, and then used the kahāpaṇas obtained from that to drink liquor..."
“You are drinking! Let it be, let it be! The king’s men seized those rogues and presented them to the king.
Then the king asked them, “Were they killed by you? “Yes, Your Majesty. “By whom were they caused to be killed? “By the followers of other sects, Your Majesty.
The king summoned the heretics, had Sundarī removed, and said, “Go through the city, speaking thus:”
He commanded: "Go about [and say], 'This Sundarī was caused to be killed by us who desired to bring disrepute upon the ascetic Gotama;
there is no fault in the ascetic Gotama, nor in the disciples of Gotama, but the fault lies with us alone.
They did accordingly. At that time, the foolish masses believed it, and even the heretics were obstructed by the penalty for the murder of a human being.
From that time forth, the gains and honors received by the Buddhas became even greater.
Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
"Friends, the heretics—who thought, 'We shall cause the Buddhas to turn black'—themselves turned black; yet the gains and honors of the Buddhas have become even greater."
“...arose. The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not possible to produce defilement in the Buddhas.
To cause a Buddha to become defiled is like trying to stain a birth-gem; as in the past—”
"Even though they strove, thinking, 'We shall defile this birth-jewel,' they were unable to defile it," he said,
and being requested by them, he related a story of the past: "In the past,
while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a certain village."
Having been reborn and reached maturity, he saw the peril in sensual pleasures, went forth, and after crossing three mountain ranges in the Himalayan region, lived as an ascetic in a leaf-hut.
Not far from it was a jewel cave where about thirty wild boars dwelt; not far from that cave, a lion roamed, and his reflection appeared upon the jewel.
Seeing the shadow of the lion, the pigs became afraid and terrified; they became thin in flesh and blood.
Thinking, "Because of the purity of this gem, this shadow appears;
let us make this gem soiled and discolored," they went to a nearby lake, stirred up the mud, and returning, they rubbed that gem with the bristles of the pigs. Because of those pig bristles...
As it was being rubbed, it became even more translucent. Seeing no other means,
the pigs approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and standing to one side,
they recited the first two verses:
“For seven years, O River, we have dwelt for about thirty [days];
‘We shall destroy the radiance of the jewel,’ such was our counsel.
But as long as we polish the jewel, the more the jewel becomes purified.”
"Now we ask this: what do you consider to be the task here?
In that context, *dariye* means "in the jewel-cave. *Vasāmasa* means "we dwell. *Haññāma* means "we shall kill," [that is,] "we too shall cause it to lose its color.
*Idañca dāni pucchāma* means "now we ask: for what reason is this jewel becoming soiled?"
“...is purified”—this is what we ask him. “What deed do you think?”—in this sense, “what deed do you think [I have done] here?
Then, explaining it to them, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:
“This beryl gem is flawless, stainless, and beautiful;
it is impossible to destroy its splendor. Depart, you pigs!

In this context, “flawless” means without roughness. “Beautiful” means radiant. “Splendor” means light. “Depart” means: it is not possible to destroy the radiance of this gem; however, you should abandon this gem-cave and go elsewhere.
Having heard his words, they did exactly as he instructed. The Bodhisatta, having attained meditative absorption (jhāna), became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, I myself was that ascetic.
This concludes the fifth narration, the Maṇisūkara-jātaka.
[286] 6. The Commentary on the Sālūka Jātaka:
"Do not envy the lily. This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction of Thullakumārikā.
That story will be made clear in the Cūḷanāradakassapa Jātaka. Then the Teacher summoned that bhikkhu.
“Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied? he asked. “It is so, Bhante,” he replied.
“Who is it that makes you dissatisfied? “A young woman of great stature, Bhante. The Teacher said, “This woman, monk, has brought you harm;
even in the past, you were the ‘upper-crust’ (*uttaribhaṅga*) for the assembly that had come for the sake of her marriage. Having said this, at the request of the monks, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a large red bull named Mahālohita, and his younger brother was a bull named Cūḷalohita.
Both bulls were performing work for a certain family in a village.
That family had a daughter who had reached marriageable age, and they had betrothed her to another family. Then that family...
Thinking, "At the time of our marriage, there will be a ceremonial cloth (uttaribhaṅga)," they raised a pig named Sālūka on rice-gruel and solid food;

it used to sleep beneath the bed. Then one day, Cūḷalohita said to his brother, "Brother, we do the work in this family, and it is by depending on us that this family lives; yet these people [treat] us..."
“They give him only a mere handful of straw; they feed this pig with rice gruel and have him sleep beneath the bed.
What indeed will he do for them? Mahālohita said, “Father, do not long for his rice gruel;
on the day of this girl’s wedding, they intend to make this [gruel] into an upper-cloth (uttaribhaṅga) for her, and they are feeding him this much meat only to make his body stout.”
“Wait, and after a few days you will see him being dragged out from the lower bed-chamber, slaughtered, and cut into pieces to be made into food for the guests.
Having said this, he uttered the first two verses: “Do not envy Sālūka;
he eats the food of the sick. ... [and so on] ...”
"Eat the husk without anxiety; this is the mark of long life.
'Now he will come here, a guest who serves with diligence;
then you shall see the lotus-root sleeping upon the pestle.'"
