Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: "Dear son, do not long for the state of a water-buffalo or a pig;
for he is eating food that causes illness, food that is a meal of death, having eaten which he will before long reach his end.
But you, being free from anxiety and without attachment, eat this chaff mixed with straw that you have received; this is for the sake of long life."

"Lakkhaṇa" means the sign for recognition. Now, in just a few days, that man from the wedding party—accompanied by a large retinue, a servant of the groom, having arrived here as a guest—will see this *sālūka* root lying there, killed and being slaughtered because it possesses an upper lip resembling a pestle;
thus it is called "pestle-lipped" (*musaluttara*).
Then, after only a few days had passed, when the wedding guests arrived, they killed a water-lily (*sālūka*) and prepared a meal of superior quality.
Seeing that misfortune befall it, both oxen thought, "Our own fodder is indeed better.
Having attained full enlightenment, the Teacher spoke this third verse, which illuminates that meaning:
“Having seen the magnificent boar lying there with his snout raised high, the old oxen reflected:
‘This is truly our own excellent prize, as it were.
In this context, *bhusāmiva* means: “It is indeed our own excellent and supreme prize.”
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
at the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “The girl at that time was the present Thullakumārikā;
the Sālūka was the bhikkhu who became dissatisfied; Cūḷalohita was Ānanda; and Mahālohita was indeed myself.”
The sixth: The Exposition of the Sālūka-jātaka.
[287] 7. The Exposition of the Lābhagaraha-jātaka.
"Not even a madman..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a co-resident disciple of the Elder Sāriputta.
He related [the story]. It is said that the Elder’s pupil approached the Elder, paid homage, and sat down to one side, asking:
“Venerable sir, please tell me the method for the arising of gains; by doing what does one become a recipient of robes and other requisites?
Then the Elder said to him: “Friend, gain and honor arise for one who is endowed with four factors.”
"Having broken down one's own sense of shame and dread of blame, having abandoned the life of a recluse, one must act like a madman though not actually mad;
one must speak malicious words, act like an actor, and be a curious person with loose speech"—thus he spoke this path for the arising of gain. Having censured that path, he rose up.
He departed. The Elder approached the Teacher, paid homage, and related what had occurred.
The Teacher said, "Sāriputta, this bhikkhu does not criticize gain only now; he has criticized it even in the past. Having spoken thus, at the Elder's request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
Having reached maturity, at the age of sixteen, he attained the culmination of the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of learning.
Becoming a world-renowned teacher, he taught the arts to five hundred young students. Among them was one student...
Endowed with virtue and good conduct, one day he approached his teacher and asked about the way to acquire gain for these beings:
"How does the acquisition of gain arise for these beings? The teacher replied, "Dear son, the acquisition of gain for these beings arises through four causes," and spoke the first verse:
“Neither deranged, nor slanderous, neither deceitful nor curious;
among the deluded, one gains profit—this is your instruction.
Therein, *nānummatto* means not deranged. This is what is meant: just as one who is deranged [behaves improperly toward] women, men, girls, and children...
Having seen them, he plunders their clothes, ornaments, and so forth; seizing fish, meat, cakes, and other such things from here and there by force, he eats them.

In exactly the same way, one who has become a householder—having abandoned shame and dread of blame arising internally and externally, disregarding what is wholesome and unwholesome, and failing to fear the terror of hell—is overcome by greed and his mind is consumed by sensual desires.

One who is heedless commits acts of violence such as breaking into homes; even one who has gone forth, having abandoned shame and dread of blame, disregarding what is wholesome and unwholesome, and failing to fear the terrors of hell, tramples upon the training rules prescribed by the Teacher.

Overcome by greed and with a mind consumed by it, relying on mere robes and other requisites, he abandons his own state of renunciation and, being heedless, engages in such things as the practice of medicine and acting as a messenger.
He performs such acts as giving bamboo and so forth, and makes his living by depending on these;
though not actually insane, because he resembles one who is insane, he is called "insane," and for such a person, gain quickly arises.
But he who is thus not insane, being modest and scrupulous, does not obtain gain among deluded and unwise men; therefore, one who desires gain should act like one who is insane.
Regarding the phrase "nor malicious speech": here too, one who is malicious brings slander to the royal court, saying, "This was done by such-and-such a person.
By doing so, he seizes the reputation of others for himself.
Kings, thinking, "This man is loyal to us," place him in high positions; and ministers and others think, "He will cause dissension within our circle at the royal court."
They think it should be given out of fear; thus, at present, gain arises for the backbiter.
However, one who is not a backbiter does not obtain gain among the deluded—this is how the meaning should be understood.
"Like an actor" means that one who seeks to produce gain must be like an actor; for just as an actor, having abandoned shame and moral dread, [performs his art].
Just as one who plays with dancing, singing, and instrumental music accumulates wealth, even so must one who desires gain conduct himself by breaking his sense of shame and dread of blame,
engaging in various kinds of play like a companion to the lecherous among women,
men, girls, and boys. He who does not play in this manner does not obtain gain from those who are deluded.
“Nākutūhala”: *kutūhala* means one whose speech is scattered. For kings ask their ministers:
“It is heard that in such-and-such a place a man has been killed, a house plundered, and another’s wife violated;
whose work could this be? In that situation, even while the others remain silent, he stands up and says: “Such-and-such a person and such-and-such a person...”

And he says, "I am Kutūhala. Because of his words, the kings search for those men and, having restrained them, bestow great honor upon him, saying, "Because of him, our city has become free of thieves.
The rest of the people also [rely] on him out of fear, thinking, "If questioned by our royal officers, he will speak what is appropriate or inappropriate."
They give wealth; thus, gain arises for one who is curious.
But he who is not curious does not obtain gain among the deluded. "This is your instruction" means: "This is our guidance regarding your gains.
Having heard his teacher's words, the pupil, censuring gain—
“Fie on that gain of fame and gain of wealth, O brahmin,
which is sustained by falling into ruin or by practicing unrighteousness!
Even better would it be to wander as a homeless renunciant, carrying a bowl.”
“This livelihood is indeed better than seeking it through unrighteousness”—thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, “that mode of life” means that way of living. “By one’s own downfall” means by one’s own ruin.
“By practicing unrighteousness” means by performing unrighteous acts, improper deeds—such as killing, binding, and censuring—thereby bringing oneself to ruin and practicing what is not Dhamma.
Whatever livelihood one has practiced, as well as fame and the acquisition of wealth—all that is woe! I despise it; I censure it;
my intention is: "I have no need for this. "Taking a bowl" means having taken up the alms-bowl.

"A homeless wanderer" means one who should live having gone forth from home and being without a house; and a true person does not practice unrighteous conduct by way of bodily misconduct and so forth.

One should practice [this]. For what reason? Because this very livelihood is better. As for "that which is by means of unrighteousness," he shows that this alms-round among other families with bowl in hand is better than that pursuit of a livelihood by unrighteous means—it is a hundredfold, a thousandfold more excellent.

Thus, having praised the virtues of the renunciant life, the young man went forth, took up the ascetic life of an *isi*, and while seeking alms in accordance with the Dhamma, he attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), eventually destined for the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, the young man who censured gain was the monk [who criticized me], and the teacher was none other than I myself.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Lābhagarahajātakavaṇṇanā.
[288] 8. The Commentary on the Fish-Net Jātaka.
"The fish are worth..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a fraudulent merchant. The story of the present has already been told above.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of householders.
Having reached maturity, he established a household. He also had a younger brother, and later their father passed away.
One day, thinking, "We shall settle our father’s business affairs," they went to a certain village;
having obtained a thousand kahāpaṇas, they were returning when, while waiting for a boat at a river crossing, they ate their packed meal. The Bodhisatta—
Having given the leftover food to the fish in the Ganges, he offered a portion to the river deity.
As soon as the deity had expressed her appreciation for the offering, she increased her divine splendor; perceiving her own increase in glory, she understood the reason for it.
Meanwhile, the Bodhisatta, having spread his upper robe upon the sand, lay down and fell asleep, while his younger brother [remained awake] for a short while.

He was a professional thief. Without giving those kahāpaṇas to the Bodhisatta, out of a desire to seize them for himself, he made a bundle of pebbles resembling a bundle of kahāpaṇas and placed both bundles together in one spot.
When they had boarded the boat and reached the middle of the Ganges, the younger brother shook the boat, saying, "I shall throw the bundle of pebbles into the water."
Having thrown down a bundle worth a thousand, he said, "Brother, the bundle worth a thousand has fallen into the water;
what shall we do? "What can we do with what has fallen into the water? Do not worry. The river deity thought:
"I shall increase my divine glory by reciting the words of thanksgiving for this gift, and I will protect what belongs to him. Then she [took] her own...
By his supernatural power, he caused that bundle to swallow a large fish and took charge of guarding it himself.
That thief also went home and, thinking, "My brother has been cheated," began to untie the bundle;
seeing the pebbles, his heart grew dry with grief, and he lay down clutching the foot of the bedstead.
Then the fishermen cast their net for the purpose of catching fish. By the power of the deity, that fish entered the net.
Having caught it, the fishermen entered the city to sell it. When people saw the great fish, they asked for its price.
The fishermen said, "Take it by paying one thousand kahāpaṇas and seven māsakas."
People laughed, saying, "We have never even seen a fish worth a thousand coins!
The fishermen took the fish, went to the door of the Bodhisatta’s house, and said, "Take this fish.
"What is its price? "Give seven māsakas and take it. "How can you give it for that when you give so much to others? "To others..."
"We will give it for seven hundred and one māsakas; you, however, take it after giving us seven māsakas.
He gave them the seven māsakas and sent the fish to his wife.
While she was cutting open the belly of the fish, she saw a bundle of a thousand [māsakas] and informed the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta looked at it and recognized his own seal.
Having seen this and recognized it as his own property, he thought: "Now these fishermen are giving this fish to others for a thousand [pieces] and seven māsakas;
but having come to us, because it was our own, they took only seven māsakas and gave it to us.
It is impossible to make anyone believe this without explaining the difference between these two cases."
He spoke the first verse:
“Fish are worth more than a thousand [pieces of gold]; there is no one who would believe this.
Even if I were to have seven months remaining here, I too would buy that gift of fish.”
In this context, "more than" means that when asked by others, the fishermen say, "They are worth more than one thousand [pieces of money] plus seven months' wages.

"There is no one who would believe this" means there is no such person who, not knowing this matter through direct perception, would believe my word; nor is there anyone who would believe that the fish are worth this much.
Thus it does not exist; for that very reason, the meaning is also that they were not taken by others. "And there were mine" means that I had seven māsakas.
"The fish-group" (macchuddāna) refers to the group of fish. For indeed, other fish were tied together with that one fish;
this was said with reference to that entire group of fish. "One would buy" means one bought; [the price was] seven [māsakas].
The meaning is that they would take such a quantity of fish for giving a single *māsaka*.
Having spoken thus, he thought: "Upon what basis did I obtain these kahāpaṇas?
At that moment, the river deity stood in the sky, her form visible, and said: "I am the deity of the Ganges; by me, the fish..."
“Having given me extra alms-food, he granted me a boon; therefore, I have come here protecting what belongs to you,” she declared, and spoke this verse:
“Having given food for the fish, he assigned the merit to me.”
“Remembering that offering, you have performed this act of reverence.

In this context, “offering” (*dakkhiṇā*) refers to the gift of merit (*pattidāna*) given in this place. “By you, remembering the reverence performed for me” means: “Remembering that reverence performed by you for me, [I thought], ‘This wealth of yours has been protected by me.
Having said this, that deity related everything regarding the fraudulent deed committed by his younger brother, saying: “This...
"Now you lie there with a parched heart; for one with a wicked mind, there is no growth.
But I brought wealth and gave it to you, thinking, 'Let not what belongs to you be lost. Do not give this to the younger thief, but take it all yourself!
Having said this, he spoke the third verse:
“For one with a corrupted mind, there is no prosperity, nor do the deities honor him;
he who, being a doer of evil deeds, deceived his brother regarding the paternal inheritance.

In this context, “there is no prosperity” means that for such a person, there is no growth whatsoever, either in this world or in the next world. “Nor do the deities honor him” means that the deities who protect what belongs to that person do not pay him respect.

Thus spoke the deity who was a friend to the deceitful thief, being unwilling to give him the kahāpaṇas. But the Bodhisatta, thinking, "It is not possible to act in this way," sent five hundred kahāpaṇas to him as well.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka;
at the conclusion of the Truths, the merchant was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the younger brother was the fraudulent merchant of today, and the elder brother..."
"But it was indeed I who was he.
The commentary on the Macchuddāna Jātaka is the eighth.
[289] 9. The commentary on the Nānāchanda Jātaka.

"O Great King, there are various desires"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the eight wonderful gains of the Venerable Ānanda. The story will appear in the Juṇhā Jātaka of the Ekādasakanipāta.
In the past, however, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen;
having reached maturity and mastered all arts at Takkasilā, he succeeded to the kingdom upon his father’s passing.
His father’s former priest, having been removed from his position, was living in poverty in an old house.
Now one day, while the Bodhisatta was wandering about the city at night in the guise of a stranger to inspect it, some thieves who had committed crimes were drinking liquor at a tavern;
they took another jar and [prepared to depart] for themselves.
As they were going home, seeing him in the middle of the street, they cried out, "Hey! Who are you?
They struck him, seized his upper garment, made him lift up a water-jar, and went along making a great noise.

At that very moment, the brahmin had gone out and was standing in the middle of the street observing the constellations; having realized that the king had fallen into the hands of his enemies, he [addressed] the brahmin lady...
He addressed her. She said, "What is it, noble sir? and hurriedly went into his presence. Then he said to her, "Madam, our king has fallen into the power of his enemies.
"Noble sir, what business do you have with the king's affairs? The brahmins will find out," she replied.
When the king heard the brahmin's words, he stepped aside a short distance and said to the rogues, "I am in trouble, sirs; [give me] my upper robe..."
“Take me and release me! Out of compassion, they released him as he pleaded again and again.
He, having observed their dwelling house, turned back. Then the former state-priest brahmin also said, “Madam, our king has been freed from the hands of his enemies.
When the king heard this and observed that man’s house as well, he returned to the palace.
"Mount it. When the night had turned to dawn, he summoned the brahmins and asked, "Teachers, what did you observe regarding the constellations during the night?
"Yes, Your Majesty," they replied. "Was it auspicious? "It was auspicious, Your Majesty. "Is there anyone who has taken anything? "There is none, Your Majesty.
The king said, "Summon the brahmin from such-and-such a house," referring to his former domestic chaplain.
Having summoned him, he asked, "Teacher, did you see an auspicious constellation tonight? "Yes, Your Majesty," he replied.
"Is there any specific omen? "Yes, Great King; tonight you went into the power of your enemies, but were released in an instant.
The king thought, "One who knows constellations must indeed be like this," and had the other brahmins expelled.
“Brāhmaṇa, I am pleased with you; choose a boon,” he said. “Great King, I will choose after consulting with my wife and children,” he replied.
“Go, consult them, and then return,” [the king said].
He went and summoned his wife, son, daughter-in-law, and slave-girl, and said, “The king is granting me a boon.”
“What shall we take? he asked. The brahmin woman said, “Bring me a hundred cows.
His son, named Chattamāṇava, said, “A noble chariot yoked with four bay horses the color of white water-lilies.
His daughter-in-law said, “All my ornaments, beginning with my jeweled earrings. A slave girl named Puṇṇā said, “Both my mortar and pestle...”
"Very well. But the brahmin, desiring to obtain an excellent village, went into the presence of the king.
When asked, "Brahmin, have you inquired about your wife and children? he replied, "Yes, Your Majesty, I have inquired; they have many desires," and spoke the first two verses:
"O Great King, we live in one house with diverse desires; ... [the rest of the verses follow]"
“I desire an excellent village, and the brahmin woman desires a hundred cows;
my son desires a chariot of thoroughbred horses, and the maiden desires jeweled earrings;
as for this wretched Puṇṇikā, she longs for a mortar.”
In this context, *iccheti* means "I desire. *Gavaṃ sataṃ* means "a hundred cows," that is, a hundred milch-cows. *Kaññā* means "a daughter-in-law.
*Yā cesā* means "this very one"—referring to the slave-girl named Puṇṇikā in our house—who is base and wretched, and who desires and longs for the mortar along with the pestles.
The king, commanding, "Give everyone whatever they desire," said:
"To the brahmin, a choice village; to the brahmin woman, a hundred cows;
to his son, a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses; to his daughter, jeweled earrings."
"Whatever this Puṇṇikā, the wretched woman, may be, place her upon the mortar," he said, speaking this verse.
Therein, "whatever this Puṇṇikā" refers to that which he calls the wretched woman; "place her upon the mortar" means "accept her [as your share].

Thus the king, having granted the Brahmin both what was requested and other great honors, said, "Henceforth, apply yourself with diligence to whatever duties we have to perform," and he kept the Brahmin in his own presence.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin was Ānanda, and the king was none other than myself.
This concludes the ninth commentary, the Nānāchanda-jātaka.
10. The Commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsaka-jātaka.
"Virtue alone is indeed beautiful"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain Brahmin who tested his own virtue.
The story, however, has already been related in detail both in the present and in the past in the *Sīlavīmaṃsaka-jātaka* of the First Book (*Ekakanipāta*).
Here, however, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, his domestic priest was endowed with virtue.
Thinking, "I shall test my own virtue," he took one kahāpaṇa coin from the money-changer's board for two days.
Then, on the third day, they seized him as a thief and led him into the presence of the king.
On the way, he saw snake-charmers playing with a snake. When the king saw him, he asked, "Why did you do such a thing? The brahmin—
Having said, "Out of a desire to test his own virtue," he spoke these verses:
"Virtue indeed is beautiful; virtue is unsurpassed in the world.
Behold: though he be a serpent of deadly venom, if he is virtuous, he is not slain."
“I shall praise that virtue which is approved in the world as auspicious;
it is the conduct of the noble way of life by which one is called ‘virtuous.
Such a person becomes dear to kinsmen and shines among friends.”
“With the breakup of the body, the virtuous person is reborn in a happy destination.
In this context, *sīla* means conduct (*ācāra*). *Kira* is a particle used in the sense of tradition. *Kalyāṇa* means beautiful;
the meaning is that the wise say, “Virtue alone is indeed beautiful. *Passa* (behold) is what he says to himself. *Na haññati* (is not slain): [he is not harmed].

One does not harm others, nor is one harmed by others. "I shall undertake what has been undertaken"—this is how it is accepted by the wise as "approved" (*anumataṃ*), meaning "secure and fearless. "By which it is called":
by means of which virtue a virtuous person, practicing the conduct of the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas, is called "one whose conduct follows the way of the Noble Ones" (*ariyavuttisamācāra*).
The meaning is: "I shall undertake that which is so called. It shines like a mass of fire on the summit of a mountain;
thus the Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma to the king while proclaiming the praise of virtue through three verses, said:
"Great King, in my house there is much wealth belonging to my father, belonging to my mother, acquired by myself, and given by you."
"There is no limit to this; however, while testing my virtue, I took the coins from the money-changer's board.
Now I have realized that in this world, birth, clan, and family status are of little consequence, whereas virtue alone is supreme.
I shall go forth into homelessness; please grant me permission to do so. Having thus obtained permission, he departed.
Although he was entreated again and again by the king, he departed, entered the Himalayas, and went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Having realized the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dharma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the Brahmin priest who tested his virtue."
The commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsaka-jātaka is the tenth.
The fourth chapter, the Abbhantara-vagga, concludes here.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
Duma, Kaṃsavara, Uttama, Byaggha, Migā, Maṇayo, Maṇi, Sālukka, Avhāyana, Anusāsaniya, Macchavara, Maṇikuṇḍalaka, and Kira—these are the ten. 5.
The Kumbha Chapter.
[291] 1. The Commentary on the Surāghaṭa Jātaka:
"The jar that grants all desires. This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the nephew of Anāthapiṇḍika.
It is said that he squandered forty crores of gold belonging to his parents through his addiction to drink.
Having lost it, he went back to the merchant. The merchant gave him a thousand [pieces] saying, "Carry out your business," but he lost that as well and returned again.
Again, the merchant had five hundred given to him; having lost those too, he returned once more. Then the merchant had two thick cloths given to him.
Having lost those as well, when he returned again, the merchant had him seized by the neck and driven out. He was left without a protector.
Having offered the oblation, he died leaning against the neighbor's wall; they dragged him out and threw him away.
Anāthapiṇḍika went to the monastery and reported the entire account of his nephew’s fate to the Tathāgata. The Teacher said, "How will you satisfy him?
Even though I previously gave him a jar that granted all desires, I was unable to satisfy him."
Having said, "He was not able," he related a story of the past when requested by him.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of merchants;
upon his father's passing, he obtained the position of treasurer. In his house, there were forty crores of wealth buried underground.
He, however, had only one son. Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, the Bodhisatta passed away and was reborn as Sakka, the king of the gods.
Then his son blocked off the street, had a pavilion constructed, and sat surrounded by a great crowd, beginning to drink liquor.
He [rewarded] those performing leaping, running, dancing, singing, and so forth, by the thousands...
Giving away his wealth, he fell into the state of being addicted to women, liquor, and meat;
becoming intoxicated and seeking out social gatherings, he wandered about thinking, "Where is the singing? Where is the dancing? Where is the instrumental music?
Before long, having squandered forty million pieces of gold along with his means of enjoyment, luxury goods, and utensils, he became destitute and wretched, wandering about clad in rags.
Sakka, perceiving his state of poverty through his supernormal knowledge, came out of affection for his son and gave him a jar that grants all desires.
He then instructed him, saying, "Dear son, protect this jar so that it does not break;
as long as you have this, there will be no limit to your wealth. Be diligent! Having thus advised him, he returned to the world of the gods. Then...
From that time on, he wandered about drinking liquor. Then one day, being intoxicated, he threw the jar into the air;
while attempting to catch it, he missed his aim once, and the jar fell to the ground and broke.
From that point forward, having become poor again, he dressed in rags and, with an alms-bowl in hand, went begging for food and died leaning against another's wall.
The Teacher, having brought up this past event,
said: “Having obtained a jar that grants all desires,
the rogue prospers in happiness for as long as he protects it.”
“When, intoxicated and arrogant, one breaks the jar through negligence,
then, naked and destitute, the fool suffers later. In the same way, he who,
having acquired wealth, consumes it with negligence [suffers likewise].”
"The fool suffers afterwards, like a rogue who has smashed a jar.
Having spoken these verses of perfect enlightenment, he identified the Jātaka.
In this context, "giving all desires" refers to a jar capable of granting all material objects of desire. "Jar" (kuṭa) is a synonym for a water-jar (kumbha).
"For as long as" means for whatever length of time. "He protects" means that whoever, having obtained such [a vessel], guards it for as long as he does, for that long he prospers in happiness;
this is the meaning. "Intoxicated and arrogant" means intoxicated by the madness of liquor and arrogant with pride.
"Through negligence he broke the jar" means he shattered the jar through carelessness. "Naked and ragged" means sometimes naked and sometimes [clad in rags].
It is called *pottha* because it is covered with rags (*pilotika*). "Even so" means just so. "Negligent" means through negligence. "He suffers" means he grieves.
"At that time, the rogue who broke the jar of liquor was the merchant’s nephew, while Sakka was none other than myself.
This is the first commentary on the *Surāghaṭa Jātaka*.
[292] 2. The Commentary on the Supatta Jātaka.

"In Benares, O Great King," etc.—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the rice-meat meal mixed with fresh ghee that the Elder Sāriputta had given to Queen Bimbā. The story of the events is as follows.

The narrative regarding the internal birth story (*abbhantarajātakavatthu*) is exactly the same. For at that time as well, the elder nun’s abdominal wind was provoked; Rāhulabhadda informed the elder [of this].

The elder had her seated in the assembly hall, went to the residence of the King of Kosala, and having brought back rice cooked with fresh ghee mixed with the broth of red fish, he gave it to her. He, having brought it back...
He gave it to the elder nun; as soon as she had eaten it, her abdominal wind was allayed. The king sent men to investigate, and from that time forth he provided the elder nun with such food.
Then one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth: "Friends, the General of the Dhamma [gave such food] to the elder nun..."
“...and satisfied them with food. The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta gives what Rāhulamātā has requested;
in the past, too, he gave it to her. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into the womb of a crow.
Having reached maturity, he became the eldest of eighty thousand crows, a king of crows named Supatta;
his chief queen was a female crow named Suphassā, and his commander-in-chief was named Sumukha. Surrounded by those eighty thousand crows, he [resided] in Bārāṇasī.
He lived there, depending upon him. One day, while Supassa was seeking food, he passed by the royal kitchen of the King of Bārāṇasī.

The cook, having prepared a meal for the king consisting of various preparations of fish and meat, stood nearby with a few dishes uncovered, fanning away the steam. Supassa [smelled] the scent of the fish and meat.
Having eaten the king’s food and wishing to eat it again, she did not mention it that day;
but on the second day, when he said, "Come, dear lady, let us go for alms," she replied, "You go; I have a certain craving.
When he asked, "What kind of craving? she said, "I wish to eat the food of the King of Bārāṇasī, but I cannot..."
“It is possible for me to obtain that; therefore, O Lord, I shall sacrifice my life,” he said. The Bodhisatta sat down reflecting.
Sumukha came and asked, “Why, Great King, are you displeased? The king explained the matter to him.
The general said, “Do not worry, Great King,” and having comforted them both, he said, “Today you two remain right here; we—”
Having said, "We shall bring food," he departed.
He gathered the crows together, explained the situation, and saying, "Come, we shall bring food," he entered Bārāṇasī with the crows;
then, having divided them into groups, he stationed them at various places not far from the kitchen.

Having stationed them for the sake of protection, he himself sat upon the roof of the kitchen together with eight *kāka-yodha* (crow-warriors), watching for the time when the king’s meal would be carried out.
He said to those crows: "When the king’s food is being carried, I shall cause the vessels to fall;
when the vessels have fallen, there will be no life left for me, but you four men must [eat] a mouthful."
“Take four portions of fish and meat, and having brought them, feed the king of crows together with his wife on a fine leaf;
when asked, ‘Where is the general? you should say, ‘He will follow behind.
Then the cook, having prepared the king’s meal and taken it in a carrying-pole, set out for the royal palace. When he reached the royal courtyard, the commander of the crows—
Having given the signal to the crows, he himself flew up, sat upon the chest of the food-bearer, struck him with his talons,
and having pierced the tip of his nose with his beak— which resembled the point of a reed— stood up and covered his face with both wings.
As the king was walking on the great terrace, he looked through the large window and observed that action of the crow.
Seeing this, he called out to the food-bearer, saying, "Ho, cook! Throw away the dishes and catch the crow!
He threw away the dishes and seized the crow firmly. The king also said to him, "Come here!
At that moment, crows arrived, ate as much as they could carry, and took the remainder according to the aforementioned method.
They arrived. Then the rest came and ate what remained. Those eight people also went and fed the king together with his queen;
thus Suphassā’s craving was appeased. The food-bearer presented a crow to the king.
Then the king asked him: "O crow, you have no shame before me, yet you have torn the nose of the food-bearer."
“You broke the food vessels and did not protect your own life; why did you commit such an act?
The crow replied, “Great King, our king dwells near Bārāṇasī, and I am his commander-in-chief.
His wife, named Suphassā, was pregnant with a longing (dohaḷa) and desired to eat your food. The king [acted] for her longing...”
He told it to me. I came right there, having renounced my own life;
now food has been sent for her, and my heart’s desire has reached its fulfillment. It was for this reason that I committed such a deed,” he said, speaking these verses.
“Great King, in Bārāṇasī there lived a king of crows,
Supatta, surrounded by eighty thousand followers.
His wife was pregnant with longing and desired to eat *suphassā*.”
“In the king’s kitchen was cooked food of great value, the king’s own meal.
‘I have been sent as a messenger to them, and I have come here from the king;
I shall perform service for my master, not this nose-wound.’”
In that context, *bārāṇasim* means "in Bārāṇasī. *Nivāsako* means "one who dwells permanently. *Pakkam* means prepared in various ways;

some recite it as *siddham*. *Paccaggham* means fresh and not stale, or alternatively, it is called *paccaggham* because there are individually high-priced items such as preparations of fish and meat therein.
"I was sent to them as a messenger, for I have come here on behalf of the king."
"I am the messenger of both of them, an executor of the king’s command, and have been sent here"—this is the meaning.
"I shall pay homage to my master": thus having come, I shall perform the homage, honor, and respect due to my own master.
"I did not make a wound on your nose, O Great King"—for this reason, [you and your own life...]
“Disregarding the food bowl, I caused it to be dropped and made a wound on the nose of the food-bearer with my beak;
thus I have shown disrespect to my own king. Now, you may inflict whatever punishment you wish.
When the king heard his words, he said, “We have already bestowed great honor upon those who were human beings. Our...”
"We cannot find a spiritual friend (sahajja) to serve; even though we give away villages and such, we do not obtain one who would grant us our very life.
Yet this crow, though being merely a bird, sacrifices his own life for the sake of his king; he is truly a virtuous man (sappurisa), a sweet-voiced preacher of the Dhamma.
Having thus gained confidence in his virtues, she honored him with a white parasol (setacchatța). He took the white parasol he had received and offered it to the king himself.

Having made his offering, he spoke of the Bodhisatta’s virtues. The king summoned him, and after hearing the Dhamma from both of them, he established a regular supply of food for each of them according to his own dietary standard;
he had one measure of rice cooked daily for the remaining crows, and himself, standing by the Bodhisatta’s instruction, granted fearlessness to all beings and observed the five precepts.
He protected [them]. However, the proclamation that Supatta was a crow lasted for seven hundred years.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the king was Ānanda; the general Sumukha was Sāriputta; Suphassā was Rāhulamātā; and Supatta was indeed myself.
This is the second commentary on the Supatta Jātaka.
[293] 3. The Commentary on the Kāyanibbinda Jātaka.
"When I am touched..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain man.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a man afflicted with jaundice who was rejected by physicians. His wife and children...
He thought, "Who is able to nurse this man? Then it occurred to him:

"If I recover from this illness, I shall go forth into homelessness. After a few days, having obtained some suitable food and recovered his health, he went to Jetavana and requested the Teacher for the going-forth.
In the presence of the Teacher, he received both the going-forth and full ordination.
Not long after receiving it, he attained Arahatship. Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth:

"Friends, such-and-such a man suffering from jaundice, thinking 'Once I have recovered from this illness, I shall go forth,' went forth and even attained Arahatship. The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what is it that you are discussing?"
“...are now sitting together in conversation. Having asked this, and being told, “Indeed, they are,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that this has happened;
in the past, wise men also spoke thus, recovered from their illnesses, went forth into homelessness, and brought about their own advancement. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
Having reached maturity and established a household, he became afflicted with jaundice. Even physicians were unable to treat him, and his wife and children were filled with remorse for him.
Thinking, "Once I have recovered from this disease, I shall go forth," he obtained some suitable food, and having been cured, he entered the Himalayas and went forth as an ascetic.
Having aroused the higher knowledges and the meditative attainments, and dwelling in the bliss of jhāna, he uttered this inspired exclamation:
"For so long a time, I did not obtain such bliss as this! And while uttering this exclamation, he spoke these verses:
"When I was afflicted by a certain disease, suffering intensely from a malady and being tormented;..."
This body quickly putrefies, like a flower placed in the dust in the heat.
It is ignoble, yet reckoned as noble; impure, yet considered pure;
filled with various kinds of filth, for one who does not see its true nature.
“Alas! This diseased, putrid body—loathsome, impure, and subject to illness—at which people, being heedless and infatuated, miss the path to rebirth in the world of the Sugata.

In this context, “by one [disease]” means by one of the ninety-eight diseases, namely the malady of jaundice (*paṇḍuroga*). It is called a “disease” (*roga*) because its intrinsic nature is to cause affliction (*rujjanasabhāvattā*).

Thus named. "Is afflicted" (*ruppati*) means being struck or oppressed. "Placed in the sun on the dust" means that just as a delicate flower placed in the sun upon hot sand would wither away, so too does it wither; this is the meaning.
"The ignoble is reckoned as noble" means that which is repulsive and unpleasant is nevertheless reckoned as pleasant by fools. "Filled with various kinds of filth."
It is filled with the thirty-two types of filth, beginning with the hair.
To one who does not see the true nature of the body—namely, the blind, foolish worldling—it appears as something pleasant, beautiful, and fit for enjoyment;
however, the nature of foulness, which has been explained in the manner of "the eye-ordure from the eye" and so forth, does not appear to such fools.
"Afflicted" means constantly ill. "Intoxicated" means excessively muddled by the intoxication of the defilements. "The folk" refers to blind, foolish worldlings.

"They lose the path to rebirth in the Happy State" means that, being stuck and clinging to this putrid body, they fill the path to the states of loss and thereby forfeit the path to rebirth in the happy realms distinguished as those of gods and humans.

Thus, the Great Being, contemplating the various forms of impurity and the state of constant illness within the body, became disenchanted with the body. Having cultivated the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) for the rest of his life, he was destined for the Brahma-world.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*), identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, many people attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) and other stages. "At that time, I myself was that ascetic.
This is the third commentary on the *Kāyanibbinda Jātaka*.
[294] 4. The Commentary on the Jambukhādaka Jātaka.
"Who is this one with a sweet voice and a nasal tone?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta and Kokālika.
At that time, when Devadatta’s gains and honor had declined, Kokālika approached various families and said, "The Elder Devadatta..."
“He was born in the lineage of Mahā Sammata, in the royal dynasty of Okkāka; he grew up in an unbroken Kṣatriya family;
he is a bearer of the Three Piṭakas, an attainer of *jhāna*, sweet-spoken, and a preacher of the Dhamma. Give [alms] and do service for this elder!”—thus he spoke in praise of Devadatta.
Devadatta, too, [praised him, saying]: “Kokālika left behind a prominent Brahmin family and went forth; he is learned...”
“A preacher of the Dhamma! Give him [alms], provide for Kokālika! Thus he spoke in praise of Kokālika.
So, having spoken in praise of one another, they wandered about eating at the homes of lay families. Then one day, in the Hall of Truth, the bhikkhus raised this discussion:
“Friends, Devadatta and Kokālika, having spoken of non-existent virtues in each other’s presence...”
“...eating as they wander about. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, with what conversation are you sitting gathered here now?
When they replied, “With this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that they eat after speaking of each other’s non-existent virtues;
in the past, too, they ate in just this way. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a certain rose-apple grove.
There, a crow sat on a branch of a rose-apple tree eating rose-apple fruits.
Then, a jackal arrived and, looking upward, saw the crow and thought, "What if I were to speak of this one's non-existent virtues?"
Having spoken thus, while praising him, saying, "He would eat the rose-apples after describing them," he recited this verse:
"Who is this one with the lovely, melodic voice, supreme among those who possess a voice?
Having escaped from the branch of the rose-apple tree, he warbles like a peacock chick."
In this context, "possessing a clear-toned voice" means endowed with a voice that is unbroken and unified by the *bindu*. "Melodious" means having a sweet sound.

"Unfallen" means not fallen away, but remaining settled. "He warbles like a young peacock chick" means that, like a young peacock, he utters a pleasing sound such that one says, "What is it that is warbling?"
Then the crow, praising him in return, spoke this second verse:
“Only a son of good family knows how to praise a son of good family;
O you with the color of a tiger’s skin, eat, my friend, I give it to you.”
In that context, "having the color of a tiger’s belly" means: "You eat with a complexion exactly like that of a young tiger;

therefore I address you as 'O you who have the color of a tiger’s belly. Eat, my friend, I give them to you!"—thus he said, "Friend, eat as much as you wish of these rose-apples; I shall give them to you."

Having spoken thus, he shook a branch of the rose-apple tree and caused its fruits to fall. Then, the deity dwelling in that rose-apple tree, seeing both of them eating the rose-apples after having spoken of non-existent virtues, recited this third verse:
“Ah, after a long time indeed I behold two speakers of falsehood come together—those who eat what has been vomited and those who eat filth—praising one another!”
In this context, "one who eats vomit" refers to the crow that eats the food vomited by others; and "one who eats from a corpse" refers to the jackal that eats corpses.
Having spoken this verse, that deity displayed a terrifying form as an object of perception and caused them to flee from that place.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, the crow was Kokālika, and the tree deity was none other than myself."
The Fourth: The Commentary on the Jambukhādaka Jātaka.
[295] 5. The Commentary on the Anta Jātaka.

"Like the hump of a bull, indeed, is yours"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning those same two individuals. The story of the present is exactly like the previous one.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a deity dwelling in an *eraṇḍa* tree on the outskirts of a certain village.
At that time, in a certain village, they had dragged out a dead old ox and discarded it in an *eraṇḍa* grove at the entrance of the village.
A jackal came and ate its flesh. A crow also came and perched upon the *eraṇḍa* tree.
Seeing him, he thought, "Suppose I were to eat his flesh by speaking of non-existent virtues," and having so reflected,
he spoke the first verse:
"Your shoulder is like that of a bull, your springing forth like that of a lion;"
"O King of Deer, let there be homage to you; may we receive something [in return].
Having heard that, the jackal spoke the second verse:
“Only a son of good family knows how to praise a son of good family;
like the neck of a peacock, O crows, fly away from here!
In this context, “fly away from here” means: having descended from the castor-oil plant, come here toward me and eat the flesh—thus he says.
Seeing their deed, the tree deity spoke this third verse:
“The jackal is the lowest among deer, the crow among birds, and the castor-oil plant is the lowest among trees; these three have come together as the lowest.”
In this context, "end" means inferior and wretched.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, the crow was Kokālika, and the tree deity was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Anta-jātaka, the fifth.
[296] 6. The Commentary on the Samuddajātakaya.
"Who is this leader?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Upananda.
For he was gluttonous and possessed great craving; it was impossible to satisfy him even with provisions filling a cart. At the time of entering the rains retreat...
Having entered the rains retreat in two or three monasteries, he places his sandals in one, his walking staff in another, and his water jar in yet another.

He himself dwells in one [monastery]; then, having gone to a monastery in the countryside and seeing monks with excellent requisites, he speaks on the Noble Lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*), causes them to take up rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*), and [takes] their robes for himself.
He takes [the bowls], and having had earthenware bowls taken, and having taken both pleasing and unpleasing bowls and basins, he fills his carriage and comes to Jetavana.
Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
"Friends, Upananda the Sakyan-son is gluttonous and full of desire; after preaching the practice to others, he [deprives them] of their requisites for the ascetic life..."
“...having filled his vehicle, he comes. When the Teacher arrived, he asked, “Monks, about what topic are you sitting here conversing now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it was improper for Upananda to speak of the noble lineage of others;
for he himself should first become one of few desires, and only afterwards [should he encourage others].”
“It is fitting to speak of the noble lineage (ariyavaṃsa) to others.
“First, one should establish oneself in what is appropriate;
then one may instruct others. Thus the wise person will not come to grief.”

Having taught this verse from the *Dhammapada* and censured Upananda, [the Buddha] said, "Monks, it is not only now that Upananda has great desire; even in the past, he thought the water of the great ocean must be guarded," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a deity of the ocean.
Then, a certain crow, wandering above the ocean, [thought]: "Drink the water of the ocean by measure, guarding it..."
“Drink! he roamed about, repeatedly warding off the schools of fish and flocks of birds. Seeing him, the deity of the ocean spoke this first verse:
“Who is this that runs all around within the salt waters?”
“He wards off fish and crocodiles, yet he is distressed by the waves. Hearing this, the ocean-crow spoke the second verse:
“Who is this that leads? Who indeed is this?
Having heard that, the ocean-crow spoke the second verse:
“The bird Anantapāyī, unsatisfied and famed in all directions, desires to drink the ocean, the lord of rivers.
Its meaning is this: “I desire to drink the infinite ocean; for that reason, I am a bird named Anantapāyī, even though [the ocean] is vast...”

"Because I am possessed of an insatiable craving, I am known as 'the unsatisfied. Though I am famous, renowned, and well-known throughout the quarters, I nevertheless desire to drink up this entire ocean—
the ocean because it is a mine of beautiful jewels, or because it is dug by the Sāgara [demon],
or because it is the lord of rivers (saritapati) by virtue of being the master of flowing waters."
Having heard that, the deity of the ocean spoke this third verse:
“This great ocean both wanes and waxes;
it is never known to be exhausted. Yet it is said that the sea is undrinkable.”
In this regard, "it diminishes" means that at the time of the water receding, it diminishes, and at the time of its emerging, it fills up.

"Its limit is not known" means that even if the entire world were to drink from this great ocean, no end would be perceived such that one could say, "This much water has been drunk from here. It is said, moreover, that this ocean cannot be drunk.
"Let someone drain the water and let us descend.
Having said this, she showed him the terrifying appearance of the object and drove away the sea-crow.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Upananda was the sea-crow, and I myself was the deity."
The Sixth: The Commentary on the Samudda Jātaka.
[297] 7. The Commentary on the Kāmavilāpa Jātaka.
"O bird, you who dwell on high," this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the seduction by his former wife.
He related it. The present-day narrative was told in the *Puppharatta Jātaka*, while the past-life narrative will be revealed in the *Indriya Jātaka*.
They impaled that man alive upon a stake. While sitting there, he saw a crow flying through the sky;
disregarding even that most excruciating pain, he sent a message to his beloved wife.
Addressing the crow as he was about to depart, she spoke these verses:
“O bird, soaring high and flying on your wings, O ranger of the skies!
You should indeed call out to her of the beautiful thighs; she will surely take a long time.”
“This woman indeed does not know that a sword and a spear have been hurled;
she, being fierce, acts out her anger, and that burns me, not this.
“Here is a garland of blue lotuses, with a coin fastened upon it.”
"And soft Kāsika cloth; satisfy your dear creditors.
Therein, "ḍemānā" means going or walking. "Pattayāna" he addresses him directly; likewise with "vihaṅgama.
For he is called "pattayāna" because he travels having made his vehicle of feet, and "vihaṅgama" because he travels through the air. "Vajjāsī" means...
"You should say: 'Vāmūru'—meaning she whose thighs are like the trunk of a plantain tree—speak of her sitting upon the stake.
'She will surely wait a long time' means that, being unaware of this situation, she will delay my arrival, thinking:
'A long time has passed since my beloved departed, yet he does not come.'"
“*Asiṃ sattiñca*”: he speaks with reference specifically to the spear, because it is similar to a sword and similar to a javelin;
for that [spear] was set up and placed there to terrify him. *Caṇḍī* means wrathful. *Kāhati kodaṃ*:
she will direct anger toward me, thinking, “He is taking too long. *Taṃ me tapati*: that anger of hers distresses me. *No idaṃ*: not this.
Furthermore, this indicates: "Here, this stake does not burn me.
With the words "This is the lotus-enclosure" (*uppalasannāho*) and so forth, he points out his own goods placed upon the head of the bed in the house.
In that context, "lotus-enclosure" (*uppalasannāho*) means both the lotus (*uppala*) and the enclosure (*sannāho*); it refers to the stalk resembling a lotus and the one who provides the enclosure.
And so is the meaning. "A *nikkha*" refers to a finger-ring made of five pieces of gold.
"And soft Kāsī cloth" refers to a pair of soft Kāsī garments; it is said that this much was placed by him at the head of the bed.
"To satisfy my dear creditor"—having taken all this, may she, who is dear to me and desirous of wealth, satisfy herself with this wealth.
"May it be full; may she be content.
Thus, while lamenting, he passed away and was reborn in hell.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, [the listeners were established in the fruits of the path].
The dejected monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, she who was his wife was my present wife;
and he who was the young god who witnessed that event was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Kāmavilāpa Jātaka.
[298] 8. The Udumbara Jātaka Commentary.
"And these udumbara fruits have ripened"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain bhikkhu.
It is said that he had built a monastery in a certain frontier village and was living there. The monastery was delightful, situated on a rocky plateau.
The place for sweeping was pleasant with water, the village for alms was neither too far nor too near, and the people gave alms with affection.
Then, while wandering on his travels, a certain monk arrived at that monastery.
The resident monk performed the duties for the guest and, on the following day, took him with him into the village for alms.
People, having given excellent almsfood, invited him for the following day. After the newcomer had eaten for a few days, he thought:
“By some means I shall deceive this monk, drive him out, and take possession of this monastery.
Then, when the elder came to attend upon him, he asked: “Friend, why did you not go to attend upon the Buddha? “Venerable sir, [I did not.]”
“There is no one to look after this monastery; that is why I have never gone there before.

“I will look after it until you return from attending upon the Buddha,” he said. “Very well, venerable sir,” the resident monk replied, and having told the people, “Do not neglect the elders until my return,” he departed.
From that time on, the newcomer alienated those people by saying, "This resident has this and that fault.
The other, too, having paid homage to the Teacher, returned; however, he did not give him a lodging.
Having stayed in one place, on the following day he entered the village for alms, but the people did not even show him the slightest mark of respect. He was filled with remorse.
Having made the offering, he returned to Jetavana and reported that matter to the monks.
Those monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, it is said that such-and-such a monk has evicted such-and-such a monk from his dwelling and is living there himself.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?"
Having asked, and being told, "It was indeed by her," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, he drove her out from her dwelling place," and he related a story of the past.
Long ago, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in the forest.
He was reborn there. During the rainy season, it rained for seven weeks.
Now, a certain small red-faced monkey, living in a rain-sheltered stone cave, sat comfortably one day in a place where he was out of the way of the water at the entrance of the cave.
There, a large black-faced monkey, drenched and tormented by the cold, wandered about until he came upon that [other] monkey sitting in such a manner.
Seeing him, he thought, “I shall get him out by some means and dwell here,” and so, hanging down from his belly and assuming the appearance of being well-fed,
he stood before him and spoke this first verse:
“These udumbara fruits are ripe, as are the nigrodhas and kapitthas.”
"Come out, eat; why are you dying of hunger?

In this context, *kapitthāni* refers to *pilakkhā* (wood-apples). "Come out": "These *udumbara* trees and others are bent down by the weight of their fruit; I too have come back having eaten my fill and being satisfied; you too go and eat.
Having heard his words and placing faith in them, he also desired to eat the fruits, and so he went out and [searched] here and there.
Failing to find anything after searching, he returned and saw him sitting inside that stone cave.
Thinking, "I will deceive him," he stood before him and spoke the second verse:
"He who honors his elders is thus well-nourished."
"Just as I am well-fed today, having subsisted on the fruits of the trees.
Therein, "having subsisted on the fruits of the trees" means that he has eaten the fruits of trees such as the udumbara, and thus is satiated, nourished, and well-fed.
Having heard this, the great monkey spoke the third verse:
“If a monkey born in the forest should deceive another monkey born in the forest, a young monkey might believe him, for an old monkey is not deceived by an old monkey.
The meaning of this is: if a monkey born in the forest were to practice deception against another monkey born in the forest, one who is like you [would believe it].
"A young monkey might believe it, but an old, decrepit, aged monkey like me would certainly not believe it;
even if you were to say it a hundred times, one such as you does not gain his trust.
For in this region of the Himalayas, all the fruit has been soaked by the rain and fallen; furthermore, this place no longer belongs to you—go! Having said this, he departed from that very spot.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the small monkey was the resident monk, the large black monkey was the visitor, and the tree deity was none other than myself.
This concludes the eighth narrative, the Udumbara Jātaka.
9. The Commentary on the Komāraputta Jātaka.
"Pure they call this," the Teacher spoke while dwelling at the Eastern Monastery concerning certain monks of frivolous character.

It seems those monks, while the Teacher was staying in the upper story of the palace, were sitting in the lower story discussing what they had seen and heard, engaging in quarrels and insults. The Teacher addressed Mahāmoggallāna: "These monks..."
"Make them feel spiritual urgency," he said. The Elder sprang into the air, struck the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe, and made the palace shake as far as its water-bound foundations.
Those monks, terrified by the fear of death, emerged and stood outside.
His habit of playing became well known among the monks. Then one day, while the monks were in the Dhamma hall—
How did they raise the issue? “Friends, some bhikkhus, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, are wandering about with a playful disposition;
they do not apply themselves to the work of insight meditation on ‘impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, “Bhikkhus, about what talk are you gathered here now? [They replied: “About this—”
When he said, "Is that so?", [the Buddha] replied, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, these were of a playful nature," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a certain village;
they knew him as "Komāraputta. Later, having gone forth, he took up the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Having gone forth, he dwelt in a region of the Himalayas. Now, there were other ascetics of a playful disposition who, having established a hermitage in a region of the Himalayas, lived there;

they did not possess even the basic practice of the *kasiṇas*. Having brought various fruits from the forest and eaten them, they spent their time in various kinds of play, laughing. Near them there was a certain monkey.
He too, being of a playful nature, displayed various kinds of play to the ascetics by making facial contortions and other such gestures.
After the ascetics had lived there for a long time, they departed for the path of men in order to partake of salt and sour food.
From the moment they had gone, the Bodhisatta went to that place and made his dwelling; the monkey showed him play just as he had shown it to them.

The Bodhisatta clapped his hands and gave him this advice: "One who dwells in the presence of those well-trained in the life of renunciation must be endowed with proper conduct, well-restrained in body and so forth, and devoted to the meditative absorptions (jhānas).
From that time forward, he became virtuous and possessed of proper conduct, while the Bodhisatta departed for elsewhere. Then they...
The ascetics, having partaken of salted sour gruel, went to that place. The monkey did not show them his antics as he had done before.
Then the ascetics, questioning him, spoke the first verse: “Friend, formerly you used to perform antics before us; now you do not. What is the reason for this?”
“You are pure in the presence of those who possess virtue, yet you play the lecher in our hermitage.
Do away with your monkeyish ways, O monkey! We do not take pleasure in one such as you, though he claim to be virtuous.

In this context, “in the presence of those who possess virtue” means in the vicinity of us, whose conduct is playful. “Lecher” (*okkantika*) refers to one who enters [the women] like a deer [into a trap].
"You play. Here, "karohare" is an address; "areti" means to call out. "Makkaṭiyāni" refers to facial distortions known as the "monkey-face" play.

"We do not delight in that virtuous conduct of yours" means: we no longer take pleasure in that former habit of yours regarding play and amusement, nor does your conduct now please us; what indeed could be the reason for this?
Having heard that, the monkey spoke this second verse:
“I have indeed heard of the supreme purity of the learned son of a noble family;
do not now think of me as you did before, friend, for I dwell devoted to meditation.”
In this context, *mayham* (of me) is used in the sense of the agent as a dative. *Visuddhi* means purification through meditation (*jhāna-visuddhi*).
*Bahussutassa* means "of one who has heard much," because he has both heard and penetrated many preparatory exercises for the *kasiṇas* and the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).
*Tuvaṃ* is addressed to one of those ascetics, meaning: "Do not now recognize me as you did before; I am no longer like I was previously."
"I have found a teacher," he declared.
Hearing this, the ascetics spoke the third verse:
"Even if one were to sow seed upon a rock, and even if the rain-god were to send down rain, it would not sprout."
"For you have merely heard of that supreme purity; you, monkey, are far from the plane of jhāna.
The meaning of this is: even if one were to sow five kinds of seed upon a rocky surface and the rain-god were to send rain properly, it would not grow there due to the unsuitability of the soil;
in the same way, you have merely heard of the supreme purity of jhāna, but you yourself—
Because he was of animal birth, they reproached the monkey, saying, "He stands far away from the plane of meditation; it is not possible for you to produce meditative absorption.

Having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, those ascetics of playful disposition were these monks, and the youth Komārabhacca was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Komārabhacca Jātaka, the ninth.
[300] 10. The Exposition of the Vakajātaka:
"Living by the withholding of the lives of others. This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning an old rug.
The story of the incident has already been recorded in detail in the Vinaya; here, however, is the summary: Venerable Upasena was two years ordained...
Having approached the Teacher together with his one-year-old *saddhivihārika*, he was rebuked by the Teacher;
then, having paid homage and departed, he established insight (*vipassanā*), attained *arahantship*, and became endowed with qualities such as fewness of desires.

Having undertaken the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) and wandering about as one who maintains the thirteen *dhutaṅgas*, he, along with his retinue, [waited] while the Blessed One remained in seclusion for three months.
Having approached the Teacher and received the first "well done" for not complying with an unrighteous agreement after having first incurred censure from the assembly,

and having been favored by the Teacher who said, "From now on, let the bhikkhus who observe the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) come and see me as they please," he departed and [informed] the bhikkhus of that matter.
He reported this. From that time forth, the bhikkhus, having become wearers of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), approached the Teacher to see him;
once the Teacher had emerged from seclusion, they would discard their rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*) here and there and take only their own bowls and robes.
The Teacher, wandering for alms-residences together with many bhikkhus, [came] to those various places.
Seeing discarded refuse-rags, and having inquired and heard the matter, he said, "Monks, the undertaking of the ascetic practices by these monks did not endure for long;
it was like the Uposatha ceremony of a crow," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, the king of the gods. Then one—
A crane lived on a stone slab on the bank of the Ganges. Then, a great flood of water came down from the Ganges and surrounded that stone.
The crane climbed up and lay down upon the surface of the stone; he had no food, nor was there any path for him to go out for food, and the water continued to rise.
He thought: "I have neither food, nor is there any path for me to go out for food."
"Since one who is inactive lies down, the Uposatha observance is better," he thought.
Thus, having resolved upon the Uposatha in his mind and undertaken the precepts, he lay down.
Then Sakka, the king of the gods, perceiving his weak commitment, thought, "I shall trouble this crane," and approaching in the form of a goat, he stood not far from him and [presented] himself.
He showed himself. Seeing him, the jackal thought, "I shall find out about the Uposatha ceremony on another day," and rising up, he lunged forward to seize him.
The goat, however, leaped hither and thither and did not allow himself to be caught.
Unable to catch him, the jackal turned back; thinking, "Let my Uposatha duty not be interrupted for now," he remained right there.
He lay down again. Sakka, remaining in the sky in his own Sakka-form, rebuked and censured him, saying, "What is the use of an observance-day rite for one with such a weak disposition?
Not knowing my status as Sakka, you were desirous of eating goat's meat!
Having thus harassed and reproached him, he departed for the world of the gods.
“Living by the slaughter of other beings, a consumer of flesh and blood,
a wolf took upon himself a vow and observed the Uposatha.
Knowing his vow, Sakka approached him in the guise of an old man.”
“Vītatapa attained the higher state; Lohitapa broke his asceticism.
‘In the same way, some here who are weak in their undertaking make light of themselves, like a calf because of a she-goat.’”
These too are verses concerning the Fully Enlightened One.
Therein, "he was reborn on the Uposatha day" means he had entered upon the Uposatha residence.
"Knowing his vow" means knowing his weak vow. "Having abandoned asceticism, he approached" means having become free from asceticism, he approached; he leapt forward to devour him.
[The word] *attha* means "meaning. *Lohitapoti* means "one who drinks blood. They broke their own undertaken asceticism (*tapas*).
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was Sakka.
This is the tenth commentary on the Vakajātaka.
The fifth chapter: The Chapter on the Jar.
Its summary verse:
Varakumbha, Supatta, Sirivhayana, Sucisammata, Bindusara, and Cusabha.
And the Lord of the River was bitten by a fierce old monkey, then by a female monkey, and then by a crow.
Now, the summary of the Vagga:
Saṅkappa, Paduma, and Udapāna as the third.
The internal analysis of the *ghaṭabhedo* [section] from the *Tikanipāta* has been completed.
The commentary on the *Tikanipāta* is finished.
(The second part is concluded.)
